Learning questions 85

The circulatory system and the three layers of the heart wall

L1Learning
What are the two components of the circulatory system?
  1. A. Blood vascular (cardiovascular) system + lymphatic vascular system
  2. B. Blood vascular (cardiovascular) system + lymphoid organs (nodes, spleen, thymus)
  3. C. Pulmonary circulation + systemic circulation, with no lymphatic part
AnswerA. Blood vascular (cardiovascular) system + lymphatic vascular system
WhyThe circulatory system = the cardiovascular (blood vascular) system (heart, arteries, capillaries, veins) + the lymphatic vascular system.
Explanation

The blood vascular system is the heart plus the closed loop of arteries, capillaries and veins. The lymphatic vascular system is a one-way set of blind-ended lymphatic capillaries and larger lymphatic vessels that collect excess tissue fluid and return it to the veins through the thoracic and right lymphatic ducts.

  • Lymphoid organs (nodes, spleen, thymus) belong to the immune system; only the lymphatic vessels are part of the circulatory system in this course.
  • Pulmonary + systemic circulation is how the blood vascular system itself is divided; it leaves out the lymphatic half altogether.
Slide (1)
L2Learning
Which circulation works at high pressure and which at low pressure?
  1. A. Pulmonary circulation high; systemic circulation low
  2. B. Both run at the same high pressure, since both ventricles eject the same volume
  3. C. Systemic circulation high; pulmonary circulation low
AnswerC. Systemic circulation high; pulmonary circulation low
WhyThe left ventricle drives the high-pressure systemic circuit; the right ventricle drives the low-pressure pulmonary circuit through the lungs.
Explanation

Both ventricles eject the same volume each beat, but the resistance they pump against differs. The systemic circuit (left ventricle → aorta → body) has a high resistance, so it needs a high pressure (about 120/80 mmHg). The pulmonary circuit (right ventricle → pulmonary trunk → lungs) has a low resistance and runs at roughly a sixth of that pressure.

  • The reverse pairing swaps the two circuits.
  • Same pressure: equal volume does not mean equal pressure; pressure depends on the resistance downstream.

This is why the left ventricular wall is about three times thicker than the right.

Slide (1)
L3Learning
In the lecture's vessel terminology, what do afferent and efferent mean?
  1. A. Afferent: arriving, moving towards a structure
    Efferent: exiting, moving outward from it
  2. B. Afferent: exiting, moving outward from a structure
    Efferent: arriving, moving towards it
  3. C. Afferent: carrying oxygenated blood
    Efferent: carrying oxygen-poor blood
AnswerA. Afferent: arriving, moving towards a structure
Efferent: exiting, moving outward from it
WhyAfferent = Arriving (moving towards); efferent = Exiting (moving outward). The words describe direction, not oxygen content.
Explanation

The terms describe the direction of flow relative to the structure being discussed. A vessel that carries blood or lymph towards an organ is afferent; one that carries it away is efferent.

  • The swapped option reverses the definitions.
  • Oxygenated vs oxygen-poor confuses direction with content: an afferent vessel can carry either kind of blood.

Hook from the slide: Afferent = Arriving, Efferent = Externalising.

Slide (1)
L4Learning
Going outward from the heart, how are the arteries subdivided?
  1. A. Muscular artery → elastic artery → small artery → arteriole
  2. B. Elastic artery → muscular artery → small artery → arteriole
  3. C. Elastic artery → small artery → muscular artery → arteriole
AnswerB. Elastic artery → muscular artery → small artery → arteriole
WhyArteries shrink in steps: elastic (aorta) → muscular (distributing) → small artery → arteriole, which feeds the capillaries.
Explanation

The lecture's list of cardiovascular elements runs heart → arteries → capillaries → veins. The elastic arteries (aorta, pulmonary trunk) leave the heart; they branch into muscular arteries that distribute blood to organs, then into small arteries, and finally arterioles, the resistance vessels just before the capillaries. Veins run the other way: venules → small veins → medium-sized veins → large veins.

  • Putting muscular before elastic reverses the first step: the aorta, right at the heart, is the elastic one.
  • Putting small artery before muscular breaks the steady fall in size.
Slide (1)
L5Learning
Name the three layers of the heart wall, from inside out.
  1. A. Epicardium → myocardium → endocardium
  2. B. Endocardium → myocardium → epicardium
  3. C. Endocardium → epicardium → myocardium
AnswerB. Endocardium → myocardium → epicardium
WhyInside out: endocardium (lining) → myocardium (muscle) → epicardium (outer covering, the visceral pericardium).
Explanation

Endo- = inside, myo- = muscle, epi- = upon. The endocardium lines the chambers and faces the blood; the myocardium is the thick muscular middle; the epicardium covers the outer surface and faces the pericardial cavity.

  • Epicardium → myocardium → endocardium is the right sequence read from outside in, not inside out.
  • Endocardium → epicardium → myocardium puts the covering layer in the middle; the muscle always sits between the two thin layers.

The heart wall is a modified vessel wall: endocardium ≈ tunica intima, myocardium ≈ tunica media, epicardium ≈ tunica adventitia.

Slides (2)
L6Learning
The endocardium is continuous with which layer of the great vessels?
  1. A. Tunica media
  2. B. Tunica adventitia
  3. C. Tunica intima
AnswerC. Tunica intima
WhyThe endocardium's endothelium and subendothelial tissue continue straight into the tunica intima of the aorta, pulmonary trunk and great veins.
Explanation

Both the endocardium and the tunica intima are an endothelium (simple squamous epithelium) on a thin layer of connective tissue, and they face the blood. Where the great vessels join the heart, one simply runs into the other, so the endothelium lining blood is one unbroken sheet from the heart to the capillaries.

  • Tunica media is the vessel's muscular/elastic middle coat; its heart equivalent is the myocardium.
  • Tunica adventitia is the outer connective-tissue coat; its heart equivalent is the epicardium.
Slide (1)
L7Learning
Which layer is the thickest part of the heart wall, and which vessel tunic does it correspond to?
  1. A. Endocardium (connective tissue) — equivalent of the tunica media
  2. B. Myocardium (cardiac muscle) — equivalent of the tunica adventitia
  3. C. Myocardium (cardiac muscle) — equivalent of the tunica media
AnswerC. Myocardium (cardiac muscle) — equivalent of the tunica media
WhyThe myocardium, closely packed cardiac muscle, is by far the thickest layer; like the vessel media, it is the contractile middle coat.
Explanation

The myocardium is the muscular wall of the heart: cardiac muscle cells arranged in spiral layers round the chambers, grouped into fascicles by connective-tissue septa that carry vessels and nerves. It does the pumping, as the smooth muscle of the tunica media does in an artery.

  • The endocardium is a thin lining (endothelium plus connective tissue), not the bulk of the wall; it matches the intima.
  • The adventitia is the outer connective-tissue coat; the epicardium, not the myocardium, corresponds to it.
Slide (1)

Pericardium and epicardium

L8Learning
What does the fibrous pericardium do, and what is its key mechanical property?
  1. A. Elastic outer sac that cushions the heart; recoils after stretch
  2. B. Tough outer sac that anchors the heart; cannot stretch quickly
  3. C. Thin serous membrane that secretes fluid; stretches readily
AnswerB. Tough outer sac that anchors the heart; cannot stretch quickly
WhyThe fibrous pericardium is the dense outer sac that anchors the heart; it is inextensible over minutes to hours, which is why sudden fluid causes tamponade.
Explanation

The fibrous pericardium is a sac of dense collagenous connective tissue attached to the diaphragm and the roots of the great vessels. It holds the heart in place and stops it overfilling. Because collagen barely stretches, the sac cannot expand to make room for fluid that collects suddenly.

  • Elastic and recoiling describes elastic tissue, not this collagen sac.
  • Secreting fluid is the job of the serous pericardium's mesothelium, which lines the inside of the fibrous sac and covers the heart.
Slide (1)
L9Learning
A shard of glass pierces the chest wall and enters the left ventricle. In what order does it cross the layers?
  1. A. Fibrous pericardium → visceral serous layer (epicardium) → pericardial cavity → parietal serous layer → myocardium → endocardium
  2. B. Fibrous pericardium → parietal serous layer → pericardial cavity → visceral serous layer (epicardium) → myocardium → endocardium
  3. C. Parietal serous layer → fibrous pericardium → pericardial cavity → visceral serous layer (epicardium) → myocardium → endocardium
AnswerB. Fibrous pericardium → parietal serous layer → pericardial cavity → visceral serous layer (epicardium) → myocardium → endocardium
WhyOutside in: fibrous pericardium → parietal serous layer → cavity → visceral serous layer (= epicardium) → myocardium → endocardium.
Explanation

The pericardium has two parts. The fibrous pericardium is the outer sac. The serous pericardium is a closed double layer of mesothelium: its parietal layer lines the inside of the fibrous sac, then folds back at the great vessels to become the visceral layer, which sticks to the heart surface and is the epicardium. The thin pericardial cavity lies between the two serous layers.

  • Putting the visceral layer first inverts the serous pair: the visceral layer is the one on the heart.
  • Putting the parietal layer outside the fibrous sac is wrong: it lines the fibrous sac from the inside.

Picture a fist (the heart) pushed into a balloon: the layer touching the fist is visceral, the outer balloon wall is parietal.

Slides (2)
L10Learning
Where is the pericardial cavity, and what does it contain?
  1. A. Between the parietal and visceral serous layers; a thin film of lubricating fluid
  2. B. Between the fibrous pericardium and the parietal serous layer; a thin film of lubricating fluid
  3. C. Between the visceral serous layer and the myocardium; a thin film of lubricating fluid
AnswerA. Between the parietal and visceral serous layers; a thin film of lubricating fluid
WhyThe pericardial cavity is the potential space between the parietal and visceral serous layers; it holds a small amount of pericardial fluid.
Explanation

Normally the cavity is only a slit holding a few tens of millilitres of serous fluid made by the mesothelium. The fluid lets the beating heart slide against the sac without friction.

  • The fibrous pericardium and parietal layer are fused to each other; there is no space between them.
  • The visceral layer and myocardium are joined by the loose subepicardial connective tissue (with fat and coronary vessels), not separated by a cavity.

Because both walls of the cavity are serous layers, any blood or fluid that collects there touches the epicardium directly.

Slide (1)
L11Learning
The epicardium is the same layer as which of these?
  1. A. The parietal layer of the serous pericardium
  2. B. The visceral layer of the serous pericardium
  3. C. The fibrous pericardium
AnswerB. The visceral layer of the serous pericardium
WhyThe epicardium is the visceral pericardium: the serous layer stuck to the heart surface.
Explanation

The serous pericardium has two layers. The visceral one covers the heart and is called the epicardium; it is mesothelium on loose connective tissue that holds fat, coronary vessels and nerves. The parietal one lines the inside of the fibrous sac.

  • The parietal layer faces the epicardium across the pericardial cavity but is part of the sac, not the heart wall.
  • The fibrous pericardium is the outermost dense sac and has no mesothelium of its own.

Hook: visceral = on the viscus (the heart itself).

Slide (1)
L12Learning
In which layer of the heart wall do the main coronary arteries and veins run?
  1. A. Epicardium
  2. B. Myocardium
  3. C. Endocardium
AnswerA. Epicardium
WhyThe coronary arteries and veins (and the cardiac nerves) run in the epicardium, embedded in its fat, and send branches inward into the myocardium.
Explanation

The epicardium's loose connective tissue holds variable amounts of fat, and the large coronary branches lie in this fat on the heart surface, for example the anterior interventricular artery in the fat of the anterior interventricular sulcus. Smaller branches then dive into the myocardium.

  • The myocardium contains only the smaller penetrating branches and a dense capillary bed, not the main vessels.
  • The endocardium is a thin lining nourished largely by diffusion from the chamber blood.

This is why a coronary bypass graft is sewn onto the surface of the heart.

Slides (2)
L13Learning
Under the microscope, what does the epicardium consist of?
  1. A. Mesothelium over loose connective tissue holding fat, nerves and coronary vessels
  2. B. Endothelium over loose connective tissue holding pale Purkinje fibres
  3. C. Dense fibrous tissue over areolar tissue, with no epithelial covering
AnswerA. Mesothelium over loose connective tissue holding fat, nerves and coronary vessels
WhyEpicardium = simple squamous mesothelium on loose connective tissue with fat, autonomic nerves and coronary vessels.
Explanation

On the slide the epicardium is the pale outer band of the heart wall. Its free surface is a single row of flat mesothelial cells. Beneath them is loose connective tissue (fibro-elastic) with fat cells, nerve bundles and branches of the coronary arteries and veins, and below that the cardiac muscle begins.

  • Endothelium with Purkinje fibres describes the endocardium on the inner side of the wall.
  • Dense fibrous tissue without a surface epithelium describes the fibrous pericardium, the outer sac.
Slides (3)
L14Learning
What secretes pericardial fluid, and why is it needed?
  1. A. The endothelium of the coronary vessels — it stops the two layers rubbing
  2. B. The mesothelium of the serous pericardium — it stops the two layers rubbing
  3. C. The fibrous pericardium — it nourishes the outer myocardium
AnswerB. The mesothelium of the serous pericardium — it stops the two layers rubbing
WhyThe mesothelial cells of both serous layers secrete a lubricating fluid that lets the beating heart slide inside the sac without friction.
Explanation

Mesothelium is the simple squamous epithelium that lines the body's serous cavities. In the heart it covers the epicardium and lines the parietal pericardium, and it secretes a thin serous fluid into the pericardial cavity. The fluid lubricates the surfaces as the heart moves with each beat.

  • Endothelium lines blood vessels and the heart chambers; it faces blood, not the pericardial cavity.
  • The fibrous pericardium is dense connective tissue with no secretory epithelium, and the fluid does not feed the myocardium (the coronary vessels do).
Slide (1)
L15Learning
Mesothelium vs endothelium: what do they share, and how do they differ?
  1. A. Both simple squamous
    Mesothelium lines the heart and vessels
    Endothelium lines a body cavity (pericardial sac)
  2. B. Both simple cuboidal
    Mesothelium lines a body cavity (pericardial sac)
    Endothelium lines the heart and vessels
  3. C. Both simple squamous
    Mesothelium lines a body cavity (pericardial sac)
    Endothelium lines the heart and vessels
AnswerC. Both simple squamous
Mesothelium lines a body cavity (pericardial sac)
Endothelium lines the heart and vessels
WhyBoth are simple squamous epithelia: mesothelium lines serous cavities (pericardium, pleura, peritoneum); endothelium lines the heart and every blood vessel.
Explanation

The two are named by where they sit, not by their shape. In the heart wall, the mesothelium is the surface of the epicardium and of the parietal pericardium, facing the pericardial cavity. The endothelium is the surface of the endocardium, facing the blood in the chambers, and it continues into the intima of every vessel.

  • The swapped option reverses where each one lies.
  • Cuboidal is wrong for both: each is a single layer of flat cells.
Slides (2)
L16Learning
In section, what are the layers of the parietal pericardium, from outside in?
  1. A. Mesothelium → areolar tissue → dense fibrous layer facing the cavity
  2. B. Dense fibrous layer → areolar tissue → mesothelium facing the cavity
  3. C. Dense fibrous layer → mesothelium → areolar tissue facing the cavity
AnswerB. Dense fibrous layer → areolar tissue → mesothelium facing the cavity
WhyThe sac is dense fibrous tissue outside, then areolar (loose) tissue, then mesothelium on the surface that faces the pericardial cavity.
Explanation

The epithelium is always on the free surface, the side that faces the cavity. So the parietal pericardium has its mesothelium on the inside, supported by a thin areolar layer, with the tough dense fibrous layer on the outside. The epicardium mirrors this across the cavity: mesothelium facing the cavity, areolar tissue beneath, then myocardium.

  • Putting mesothelium on the outside turns the sac inside out; the outside of the sac faces the mediastinum, not a serous cavity.
  • Putting areolar tissue on the cavity side would leave the cavity without its lining epithelium.
Slide (1)
L17Learning
About 400 mL of blood is found in the pericardial cavity at autopsy. Which structure is it in direct contact with?
  1. A. Fibrous pericardium
  2. B. Myocardium
  3. C. Epicardium
AnswerC. Epicardium
WhyThe pericardial cavity lies between the parietal serous layer and the epicardium (visceral serous layer), so blood in it touches the epicardium.
Explanation

The two walls of the pericardial cavity are the two serous layers. The inner wall is the epicardium, whose mesothelium covers the heart; the outer wall is the parietal serous layer lining the fibrous sac. Blood that escapes into the cavity (haemopericardium) therefore bathes the epicardial surface.

  • The fibrous pericardium is outside the parietal serous layer, so the blood is separated from it by that mesothelial lining.
  • The myocardium lies beneath the epicardium and is not exposed to the cavity unless the wall has ruptured.
Slides (2)
L18Learning
What is the mechanism of cardiac tamponade?
  1. A. Fluid or blood fills the pericardial cavity → the fibrous sac stretches → the heart dilates and cannot contract
  2. B. Fluid or blood fills the pericardial cavity → the fibrous sac cannot stretch → the heart is squeezed and cannot fill
  3. C. The pericardium scars and thickens → the heart is encased and cannot fill, with no fluid present
AnswerB. Fluid or blood fills the pericardial cavity → the fibrous sac cannot stretch → the heart is squeezed and cannot fill
WhyIn tamponade, fluid in the sac cannot push the inextensible fibrous pericardium outward, so it presses on the heart and stops the chambers filling.
Explanation

The pericardial cavity normally holds only a thin film of fluid. When blood or fluid collects quickly, the fibrous pericardium cannot expand, so the pressure in the sac rises and compresses the heart, first the thin-walled right atrium and ventricle. Less filling means a smaller stroke volume, falling blood pressure and, without drainage, death.

  • If the sac stretched, there would be room for the fluid and no compression; it is the failure to stretch that matters.
  • Scarring and thickening with no fluid is constrictive pericarditis, a different disease that also limits filling.
Slides (2)
L19Learning
What is the difference between a pericardial effusion and cardiac tamponade?
  1. A. Effusion: enough fluid to compress the heart and stop it filling
    Tamponade: fluid in the pericardial sac
  2. B. Effusion: fluid in the myocardium
    Tamponade: fluid in the pericardial sac
  3. C. Effusion: fluid in the pericardial sac
    Tamponade: enough fluid to compress the heart and stop it filling
AnswerC. Effusion: fluid in the pericardial sac
Tamponade: enough fluid to compress the heart and stop it filling
WhyEffusion just means extra fluid in the sac; tamponade is when that fluid raises the pressure enough to compress the heart.
Explanation

An effusion can be small and harmless, or large but slow enough for the sac to adapt. It becomes tamponade once the pressure in the sac stops the chambers filling, shown on the slide as a moderate effusion progressing to ventricular collapse.

  • The swapped option reverses the two terms: tamponade is the severe, compressive end of an effusion.
  • Fluid in the myocardium is myocardial oedema; an effusion is by definition in the pericardial cavity.
Slides (2)
L20Learning
Two weeks after a massive heart attack, a man has sharp chest pain, BP 80/40 and pulse 100, and dies. Autopsy shows a rupture in the left ventricular wall. What killed him?
  1. A. Pulmonary oedema
  2. B. Cardiac tamponade
  3. C. Pulmonary thromboembolism
AnswerB. Cardiac tamponade
WhyThe softened infarct ruptured; blood poured into the pericardial cavity (haemopericardium) and compressed the heart: cardiac tamponade.
Explanation

After a myocardial infarction the dead muscle is soft while it is being removed and before the scar is strong, typically in the first one to two weeks. A free-wall rupture lets ventricular blood under high pressure flood the pericardial cavity. The inextensible fibrous pericardium cannot expand, so the heart cannot fill: low blood pressure, fast pulse and sudden death.

  • Pulmonary oedema comes from left heart failure raising pulmonary venous pressure; it does not follow from a hole that empties the ventricle into the sac.
  • Pulmonary thromboembolism starts from deep vein thrombi in the legs, not from a ruptured ventricle.
Slide (1)
L21Learning
What is constrictive pericarditis?
  1. A. Pericardium filled with fluid and stretched → restricted outflow from the ventricles
  2. B. Pericardium scarred and thickened (over 5 mm), with loss of elasticity → restricted filling of the heart
  3. C. Myocardium scarred and thickened, with loss of elasticity → restricted contraction of the ventricles
AnswerB. Pericardium scarred and thickened (over 5 mm), with loss of elasticity → restricted filling of the heart
WhyIn constrictive pericarditis the pericardium becomes a thick (>5 mm), scarred, inelastic shell that limits venous inflow, with no fluid needed.
Explanation

Chronic inflammation of the pericardium (for example after tuberculosis) replaces it with dense scar tissue, sometimes calcified. The rigid shell stops the heart expanding in diastole, so blood backs up in the veins; the heart looks 'quiet' because it barely moves. The problem is filling, not pumping.

  • Fluid-filled and stretched describes an effusion, and the problem in tamponade is also filling, not outflow.
  • Scarred myocardium is a disease of the muscle; constrictive pericarditis spares the muscle.
Slides (3)
L22Learning
How is constrictive pericarditis treated?
  1. A. Pericardiectomy (removing the pericardium)
  2. B. Pericardiocentesis (draining fluid with a needle)
  3. C. Coronary artery bypass grafting
AnswerA. Pericardiectomy (removing the pericardium)
WhyCutting away the rigid shell (pericardiectomy) frees the heart; on imaging its movement returns to normal.
Explanation

The disease is a thick scarred sac, so the cure is to remove it. The lab's moving images show the same patient's heart barely moving before surgery and beating normally after pericardiectomy.

  • Pericardiocentesis (needle drainage) treats tamponade, where the problem is fluid; there is no fluid to drain in constriction.
  • Bypass grafting treats blocked coronary arteries, which are not the problem here.
Slide (1)
L23Learning
An H&E section of atrial wall shows a row of flat cells on the free surface, over loose tissue with fat cells, a nerve bundle and a small artery; cardiac muscle lies beneath. Which layer is this?
  1. A. Epicardium
  2. B. Endocardium
  3. C. Parietal pericardium
AnswerA. Epicardium
WhyFlat surface cells over fat, nerves and vessels, with muscle directly below, is the epicardium: mesothelium on subepicardial loose connective tissue.
Explanation

Three clues point to the epicardium: a mesothelium on the surface, adipocytes (empty round spaces) and a nerve in the loose connective tissue, and cardiac muscle directly underneath. Coronary branches also run here.

  • The endocardium also has flat surface cells (endothelium), but its connective tissue holds no fat or nerve bundles; it may hold pale Purkinje fibres, and it faces a chamber full of blood.
  • The parietal pericardium has mesothelium too, but under it lies dense fibrous tissue, not cardiac muscle.
Slides (2)
L24Learning
In a heart section, how can you tell that a layer of flat surface cells is endothelium rather than mesothelium?
  1. A. It faces the pericardial cavity, and the connective tissue beneath has fat and nerve bundles
  2. B. Its cells are cuboidal, while mesothelial cells are flat
  3. C. It faces a chamber lumen, and the connective tissue beneath has no fat or nerve bundles
AnswerC. It faces a chamber lumen, and the connective tissue beneath has no fat or nerve bundles
WhyBoth are flat single layers; the endothelium faces the chamber blood and sits on thin connective tissue without fat or nerves (often with Purkinje fibres below).
Explanation

The cells themselves look the same: one layer of flattened cells with flat nuclei. What gives them away is the company they keep. Endothelium lines the endocardium, faces the lumen of a chamber and sits on thin connective tissue that runs into the subendocardium, where pale Purkinje fibres may appear. Mesothelium covers the epicardium, faces the pericardial cavity and sits on loose tissue with fat lobules, nerves and coronary vessels.

  • Facing the pericardial cavity with fat and nerves below is the description of mesothelium.
  • Cuboidal is wrong: both are simple squamous epithelia.
Slides (2)

Myocardium and intercalated discs

L25Learning
How are the cardiac muscle cells of the myocardium arranged?
  1. A. In concentric, spiral layers round the chambers, grouped into fascicles by sheets of elastic laminae with no vessels
  2. B. In concentric, spiral layers round the chambers, grouped into fascicles by connective-tissue septa carrying vessels and nerves
  3. C. In straight longitudinal sheets from base to apex, forming one continuous mass with no septa
AnswerB. In concentric, spiral layers round the chambers, grouped into fascicles by connective-tissue septa carrying vessels and nerves
WhyMyocardial cells wind round the chambers in spiral layers; connective-tissue septa carrying vessels and nerves group them into fascicles.
Explanation

The spiral arrangement wrings blood out of the ventricles: when the layers contract, the chamber shortens and twists, squeezing blood toward the outflow valves. Between the fascicles, thin connective-tissue septa carry the rich capillary network and autonomic nerves that the working muscle needs. Ventricular fascicles are larger than atrial ones.

  • Elastic laminae without vessels is wrong twice: the septa are ordinary connective tissue, and they carry the vessels and nerves.
  • Straight longitudinal sheets would only shorten the chamber, not wring it; the slide shows spiral bands.
Slides (2)
L26Learning
Why is the left ventricular wall much thicker than the right?
  1. A. It pumps into the high-pressure systemic circulation
  2. B. It pumps into the low-pressure pulmonary circulation
  3. C. It must hold a larger volume of blood than the right ventricle
AnswerA. It pumps into the high-pressure systemic circulation
WhyThe left ventricle must generate systemic pressure (~120 mmHg), so its wall is about three times thicker than the right's.
Explanation

Wall thickness follows the pressure a chamber must produce. The left ventricle ejects into the aorta against the high systemic resistance; the right ventricle ejects the same volume into the low-resistance pulmonary circuit. In cross-section the left ventricle is a thick ring and the right a thin crescent wrapped against the interventricular septum.

  • The pulmonary circulation is the right ventricle's target, and it is low pressure.
  • Both ventricles hold and eject the same volume; otherwise blood would pile up in one circuit.

The slide also shows epicardial fat in the anterior interventricular sulcus, where the anterior interventricular artery runs.

Slides (2)
L27Learning
How do ventricular muscle cells compare with atrial muscle cells?
  1. A. Atrial cells are thicker and grouped into larger fascicles
  2. B. Ventricular cells are thicker and grouped into larger fascicles
  3. C. Ventricular cells are thinner but grouped into larger fascicles
AnswerB. Ventricular cells are thicker and grouped into larger fascicles
WhyVentricular myocytes are thicker than atrial ones and form larger fascicles, matching the heavier work of the ventricles.
Explanation

The ventricles do most of the pumping, so their cells are wider and packed into bigger bundles. Atrial myocytes are thinner, and they have a second job: they carry small secretory granules of atrial natriuretic factor.

  • The atrial-thicker option reverses the sizes.
  • Thinner ventricular cells contradicts the lab manual: ventricular cells are the thicker ones.
Slide (1)
L28Learning
What do atrial muscle cells store in small secretory granules?
  1. A. Atrial natriuretic factor (ANF)
  2. B. Renin
  3. C. Antidiuretic hormone (ADH)
AnswerA. Atrial natriuretic factor (ANF)
WhyAtrial myocytes store the peptide hormone atrial natriuretic factor in small granules near the nucleus, so the atria are also an endocrine organ.
Explanation

When the atria are stretched by a high blood volume, the cells release ANF (also called atrial natriuretic peptide). The granules are tiny and are seen with the electron microscope rather than on routine H&E.

  • Renin is made by the juxtaglomerular cells of the kidney, not by heart muscle.
  • ADH is made by hypothalamic neurons and released from the posterior pituitary.
Slide (1)
L29LearningBorderline
What does atrial natriuretic factor do?
  1. A. Makes the kidney retain more sodium and water, raising blood volume and pressure
  2. B. Constricts arterioles, raising blood pressure
  3. C. Makes the kidney excrete more sodium and water, lowering blood volume and pressure
AnswerC. Makes the kidney excrete more sodium and water, lowering blood volume and pressure
WhyANF is released when the atria are overstretched and makes the kidneys lose sodium and water (natriuresis), so blood volume and pressure fall.
Explanation

'Natriuretic' means causing sodium loss in the urine. ANF increases the glomerular filtration rate and blocks sodium reabsorption, and it also relaxes vascular smooth muscle. All its effects lower blood volume and pressure, the opposite of the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system.

  • Retaining sodium and water is what aldosterone and ADH do.
  • Constricting arterioles is the action of angiotensin II and sympathetic stimulation; ANF dilates.
L30Learning
Which three features together identify cardiac muscle on a slide?
  1. A. Striated
    Central nucleus
    Intercalated discs
  2. B. Non-striated
    Central nucleus
    Intercalated discs
  3. C. Striated
    Peripheral nuclei
    Intercalated discs
AnswerA. Striated
Central nucleus
Intercalated discs
WhyCardiac muscle is striated like skeletal muscle, but has one or two central nuclei and intercalated discs joining the branched cells end to end.
Explanation

In longitudinal section, cardiac muscle shows fine cross-striations, oval nuclei sitting in the middle of each cell (often with a pale zone at each pole), branching cells, and dark, irregular, step-like intercalated discs crossing the fibres at intervals.

  • Non-striated with central nuclei describes smooth muscle (which has no intercalated discs).
  • Peripheral nuclei describes skeletal muscle, whose long multinucleated fibres push their nuclei under the cell membrane.
Slides (3)
L31Learning
Cardiac vs skeletal muscle: how do the nuclei differ?
  1. A. Cardiac: one (or two), at the periphery
    Skeletal: many, central
  2. B. Cardiac: one (or two), central
    Skeletal: many, at the periphery
  3. C. Cardiac: many, at the periphery
    Skeletal: one (or two), central
AnswerB. Cardiac: one (or two), central
Skeletal: many, at the periphery
WhyEach cardiac cell has one or two central nuclei; a skeletal fibre is one huge cell with many peripheral nuclei.
Explanation

A skeletal muscle fibre forms by fusion of many myoblasts, so it is multinucleated and its nuclei lie just under the sarcolemma. A cardiac 'fibre' is a chain of separate cells joined end to end, each with its own one or two nuclei in the centre, surrounded by myofibrils.

  • Cardiac peripheral / skeletal central puts both nuclei in the wrong place.
  • Cardiac many / skeletal one swaps the whole pattern.
Slide (1)
L32Learning
Cardiac vs skeletal muscle: how do the cell shapes differ?
  1. A. Cardiac: long, unbranched fibres
    Skeletal: short, branching cells joined end to end
  2. B. Cardiac: short, branching cells joined end to end
    Skeletal: long, unbranched fibres
  3. C. Cardiac: short, unbranched cells joined side to side
    Skeletal: long, branching fibres
AnswerB. Cardiac: short, branching cells joined end to end
Skeletal: long, unbranched fibres
WhyCardiac cells are short and branched, linked end to end into a network; skeletal fibres are long, unbranched cylinders.
Explanation

The branching lets cardiac cells form a three-dimensional meshwork that contracts as a unit, which suits emptying a chamber. A skeletal muscle fibre is one long cylindrical cell running much of the muscle's length.

  • The swapped option gives each tissue the other's shape.
  • Side-to-side, unbranched cardiac cells and branching skeletal fibres are both wrong: cardiac cells branch and meet end to end at intercalated discs.
Slides (2)
L33Learning
In routine H&E, which feature distinguishes cardiac from skeletal muscle?
  1. A. Fibres showing regular cross-striations along their length
  2. B. Sarcomeres lying between adjacent Z lines in each myofibril
  3. C. Muscle cells in series, joined by end-to-end connections
AnswerC. Muscle cells in series, joined by end-to-end connections
WhyCardiac 'fibres' are chains of separate cells joined end to end at intercalated discs; skeletal fibres are single multinucleated cells.
Explanation

The end-to-end junctions are the intercalated discs, the dark step-like lines crossing cardiac fibres. Skeletal muscle has nothing like them because each fibre is one continuous cell.

  • Cross-striations are present in both cardiac and skeletal muscle, so they cannot tell them apart.
  • Sarcomeres between Z lines is the structure of every striated muscle, cardiac and skeletal alike.

Exam tip: when an option is true of both tissues, it cannot be the distinguishing feature.

Slide (1)
L34Learning
How do intercalated discs look on an H&E slide?
  1. A. Dark, irregular cross-lines joining cells end to end — also seen in skeletal muscle
  2. B. Pale longitudinal lines between myofibrils — unique to cardiac muscle
  3. C. Dark, irregular cross-lines joining cells end to end — unique to cardiac muscle
AnswerC. Dark, irregular cross-lines joining cells end to end — unique to cardiac muscle
WhyIntercalated discs are dark, step-like lines across the fibres, more widely spaced than the striations, found only in cardiac muscle.
Explanation

Each disc marks the boundary between two cardiac cells, so the discs occur at irregular intervals of one cell length, much farther apart than the closely spaced, regular striations. They stain darkly because the junctions are dense with protein.

  • Skeletal muscle has no intercalated discs; its fibres are single cells with no end-to-end boundaries.
  • Pale longitudinal lines run the wrong way: the discs cross the fibre.

Do not confuse them with contraction bands in infarcted muscle: those are many dense bands within a single cell.

Slides (2)
L35Learning
Which three junctions make up an intercalated disc?
  1. A. Fascia adherens
    Desmosomes
    Gap junctions
  2. B. Tight junctions
    Desmosomes
    Gap junctions
  3. C. Fascia adherens
    Hemidesmosomes
    Gap junctions
AnswerA. Fascia adherens
Desmosomes
Gap junctions
WhyAn intercalated disc is a junctional complex of fasciae adherentes and desmosomes (holding) plus gap junctions (signalling).
Explanation

In the electron microscope the disc runs like a staircase. Its transverse parts (the 'treads') carry the fasciae adherentes, where actin filaments anchor, and the desmosomes, which bind the cells against the pull of contraction. Its lateral parts (the 'risers') carry the gap junctions, which pass ions from cell to cell.

  • Tight junctions seal epithelia; there are none in the intercalated disc.
  • Hemidesmosomes fix a cell to its basement membrane, not to a neighbouring cell.
Slides (2)
L36Learning
What do the fasciae adherentes and desmosomes of the intercalated disc do?
  1. A. Let the electrical signal pass from cell to cell
  2. B. Hold the cells together against the pull of contraction
  3. C. Anchor the cells to the basement membrane
AnswerB. Hold the cells together against the pull of contraction
WhyFasciae adherentes anchor actin filaments at the cell ends and desmosomes bind the cells, so contraction cannot pull them apart.
Explanation

Each contraction pulls hard on the ends of every cardiac cell. The fascia adherens is where the actin of the last sarcomere attaches to the cell membrane, passing the force to the next cell; desmosomes act as spot welds anchored to intermediate filaments.

  • Passing the electrical signal is the job of the gap junctions in the same disc.
  • Anchoring to the basement membrane is done by hemidesmosomes, which are not part of the disc.
Slide (1)
L37Learning
Which component of the intercalated disc spreads electrical signals between cardiac myocytes to keep a normal rhythm?
  1. A. Gap junctions
  2. B. Fasciae adherentes
  3. C. Desmosomes (maculae adherentes)
AnswerA. Gap junctions
WhyGap junctions are low-resistance channels that let ions, and so the action potential, pass straight from one cardiac cell to the next.
Explanation

A gap junction is a cluster of connexon channels that join the cytoplasm of two neighbouring cells. Current flows through them easily, so depolarisation spreads quickly through the myocardium and the cells contract together as a functional syncytium.

  • Fasciae adherentes anchor actin filaments; they hold, they do not conduct.
  • Desmosomes (maculae adherentes) are spot welds for mechanical strength.
Slide (1)
L38Learning
Intercalated discs contain all of these molecules EXCEPT:
  1. A. Collagen VII
  2. B. Desmoglein and desmocollin
  3. C. Cadherin
AnswerA. Collagen VII
WhyCollagen VII forms anchoring fibrils beneath epithelia; the disc's junctions use desmogleins/desmocollins (desmosomes), cadherins (fascia adherens) and connexins (gap junctions).
Explanation

Each junction of the intercalated disc has its own adhesion proteins. Desmosomes bind neighbouring cells with the cadherin-family proteins desmoglein and desmocollin, held inside by desmoplakin. The fascia adherens uses N-cadherin linked to actin. Gap junctions are built from connexins.

  • Collagen VII is an extracellular matrix protein that anchors the basal lamina of skin to the dermis; it plays no part in cell-to-cell junctions.
  • The other two options are genuine disc proteins.

Likewise, hemidesmosomes are never part of an intercalated disc.

Slide (1)
L39LearningBorderline
In cardiac muscle from an elderly person, yellow-brown granules cluster at the poles of the central nuclei. What are they?
  1. A. Glycogen granules: stored fuel for contraction
  2. B. Atrial natriuretic factor granules: stored hormone
  3. C. Lipofuscin: undigested residues of lysosomal digestion
AnswerC. Lipofuscin: undigested residues of lysosomal digestion
WhyLipofuscin, the 'wear-and-tear' pigment, is indigestible material left in residual bodies after lysosomal digestion; it builds up near the nucleus with age.
Explanation

Cardiac myocytes live for the whole lifetime and do not divide, so the leftovers of years of lysosomal digestion accumulate as golden-brown lipofuscin granules in the pale zone at each pole of the nucleus.

  • Glycogen washes out in routine processing and leaves pale, clear sarcoplasm, not brown granules (it is plentiful in Purkinje fibres).
  • ANF granules lie in atrial cells but are tiny, colourless and visible only by electron microscopy.
L40Learning
A section shows a thick layer of branching striated cells with central nuclei, joined end to end by dark cross-lines, with capillaries between them. Which heart layer is this?
  1. A. Endocardium
  2. B. Epicardium
  3. C. Myocardium
AnswerC. Myocardium
WhyBranching striated cells with central nuclei and intercalated discs filling the field is the myocardium.
Explanation

The myocardium is almost entirely cardiac muscle: striated, branched cells with one or two central nuclei, intercalated discs, and a rich capillary network in the thin connective tissue between fascicles.

  • The endocardium is a thin layer of endothelium and connective tissue on the luminal side; its only muscle-like cells are the pale Purkinje fibres.
  • The epicardium is mesothelium over loose tissue with fat, nerves and coronary vessels on the outer surface.
Slides (2)

Endocardium and Purkinje fibres

L41Learning
What makes up the endocardium?
  1. A. Endothelium → connective tissue with scattered smooth muscle → deeper subendocardial connective tissue
  2. B. Mesothelium → loose connective tissue with fat → deeper subendocardial connective tissue
  3. C. Endothelium resting directly on cardiac muscle, with no connective tissue
AnswerA. Endothelium → connective tissue with scattered smooth muscle → deeper subendocardial connective tissue
WhyEndocardium = endothelium + a middle layer of connective tissue with some smooth muscle + a deeper subendocardium that blends into the myocardium.
Explanation

The inner lining of the heart has three parts: a simple squamous endothelium facing the blood; a middle myoelastic layer of connective tissue with scattered smooth muscle cells; and the subendocardial layer, loose connective tissue continuous with the myocardium's connective tissue. The subendocardium of the ventricles carries the Purkinje fibres.

  • Mesothelium with fat describes the epicardium on the outside of the heart.
  • Endothelium directly on muscle leaves out the connective-tissue layers in which the Purkinje fibres run.
Slide (1)
L42Learning
Which layer of the heart wall contains the Purkinje fibres?
  1. A. Myocardium (among the contractile fibres)
  2. B. Epicardium (its subepicardial fatty layer)
  3. C. Endocardium (its subendocardial layer)
AnswerC. Endocardium (its subendocardial layer)
WhyPurkinje fibres run in the subendocardial layer, the deepest part of the endocardium, just above the myocardium.
Explanation

The subendocardium is loose connective tissue between the endothelium-covered lining and the cardiac muscle. In the ventricles it carries the network of Purkinje fibres that spreads the impulse; from there the fibres contact the contractile muscle. The lecture slide calls it the 'subendothelial layer', meaning the same place.

  • The myocardium is the contractile muscle the Purkinje fibres feed into, not the layer they run in.
  • The epicardium carries coronary vessels, fat and nerves on the outer surface.
Slide (1)
L43Learning
An H&E section of ventricle shows a thin endothelium, then a band of connective tissue holding large pale fibres with central nuclei, then deep-pink cardiac muscle. Name the band and the pale fibres.
  1. A. Subepicardium; adipocytes
  2. B. Myoelastic layer; smooth muscle cells
  3. C. Subendocardium; Purkinje fibres
AnswerC. Subendocardium; Purkinje fibres
WhyLarge pale fibres in the connective tissue between endothelium and myocardium are Purkinje fibres in the subendocardium.
Explanation

Read the section from the lumen: endothelium (En), then the subendocardium (SEn) with Purkinje fibres (P), then the myocardium (M). Purkinje fibres are wider than the contractile cells and pale because their glycogen dissolves during processing.

  • Subepicardium with adipocytes is on the other side of the wall, under a mesothelium; fat cells are empty rings with flattened peripheral nuclei, not fibres with central nuclei.
  • The myoelastic layer lies just under the endothelium; its smooth muscle cells are thin and spindle-shaped, not large and pale.
Slide (1)
L44Learning
How do Purkinje fibres look compared with ordinary cardiac muscle cells?
  1. A. Smaller and darker — little glycogen, more myofibrils
  2. B. Larger and paler — abundant glycogen, fewer myofibrils
  3. C. Larger and darker — abundant myoglobin, more myofibrils
AnswerB. Larger and paler — abundant glycogen, fewer myofibrils
WhyPurkinje fibres are larger and paler than contractile cells: they are packed with glycogen and have fewer myofibrils.
Explanation

Purkinje fibres are modified cardiac muscle cells built for conduction, not force. Much of their cytoplasm is glycogen instead of myofibrils, so in H&E they look swollen and pale beside the dense pink working muscle; in a trichrome stain they are pale lavender above the deep-red myocardium.

  • Smaller and darker with more myofibrils describes the contractile cells, not the conducting ones.
  • Myoglobin and extra myofibrils would make them darker; their pallor comes from glycogen.

Giveaway: big pale cells just under the endocardium = Purkinje fibres.

Slides (2)
L45Learning
Why do Purkinje fibres look pale in routine sections?
  1. A. Lipid dissolves in processing → clear sarcoplasm round a peripheral nucleus, myofibrils packed centrally
  2. B. Glycogen washes out in processing → clear sarcoplasm round a central nucleus, myofibrils pushed to the edge
  3. C. Glycogen stains intensely → nucleus pushed to the edge by packed myofibrils
AnswerB. Glycogen washes out in processing → clear sarcoplasm round a central nucleus, myofibrils pushed to the edge
WhyTheir abundant glycogen dissolves during processing, leaving clear sarcoplasm round a central nucleus, with the sparse myofibrils at the cell periphery.
Explanation

The glycogen occupies the middle of the cell. When it is removed by routine fixation and staining, empty-looking sarcoplasm is left around the centrally placed nucleus, and the few myofibrils sit mainly near the cell edge.

  • Lipid is not what fills them, and their nucleus stays central.
  • Glycogen does not stain with H&E; it shows up only with a special stain such as PAS, where it turns magenta.
Slide (1)
L46Learning
A PAS stain turns the large pale subendocardial fibres dark magenta. Which substance in them does PAS reveal?
  1. A. Lipid
  2. B. Collagen
  3. C. Glycogen
AnswerC. Glycogen
WhyPAS (periodic acid–Schiff) stains glycogen magenta, and Purkinje fibres are full of it.
Explanation

The glycogen that washes out in routine H&E, leaving Purkinje fibres pale, is kept and coloured by PAS. So the same fibres that look empty in H&E turn deep magenta in PAS, which confirms both their identity and their location in the endocardium.

  • Lipid is dissolved by routine processing and is shown with fat stains on frozen sections, not PAS.
  • Collagen is blue in trichrome; PAS colours it only faintly. The fibres here are muscle cells, not connective tissue.
Slide (1)
L47Learning
How do the intercalated discs of Purkinje fibres differ from typical ones?
  1. A. Fasciae adherentes and desmosomes present; gap junctions absent
  2. B. Tight junctions replace gap junctions; desmosomes well developed
  3. C. Desmosomes and gap junctions present; fasciae adherentes poorly developed
AnswerC. Desmosomes and gap junctions present; fasciae adherentes poorly developed
WhyPurkinje fibre discs are atypical: they keep desmosomes and gap junctions but lack well-developed fasciae adherentes.
Explanation

The fascia adherens anchors actin of the contractile apparatus; Purkinje fibres have few myofibrils and do little contracting, so they need little of it. They do need gap junctions, because conducting the impulse quickly is their whole job.

  • No gap junctions would stop them conducting.
  • Tight junctions are not found in intercalated discs of any kind.
Slide (1)

The conduction system

L48Learning
What are the cells of the cardiac conduction system?
  1. A. Modified cardiac muscle cells, specialised for conduction rather than contraction
  2. B. Specialised neurons of the autonomic nervous system
  3. C. Modified smooth muscle cells, specialised for conduction rather than contraction
AnswerA. Modified cardiac muscle cells, specialised for conduction rather than contraction
WhyThe nodes, the AV bundle and the Purkinje fibres are all modified cardiac muscle cells that generate and conduct the impulse instead of contracting strongly.
Explanation

The SA and AV nodes are small masses of specialised myocardial tissue in the right atrial wall; the AV bundle, bundle branches and Purkinje fibres are conducting muscle cells joined by gap junctions. They contain few myofibrils.

  • Neurons: the heart beats without its nerves; autonomic nerves only speed or slow the rate set by the SA node. 'Purkinje cells' of the cerebellum are neurons, but Purkinje fibres of the heart are muscle.
  • Smooth muscle occurs in the endocardium's myoelastic layer and in vessel walls, but it does not conduct the heartbeat.
Slide (1)
L49Learning
Trace the cardiac conduction pathway.
  1. A. SA node → AV bundle (of His) → AV node → right and left bundle branches → Purkinje fibres
  2. B. SA node → AV node → AV bundle (of His) → right and left bundle branches → Purkinje fibres
  3. C. AV node → SA node → AV bundle (of His) → right and left bundle branches → Purkinje fibres
AnswerB. SA node → AV node → AV bundle (of His) → right and left bundle branches → Purkinje fibres
WhySA node fires → atria → AV node (delay) → bundle of His through the skeleton → bundle branches in the septum → Purkinje fibres → ventricles.
Explanation

The impulse starts in the SA node in the right atrial wall and spreads over both atria. It is funnelled into the AV node, which delays it, then into the AV bundle (of His), the only path through the insulating cardiac skeleton. The bundle splits into right and left branches in the interventricular septum; about halfway down these become the subendocardial Purkinje network that reaches all of both ventricles.

  • Putting the bundle of His before the AV node skips the delay: the AV node feeds the bundle, not the other way round.
  • Starting at the AV node makes it the pacemaker; the SA node fires first because it is the fastest.
Slides (2)
L50Learning
After the SA node fires, which tissue depolarises before the AV node?
  1. A. Ventricular myocardium
  2. B. Bundle of His
  3. C. Atrial myocardium
AnswerC. Atrial myocardium
WhyOrder: SA node → atrial myocardium → AV node → bundle of His → Purkinje fibres → ventricular myocardium.
Explanation

The SA node's impulse spreads cell to cell through the atrial muscle (through gap junctions), so the atria contract first. The wave converges on the AV node in the floor of the right atrium, which passes it on after a delay.

  • The ventricular myocardium is the last to depolarise, after the Purkinje fibres.
  • The bundle of His comes after the AV node, carrying the impulse through the cardiac skeleton.
Slides (2)
L51Learning
Where is the sinoatrial (SA) node, and what is its role?
  1. A. Wall of the left atrium — pacemaker of the heart
  2. B. Interventricular septum — pacemaker of the heart
  3. C. Wall of the right atrium — pacemaker of the heart
AnswerC. Wall of the right atrium — pacemaker of the heart
WhyThe SA node sits in the right atrial wall near the entrance of the superior vena cava and is the pacemaker: it fires fastest and sets the heart rate.
Explanation

The SA node is a small mass of specialised cardiac muscle under the epicardium at the junction of the superior vena cava with the right atrium. Its cells depolarise spontaneously faster than any other part of the conduction system, so each beat starts there. When it fails, an artificial pacemaker can take over.

  • The left atrium has no node; both nodes are on the right side.
  • The interventricular septum carries the AV bundle and its branches, not the pacemaker.
Slides (2)
L52Learning
Electrophysiological mapping shows the earliest spontaneous depolarisation in a small nodal structure in the upper right atrial wall, where the superior vena cava enters. What is it?
  1. A. Sinoatrial (SA) node
  2. B. Atrioventricular (AV) node
  3. C. Bundle of His
AnswerA. Sinoatrial (SA) node
WhyThe first site to fire, at the superior vena cava–right atrium junction, is the SA node, the pacemaker.
Explanation

The SA node lies along the crista terminalis where the superior vena cava enters the right atrium. Because its cells reach threshold fastest, every normal beat begins there.

  • The AV node lies lower, in the floor of the right atrium at the atrioventricular junction; it fires spontaneously only if the SA node fails, and more slowly.
  • The bundle of His is in the interventricular septum and only conducts what the AV node passes to it.
Slides (2)
L53Learning
Where is the atrioventricular (AV) node?
  1. A. Floor of the left atrium, at the junction between atria and ventricles
  2. B. Upper interventricular septum, below the cardiac skeleton
  3. C. Floor of the right atrium, at the junction between atria and ventricles
AnswerC. Floor of the right atrium, at the junction between atria and ventricles
WhyThe AV node lies in the floor of the right atrium, at the atrioventricular junction, just above the cardiac skeleton.
Explanation

The lecture places the AV node at the junction between atria and ventricles; the textbook puts it more precisely in the floor of the right atrium. It collects the atrial impulse and passes it into the AV bundle, which pierces the cardiac skeleton.

  • The left atrium has no nodal tissue.
  • The upper interventricular septum below the skeleton is where the AV bundle runs and divides, after it has left the node.
Slides (2)
L54Learning
Why is the delay at the AV node useful?
  1. A. It lets the atria finish emptying before the ventricles contract
  2. B. It lets the ventricles finish emptying before the atria contract
  3. C. It lets the ventricles contract before the atria fill
AnswerA. It lets the atria finish emptying before the ventricles contract
WhyThe AV-node delay gives the atria time to finish pushing blood into the ventricles before the ventricles contract.
Explanation

The atria contract first and top up the ventricles at the end of their filling. If the impulse reached the ventricles at once, they would contract while the atria were still emptying, and the AV valves would close on incomplete filling.

  • Ventricles emptying before the atria contract reverses the sequence: atrial contraction comes first.
  • Ventricles contracting before the atria fill has nothing to do with the delay; the atria fill throughout ventricular contraction.
Slide (1)
L55Learning
What course does the AV bundle (of His) take?
  1. A. Through an opening in the cardiac skeleton → interventricular septum → splits into right and left bundle branches
  2. B. Around the cardiac skeleton → right atrial wall → splits into anterior and posterior branches
  3. C. Through an opening in the cardiac skeleton → left ventricular free wall → splits straight into Purkinje fibres
AnswerA. Through an opening in the cardiac skeleton → interventricular septum → splits into right and left bundle branches
WhyThe AV bundle passes through the cardiac skeleton into the interventricular septum, where it divides into right and left bundle branches.
Explanation

The bundle is the only muscular link between atria and ventricles. After piercing the fibrous skeleton it runs along the top of the muscular interventricular septum and bifurcates. About halfway down the septum the branches break up into the subendocardial Purkinje network.

  • It cannot go around the skeleton: the skeleton insulates the atria from the ventricles all the way round, and the bundle runs in the septum, not the atrial wall.
  • It does not enter the left ventricular free wall; it divides in the septum first, and both ventricles are reached through their own branch.
Slide (1)
L56Learning
What do Purkinje fibres do?
  1. A. Carry the signal slowly to both atria, ending on contractile muscle → atria contract together
  2. B. Carry the signal rapidly to all parts of both ventricles, ending on contractile muscle → ventricles contract together
  3. C. Carry the signal rapidly to the right ventricle only → ventricles contract one after the other
AnswerB. Carry the signal rapidly to all parts of both ventricles, ending on contractile muscle → ventricles contract together
WhyThe His–Purkinje network rapidly delivers the impulse to all parts of both ventricles, so the ventricular muscle contracts in one coordinated wave.
Explanation

Purkinje fibres are the terminal branches of the right and left bundle branches, running in the subendocardium of both ventricles. They conduct faster than ordinary myocardium and end on the contractile cells, triggering contraction throughout both ventricles almost at once.

  • The atria are reached directly from the SA node through atrial muscle, not through Purkinje fibres.
  • Both bundle branches carry Purkinje fibres, so both ventricles are activated together.
Slide (1)
L57Learning
A simple squamous epithelium covers or lines the free surface of all of these EXCEPT:
  1. A. The mitral valve
  2. B. The sinoatrial node
  3. C. The epicardium
AnswerB. The sinoatrial node
WhyThe SA node sits inside the right atrial wall and reaches neither surface; valves are covered by endothelium and the epicardium by mesothelium.
Explanation

Every free surface of the heart has a simple squamous epithelium: endothelium on the endocardium and both faces of every valve, mesothelium on the epicardium, and endothelium continuing into the aorta's intima. The SA node is a buried mass of specialised muscle at the superior vena cava–right atrium junction, under the epicardium, so it has no free surface of its own.

  • The mitral valve is a fold of endocardium; endothelium covers both its surfaces.
  • The epicardium is covered by mesothelium, which is also simple squamous.
Slide (1)
L58Learning
What does an electrocardiogram (ECG) record?
  1. A. The sound of the heart valves closing, from a microphone on the chest
  2. B. The blood flow through the coronary arteries, from electrodes on the skin
  3. C. The spread of the electrical impulse through the heart, from electrodes on the skin
AnswerC. The spread of the electrical impulse through the heart, from electrodes on the skin
WhyAn ECG records the voltage differences that the spreading impulse produces, measured between skin electrodes; Einthoven built the first practical one in 1903.
Explanation

As the impulse spreads through the myocardium, it creates voltage differences that reach the body surface. Electrodes at different points record them. The tracing shows heart rate, rhythm, conduction times through each part of the conduction system, effects of electrolytes and drugs, and the location of damaged muscle.

  • Valve sounds are heard with a stethoscope or recorded by phonocardiography.
  • Coronary flow is studied by angiography or perfusion scans, not by the ECG.
Slide (1)

The cardiac skeleton

L59Learning
What tissue forms the cardiac skeleton?
  1. A. Dense irregular connective tissue
  2. B. Dense regular connective tissue
  3. C. Elastic connective tissue
AnswerA. Dense irregular connective tissue
WhyThe cardiac skeleton is dense irregular connective tissue: thick collagen bundles running in many directions.
Explanation

The skeleton must resist pull from every direction, as valves snap shut and muscle contracts on all sides, so its collagen bundles are woven in many directions, like the dermis. It lies mainly in the endocardium at the junction of atria and ventricles.

  • Dense regular tissue has parallel bundles that resist pull in one direction only, as in tendons.
  • Elastic tissue stretches and recoils, as in the aortic wall; the skeleton has to stay rigid to hold the valve openings in shape.
Slide (1)
L60Learning
How is the cardiac skeleton arranged?
  1. A. Four fibrous rings (annuli) around the four valves, joined by the left and right fibrous trigones
  2. B. Four cartilaginous rings around the four valves, joined by the left and right fibrous trigones
  3. C. Four fibrous rings (annuli) around the four valves, joined by the anterior and posterior papillary muscles
AnswerA. Four fibrous rings (annuli) around the four valves, joined by the left and right fibrous trigones
WhyThe skeleton is four fibrous rings round the valve openings (including the bases of the aorta and pulmonary trunk), linked by the fibrous trigones and the membranous septum.
Explanation

Seen from above with the atria removed, the skeleton is a flat plate between atria and ventricles: rings around the tricuspid, mitral, aortic and pulmonary openings, joined in the middle by the right and left fibrous trigones. The membranous part of the interventricular septum hangs down from it. The AV bundle passes through the right fibrous trigone.

  • Cartilage: the human cardiac skeleton is fibrous connective tissue, not cartilage.
  • Papillary muscles are muscular projections inside the ventricles; they pull on the chordae and are not part of the skeleton.
Slides (2)
L61Learning
Into which structures does the cardiac skeleton extend?
  1. A. Valve cusps
    Papillary muscles
    Muscular part of the interventricular septum
  2. B. Valve cusps
    Purkinje fibres
    Membranous part of the interventricular septum
  3. C. Valve cusps
    Chordae tendineae
    Membranous part of the interventricular septum
AnswerC. Valve cusps
Chordae tendineae
Membranous part of the interventricular septum
WhyThe skeleton's collagen runs into the valve cusps and chordae tendineae and forms the membranous interventricular septum.
Explanation

The dense connective tissue core of each valve leaflet is continuous with the fibrous ring it hangs from, and the chordae tendineae are cords of the same collagen. The small upper, membranous part of the interventricular septum is skeleton too.

  • Papillary muscles and the muscular septum are cardiac muscle, not connective tissue.
  • Purkinje fibres are modified muscle cells in the subendocardium; only the AV bundle passes through the skeleton.
Slide (1)
L62Learning
Which part of the interventricular septum is formed by the cardiac skeleton?
  1. A. The muscular part: large, lower part running toward the apex
  2. B. The membranous part: large, lower part running toward the apex
  3. C. The membranous part: small, uppermost, just below the aortic valve
AnswerC. The membranous part: small, uppermost, just below the aortic valve
WhyThe membranous septum is a small, thin, fibrous area at the top of the septum below the aortic valve; the rest is the thick muscular septum.
Explanation

In a four-chamber slice, nearly all of the interventricular septum is thick muscle. Only a small, thin patch at its top, just below the aortic root, is fibrous. This membranous septum is part of the cardiac skeleton; the AV bundle runs along its lower edge as it reaches the muscular septum.

  • The muscular part is cardiac muscle, not skeleton.
  • The membranous part is small and high, not the large lower portion.
Slides (2)
L63Learning
What are the jobs of the cardiac skeleton?
  1. A. Anchors the valves
    Generates the pacemaker impulse
    Electrically couples atria to ventricles
  2. B. Anchors the valves
    Insertion for atrial and ventricular muscle
    Electrically insulates atria from ventricles
  3. C. Anchors the coronary arteries
    Insertion for atrial and ventricular muscle
    Conducts the impulse from atria to ventricles
AnswerB. Anchors the valves
Insertion for atrial and ventricular muscle
Electrically insulates atria from ventricles
WhyThe skeleton stabilises the valves, gives the atrial and ventricular muscle something to pull on, and electrically insulates the atria from the ventricles.
Explanation

The fibrous rings keep each valve opening the right shape so the cusps meet. The atrial and ventricular muscle bundles insert on the skeleton. Because connective tissue has no gap junctions, the skeleton blocks the atrial impulse everywhere except at the AV bundle.

  • Pacemaking and coupling are done by the SA node and the AV node/bundle; the skeleton does the opposite of coupling.
  • The skeleton does not conduct; and the coronary arteries are anchored in the epicardium, not by the skeleton.
Slide (1)
L64Learning
What is the only electrical path from the atria to the ventricles?
  1. A. The AV bundle (of His), which pierces the cardiac skeleton
  2. B. Purkinje fibres, which run through the fibrous trigones
  3. C. Gap junctions spread evenly across the whole cardiac skeleton
AnswerA. The AV bundle (of His), which pierces the cardiac skeleton
WhyThe insulating skeleton leaves one gap: the AV bundle passing through it, so every impulse must go through the AV node and bundle.
Explanation

This arrangement makes the AV node the gatekeeper. It delays the impulse so the atria can empty, and it limits how fast the ventricles can be driven if the atria beat abnormally fast. If the skeleton did not insulate, impulses could cross anywhere and the ventricles would contract out of step with the atria.

  • Purkinje fibres are downstream, in the ventricular subendocardium; they do not cross the skeleton.
  • Connective tissue has no gap junctions; that is exactly why it insulates.
Slides (2)

Heart valves

L65Learning
What separates the atria from the ventricles, and what separates the ventricles from the great arteries?
  1. A. Atria/ventricles: atrioventricular valves
    Ventricles/arteries: semilunar valves
  2. B. Atria/ventricles: semilunar valves
    Ventricles/arteries: atrioventricular valves
  3. C. Atria/ventricles: the cardiac skeleton alone, with no valves
    Ventricles/arteries: semilunar valves
AnswerA. Atria/ventricles: atrioventricular valves
Ventricles/arteries: semilunar valves
WhyValves keep flow one-way: atrioventricular valves between atria and ventricles, semilunar valves between ventricles and the aorta or pulmonary trunk.
Explanation

There are two types of heart valve. The two AV valves (tricuspid on the right, mitral on the left) stop blood going back into the atria when the ventricles contract. The two semilunar valves (pulmonary and aortic) stop blood falling back into the ventricles when they relax.

  • The swapped option reverses the two types.
  • The cardiac skeleton surrounds the AV openings but does not close them; the AV valves hang from it.
Slides (2)
L66Learning
Name the atrioventricular valves.
  1. A. Right: bicuspid (mitral)
    Left: tricuspid
  2. B. Right: tricuspid
    Left: bicuspid (mitral)
  3. C. Right: pulmonary
    Left: aortic
AnswerB. Right: tricuspid
Left: bicuspid (mitral)
WhyThe tricuspid valve guards the right AV opening; the bicuspid (mitral) valve guards the left.
Explanation

The right AV valve has three cusps, the left two. The mitral valve is named for its resemblance to a bishop's mitre.

  • Mitral on the right swaps the sides.
  • Pulmonary and aortic are the semilunar valves at the exits of the ventricles.

Hook: 'Tricuspid on the Right'; the Left has the mitraL.

Slide (1)
L67Learning
Name the semilunar valves and where each sits.
  1. A. Pulmonary: left ventricle → pulmonary trunk
    Aortic: right ventricle → aorta
  2. B. Pulmonary: right ventricle → aorta
    Aortic: left ventricle → pulmonary trunk
  3. C. Pulmonary: right ventricle → pulmonary trunk
    Aortic: left ventricle → aorta
AnswerC. Pulmonary: right ventricle → pulmonary trunk
Aortic: left ventricle → aorta
WhyThe pulmonary semilunar valve guards the right ventricle's exit into the pulmonary trunk; the aortic valve guards the left ventricle's exit into the aorta.
Explanation

Each semilunar valve sits at the root of the great artery leaving a ventricle. The right ventricle feeds the lungs through the pulmonary trunk; the left feeds the body through the aorta.

  • The first wrong option swaps which ventricle each valve serves.
  • The second swaps which artery each valve opens into.

The mitral valve is an AV valve, never a semilunar one.

Slide (1)
L68Learning
What forms the core of a heart valve?
  1. A. Vascular loose connective tissue, covered on both surfaces by endothelium
  2. B. Avascular dense connective tissue, covered on both surfaces by endothelium
  3. C. Cardiac muscle, covered on both surfaces by endothelium
AnswerB. Avascular dense connective tissue, covered on both surfaces by endothelium
WhyA valve is a fold of endocardium with an avascular dense connective tissue core (the fibrosa), covered by endothelium; it moves passively.
Explanation

The collagen core (blue in trichrome) is continuous with the fibrous ring of the cardiac skeleton. It has no blood vessels: the thin leaflet is nourished by diffusion from the blood on both sides. Valves contain no muscle and open and close only with the pressure difference across them.

  • Vascular loose tissue would be too weak and would bleed; the core is dense and avascular.
  • Cardiac muscle stays in the myocardium and papillary muscles; the leaflet itself does not contract.

Because they are avascular, infected valves are hard for white cells and antibiotics to reach.

Slide (1)
L69Learning
Which layer of the heart wall do the valves belong to?
  1. A. Myocardium (extensions of the muscle), with a core continuous with the papillary muscles
  2. B. Endocardium (folds of the lining), with a core continuous with the cardiac skeleton
  3. C. Epicardium (folds of the serous layer), with a core continuous with the pericardium
AnswerB. Endocardium (folds of the lining), with a core continuous with the cardiac skeleton
WhyValves are folds of endocardium: endothelium over a connective-tissue core anchored in the cardiac skeleton.
Explanation

At the atrioventricular junction the skeleton lies mainly within the endocardium, and each leaflet grows out of it: its dense collagen core continues from the fibrous ring, and its endothelial covering continues from the endocardium of the atrium and ventricle.

  • The myocardium stops at the base of the valve; the papillary muscles attach to the chordae, not to the leaflet core.
  • The epicardium covers the outside of the heart and never reaches the valve openings.
Slide (1)
L70Learning
What closes the atrioventricular valves at the start of ventricular contraction?
  1. A. Contraction of the papillary muscles pulls the cusps together
  2. B. Contraction of muscle within the cusps draws them shut
  3. C. Rising ventricular blood pressure pushes the cusps together
AnswerC. Rising ventricular blood pressure pushes the cusps together
WhyAV valves close passively: when ventricular pressure exceeds atrial pressure, blood pressure pushes the cusps shut.
Explanation

The lecture lists the two forces: 'blood pressure closes valve' and 'papillary muscles tense chordae tendineae'. The pressure gradient does the closing; the papillary muscles, contracting with the rest of the ventricle, only keep the closed cusps from being blown back into the atrium.

  • Papillary muscles pull the cusps toward the ventricle through the chordae; they brace the closed valve rather than shutting it.
  • The cusps contain no muscle: they are dense connective tissue covered by endothelium.
Slides (2)
L71Learning
What stops the atrioventricular valve cusps turning inside out into the atria?
  1. A. Papillary muscles contract → tense the chordae tendineae
  2. B. Papillary muscles relax → slacken the chordae tendineae
  3. C. The three cusps brace against one another like a tripod
AnswerA. Papillary muscles contract → tense the chordae tendineae
WhyDuring ventricular contraction the papillary muscles contract too and tense the chordae tendineae, holding the closed AV cusps against the pressure.
Explanation

The chordae tendineae are collagen cords running from the free edges of the AV cusps to the papillary muscles on the ventricular wall. As ventricular pressure rises, the papillary muscles shorten in step and keep the cords taut, so the cusps meet but cannot evert (prolapse) into the atria. If a papillary muscle ruptures after an infarct, the valve flips back and blood regurgitates into the atrium.

  • Slack chordae would let the cusps blow back.
  • Bracing like a tripod is how the semilunar valves stay shut; they have no chordae or papillary muscles.
Slides (2)
L72Learning
Semilunar valves have no muscular support. How do they stay shut against the back-pressure?
  1. A. Their three cusps fill with blood and brace against one another like a tripod
  2. B. Papillary muscles tense chordae tendineae attached to each cusp
  3. C. Smooth muscle in the cusps contracts during diastole
AnswerA. Their three cusps fill with blood and brace against one another like a tripod
WhyThe semilunar valves have no chordae or papillary muscles; their three cusps fill with back-flowing blood and press together, supporting each other like a tripod.
Explanation

When the ventricle relaxes, blood in the aorta or pulmonary trunk falls back toward it, fills the pocket-shaped cusps and pushes them together at the centre. The three cusps meet along their thick edges, with the nodules sealing the middle, and hold one another up.

  • Chordae and papillary muscles belong to the AV valves only.
  • Smooth muscle is not present in the cusps; valve movement is passive.

Exam point: 'three cusps, no muscular support' = semilunar.

Slide (1)
L73Learning
While the ventricles are contracting and ejecting blood, which valves are open?
  1. A. Tricuspid and mitral open; aortic and pulmonary closed
  2. B. Aortic and pulmonary open; tricuspid and mitral closed
  3. C. Mitral and aortic open; tricuspid and pulmonary closed
AnswerB. Aortic and pulmonary open; tricuspid and mitral closed
WhyDuring ejection the semilunar valves are open and the AV valves closed; in relaxation it is the reverse.
Explanation

The two ventricles work together, so valves of the same type always do the same thing on both sides. When the ventricles contract, their pressure rises above atrial pressure (closing the tricuspid and mitral valves) and above arterial pressure (opening the aortic and pulmonary valves). When they relax, the AV valves open to let them fill and the semilunar valves close.

  • AV open, semilunar closed is the picture of relaxed, filling ventricles.
  • Mitral and aortic open together mixes the two states; a valve and its partner on the other side always move together.
Slide (1)
L74Learning
Name the parts of a semilunar cusp and what lies behind it.
  1. A. Lunule at the middle of the free edge; nodule on either side
    Sinus: a bulge of the vessel wall behind each cusp
  2. B. Nodule at the middle of the free edge; lunule on either side
    Chordae tendineae: cords behind each cusp
  3. C. Nodule at the middle of the free edge; lunule on either side
    Sinus: a bulge of the vessel wall behind each cusp
AnswerC. Nodule at the middle of the free edge; lunule on either side
Sinus: a bulge of the vessel wall behind each cusp
WhyEach cusp has a central nodule on its free edge, thin crescent lunules on either side, and a pocket of vessel wall behind it, the aortic or pulmonary sinus.
Explanation

When the valve closes, the lunules of neighbouring cusps press against each other and the three nodules meet in the centre to seal the gap. Behind each cusp the vessel wall bulges out as a sinus; blood fills the sinuses during diastole and keeps the cusps from sticking to the wall.

  • Swapping nodule and lunule reverses them: the nodule is the single thickening in the middle.
  • Chordae tendineae belong to the AV valves; nothing tethers a semilunar cusp.
Slide (1)
L75Learning
Behind which cusps of the aortic valve do the coronary arteries open?
  1. A. Right and posterior cusps; the left cusp has no coronary opening
  2. B. Anterior and left cusps; the right cusp has no coronary opening
  3. C. Right and left cusps; the posterior cusp has no coronary opening
AnswerC. Right and left cusps; the posterior cusp has no coronary opening
WhyThe right coronary artery opens from the right aortic sinus and the left coronary artery from the left; the posterior (non-coronary) sinus has none.
Explanation

The aortic valve has right, left and posterior cusps, each with a sinus behind it. The coronary ostia sit in the right and left aortic sinuses, just above the valve. The pulmonary valve's cusps are named left, anterior and right, and it has no coronary openings.

  • The posterior sinus is the non-coronary one, so it cannot be one of the two.
  • Anterior is a pulmonary cusp name; the aortic valve has no anterior cusp.
Slide (1)
L76Learning
A trichrome section shows a thin flap with a blue-staining core, covered by a thin cellular lining, with thin blue cords attached to it; its base blends with blue tissue between atrium and ventricle. What is it?
  1. A. An atrioventricular valve leaflet with chordae tendineae
  2. B. A semilunar valve cusp attached to its aortic sinus wall
  3. C. A papillary muscle with a tendon arising from its tip
AnswerA. An atrioventricular valve leaflet with chordae tendineae
WhyBlue (collagen) core, endothelial covering and attached chordae tendineae = an AV valve leaflet, its base continuous with the fibrous skeleton.
Explanation

Trichrome stains collagen blue and muscle red/purple. A leaflet whose dense connective-tissue core (C) is continuous at its base with the fibrous skeleton in the endocardium (En), between atrium (A) and ventricle (V), with cords (CT) attached, is an atrioventricular valve. The chordae are the cords tying its free edge to the papillary muscles.

  • A semilunar cusp has no chordae tendineae, and it hangs from the root of the aorta or pulmonary trunk, not between atrium and ventricle.
  • A papillary muscle would stain red like the myocardium; only its chordae are blue.
Slide (1)
L77Learning
Three weeks after a dental extraction, a 19-year-old has palpitations, and echocardiography shows vegetations on his heart valves. Which layer of the heart is infected?
  1. A. Endocardium
  2. B. Myocardium
  3. C. Epicardium
AnswerA. Endocardium
WhyHeart valves are folds of endocardium, so vegetations on them are infective endocarditis.
Explanation

Mouth bacteria (often viridans streptococci) can enter the blood during dental work and settle on the valves, which are covered by endothelium and have an avascular connective-tissue core. Clumps of bacteria, platelets and fibrin grow there as vegetations and can damage the valve.

  • Myocardium: infection of the muscle is myocarditis, not lesions on the valves.
  • Epicardium: infection of the outer surface is pericarditis; the epicardium never covers a valve.
Slide (1)

Coronary circulation and myocardial infarction

L78Learning
Where do the right and left coronary arteries arise?
  1. A. From the aortic arch, beside the brachiocephalic trunk
  2. B. From the aortic sinuses, just above the aortic valve
