  3. C. From the left ventricle, just below the aortic valve
AnswerB. From the aortic sinuses, just above the aortic valve
WhyThe coronary arteries are the first branches of the aorta, opening from the right and left aortic sinuses just above the valve cusps.
Explanation

The aortic sinuses are the three bulges of the aortic root behind the valve cusps. The right coronary artery leaves the right sinus and the left coronary artery the left sinus, so the heart muscle is the first tissue supplied with freshly ejected blood.

  • The aortic arch is farther along and gives off the vessels to the head and arms.
  • Nothing arises below the valve: that is still inside the ventricle.
Slides (2)
L79Learning
When do the coronary arteries mainly fill, and what drives the flow?
  1. A. Between contractions — the stretched elastic aortic wall recoils and pushes blood in
  2. B. During contraction — the squeeze of the ventricle pushes blood directly into them
  3. C. Between contractions — the pulmonary trunk recoils and pushes blood in
AnswerA. Between contractions — the stretched elastic aortic wall recoils and pushes blood in
WhyCoronary flow is greatest between contractions (diastole): the elastic rebound of the stretched aortic wall drives blood into the coronary openings.
Explanation

During ejection the aorta stretches and stores energy in its elastic wall. When the ventricle relaxes and the aortic valve closes, the wall recoils and keeps the aortic pressure high, pushing blood into the coronary arteries from the aortic sinuses. During contraction, the squeezing myocardium compresses its own vessels, so flow, especially to the left ventricle, falls.

  • The ventricular squeeze squashes the intramural coronary vessels rather than filling them.
  • The pulmonary trunk does not give rise to the coronary arteries.

A fast heart rate shortens diastole and so shortens the time for coronary filling.

Slide (1)
L80Learning
What are the main branches of the left coronary artery?
  1. A. Anterior interventricular artery
    Circumflex artery
  2. B. Anterior interventricular artery
    Right marginal artery
  3. C. Circumflex artery
    Posterior interventricular artery
AnswerA. Anterior interventricular artery
Circumflex artery
WhyThe left coronary artery divides into the anterior interventricular (left anterior descending) and the circumflex arteries.
Explanation

The anterior interventricular artery runs down the anterior interventricular sulcus, in epicardial fat, supplying the front of both ventricles and most of the septum. The circumflex runs round the left side in the coronary (atrioventricular) groove.

  • The right marginal artery is a branch of the right coronary artery.
  • The posterior interventricular artery usually comes from the right coronary artery.
Slide (1)
L81Learning
What are the main branches of the right coronary artery?
  1. A. Anterior interventricular artery
    Circumflex artery
  2. B. Right marginal artery
    Usually the posterior interventricular artery
  3. C. Left marginal artery
    Usually the anterior interventricular artery
AnswerB. Right marginal artery
Usually the posterior interventricular artery
WhyThe right coronary artery gives the right marginal artery and, in most hearts, the posterior interventricular artery.
Explanation

The right coronary artery runs in the right coronary groove, gives the right marginal artery along the lower border of the heart, and usually continues as the posterior interventricular artery in the posterior interventricular sulcus (a 'right-dominant' heart).

  • The anterior interventricular and circumflex arteries are the two branches of the left coronary artery.
  • A left marginal artery arises from the circumflex, a left coronary branch.
Slide (1)
L82Learning
What is a myocardial infarction?
  1. A. Death of heart muscle when a coronary artery is blocked, usually by a thrombus
  2. B. Brief coronary spasm that reduces flow without killing any muscle
  3. C. Scarring of the pericardium that restricts filling of the heart
AnswerA. Death of heart muscle when a coronary artery is blocked, usually by a thrombus
WhyMyocardial infarction = death of myocardium in the territory of a blocked coronary artery, most often blocked by a thrombus on an atherosclerotic plaque.
Explanation

A clot that blocks a coronary artery (coronary thrombosis) cuts off oxygen to the muscle it supplies. After about 20–30 minutes of severe ischaemia the cells start to die. The slides show a coronary artery whose lumen is filled by a thrombus and the infarcted muscle.

  • Spasm without cell death describes angina-type ischaemia, which is reversible.
  • Pericardial scarring is constrictive pericarditis, a different disease.
Slides (2)
L83LearningBorderline
One month after a myocardial infarction, what has replaced the dead heart muscle?
  1. A. New cardiac muscle cells formed by division of the surviving myocytes
  2. B. New smooth muscle cells converted from the surviving myocytes
  3. C. A scar of dense collagenous connective tissue
AnswerC. A scar of dense collagenous connective tissue
WhyAdult cardiac myocytes cannot divide, so an infarct heals as a fibrous (collagen) scar that does not contract.
Explanation

After macrophages clear the dead muscle, granulation tissue grows in and fibroblasts lay down collagen. By about a month the infarct is largely fibrous tissue, which matures into a dense, pale collagen scar over the following weeks (complete by about two months). Because the scar cannot contract, the heart pumps less well, and a large scar can lead to heart failure.

  • Myocyte division (hyperplasia) does not happen in the adult heart to any useful degree; the muscle is a permanent tissue.
  • Myocytes do not turn into smooth muscle.
L84LearningBorderline
A young woman with years of untreated severe hypertension dies of heart failure; her heart weighs 540 g. What process in the myocardial fibres enlarged it?
  1. A. Hyperplasia (myocytes divide to increase in number)
  2. B. Fatty change (fat droplets accumulate in each myocyte)
  3. C. Hypertrophy (each myocyte grows larger)
AnswerC. Hypertrophy (each myocyte grows larger)
WhyCardiac myocytes cannot divide, so a heart working against high pressure enlarges by hypertrophy: each cell adds myofibrils and grows.
Explanation

A raised afterload makes the left ventricle work harder. It responds by thickening its wall: each muscle cell makes more sarcomeres and becomes larger, while the number of cells stays about the same.

  • Hyperplasia needs cells that can divide; adult cardiac muscle cells, like neurons, essentially cannot.
  • Fatty change makes cells pale and vacuolated but does not double the weight of the heart.
L85LearningBorderline
In myocardium from a patient who died of a heart attack, single myocytes show many dense pink transverse bands close together. What are they?
  1. A. Intercalated discs of normal muscle
  2. B. Contraction bands of infarcted (dying) muscle
  3. C. Lipofuscin granules of ageing muscle
AnswerB. Contraction bands of infarcted (dying) muscle
WhyMany dense bands within one cell are contraction bands, a sign of myocardial infarction; intercalated discs occur only between cells.
Explanation

When dying cardiac muscle is flooded with calcium (for example when blood flow returns), its myofibrils hypercontract into thick, dense, eosinophilic bands crowded together across the cell. Healthy muscle shows only one intercalated disc at each end of a cell.

  • Intercalated discs are thin, step-like lines at the cell borders, roughly one cell length apart.
  • Lipofuscin is golden-brown granules at the nuclear poles, not bands across the cell.

1High-yield
Two weeks after suffering a massive heart attack, a 54-year-old man presents to the emergency room complaining of sharp pain on the left side of his chest. On physical examination, the patient is apprehensive and sweating. His blood pressure is 80/40 mm Hg, and the pulse rate is 100 per minute. The patient expires shortly after admission. At autopsy, the left ventricle shows a rupture in the myocardial wall. What was the most likely cause of the patient’s death?
  1. (A) Cardiac tamponade
  2. (B) Dissecting aortic aneurysm
  3. (C) Pulmonary edema
  4. (D) Pulmonary thromboembolism
  5. (E) Septic shock
AnswerA. Cardiac tamponade
WhyRupture of a softened infarct floods the pericardial cavity with blood (hemopericardium), compressing the heart and blocking ventricular filling, which is cardiac tamponade.
Explanation from the source
Rupture of a myocardial infarct causes blood to fill the peritoneal cavity (hemopericardium). This medical catastrophe restricts the motion of the heart and is referred to as cardiac tamponade. When it happens, it typically occurs within the first 3 weeks following myocardial infarction. Pulsus paradoxus (>10 mm Hg drop in arterial blood pressure with inspiration) is commonly observed in patients with hemopericardium. Although aortic dissections (choice B) can break through to the pericardium, they do not rupture the heart wall. None of the other cardiovascular diseases are associated with rupture of the heart wall and cardiac tamponade. Keywords: Hemopericardium, cardiac tamponade
ConceptVentricular rupture after MI causes hemopericardium and cardiac tamponade

Q6 – The sinoatrial node is located within which of the following structures?
  1. A. Right atrial wall
  2. B. Left atrial wall
  3. C. Cardiac skeleton
  4. D. Epicardium
  5. E. Endocardium
AnswerA. Right atrial wall
WhyThe sinoatrial node sits in the right atrial wall near the entrance of the superior vena cava, where it generates the impulse that starts each heartbeat.
Explanation from the source
Both the sinoatrial (SA) node (pacemaker) and atrioventricular (AV) node are located in the walls of the right atrium. The AV node is continuous with a specialized bundle of cardiac muscle fibers, the AV bundle of His, which gives rise to the right and left bundle branches that run along both sides of the interventricular septum to the apex of the heart. As the bundle branches approach the apex, they subdivide further as a network of subendocardial Purkinje fibers that spread the electrical impulse to the muscle of the myocardium from the apex to the base. Sinoatrial nodeThe SA node is a 6-7 mm structure that is generally not visible grossly, although it is recognizable histologically. It is located subepicardially within the right atrial wall where the muscular ridge known as the crista terminalis meets the superior vena cava. The SA node is identifiable in the histologic image where it is the paler staining region (indicated by asterisks) surrounding the sinoatrial nodal artery. At high magnification (not shown here), the SA node fibers are thinner, have fewer myofibrils, and are less intensely staining on H&E compared to the neighboring contractile fibers. Darker contractile cardiac muscle cells and endocardium of the right atrium can be seen to the left of the node, and fat tissue of the epicardium to the right.
ConceptThe SA node lies in the right atrial wall

[Question 1] A 68-year-old man develops sudden, severe substernal chest pain. Laboratory studies and ECG confirm an acute myocardial infarction (heart attack). The patient cannot maintain his blood pressure and expires 4 hours later. Which of the following was the most likely cause of the patient’s death? [Question 2] The heart of the patient described in Question 1 is examined at autopsy. Routine H&E staining reveals layered structures within the wall of the heart (shown in the image). Identify the indicated layer.
  1. (A) Endocardium
  2. (B) Epicardium
  3. (C) Myocardium
  4. (D) Parietal layer of the pericardium
  5. (E) Visceral layer of the pericardium
AnswerC. Myocardium
WhyThe thick middle layer of branching, striated cardiac muscle with central nuclei and intercalated discs is the myocardium, the contractile layer that dies in a myocardial infarction.
Explanation from the source
The heart is a folded endothelial tube with a thickened muscular wall that pumps blood through the circulatory system. The principal functional component of the heart is the myocardial layer (myocardium) that is composed of cardiac muscle. The myocardium is covered externally by an epicardium (choice B), consisting of a layer of mesothelium and associated adipose connective tissue. The inner (luminal) surface of the myocardium is lined by endocardium (choice A), consisting of a layer of endothelium and associated connective tissue. Parietal layer of pericardium (choice D) lines the fibrous pericardial sac and is not visible in this section. Visceral layer of pericardium (choice E) refers to the mesothelial cell layer of epicardium. The myocardium is considerably thicker in the ventricles, than in the atria, reflecting the needs of the ventricles to propel blood through pulmonary and systemic circulations. Keywords: Heart, myocardium
ConceptThick muscular middle layer of the heart wall (image) is the myocardium

The adipose tissue functions as a cushion for the heart as it moves within the pericardial sac. Blood vessels and nerves supplying the heart travel through the epicardium. Endocardium (choice A) lines the luminal surface of the heart and is typically devoid of adipose tissue. Fibrous pericardium (choice C) is composed of dense connective tissue and is not visible in this image. Visceral pleura (choice E) represents a layer of mesothelium that is adherent to the surface of the lungs. Keywords: Heart, epicardium

[Question 5] Two weeks after suffering a massive heart attack, a 54-year-old man presents to the emergency room complaining of sharp pain on the left side of his chest. On physical examination, the patient is apprehensive and sweating. His blood pressure is 80/40 mm Hg, and the pulse rate is 100 per minute. The patient expires shortly after admission. At autopsy, the left ventricle shows a rupture in the myocardial wall. What was the most likely cause of the patient’s death? [Question 6] Autopsy of the patient described in Question 5 reveals 400 mL of blood in the pericardial cavity. This blood is in direct contact with which of the following anatomic structures?
  1. (A) Endocardium
  2. (B) Epicardium
  3. (C) Fibrous pericardium
  4. (D) Myocardium
  5. (E) Parietal pleura
AnswerB. Epicardium
WhyBlood from a ruptured ventricle fills the pericardial cavity, which is lined on the heart side by the mesothelium of the visceral serous pericardium, the surface of the epicardium; the fibrous pericardium is outside the parietal layer.
Explanation from the source
The pericardial sac is lined by visceral and parietal mesothelia that together are referred to as serous pericardium. The visceral layer of serous pericardium represents the mesothelial layer of the epicardium. The parietal layer of serous pericardium lines the inner surface of the fibrous pericardium (choice C). The space between the visceral and parietal layers of serous pericardium defines the pericardial cavity. In normal condition, a thin layer of serous fluid within the pericardial cavity (about 50 mL) provides lubrication for movement of the heart during contraction. Myocardial rupture, pericarditis, or chest injuries can cause excess fluid or blood to accumulate in the pericardial cavity. Accumulation of excess fluid or blood restricts ventricular filling, a life-threatening condition referred to as cardiac tamponade. Pericardiocentesis is often required to drain excess pericardial fluid to relieve pressure on the heart. None of the other structures are in direct contact with the pericardial cavity. Keywords: Cardiac tamponade, heart, epicardium
ConceptBlood in the pericardial cavity contacts the epicardium (visceral serous pericardium)

WhyRupture of a softened infarct fills the pericardial sac with blood (hemopericardium); the rigid fibrous pericardium cannot stretch, so pressure compresses the heart and stops ventricular filling, causing cardiac tamponade and shock.
Explanation from the source
The answer is A: Cardiac tamponade. Rupture of a myocardial infarct causes blood to fill the peritoneal cavity (hemopericardium). This medical catastrophe restricts the motion of the heart and is referred to as cardiac tamponade. When it happens, it typically occurs within the first 3 weeks following myocardial infarction. Pulsus paradoxus (>10 mm Hg drop in arterial blood pressure with inspiration) is commonly observed in patients with hemopericardium. Although aortic dissections (choice B) can break through to the pericardium, they do not rupture the heart wall. None of the other cardiovascular diseases are associated with rupture of the heart wall and cardiac tamponade. Keywords: Hemopericardium, cardiac tamponade
ConceptVentricular rupture after MI causes hemopericardium and cardiac tamponade
Slides (2)
33High-yield
Autopsy of the patient described in Question 5 reveals 400 mL of blood in the pericardial cavity. This blood is in direct contact with which of the following anatomic structures?
  1. (A) Endocardium
  2. (B) Epicardium
  3. (C) Fibrous pericardium
  4. (D) Myocardium
  5. (E) Parietal pleura
Answer(B) Epicardium
WhyBlood in the pericardial cavity touches the mesothelium of the visceral serous pericardium, which is the surface of the epicardium; the parietal layer lines the fibrous pericardium.
Explanation from the source
The answer is B: Epicardium. The pericardial sac is lined by visceral and parietal mesothelia that together are referred to as serous pericardium. The visceral layer of serous pericardium represents the mesothelial layer of the epicardium. The parietal layer of serous pericardium lines the inner surface of the fibrous pericardium (choice C). The space between the visceral and parietal layers of serous pericardium defines the pericardial cavity. In normal condition, a thin layer of serous fluid within the pericardial cavity (about 50 mL) provides lubrication for movement of the heart during contraction. Myocardial rupture, pericarditis, or chest injuries can cause excess fluid or blood to accumulate in the pericardial cavity. Accumulation of excess fluid or blood restricts ventricular filling, a lifethreatening condition referred to as cardiac tamponade. Pericardiocentesis is often required to drain excess pericardial fluid to relieve pressure on the heart. None of the other structures are in direct contact with the pericardial cavity. Keywords: Cardiac tamponade, heart, epicardium
ConceptBlood in the pericardial cavity contacts the epicardium (visceral serous pericardium)
Slides (2)
34High-yield
A 56-year-old man complains of recurring heart palpitations and is subsequently diagnosed with a cardiac arrhythmia. Which of the following cardiac structures functions as the “pacemaker” of the heart?
  1. (A) Atrioventricular bundle of His
  2. (B) Atrioventricular node
  3. (C) Purkinje fibers
  4. (D) Sinoatrial node
  5. (E) Sympathetic fibers
Answer(D) Sinoatrial node
WhyThe sinoatrial node in the right atrial wall has the fastest spontaneous depolarization rate, so it sets the heart rhythm as the pacemaker.
Explanation from the source
The answer is D: Sinoatrial node. Rhythmic cardiac muscle contractions are initiated and propagated by the conducting system of the heart. The conducting system of the heart consists of the (1) sinoatrial (SA) node, (2) atrioventricular (AV) node, (3) AV bundle of His, and (4) right and left bundle branches. The SA node, situated at the junction of superior vena cava and the right atrium, is composed of specialized nodal cardiac muscle cells. Because the SA node generates electrical impulses and has the fastest depolarization rate, it is commonly referred to as the “pacemaker” of the heart. Impulses from the SA node are conducted to the AV node (choice B) through an internodal pathway. The AV node is located in the interatrial septum near the orifice of the coronary sinus. The AV node generates impulses at a considerably lower rate than the SA node and, therefore, cannot function as pacemaker of the heart. The AV bundle of His (choice A) and Purkinje fibers (choice C) transmit impulses from the AV node to ventricular cardiac muscle. Sympathetic fibers (choice E) regulate heart rate, but they do not initiate cardiac muscle contraction. Keywords: Heart, sinoatrial node
ConceptThe sinoatrial node is the pacemaker of the heart

You are asked to lead a problem-based learning session on valvular heart disease. Which of the following tissues forms the central core of heart valves?
  1. (A) Avascular dense connective tissue
  2. (B) Cardiac muscle fibers
  3. (C) Elastic connective tissue
  4. (D) Smooth muscle fibers
  5. (E) Vascular loose connective tissue
Answer(A) Avascular dense connective tissue
WhyValve cusps have a core of avascular dense connective tissue continuous with the fibrous skeleton and covered by endothelium, getting nutrients by diffusion from blood.
Explanation from the source
The answer is A: Avascular dense connective tissue. Mitral, tricuspid, aortic, and pulmonary heart valves have an avascular, dense connective tissue core (termed fibrosa) that is continuous with collagen fibers forming the fibrous skeleton of the heart. These valves are covered by a layer of loose connective tissue on the atrial or blood vessel side and by endothelium on the ventricular side. Heart valves are normally lacking in blood vessels, since they are continuously exposed to oxygen and nutrients in the blood. None of the other tissues characterize the central core of heart valves. Keywords: Heart, valves
ConceptHeart valve core is avascular dense connective tissue

AnswerD. Collagen VII
WhyIntercalated discs contain cadherins, desmoglein, desmocollin and desmoplakin of fasciae adherentes and desmosomes, while collagen VII forms anchoring fibrils beneath basal laminae, not cell-cell junctions.
Explanation from the source
The intercalated disc is a junctional complex. This higher magnification EM shows the 3 types of cell junction that make up an intercalated disc. The 3 components are arranged in a step-like fashion with fascia adherens and desmosomes transversely oriented between muscle fibers and gap junctions parallel to their long axis. Fascia adherens (contains cadherin protein) Desmosome (contains desmocollin, desmoglein, and desmoplakin protein) Gap Junction (contains connexin protein) Hemidesmosome In hemidesmosomes, collagen type VII forms anchoring fibril loops that bind the basal lamina to underlying connective tissue. Therefore, collagen type VII does not contribute to formation of the intercalated disc.
Recognizing intercalated discs is CP1, but the molecular make-up of junctions (collagen VII anchoring fibrils) comes from the earlier cell-junction lecture.

HIST-7B Vessels & lymphatics

120 questions · 98 concepts · 29 high-yield
Learning questions 99

The three tunics and the vasa vasorum

L1Learning
Name the three tunics of a blood-vessel wall, from the lumen outward.
  1. A. Tunica media → tunica intima → tunica adventitia
  2. B. Tunica intima → tunica media → tunica adventitia
  3. C. Tunica adventitia → tunica media → tunica intima
AnswerB. Tunica intima → tunica media → tunica adventitia
WhyFrom the lumen outward: intima (endothelium), media (smooth muscle and elastic tissue), adventitia (connective tissue).
Explanation

A tunic is a concentric coat of the vessel wall. The intima lines the lumen (endothelium plus a thin subendothelial layer); the media is the middle coat of smooth muscle and elastic tissue; the adventitia (tunica externa) is the outer connective-tissue coat that blends with the surrounding tissue.

  • Media first is impossible: the endothelium always faces the blood, and it belongs to the intima.
  • Adventitia first reverses the order; adventitia means the coat that comes from outside.

Almost every vessel-identification question is really asking which of these three coats dominates. Hook: I-M-A, from inside out.

Slide (1)
L2Learning
What makes up the tunica intima?
  1. A. Endothelium on its basal lamina + a thin subendothelial layer of loose connective tissue
  2. B. Endothelium on its basal lamina + a thick layer of circular smooth muscle
  3. C. Loose connective tissue with collagen, nerves and vasa vasorum
AnswerA. Endothelium on its basal lamina + a thin subendothelial layer of loose connective tissue
WhyThe intima is the endothelium (simple squamous) plus a thin subendothelial connective-tissue layer; in arteries the internal elastic lamina closes it off.
Explanation

The endothelium is a single layer of flat cells resting on a basal lamina. Beneath it lies the subendothelial layer, a thin band of loose connective tissue (in large arteries it also holds a few smooth muscle cells). In arteries the internal elastic lamina marks the outer edge of the intima.

  • A thick layer of circular smooth muscle is the tunica media, the next coat out.
  • Loose connective tissue with nerves and vasa vasorum describes the adventitia.
Slides (2)
L3Learning
Which tunic does every blood vessel have, right down to a capillary?
  1. A. Tunica adventitia
  2. B. Tunica media
  3. C. Tunica intima
AnswerC. Tunica intima
WhyA capillary is endothelium only, the core of the tunica intima; it has no media and no adventitia.
Explanation

The lecture describes the capillary wall as intima: endothelium only; media: "none" (pericytes); adventitia: none. So the one coat every vessel shares is the intima, whose essential part is the endothelium lining the lumen.

  • Tunica media (smooth muscle) is missing from capillaries and from postcapillary venules; scattered pericytes are the closest a capillary comes to a media.
  • Tunica adventitia is also absent from capillaries; it is very thin even in arterioles.
Slide (1)
L4Learning
In arteries, what marks the boundary between the intima and the media?
  1. A. Internal elastic lamina, a wavy fenestrated sheet of elastin
  2. B. External elastic lamina, a wavy fenestrated sheet of elastin
  3. C. Basal lamina, a thin sheet of type IV collagen under the endothelium
AnswerA. Internal elastic lamina, a wavy fenestrated sheet of elastin
WhyThe internal elastic lamina is a fenestrated elastin sheet, wavy in fixed tissue, that forms the outer edge of the intima, separating it from the media.
Explanation

The internal elastic lamina is a sheet of elastin with small holes (fenestrae) that let nutrients diffuse to the media. After death or fixation the artery contracts, so the lamina buckles into a crisp wavy line, dark in an elastic stain. It is most prominent in muscular arteries; most veins lack one.

  • The external elastic lamina sits at the other side of the media, between media and adventitia.
  • The basal lamina lies directly under the endothelial cells; it is an electron-microscope structure, not the wavy line seen in the light microscope.
Slides (2)
L5Learning
What makes up the tunica media?
  1. A. Loose collagenous connective tissue carrying vasa vasorum and nerves
  2. B. Concentric layers of skeletal muscle with elastic fibres between them
  3. C. Concentric layers of smooth muscle with elastic fibres or lamellae between them
AnswerC. Concentric layers of smooth muscle with elastic fibres or lamellae between them
WhyThe media is smooth muscle + elastic tissue; the ratio of the two changes with the vessel type (elastin dominates in the aorta, muscle in muscular arteries).
Explanation

The media is built of circumferentially arranged smooth muscle cells with elastic fibres and lamellae (and some collagen) between them. The smooth muscle cells themselves secrete this matrix. In elastic arteries the elastic lamellae dominate; in muscular arteries the smooth muscle does; in veins the media is thin.

  • Skeletal muscle is never part of a vessel wall; it is voluntary muscle.
  • Loose connective tissue with vasa vasorum and nerves is the adventitia.
Slides (2)
L6Learning
Which tunic is mainly responsible for vasoconstriction and vasodilation?
  1. A. Tunica adventitia
  2. B. Tunica media
  3. C. Tunica intima
AnswerB. Tunica media
WhyThe tunica media holds the vessel's smooth muscle; its contraction narrows the lumen and its relaxation widens it.
Explanation

Vasoconstriction and vasodilation are changes in lumen diameter produced by contraction or relaxation of the circular smooth muscle of the media. That is how muscular arteries distribute blood and arterioles set resistance.

  • The intima (endothelium) releases signals such as nitric oxide and endothelin-1 that act on the media, but it does not itself contract.
  • The adventitia is connective tissue that anchors the vessel; its smooth muscle bundles appear only in large veins, and it does not set lumen size.
Slide (1)
L7Learning
In arteries, what marks the boundary between the media and the adventitia?
  1. A. External elastic lamina
  2. B. Basal lamina
  3. C. Internal elastic lamina
AnswerA. External elastic lamina
WhyThe external elastic lamina lies at the outer edge of the media; the internal elastic lamina lies at its inner edge.
Explanation

Arteries are bounded on both sides of the media by elastic sheets: the internal elastic lamina between intima and media, and the thinner, less distinct external elastic lamina between media and adventitia. It is clearest in large muscular arteries in an elastic stain and is often hard to see in H&E. Having both laminae is a feature of arteries; veins usually have neither, or only a thin internal one in the largest veins.

  • Internal elastic lamina is the inner border, under the intima.
  • Basal lamina underlies the endothelium (and surrounds smooth muscle cells); it is not a tunic border.
Slides (2)
L8Learning
What is the tunica adventitia, and what does it do?
  1. A. The outer smooth-muscle coat that sets the diameter of the vessel
  2. B. The inner connective-tissue coat that lines the lumen under the endothelium
  3. C. The outer connective-tissue coat that anchors the vessel to the surrounding tissue
AnswerC. The outer connective-tissue coat that anchors the vessel to the surrounding tissue
WhyThe adventitia is the outermost coat of collagen and elastic fibres; it merges with surrounding connective tissue and anchors the vessel.
Explanation

The tunica adventitia (tunica externa) is mostly type I collagen and elastic fibres with fibroblasts. It blends into the surrounding connective tissue, holding the vessel in place, and it carries the vessel's own nerves and, in large vessels, the vasa vasorum. It is thin in arteries and is the thickest coat of veins.

  • The inner coat that lines the lumen is the intima with its subendothelial layer.
  • The smooth-muscle coat that sets diameter is the media.
Slide (1)
L9Learning
Although the tunics vary in thickness, which tunic tends to be the most prominent layer of an artery?
  1. A. Tunica media
  2. B. Tunica intima
  3. C. Tunica adventitia
AnswerA. Tunica media
WhyArteries carry blood at high pressure, so their media (smooth muscle and elastic tissue) is the thickest, most prominent coat.
Explanation

An artery must withstand and smooth out high, pulsatile pressure (elastic arteries) or actively change diameter (muscular arteries and arterioles). Both jobs belong to the media, so it is the thickest tunic, and the artery's wall is thick compared with its lumen.

  • The intima is thin in every healthy vessel; a thick intima suggests disease such as atherosclerosis.
  • The adventitia is the thickest tunic of veins, not arteries.

Rule for slides: thickest layer media → artery; thickest layer adventitia → vein.

Slide (1)
L10Learning
Although the tunics vary in thickness, which tunic tends to be the most prominent layer of a vein?
  1. A. Tunica adventitia
  2. B. Tunica intima
  3. C. Tunica media
AnswerA. Tunica adventitia
WhyVeins work at low pressure, so their media is thin; the connective-tissue adventitia is their thickest coat.
Explanation

Veins carry blood at low pressure and do not need a strong muscular media. Their wall is mainly a thick adventitia of collagen and elastic fibres, which gets thicker as veins get larger; in the largest veins (venae cavae) it also contains longitudinal bundles of smooth muscle.

  • The media is the most prominent layer of arteries; in veins it is only a few layers of smooth muscle.
  • The intima of veins is well developed enough to fold into valves, but it is still thin.
Slides (2)
L11Learning
In large vessels, what extra structure runs in the adventitia?
  1. A. The vessel's own smooth-muscle coat, the tunica media
  2. B. The vessel's own small blood vessels, the vasa vasorum
  3. C. The vessel's own lymphatic capillaries, the lacteals
AnswerB. The vessel's own small blood vessels, the vasa vasorum
WhyVasa vasorum ("vessels of the vessels") are small arterioles, capillaries and venules in the adventitia that supply the wall of large vessels.
Explanation

The vasa vasorum are a microvasculature (arterioles, capillaries and venules) running in the adventitia of large arteries and veins and sending branches into the outer part of the media. They are larger and more numerous in veins than in arteries, because venous blood in the lumen carries less oxygen.

  • Lacteals are the lymphatic capillaries of intestinal villi, not part of a vessel wall.
  • The tunica media is the middle coat, not something carried inside the adventitia.
Slide (1)
L12Learning
Why do large arteries and veins need vasa vasorum?
  1. A. Their endothelium is impermeable to oxygen and nutrients
  2. B. Their walls are too thick to be fed by diffusion from the lumen
  3. C. The blood in their lumen carries too little oxygen to feed any of the wall
AnswerB. Their walls are too thick to be fed by diffusion from the lumen
WhyOxygen and nutrients from the lumen diffuse only into the inner wall; the outer media and adventitia of thick-walled vessels need their own supply.
Explanation

Diffusion works only over short distances. Small vessels are fed entirely from their lumen, but the outer media and adventitia of large vessels lie too far away, so they are supplied by vasa vasorum in the adventitia. They do for the wall of a large vessel what the coronary arteries do for the heart wall.

  • Too little oxygen in the lumen is false for the aorta, which carries fully oxygenated blood and still needs vasa vasorum (lower venous oxygen only explains why veins have more of them).
  • Impermeable endothelium is false: the inner wall is fed by diffusion across the endothelium.
Slide (1)
L13Learning
A scanning electron micrograph of a small artery shows a central lumen (Lu) lined by flattened cells (EC). Around them is a ring of tightly folded, compact wall (TM), and outside that a loose meshwork of fibres (TA). What is the compact ring labelled TM?
  1. A. Tunica adventitia
  2. B. Tunica intima
  3. C. Tunica media
AnswerC. Tunica media
WhyBetween the endothelial lining (intima) and the outer fibrous coat (adventitia) lies the compact muscular tunica media (TM).
Explanation

In this scanning micrograph the three tunics are labelled by their initials: TI/EC (tunica intima with endothelial cells facing the lumen), TM (tunica media, the compact smooth-muscle ring, thrown into folds because the artery contracted when fixed) and TA (tunica adventitia, the loose connective-tissue fibres outside).

  • The tunica intima is the thin lining of endothelial cells (EC) at the lumen surface.
  • The tunica adventitia is the loose fibrous meshwork (TA) at the periphery.
Slide (1)
L14Learning
In an elastic-stained section of aorta, small round channels with their own thin walls, some holding red blood cells, are scattered in the outer connective-tissue coat and the outermost media. What are they?
  1. A. Nerve bundles (nervi vasorum)
  2. B. Vasa vasorum
  3. C. Lymphatic capillaries
AnswerB. Vasa vasorum
WhySmall blood vessels with red cells in the adventitia and outer media of a large vessel are the vasa vasorum that feed its wall.
Explanation

The lab aorta slide shows the vasa vasorum as small clear spaces lined by simple squamous endothelium in the adventitia and outer media. They are arterioles, capillaries and venules, so they hold red blood cells.

  • Lymphatic capillaries also have thin walls but never contain red blood cells.
  • Nerve bundles (nervi vasorum) also run in the adventitia, but they are solid with no lumen.
Slides (2)

Endothelium and atherosclerosis

L15Learning
What is the structure of the endothelium?
  1. A. Several layers of cuboidal cells on a basal lamina, joined by desmosomes only
  2. B. One layer of flat cells on a basal lamina, joined by junctional complexes
  3. C. One layer of columnar cells on a basal lamina, joined by junctional complexes
AnswerB. One layer of flat cells on a basal lamina, joined by junctional complexes
WhyEndothelium is a simple squamous epithelium: one layer of thin, flat cells on a basal lamina, held together by junctional complexes.
Explanation

The endothelium lines the heart, every blood vessel and the lymphatics. Its cells are elongated and very thin, aligned with the direction of flow, and rest on a basal lamina; junctional complexes (tight junctions and adherens junctions) hold them together. Being so thin, it lets substances pass quickly between blood and tissue.

  • Columnar cells are tall; endothelial cells are flat (squamous).
  • Several layers of cuboidal cells describes a stratified cuboidal epithelium (e.g. sweat-gland ducts), not a vessel lining.
Slide (1)
L16Learning
What is the endothelium's basic role, as the lecture puts it?
  1. A. A passive, smooth lining that plays no part in exchange or regulation
  2. B. The interface between blood and the organs, a selective barrier and an active regulator of the vessel
  3. C. The structural layer that gives the vessel its tensile strength
AnswerB. The interface between blood and the organs, a selective barrier and an active regulator of the vessel
WhyThe endothelium is the interface between blood and the organs: everything exchanged with the tissues crosses it, and it actively regulates tone, growth, clotting and inflammation.
Explanation

Every molecule or cell moving between blood and tissue must cross the endothelium, so it acts as a selective barrier. It is also an active organ: it keeps four pairs of opposing signals in balance (dilatation vs constriction, growth inhibition vs growth promotion, antithrombosis vs prothrombosis, anti-inflammation vs proinflammation).

  • Passive lining ignores all of these functions.
  • Tensile strength comes from collagen in the adventitia and media, not from a single layer of thin cells.
Slides (2)
L17LearningBorderline
Which endothelial products dilate vessels, and which one constricts them?
  1. A. Dilate: nitric oxide, prostacyclin
    Constrict: endothelin-1
  2. B. Dilate: endothelin-1
    Constrict: nitric oxide, prostacyclin
  3. C. Dilate: prostacyclin, endothelin-1
    Constrict: nitric oxide
AnswerA. Dilate: nitric oxide, prostacyclin
Constrict: endothelin-1
WhyHealthy endothelium releases the dilators nitric oxide and prostacyclin and the constrictor endothelin-1; the balance sets the tone of the media.
Explanation

This is the dilatation vs constriction pair on the lecture's balance. Endothelial cells make nitric oxide (NO), which diffuses into the smooth muscle of the media and relaxes it, and prostacyclin (PGI2), which also relaxes muscle and inhibits platelets. Endothelin-1 is a peptide that strongly contracts vascular smooth muscle.

  • The two wrong options each put endothelin-1 among the dilators or nitric oxide among the constrictors; NO is the classic endothelium-derived relaxing factor.

The molecules come from the textbook; the slide shows the pair as dilatation vs constriction.

L18Learning
On the lecture's balance of endothelial functions, which item sits on the same side as dilatation, antithrombosis and anti-inflammation?
  1. A. Growth promotion
  2. B. Prothrombosis
  3. C. Growth inhibition
AnswerC. Growth inhibition
WhyOne side of the balance is dilatation, growth inhibition, antithrombosis, anti-inflammation; the other is constriction, growth promotion, prothrombosis, proinflammation.
Explanation

The slide pictures normal endothelial function as a balance between two sets of four:

Protective sideOpposing side
DilatationConstriction
Growth inhibitionGrowth promotion
AntithrombosisProthrombosis
Anti-inflammationProinflammation
  • Growth promotion (stimulating smooth-muscle proliferation, e.g. by growth factors) is on the opposing side.
  • Prothrombosis is also on the opposing side, paired against antithrombosis.
Slide (1)
L19LearningBorderline
Which features make healthy endothelium antithrombotic?
  1. A. Exposed subendothelial collagen
    Heparin-like molecules
    Plasminogen activator inhibitor
  2. B. A smooth non-thrombogenic surface
    von Willebrand factor
    Tissue plasminogen activator
  3. C. A smooth non-thrombogenic surface
    Heparin-like molecules
    Tissue plasminogen activator
AnswerC. A smooth non-thrombogenic surface
Heparin-like molecules
Tissue plasminogen activator
WhyIntact endothelium keeps blood fluid: its non-thrombogenic surface hides collagen, heparin-like molecules help inactivate thrombin, and tissue plasminogen activator dissolves fibrin.
Explanation

Antithrombosis means preventing clots. The intact endothelium separates blood from the thrombogenic subendothelial collagen; its surface carries heparin-like molecules (heparan sulfate) that act with antithrombin to inactivate thrombin; it secretes tissue plasminogen activator (tPA), which turns plasminogen into fibrin-dissolving plasmin; and its NO and prostacyclin inhibit platelets.

  • von Willebrand factor is prothrombotic: it tethers platelets to exposed collagen.
  • Exposed collagen and plasminogen activator inhibitor both favour clotting.
L20LearningBorderline
Which endothelial product is prothrombotic?
  1. A. Prostacyclin
  2. B. von Willebrand factor
  3. C. Tissue plasminogen activator
AnswerB. von Willebrand factor
Whyvon Willebrand factor, stored in endothelial Weibel–Palade bodies, binds platelets to exposed collagen and so promotes clotting.
Explanation

von Willebrand factor (vWF) is a large glycoprotein made by endothelial cells and stored in rod-shaped Weibel–Palade bodies. When the vessel is injured it bridges platelet receptors to exposed subendothelial collagen, the first step of the platelet plug. It sits on the prothrombosis side of the endothelial balance.

  • Tissue plasminogen activator breaks clots down (fibrinolysis), so it is antithrombotic.
  • Prostacyclin inhibits platelet aggregation and dilates vessels, so it is antithrombotic too.
L21Learning
What does endothelium do when it tips toward proinflammation?
  1. A. Lets white blood cells stick to it and migrate out into the tissue
  2. B. Releases nitric oxide that relaxes the smooth muscle of the media
  3. C. Secretes tissue plasminogen activator that dissolves fibrin
AnswerA. Lets white blood cells stick to it and migrate out into the tissue
WhyProinflammatory endothelium expresses adhesion molecules, so circulating white cells stick and emigrate, mainly through postcapillary venules.
Explanation

In infection or tissue damage, signals such as histamine and cytokines activate the endothelium. It becomes leakier and displays adhesion molecules (selectins, then integrin ligands) on its luminal surface; leukocytes roll, adhere and squeeze between the endothelial cells into the tissue. The postcapillary venule is the main site.

  • Nitric oxide release is the dilatation function.
  • Tissue plasminogen activator is part of the antithrombotic function.
Slides (2)
L22Learning
When endothelium is damaged or dysfunctional, which way does the balance tip, and what does that set off?
  1. A. Toward dilatation, growth inhibition, antithrombosis and anti-inflammation → aneurysm and haemorrhage
  2. B. Toward constriction, growth inhibition, antithrombosis and proinflammation → vasculitis only
  3. C. Toward constriction, growth promotion, prothrombosis and proinflammation → thrombosis and atherosclerosis
AnswerC. Toward constriction, growth promotion, prothrombosis and proinflammation → thrombosis and atherosclerosis
WhyDamaged endothelium loses its protective side: vessels constrict, smooth muscle grows, blood clots and white cells infiltrate, leading to thrombosis and atherosclerosis.
Explanation

Injury from high blood pressure, high LDL, smoking or hyperglycaemia removes the protective signals (NO, prostacyclin, tPA). The four functions then all tip to the same side:

FunctionHealthyDamaged
ToneDilatationConstriction
GrowthInhibitionPromotion
ClottingAntithrombosisProthrombosis
InflammationAnti-Pro-
  • The second option describes the healthy side, not damage.
  • The third mixes the two sides; damage tips all four the same way.
Slides (2)
L23Learning
Which sequence describes how atherosclerosis develops?
  1. A. Foam cells form in the media → smooth muscle proliferates in the adventitia → the endothelium is injured → partial occlusion
  2. B. Endothelial injury → LDL enters the intima and is oxidised → macrophages engulf it and become foam cells → smooth muscle and collagen form a fibrous plaque → partial occlusion
  3. C. LDL enters the intima → foam cells form → the endothelium is injured → macrophages engulf oxidised LDL → partial occlusion
AnswerB. Endothelial injury → LDL enters the intima and is oxidised → macrophages engulf it and become foam cells → smooth muscle and collagen form a fibrous plaque → partial occlusion
WhyAtherosclerosis starts with endothelial injury; LDL then leaks into the intima, is oxidised and taken up by macrophages (foam cells), and a fibrous plaque grows.
Explanation

Chronic endothelial injury (hypertension, high LDL, smoking, diabetes) makes the endothelium more permeable. LDL enters the subendothelial intima and is oxidised; monocytes follow, become macrophages, and engulf oxidised LDL to become lipid-laden foam cells (a fatty streak). Smooth muscle cells migrate into the intima and lay down collagen, forming the fibrous cap of an atheroma that narrows the lumen.

  • The second sequence puts endothelial injury after LDL entry; injury comes first and lets LDL in.
  • The third places the lesion in the media and adventitia; atheromas are intimal lesions.
Slide (1)
L24Learning
A coronary artery from a patient who died of a heart attack shows an atheroma. In which tunic does it lie, and what does it contain?
  1. A. Intima: extracellular lipid, foam cells (lipid-laden macrophages), smooth muscle cells and collagen
  2. B. Media: extracellular lipid, foam cells (lipid-laden macrophages), smooth muscle cells and collagen
  3. C. Adventitia: acute inflammatory cells around obliterated vasa vasorum
AnswerA. Intima: extracellular lipid, foam cells (lipid-laden macrophages), smooth muscle cells and collagen
WhyAn atheroma is a fibro-fatty plaque in the tunica intima: lipid, foam cells and proliferating smooth muscle under a collagenous fibrous cap.
Explanation

The atheroma grows in the intima, between the endothelium and the internal elastic lamina, which is why it bulges into and narrows the lumen. It contains pools of lipid and cholesterol, foam cells, lymphocytes, and smooth muscle cells that have migrated from the media and secrete the collagen of the fibrous cap.

  • Media is wrong: the media under a large plaque may thin, but the plaque itself is intimal.
  • Adventitial inflammation around obliterated vasa vasorum is syphilitic aortitis, which weakens the media and causes aneurysm, not an atheroma.
Slides (2)

Elastic and muscular arteries

L25Learning
Which vessels are the elastic arteries, and what is their functional name?
  1. A. The aorta and its large branches (and the pulmonary trunk): low-resistance conducting vessels
  2. B. The named arteries of the limbs, such as the femoral and radial: distributing vessels
  3. C. The aorta and its large branches (and the pulmonary trunk): high-resistance resistance vessels
AnswerA. The aorta and its large branches (and the pulmonary trunk): low-resistance conducting vessels
WhyElastic arteries (aorta, its large branches, pulmonary trunk) are conducting vessels, a low-resistance pathway carrying blood away from the heart.
Explanation

The lecture's functional names: elastic arteries = conducting (low-resistance pathway); muscular arteries = distributing; arterioles = resistance; capillaries = exchange. The elastic arteries are the largest arteries, closest to the heart: the aorta, the large arteries leaving its arch (brachiocephalic, common carotid, subclavian), the common iliacs, and the pulmonary trunk and arteries.

  • Resistance vessels are the arterioles; the wide aorta offers little resistance.
  • Femoral and radial arteries are muscular (distributing) arteries.
Slides (2)
L26Learning
What fills the media of an elastic artery?
  1. A. Loose connective tissue with vasa vasorum and few elastic fibres
  2. B. Many concentric layers of smooth muscle with only a little elastic material
  3. C. Many concentric, fenestrated elastic lamellae alternating with layers of smooth muscle
AnswerC. Many concentric, fenestrated elastic lamellae alternating with layers of smooth muscle
WhyThe elastic-artery media is thick and dominated by dozens of concentric fenestrated elastic lamellae, with smooth muscle layers between them.
Explanation

In the adult aorta the media contains dozens (about 50) of elastic lamellae: sheets of elastin with holes (fenestrae) that let nutrients diffuse. Between them lie smooth muscle cells (which secrete the elastin and collagen), collagen and a few fibroblasts. In an elastic stain (Verhoeff or Weigert) the lamellae are dark wavy lines filling the whole media; in H&E they are pink and refractile.

  • Many smooth-muscle layers with little elastic material is the media of a muscular artery.
  • Loose connective tissue with vasa vasorum is the adventitia.
Slides (2)
L27Learning
How does the elastic media of the aorta help the circulation?
  1. A. It contracts rhythmically during diastole, pumping blood forward like a second heart
  2. B. It stretches when the ventricle ejects and recoils during diastole, keeping blood flowing between beats
  3. C. It stays rigid so that the pressure falls to zero during diastole
AnswerB. It stretches when the ventricle ejects and recoils during diastole, keeping blood flowing between beats
WhyThe elastic lamellae stretch in systole (storing energy) and recoil in diastole, turning the heart's pulsatile output into continuous flow.
Explanation

During systole the aorta takes the full force of each ejection; its elastic lamellae stretch and absorb part of the stroke volume. During diastole they recoil, pushing that stored blood onward and keeping arterial pressure up (to about 80 mmHg rather than zero). This damps the pressure swings and keeps flow continuous. Elastic recoil also drives coronary filling in diastole.

  • Rhythmic contraction is wrong: the recoil is passive and elastic, not muscular pumping.
  • Rigid wall, pressure falling to zero is the opposite; a stiff aorta (as in old age) gives a higher systolic and lower diastolic pressure.
Slide (1)
L28Learning
What is the thickest tunic of the aorta, and how does it look in an elastic stain?
  1. A. Adventitia, made of dense collagen with vasa vasorum and few elastic fibres
  2. B. Media, filled with many black, wavy, concentric elastic lamellae
  3. C. Intima, filled with many black, wavy, concentric elastic lamellae
AnswerB. Media, filled with many black, wavy, concentric elastic lamellae
WhyIn the aorta the media forms most of the wall; an elastic stain shows it packed with black wavy elastic lamellae.
Explanation

The aorta's three tunics in an elastic stain: a pale, narrow intima (endothelium and subendothelium); a very thick media crowded with concentric, wavy, black-staining fenestrated elastic membranes; and a relatively thin adventitia of collagen with vasa vasorum.

  • The intima is the thin, lighter strip next to the lumen; it has no stack of lamellae.
  • The adventitia is the thickest layer of the vena cava, not the aorta.
Slide (1)
L29Learning
A tall young man with long fingers and hypermobile joints has a mutation in the fibrillin gene (Marfan syndrome) and develops an aortic aneurysm. Which part of the aortic wall is most affected?
  1. A. Tunica media, with its elastic lamellae
  2. B. Tunica intima, with its endothelium
  3. C. Tunica adventitia, with its collagen and vasa vasorum
AnswerA. Tunica media, with its elastic lamellae
WhyFibrillin is the scaffold for elastic fibres; the aorta's elastic tissue is concentrated in the media, so Marfan syndrome weakens the media → aneurysm and dissection.
Explanation

Fibrillin-1 forms the microfibrils on which elastin is laid down. In Marfan syndrome the elastic fibres are defective (and excess TGF-β activity degrades them further). The structure richest in elastic tissue is the media of elastic arteries, especially the ascending aorta. Its weakened lamellae let the wall bulge (aneurysm) or split within the media (dissection), presenting as tearing chest pain radiating to the back.

  • The intima is the site of atherosclerosis, not of the Marfan defect.
  • The adventitia is mostly collagen; damage to its vasa vasorum is the mechanism of syphilitic aneurysm.
Slide (1)
L30LearningBorderline
In tertiary syphilis, inflammation obliterates the vasa vasorum of the ascending aorta. What is the result?
  1. A. The media thickens with extra smooth muscle → systemic hypertension
  2. B. Ischaemic damage to the outer media weakens the wall → aortic aneurysm
  3. C. Lipid builds up in the intima → atheroma that occludes the aortic lumen
AnswerB. Ischaemic damage to the outer media weakens the wall → aortic aneurysm
WhyWithout its vasa vasorum the outer media of the aorta becomes ischaemic and loses its elastic tissue, so the wall weakens and balloons into an aneurysm.
Explanation

The vasa vasorum feed the adventitia and outer media of the aorta. In syphilitic aortitis an obliterative endarteritis of these small vessels starves the outer media; patches of smooth muscle and elastic lamellae die and are replaced by scar. The weakened wall stretches under arterial pressure, typically forming an aneurysm of the ascending aorta. This shows why thick walls need their own blood supply.

  • Intimal lipid and atheroma is atherosclerosis, which begins with endothelial injury.
  • Medial thickening and hypertension is the wrong direction: loss of the vasa vasorum destroys media; it does not add muscle.
L31Learning
What is the functional name of muscular arteries, and what do they do?
  1. A. Conducting vessels: carry the full output of the heart away from it at low resistance
  2. B. Distributing vessels: deliver blood to individual organs and adjust how much each receives
  3. C. Exchange vessels: let nutrients and gases pass between blood and the tissues
AnswerB. Distributing vessels: deliver blood to individual organs and adjust how much each receives
WhyMuscular (medium) arteries are distributing vessels: they carry blood to individual organs and, by contracting or relaxing, adjust flow and help regulate blood pressure.
Explanation

Most named arteries (radial, femoral, coronary, renal, splenic) are muscular arteries. The lecture says they are distributing vessels that respond to stimulus and regulate blood pressure: sympathetic nerves and local signals change the tone of their thick smooth-muscle media.

  • Conducting vessels are the elastic arteries (aorta, pulmonary trunk).
  • Exchange vessels are the capillaries.
Slide (1)
L32Learning
What makes up the media of a muscular artery, and why?
  1. A. Many fenestrated elastic lamellae with little smooth muscle, to recoil in diastole
  2. B. One to three layers of smooth muscle only, to set resistance just before the capillaries
  3. C. Many layers of smooth muscle with little elastic material, to change diameter and direct flow
AnswerC. Many layers of smooth muscle with little elastic material, to change diameter and direct flow
WhyThe media of a muscular artery is many layers of smooth muscle (less elastic material), so it can constrict or dilate to distribute blood to organs.
Explanation

Moving away from the heart, arteries gradually lose elastin and gain smooth muscle. A muscular artery's media is several to about 40 layers of circular smooth muscle cells, with a few elastic fibres between them, and is bounded by a prominent internal and a thinner external elastic lamina. Contraction of this muscle lets the vessel regulate flow to its organ.

  • Many elastic lamellae with little muscle is the elastic artery.
  • One to three smooth-muscle layers is an arteriole.
Slide (1)
L33Learning
What is the most distinctive feature of a muscular artery on a slide?
  1. A. A prominent external elastic lamina: one crisp wavy line at the outer edge of the adventitia
  2. B. Many wavy elastic lamellae running through the whole thickness of the media
  3. C. A prominent internal elastic lamina: one crisp wavy line at the inner edge of the media
AnswerC. A prominent internal elastic lamina: one crisp wavy line at the inner edge of the media
WhyA prominent internal elastic lamina, seen as a single sharp wavy line between intima and media, is the hallmark of a muscular artery.
Explanation

The lecture lists "prominent internal elastic lamina" in the intima of muscular arteries; the lab notes it is visible even in H&E. Behind it lies a thick media of smooth muscle. Smooth muscle alone is not distinctive (every artery has some), and vasa vasorum are only sometimes present.

  • The external elastic lamina lies at the outer edge of the media (not the adventitia) and is thinner and less obvious.
  • Many lamellae through the whole media identifies an elastic artery.
Slides (2)
L34Learning
On a slide, how do you tell an elastic artery from a muscular artery?
  1. A. Elastic: wavy elastic lamellae through the whole media
    Muscular: one crisp wavy line at the inner border, smooth muscle behind it
  2. B. Elastic: one crisp wavy line at the inner border, smooth muscle behind it
    Muscular: wavy elastic lamellae through the whole media
  3. C. Elastic: wavy elastic lamellae through the whole media
    Muscular: no elastic lamina at all, smooth muscle only
AnswerA. Elastic: wavy elastic lamellae through the whole media
Muscular: one crisp wavy line at the inner border, smooth muscle behind it
WhyLook at the media: lamellae everywhere → elastic artery; one internal elastic lamina with smooth muscle behind it → muscular artery.
Explanation

Both have three tunics and a thick media; what differs is what the media is made of, and it follows from the job. The elastic artery must recoil, so its media is a stack of elastic lamellae (it looks like a patch of curly ramen). The muscular artery must change diameter, so its media is smooth muscle, bordered by a prominent internal elastic lamina.

  • The swapped option reverses the two.
  • No elastic lamina at all is wrong for a muscular artery; its internal elastic lamina is its best clue (arterioles may lack one).
Slides (3)

Arterioles and the microcirculation

L35Learning
What is the functional name of arterioles?
  1. A. Resistance vessels
  2. B. Exchange vessels
  3. C. Capacitance vessels
AnswerA. Resistance vessels
WhyArterioles are resistance vessels, the primary site of vascular resistance in the circulation.
Explanation

The lecture calls arterioles "resistance vessels, the primary site of vascular resistance". The largest drop in blood pressure occurs across them, and the tone of their smooth muscle sets both systemic vascular resistance and how much blood enters each capillary bed.

  • Exchange vessels are the capillaries.
  • Capacitance vessels are the veins, which hold most of the blood volume at low pressure.
Slide (1)
L36Learning
What does the wall of an arteriole consist of?
  1. A. Intima of endothelium only; media of 1–3 layers of smooth muscle; very thin adventitia
  2. B. Intima of endothelium only; no smooth muscle, just scattered pericytes; no adventitia
  3. C. Intima with a prominent internal elastic lamina; media of many smooth-muscle layers; thick adventitia
AnswerA. Intima of endothelium only; media of 1–3 layers of smooth muscle; very thin adventitia
WhyArteriole: endothelium with no subendothelial connective tissue or muscle, a media of 1–3 smooth-muscle layers, and a very thin adventitia.
Explanation

The lecture's arteriole: intima endothelium, no connective tissue or smooth muscle; media 1–3 layers of smooth muscle; adventitia very thin connective tissue. On a slide its lumen is narrow, roughly as wide as its wall is thick, and an internal elastic lamina is usually absent (at most a thin one in the largest arterioles). A small artery has more muscle layers.

  • No smooth muscle, scattered pericytes describes a capillary or postcapillary venule.
  • Prominent internal elastic lamina and many muscle layers describes a muscular artery.
Slide (1)
L37LearningBorderline
Arterioles have only one to three layers of smooth muscle. Why can they still control flow through the whole circulation?
  1. A. Resistance varies in direct proportion to the radius, so arterioles must change diameter a lot
  2. B. Resistance depends mainly on blood viscosity, which the arteriolar wall regulates
  3. C. Resistance varies with the fourth power of the radius, so small changes in diameter change resistance greatly
AnswerC. Resistance varies with the fourth power of the radius, so small changes in diameter change resistance greatly
WhyBy Poiseuille's law resistance ∝ 1/r4: halving an arteriole's radius raises its resistance about 16-fold.
Explanation

Arterioles are numerous, narrow and sit just upstream of the capillary beds. Because resistance rises with the inverse fourth power of the radius, a small contraction of their thin muscle coat changes resistance, and therefore flow, a great deal. That is why they are the main site of vascular resistance and the main way blood is redistributed between organs.

  • Direct proportion to radius understates the effect and gets the direction wrong: a wider vessel has less resistance.
  • Viscosity depends mainly on haematocrit; the vessel wall does not regulate it.
L38Learning
During a football game, which part of the circulation does most to direct extra blood into the capillaries of the players' skeletal muscles?
  1. A. The aorta
  2. B. Arterioles
  3. C. Medium (muscular) arteries
AnswerB. Arterioles
WhyRelaxation of the smooth muscle of arterioles in active muscle lowers their resistance and lets more blood into those capillary beds.
Explanation

The tone of arteriolar smooth muscle resists blood flow, helps set systemic blood pressure and controls flow into the capillaries. In exercising muscle, local metabolites relax these arterioles, so the muscle's share of cardiac output rises while arterioles elsewhere (gut, kidney) constrict.

  • The aorta is a low-resistance conducting vessel; it cannot steer blood to one organ.
  • Muscular arteries distribute blood to whole organs and adjust somewhat, but the fine control of flow into capillary beds is at the arterioles, the main site of resistance.
Slide (1)
L39LearningBorderline
In long-standing hypertension, what happens to small arteries and arterioles?
  1. A. Their elastic lamellae fragment and the vessels balloon into aneurysms → resistance is unchanged
  2. B. Their walls thin and their lumens widen → peripheral resistance falls
  3. C. Their walls thicken (more smooth muscle, thicker intima) and their lumens narrow → peripheral resistance rises further
AnswerC. Their walls thicken (more smooth muscle, thicker intima) and their lumens narrow → peripheral resistance rises further
WhyChronic high pressure makes small arteries and arterioles thicken their walls and narrow their lumens, which raises peripheral resistance and sustains the hypertension.
Explanation

The common end point of all forms of primary hypertension is increased peripheral vascular resistance, set by small arteries and arterioles. Under chronic high pressure their smooth muscle hypertrophies and multiplies and the intima thickens, so the wall gets thicker and the lumen smaller, and resistance rises further.

  • Thinner walls and wider lumens would lower resistance and blood pressure, the opposite.
  • Fragmented elastic lamellae and aneurysm is a lesion of large elastic arteries (Marfan, dissection), not of arterioles.
L40Learning
What is the usual (simple) pathway through a capillary bed?
  1. A. Venule → capillaries → arteriole
  2. B. Arteriole → venule → capillaries
  3. C. Arteriole → capillaries → venule
AnswerC. Arteriole → capillaries → venule
WhyIn the simple pathway an arteriole feeds a capillary bed, which drains into a venule.
Explanation

The lecture's microvasculature diagram shows three arrangements: the simple pathway (artery → arteriole → capillary bed → venule → vein), the arteriovenous shunt (arteriole joined directly to venule, bypassing capillaries), and the portal system (two capillary beds in series joined by a portal vein).

  • Venule → capillaries → arteriole runs backwards; blood flows from the arterial to the venous side.
  • Arteriole → venule → capillaries puts the capillaries after the venule.
Slides (2)
L41Learning
What vessel often feeds the true capillaries of a bed, and what guards the capillary openings?
  1. A. A muscular artery, with a continuous media forming a precapillary sphincter
  2. B. A thoroughfare channel, with elastic lamellae forming precapillary valves
  3. C. A metarteriole, with scattered smooth muscle cells forming precapillary sphincters
AnswerC. A metarteriole, with scattered smooth muscle cells forming precapillary sphincters
WhyA metarteriole has a discontinuous coat of smooth muscle; rings of smooth muscle where true capillaries branch off are the precapillary sphincters.
Explanation

Capillaries arise either directly from arterioles or from metarterioles, short vessels with scattered smooth muscle cells. Each true capillary leaving a metarteriole is guarded by a small ring of smooth muscle, the precapillary sphincter, which controls whether blood enters it. The metarteriole continues as a thoroughfare channel that drains into a postcapillary venule.

  • The thoroughfare channel is the distal, muscle-free continuation of the metarteriole; there are no elastic valves.
  • A muscular artery is far larger and never feeds capillaries directly.
Slides (2)
L42Learning
What happens in a capillary bed when the precapillary sphincters relax?
  1. A. Blood spreads through the true capillaries → the bed is well perfused
  2. B. Blood stops flowing through the metarteriole → the bed becomes ischaemic
  3. C. Blood is routed through the thoroughfare channel → the bed is bypassed
AnswerA. Blood spreads through the true capillaries → the bed is well perfused
WhyRelaxed precapillary sphincters open the true capillaries, so blood flows through the whole bed: the bed is well perfused.
Explanation

Precapillary sphincters work like switches at the entrance of each true capillary. When tissue activity rises (more CO2, H+, adenosine, less O2), they relax and blood spreads through the network for exchange.

  • No flow through the metarteriole is wrong: the metarteriole stays open whatever the sphincters do.
  • Routing through the thoroughfare channel is what happens when the sphincters contract.
Slide (1)
L43Learning
What happens when the precapillary sphincters contract?
  1. A. Blood bypasses the bed through the thoroughfare channel, straight into the postcapillary venule
  2. B. Blood spreads through all the true capillaries, so the bed is well perfused
  3. C. Blood is diverted into a portal vein that feeds a second capillary bed
AnswerA. Blood bypasses the bed through the thoroughfare channel, straight into the postcapillary venule
WhyContracted sphincters close the true capillaries; blood runs from the metarteriole through the thoroughfare channel into the postcapillary venule, bypassing the bed.
Explanation

With the sphincters shut, only the central metarteriole-to-thoroughfare-channel route stays open, so most of the bed receives little flow. This lets a resting tissue limit its perfusion while blood still passes on to the venous side.

  • Spreading through all capillaries is the relaxed state.
  • Diversion into a portal vein describes a portal system, a fixed anatomical arrangement, not a sphincter response.
Slide (1)
L44Learning
What is an arteriovenous shunt, and where is it used?
  1. A. A link from an arteriole into a lymphatic vessel that skips the venules; used in the gut to absorb fat
  2. B. A direct link from the arterial to the venous side that skips the capillaries; used in the liver to filter gut blood
  3. C. A direct link from the arterial to the venous side that skips the capillaries; used in the skin to regulate heat loss
AnswerC. A direct link from the arterial to the venous side that skips the capillaries; used in the skin to regulate heat loss
WhyAn arteriovenous shunt (anastomosis) joins an arteriole directly to a venule; in the skin it controls blood flow for temperature regulation.
Explanation

Arteriovenous shunts are muscular channels connecting arterioles straight to venules. When they open, blood bypasses the capillary bed; when they constrict, blood is forced through the capillaries. They are common in the skin of the fingertips, nose and ears, where coiled shunts wrapped in a capsule form glomus bodies, and they help the body conserve or shed heat.

  • The liver receives gut blood through a portal system, two capillary beds in series, not a shunt.
  • Fat absorption in the gut goes into lacteals; no arteriole drains into a lymphatic.
Slide (1)
L45Learning
What is a portal system, and where is one found?
  1. A. Two capillary beds in series joined by a portal vein: the liver, the anterior pituitary
  2. B. Two capillary beds in series joined by a portal vein: the spleen, the posterior pituitary
  3. C. Two capillary beds in parallel fed by the same arteriole: the lung, the skin
AnswerA. Two capillary beds in series joined by a portal vein: the liver, the anterior pituitary
WhyA portal system carries blood from one capillary bed through a portal vein to a second capillary bed: hepatic portal (gut → liver) and hypophyseal portal (hypothalamus → anterior pituitary).
Explanation

Normally blood passes through one capillary bed between artery and vein. In a portal system the pathway is artery → capillary bed → portal vein → second capillary bed → vein. The hepatic portal vein carries absorbed nutrients from the intestine to the liver sinusoids; the hypophyseal portal veins carry hypothalamic releasing hormones to the anterior pituitary.

  • The spleen and posterior pituitary are not portal systems (the posterior pituitary is supplied directly by the inferior hypophyseal arteries).
  • Parallel beds fed by one arteriole are just an ordinary capillary network; "portal" means beds in series.
Slide (1)

Capillaries and pericytes

L46Learning
What is the functional name of capillaries?
  1. A. Conducting vessels
  2. B. Exchange vessels
  3. C. Resistance vessels
AnswerB. Exchange vessels
WhyCapillaries are exchange vessels: gases, nutrients and wastes pass between blood and tissue across their thin wall.
Explanation

The capillary wall is a single thin endothelial cell, the shortest possible diffusion distance, and capillaries have the largest total cross-sectional area and the slowest flow of any vessel, giving time for exchange.

  • Conducting vessels are the elastic arteries.
  • Resistance vessels are the arterioles.
Slide (1)
L47Learning
What does a capillary wall consist of?
  1. A. Endothelium + basal lamina + scattered pericytes; no media and no adventitia
  2. B. Endothelium + basal lamina + a thin smooth-muscle media; no adventitia
  3. C. Endothelium + internal elastic lamina + scattered pericytes; thin adventitia
AnswerA. Endothelium + basal lamina + scattered pericytes; no media and no adventitia
WhyThe lecture: capillary intima = endothelium only, media = "none" (pericytes), adventitia = none.
Explanation

A capillary is a tube of one to three endothelial cells rolled around a lumen just wide enough for a red cell (about 5–10 µm). The endothelium rests on a basal lamina, and here and there a pericyte wraps around it. There is no smooth-muscle layer and no connective-tissue coat.

  • A thin smooth-muscle media first appears in arterioles (and muscular venules).
  • An internal elastic lamina belongs to arteries; capillaries have none.
Slides (2)
L48Learning
Why is a capillary wall only one thin cell thick?
  1. A. A thin wall withstands higher pressure than a thick one
  2. B. A thicker wall would lengthen the diffusion distance and slow exchange
  3. C. A thin wall stops red blood cells leaking out of the vessel
AnswerB. A thicker wall would lengthen the diffusion distance and slow exchange
WhyExchange is by diffusion, which is fast only over very short distances, so the wall is reduced to a single thin endothelial cell.
Explanation

Structure follows function: capillaries exist for exchange, and the rate of diffusion falls steeply with distance. A single attenuated endothelial cell (often less than 1 µm thick away from the nucleus) on a basal lamina keeps the barrier as thin as possible.

  • Withstanding higher pressure needs a thicker wall (law of Laplace); capillaries cope only because their radius is tiny.
  • Keeping red cells in depends on the endothelium being continuous, not on how thin it is; sinusoids are thin and do let cells through.
L49Learning
What are pericytes, and which vessels do they wrap?
  1. A. Small cells whose long processes wrap the endothelium of capillaries and postcapillary venules
  2. B. Smooth muscle cells forming a continuous circular coat around capillaries
  3. C. Small cells whose long processes wrap the endothelium of arterioles and muscular arteries
AnswerA. Small cells whose long processes wrap the endothelium of capillaries and postcapillary venules
WhyPericytes are small cells with branching processes that surround the endothelium of capillaries and postcapillary venules.
Explanation

The lecture defines pericytes as small cells that surround the endothelial cells; they are the capillary's only cells outside the endothelium ("media: none, pericytes"). On a slide their nucleus sits on the outside of the endothelium, and scanning micrographs show their processes clasping the capillary. Postcapillary venules have them too ("intima: endothelium, pericytes").

  • A continuous smooth-muscle coat is a media, which capillaries lack; pericytes are scattered.
  • Arterioles and muscular arteries have a true smooth-muscle media instead.
Slides (3)
L50Learning
What basal lamina surrounds a pericyte?
  1. A. None: pericytes sit bare on the endothelial cells
  2. B. Its own basal lamina, which may fuse with that of the endothelial cell
  3. C. The internal elastic lamina of the vessel
AnswerB. Its own basal lamina, which may fuse with that of the endothelial cell
WhyA pericyte is enclosed in its own basal lamina, which can fuse with the endothelial basal lamina, so it lies within the capillary's basement membrane.
Explanation

In a transmission electron micrograph of a capillary (labels E, P, L, BL) the pericyte's processes lie against the outer surface of the endothelium, and both cells are wrapped in basal lamina. The pericyte has its own basal lamina, which often merges with the endothelial one, so the pericyte appears enclosed within it.

  • Bare is wrong: the basal lamina is always present around both cells.
  • The internal elastic lamina is an arterial structure; capillaries have none.
Slides (2)
L51Learning
What do pericytes contain, and what does that let them do?
  1. A. Fenestrae, which let large molecules pass out of the capillary
  2. B. Contractile proteins (actin and myosin), which let them help regulate capillary flow
  3. C. Phagocytic lysosomes, which let them engulf bacteria in the vessel wall
AnswerB. Contractile proteins (actin and myosin), which let them help regulate capillary flow
WhyPericytes contain actin, myosin and tropomyosin, so they are contractile and help control capillary blood flow.
Explanation

Pericytes have contractile proteins like smooth muscle cells. By contracting they can narrow a capillary, which is why the lecture lists them where the media would be. They also stabilise the capillary wall; their loss in diabetes contributes to retinal microaneurysms.

  • Fenestrae are pores in the endothelial cells of fenestrated capillaries.
  • Phagocytosis is the job of macrophages (such as the macrophages lining liver sinusoids), not pericytes.
Slide (1)
L52LearningBorderline
Besides being contractile, what is special about pericytes?
  1. A. They are adult (mesenchymal) stem cells that can form new smooth muscle cells and fibroblasts after injury
  2. B. They are terminally differentiated cells that can never divide or change type
  3. C. They are resident macrophages derived from blood monocytes
AnswerA. They are adult (mesenchymal) stem cells that can form new smooth muscle cells and fibroblasts after injury
WhyPericytes act as adult stem cells: after vessel injury they can divide and differentiate into smooth muscle cells and fibroblasts, helping repair.
Explanation

Pericytes are mesenchymal cells that keep stem-cell potential. When a vessel is injured or new vessels form, they proliferate and become smooth muscle cells of the new vessel wall or fibroblasts, so they take part in vessel repair and in building the media of new venules and arterioles. On a micrograph, the cell hugging the outside of a capillary is the pericyte, an adult stem cell.

  • Terminally differentiated is the opposite of what textbooks describe.
  • Macrophages come from monocytes and are phagocytic; pericytes are not.
L53Learning
In an H&E section of a capillary, two flattened nuclei lie at its wall. How do you tell the pericyte nucleus from the endothelial nucleus?
  1. A. The pericyte nucleus forms the lining and bulges into the lumen; the endothelial nucleus lies outside it, wrapped around the outer surface
  2. B. The pericyte nucleus is surrounded by a wavy internal elastic lamina; the endothelial nucleus is not
  3. C. The endothelial nucleus forms the lining and bulges into the lumen; the pericyte nucleus lies outside it, wrapped around the outer surface
AnswerC. The endothelial nucleus forms the lining and bulges into the lumen; the pericyte nucleus lies outside it, wrapped around the outer surface
WhyThe endothelial cell lines the lumen, so its nucleus bulges into the lumen; the pericyte sits outside the endothelium, so its nucleus lies further out.
Explanation

Position gives it away. Endothelial cells form the tube itself, and their nuclei protrude into the lumen. Pericytes hug the outside of the tube, so their nuclei sit outward, on the far side of the endothelium, inside the basal lamina. In the classic transmission micrograph the endothelial cell (E) faces the lumen (L) and the pericyte (P) lies outside it, with basal lamina (BL) around both.

  • The swapped option reverses inner and outer.
  • Capillaries have no internal elastic lamina.
Slides (2)

The three types of capillary

L54Learning
How are the three capillary types (continuous, fenestrated, sinusoidal) told apart?
  1. A. In the electron microscope, by the number of pericytes around each capillary
  2. B. In the electron microscope, by how continuous the endothelium and basement membrane are
  3. C. In the light microscope, by the thickness of their smooth-muscle layer
