AnswerB. In the electron microscope, by how continuous the endothelium and basement membrane are
WhyCapillaries all look alike in the light microscope; the types differ in the continuity of the endothelium and basement membrane, seen by electron microscopy.
Explanation

The lab manual notes that capillaries in all tissues look very similar in the light microscope but differ markedly in the electron microscope. The types are defined by whether the endothelium has pores (fenestrae) or gaps, and whether the basement membrane is continuous. Each type occurs where its leakiness suits the organ.

  • Capillaries have no smooth-muscle layer, so it cannot be used.
  • Pericyte number varies but does not define the type.
Slides (2)
L55Learning
Describe the wall of a continuous capillary.
  1. A. Unbroken endothelium sealed by tight junctions, with marginal folds and many pinocytotic vesicles; continuous basement membrane
  2. B. Unbroken endothelium sealed by tight junctions, with few vesicles; discontinuous basement membrane
  3. C. Endothelium pierced by pores closed by thin diaphragms; continuous basement membrane
AnswerA. Unbroken endothelium sealed by tight junctions, with marginal folds and many pinocytotic vesicles; continuous basement membrane
WhyA continuous capillary has an uninterrupted endothelium (tight junctions, marginal folds, pinocytotic vesicles or caveolae) on a continuous basement membrane.
Explanation

The lecture: most common type; uninterrupted endothelium; continuous basement membrane. The lab table adds tight junctions with adjacent cells plus marginal folds (flaps of cytoplasm projecting into the lumen at the cell junctions), no fenestrae, and the smallest diameter. Substances cross by diffusion, through intercellular clefts or in pinocytotic vesicles (caveolae) that shuttle across the cell.

  • Pores closed by diaphragms define the fenestrated capillary.
  • A discontinuous basement membrane belongs to sinusoids only.
Slides (2)
L56Learning
Where are continuous capillaries found?
  1. A. Muscle, brain, connective tissue, lung, thymus
  2. B. Endocrine glands, pancreas, intestinal villi
  3. C. Bone marrow, liver, spleen, lymph nodes
AnswerA. Muscle, brain, connective tissue, lung, thymus
WhyContinuous capillaries are the most common type: muscle, brain, connective tissue, lung (and thymus), where exchange must be selective.
Explanation

The lab table lists muscle, brain, connective tissue and lung; the lab manual adds striated muscle, thymus and loose connective tissue. Their tight, unbroken lining restricts what crosses, which suits the brain (blood–brain barrier) and the thymus (blood–thymus barrier).

  • Endocrine glands, pancreas, intestinal villi are the fenestrated sites (fast exchange of hormones and absorbed nutrients).
  • Bone marrow, liver, spleen, lymph nodes are the sinusoid sites, where cells and large proteins must cross.
Slides (2)
L57Learning
Alcohol, nicotine and caffeine cross the blood–brain barrier. Which capillary type forms that barrier, and what feature makes it tight?
  1. A. Continuous capillaries: an unbroken endothelium sealed by tight junctions, with no pores or gaps
  2. B. Sinusoidal capillaries: gaps between cells that are sealed by pericytes
  3. C. Fenestrated capillaries: pores closed by diaphragms that only small molecules can pass
AnswerA. Continuous capillaries: an unbroken endothelium sealed by tight junctions, with no pores or gaps
WhyBrain capillaries are continuous: tight junctions and no pores or gaps, so only lipid-soluble molecules or those with carriers get through.
Explanation

Continuous capillaries give the tightest control of exchange of the three types, so they form barriers such as the blood–brain barrier. Lipid-soluble molecules like alcohol, nicotine and caffeine cross by dissolving through the endothelial membranes; most other solutes need specific transporters. Pericytes and astrocyte end-feet support the barrier.

  • Fenestrated capillaries are leaky by design (endocrine glands, gut, kidney); a barrier cannot be built from pores.
  • Sinusoids are the leakiest type, with gaps and a broken basement membrane.
Slide (1)
L58Learning
Describe the wall of a fenestrated capillary.
  1. A. Endothelial cells separated by large gaps as well as pores; discontinuous basement membrane
  2. B. Endothelial cells joined by tight junctions, thick cytoplasm full of caveolae, no pores; continuous basement membrane
  3. C. Endothelial cells joined by tight junctions, their thin cytoplasm pierced by pores (fenestrae), many closed by a thin diaphragm; continuous basement membrane
AnswerC. Endothelial cells joined by tight junctions, their thin cytoplasm pierced by pores (fenestrae), many closed by a thin diaphragm; continuous basement membrane
WhyA fenestrated capillary has numerous pores in its thin endothelial cells, often bridged by a diaphragm, but its basement membrane stays continuous.
Explanation

The lecture: numerous openings in the capillary wall; continuous basement membrane. The fenestrae (about 60–80 nm) pass through the thinned cytoplasm itself, not between cells; the cells are still joined by tight junctions (with marginal folds). Many pores are spanned by a thin diaphragm; on an electron micrograph the diaphragm-covered pores sit above an intact basal lamina.

  • Gaps plus pores with a discontinuous basement membrane is the sinusoid.
  • No pores, many caveolae is the continuous capillary.
Slides (2)
L59Learning
Where are fenestrated capillaries found, and why there?
  1. A. Bone marrow, liver, spleen: passage of whole cells and large proteins
  2. B. Endocrine glands, pancreas, intestinal villi (and the kidney glomerulus): rapid exchange of small molecules such as hormones and absorbed nutrients
  3. C. Muscle, brain, lung: tight control so that only selected small solutes cross
AnswerB. Endocrine glands, pancreas, intestinal villi (and the kidney glomerulus): rapid exchange of small molecules such as hormones and absorbed nutrients
WhyFenestrated capillaries are found in endocrine glands, the pancreas and intestinal villi (and the renal glomerulus), where molecules must move quickly between blood and tissue.
Explanation

The lab table gives endocrine glands, pancreas and intestinal villi. In these organs hormones must enter the blood quickly, or absorbed nutrients and filtered fluid must cross in bulk; the pores make this fast while the intact basement membrane still holds back cells and most large proteins. The renal glomerulus is a special fenestrated capillary whose pores lack diaphragms.

  • Muscle, brain, lung have continuous capillaries.
  • Bone marrow, liver, spleen have sinusoids.
Slide (1)
L60Learning
Describe the wall of a sinusoidal (discontinuous) capillary.
  1. A. Gaps between endothelial cells but a continuous basement membrane; narrow, round lumen
  2. B. Pores closed by diaphragms in otherwise unbroken cells; continuous basement membrane; narrow lumen
  3. C. Large openings and gaps between endothelial cells; discontinuous basement membrane; wide, irregular lumen
AnswerC. Large openings and gaps between endothelial cells; discontinuous basement membrane; wide, irregular lumen
WhyA sinusoid has intercellular gaps and large openings, a discontinuous basement membrane and a wide, irregular lumen.
Explanation

The lecture: sinusoidal capillaries or sinusoids; larger diameter and larger openings; intercellular gaps; discontinuous basement membrane. The lab table gives "discontinuous endothelium", fenestrae "present + gaps" and the largest diameter. The lining may include macrophages (as in the liver).

  • Diaphragm-covered pores with a continuous basement membrane is the fenestrated capillary.
  • Gaps with a continuous basement membrane mixes features; in sinusoids both layers are broken.
Slides (2)
L61Learning
Where are sinusoidal capillaries found?
  1. A. Muscle, brain, connective tissue, lung, thymus
  2. B. Endocrine glands, pancreas, intestinal villi, kidney glomerulus
  3. C. Bone marrow, liver, spleen, lymph nodes, some endocrine glands
AnswerC. Bone marrow, liver, spleen, lymph nodes, some endocrine glands
WhySinusoids occur where cells and large molecules must cross: bone marrow, liver, spleen (the lab table adds lymph nodes and certain endocrine glands).
Explanation

New blood cells leave the marrow through sinusoids; plasma proteins made by hepatocytes enter the blood through liver sinusoids; old red cells squeeze through the splenic sinusoids. The lab table lists bone marrow, spleen, liver, lymph nodes and certain endocrine glands; most textbooks name only marrow, liver, spleen and some endocrine organs.

  • Muscle, brain, connective tissue, lung, thymus have continuous capillaries.
  • Endocrine glands, pancreas, villi, glomerulus are the fenestrated list (only some endocrine glands have sinusoids).
Slide (1)
L62Learning
What can cross a sinusoid wall, and what is the classic example?
  1. A. Large molecules but not cells: albumin leaves the bone marrow this way
  2. B. Large molecules and whole cells: newly formed blood cells leave the bone marrow this way
  3. C. Only water and small solutes: oxygen reaches the neurons this way
AnswerB. Large molecules and whole cells: newly formed blood cells leave the bone marrow this way
WhyWith gaps in both endothelium and basement membrane, sinusoids allow maximal molecular exchange and the movement of blood cells; new blood cells enter the circulation through bone-marrow sinusoids.
Explanation

The lecture's bone-marrow slide: sinusoids have a greater diameter than most capillaries and allow maximal molecular exchange and movement of blood cells across the endothelium. That is exactly what the marrow needs: newly made red cells, white cells and platelets must enter the blood.

  • Molecules but not cells understates sinusoids; it fits a fenestrated capillary better (albumin is made in the liver, not the marrow).
  • Only water and small solutes is the continuous capillary of the brain.
Slide (1)
L63Learning
In the liver, into what do the pores of the sinusoid endothelium cluster?
  1. A. Sieve plates
  2. B. Caveolae
  3. C. Marginal folds
AnswerA. Sieve plates
WhyScanning electron micrographs of liver sinusoids show the endothelial fenestrations grouped in clusters called sieve plates.
Explanation

The lab's scanning micrograph shows the lumen of a hepatic sinusoid with the endothelial coat perforated by fenestrations arranged in clusters, the sieve plates. They let plasma pass freely into the space between the endothelium and the hepatocytes.

  • Marginal folds are flaps of cytoplasm at the junctions of continuous and fenestrated capillary cells.
  • Caveolae are the small membrane vesicles of continuous capillaries.
Slide (1)
L64Learning
How do the three capillary types rank by diameter?
  1. A. Fenestrated smallest < continuous intermediate < sinusoidal largest
  2. B. Sinusoidal smallest < fenestrated intermediate < continuous largest
  3. C. Continuous smallest < fenestrated intermediate < sinusoidal largest
AnswerC. Continuous smallest < fenestrated intermediate < sinusoidal largest
WhyThe lab table: continuous = smallest, fenestrated = intermediate, sinusoidal = largest; diameter rises with leakiness.
Explanation

Continuous capillaries are just wide enough for a red cell to pass. Fenestrated capillaries are somewhat wider. Sinusoids are the widest, with large irregular lumens (up to about 30–40 µm) that slow the blood and allow cells to cross.

  • The second option swaps continuous and fenestrated.
  • The third reverses the whole order; the lecture stresses that sinusoids have a larger diameter than most capillaries.
Slide (1)
L65Learning
On an electron micrograph, how do you name the capillary type from its wall?
  1. A. Unbroken cytoplasm + tight junctions → fenestrated
    Thin cytoplasm with pores, intact basement membrane → continuous
    Gaps between cells, broken basement membrane, wide lumen → sinusoid
  2. B. Unbroken cytoplasm + tight junctions → continuous
    Gaps between cells, broken basement membrane, wide lumen → fenestrated
    Thin cytoplasm with pores, intact basement membrane → sinusoid
  3. C. Unbroken cytoplasm + tight junctions → continuous
    Thin cytoplasm with pores, intact basement membrane → fenestrated
    Gaps between cells, broken basement membrane, wide lumen → sinusoid
AnswerC. Unbroken cytoplasm + tight junctions → continuous
Thin cytoplasm with pores, intact basement membrane → fenestrated
Gaps between cells, broken basement membrane, wide lumen → sinusoid
WhyAsk two questions: are there pores? (no → continuous) and is the basement membrane broken? (yes → sinusoid; no → fenestrated).
Explanation
TypeEndotheliumBasement membraneWhere
ContinuousUnbroken; tight junctions, marginal folds, caveolaeContinuousMuscle, brain, connective tissue, lung
FenestratedPores (often with diaphragm); tight junctionsContinuousEndocrine glands, pancreas, villi
SinusoidalPores + gaps between cellsDiscontinuousMarrow, liver, spleen

The two wrong options each swap a pair of definitions.

Slide (1)
L66Learning
In a transmission electron micrograph of a continuous capillary, small flap-like projections of endothelial cytoplasm jut into the lumen where neighbouring endothelial cells meet. What are they?
  1. A. Fenestrae with diaphragms
  2. B. Marginal folds
  3. C. Pericyte processes
AnswerB. Marginal folds
WhyMarginal folds are small flaps of endothelial cytoplasm that project into the lumen at the junctions between cells (labelled M in the lab micrographs).
Explanation

The lab table lists "tight junction with adjacent cells + marginal fold" as the endothelial feature of continuous (and fenestrated) capillaries, and the lab micrographs label the folds M at the cell borders. They mark where two endothelial cells overlap and are sealed by tight junctions.

  • Fenestrae are holes through the thin cytoplasm, not flaps; continuous capillaries have none.
  • Pericyte processes lie on the outside of the endothelium, within the basal lamina, never in the lumen.
Slide (1)
L67Learning
An electron micrograph shows a capillary whose lumen is enclosed by thin endothelial cells forming an unbroken ring, joined by tight junctions, with many small vesicles along both surfaces and no pores; a basal lamina surrounds it without interruption. Which type is it, and where might it come from?
  1. A. Fenestrated capillary, as in the pancreas or intestine
  2. B. Sinusoidal capillary, as in the liver or bone marrow
  3. C. Continuous capillary, as in muscle or brain
AnswerC. Continuous capillary, as in muscle or brain
WhyNo pores, tight junctions, pinocytotic vesicles and an unbroken basal lamina define a continuous capillary (muscle, brain, lung, connective tissue).
Explanation

The lab micrographs of continuous capillaries show exactly these features: smooth, unbroken endothelium with junctional complexes (JC), caveolae and vesicles (C, V), and a continuous basal lamina (BL), sometimes with a pericyte (P) outside it. Tip: no "bubbles" of pores along the basal lamina means continuous.

  • A fenestrated capillary would show many small pores, often spanned by diaphragms.
  • A sinusoid would show gaps between cells, a broken basal lamina and a wide, irregular lumen.
Slides (2)
L68Learning
An electron micrograph shows a capillary whose very thin endothelium is perforated at many points by tiny pores, each bridged by a thin diaphragm, while the underlying basal lamina is continuous. In which organ would you expect it?
  1. A. Brain
  2. B. Pancreatic islet
  3. C. Liver
AnswerB. Pancreatic islet
WhyPores with diaphragms over a continuous basal lamina = fenestrated capillary, found in endocrine glands, the pancreas and intestinal villi.
Explanation

The arrows on the lab's fenestrated-capillary micrograph point to the fenestrae: thin regions of endothelial cytoplasm crossed by pores, many closed by a diaphragm. The basal lamina (BL) under them stays intact. This combination lets hormones and absorbed nutrients cross quickly while cells stay in.

  • The brain has continuous capillaries with no pores (the blood–brain barrier).
  • The liver has sinusoids, with gaps between cells and a discontinuous basal lamina.
Slides (2)
L69Learning
A bone-marrow section shows wide, irregular, thin-walled blood channels lined by a discontinuous layer of endothelium, lying among fat cells and clusters of developing blood cells. What are these channels?
  1. A. Fenestrated capillaries
  2. B. Sinusoidal (discontinuous) capillaries
  3. C. Postcapillary venules
AnswerB. Sinusoidal (discontinuous) capillaries
WhyWide, irregular channels with a discontinuous lining in bone marrow are sinusoids, the route by which new blood cells enter the circulation.
Explanation

The lecture's bone-marrow slide labels the sinusoids (S) among adipocytes (A) and haematopoietic tissue: larger diameter than most capillaries and maximal exchange, including movement of blood cells. Shortcut: purple developing blood cells plus fat cells = marrow = sinusoids.

  • Fenestrated capillaries are narrower and keep a continuous basement membrane; they belong to endocrine glands and the gut.
  • Postcapillary venules are round, with a continuous endothelium and pericytes; they are where white cells leave the blood in inflammation, not where marrow cells enter it.
Slide (1)

Venules and veins

L70Learning
How does the lecture grade veins by diameter?
  1. A. Small veins <0.1 mm
    Medium veins <1 mm
    Large veins >1 mm
  2. B. Small veins <5 mm
    Medium veins <20 mm
    Large veins >20 mm
  3. C. Small veins <1 mm
    Medium veins <10 mm
    Large veins >10 mm
AnswerC. Small veins <1 mm
Medium veins <10 mm
Large veins >10 mm
WhyVenules → small veins (<1 mm) → medium veins (<10 mm) → large veins (>10 mm), such as the venae cavae.
Explanation

The veins slide grades them as venule, small vein (<1 mm), medium-sized vein (<10 mm) and large vein (10 mm and over). Medium veins (1–10 mm) are the ones that accompany muscular arteries in neurovascular bundles; large veins include the venae cavae and the portal, pulmonary and subclavian veins.

  • The 5/20 mm and 0.1/1 mm cut-offs are invented.

Slide note: the lecture lists venules as <0.01 mm and the summary slide as <0.001 mm. Textbooks give venules about 0.01–0.1 mm (10–100 µm); 0.001 mm (1 µm) is smaller than a red cell and must be a typo.

Slide (1)
L71Learning
What does the wall of a postcapillary venule consist of?
  1. A. Endothelium + internal elastic lamina
  2. B. Endothelium + pericytes
  3. C. Endothelium + a thick adventitia
AnswerB. Endothelium + pericytes
WhyThe lecture: postcapillary venule intima = endothelium + pericytes; like a capillary, it has no smooth-muscle media.
Explanation

Postcapillary venules collect blood from capillaries. Their wall is still very thin: an endothelium with scattered pericytes and a thin layer of surrounding connective tissue. Only further downstream (muscular venules, then small veins) does smooth muscle appear. Their thin, responsive endothelium is why they are the main site of leukocyte emigration and of fluid leakage in inflammation.

  • Internal elastic lamina is an arterial feature.
  • Thick adventitia belongs to larger veins.
Slide (1)
L72Learning
In infection or tissue damage, where do white blood cells mainly stick to the vessel wall and leave the circulation?
  1. A. Postcapillary venules
  2. B. Continuous capillaries
  3. C. Arterioles
AnswerA. Postcapillary venules
WhyPostcapillary venules are the primary site where white cells adhere to the endothelium and emigrate (diapedesis) into the tissue.
Explanation

Inflammatory signals (histamine, cytokines) act mainly on the endothelium of postcapillary venules: it expresses adhesion molecules and its junctions loosen, so leukocytes roll, stick and squeeze out into the tissue, and plasma leaks out (swelling). Flow here is slow and the wall is thin, which helps.

  • Continuous capillaries are too narrow and tightly sealed; they are the exchange site, not the emigration site.
  • Arterioles have a muscular wall and fast flow.
Slide (1)
L73Learning
Next to an arteriole of similar overall size, how does a venule look?
  1. A. Narrower lumen, thicker wall
  2. B. Same lumen, thicker wall
  3. C. Wider lumen, thinner wall
AnswerC. Wider lumen, thinner wall
WhyVenules have a large diameter and a relatively thin wall; arterioles have a narrow, round lumen inside a thick muscular wall.
Explanation

The lecture's "arterioles vs venules" micrograph places them side by side: the venule (V) is a wide, thin-walled channel full of red cells, edged by a pericyte (P); the arteriole (A) has a small round lumen in a thick ring of smooth muscle. The same rule holds at every size: veins have larger lumens and thinner walls than their companion arteries.

  • Narrower lumen, thicker wall describes the arteriole.
  • Same lumen, thicker wall is wrong on both counts.
Slide (1)
L74Learning
Which rules hold for small, medium and large veins?
  1. A. The lumen is wider than the wall is thick; the adventitia gets thicker as the vein gets bigger
  2. B. The lumen is wider than the wall is thick; the intima gets thicker as the vein gets bigger
  3. C. The wall is thicker than the lumen is wide; the media gets thicker as the vein gets bigger
AnswerA. The lumen is wider than the wall is thick; the adventitia gets thicker as the vein gets bigger
WhyIn veins the lumen diameter exceeds the wall thickness, and the connective-tissue adventitia thickens as veins get larger.
Explanation

The lecture: lumen diameter exceeds wall thickness; intima well developed and forms valves; media relatively thin, a few layers of smooth muscle; adventitia connective tissue that gets thicker as the vein gets bigger.

  • Wall thicker than lumen, thickening media describes arteries.
  • The intima forms valves but does not become the thick layer; the adventitia does.
Slide (1)
L75Learning
A large vessel has a thin tunica media and a thick adventitia of collagen with smooth-muscle bundles. What is the main functional point of this design?
  1. A. To regulate how much blood enters the capillary beds
  2. B. To support a thin-walled vessel that stores a large volume of blood at low pressure
  3. C. To resist high, pulsatile pressure and recoil between heartbeats
AnswerB. To support a thin-walled vessel that stores a large volume of blood at low pressure
WhyThis is a large vein: a capacitance vessel that holds much of the blood volume at low pressure, with a supportive adventitia rather than a strong muscular media.
Explanation

Venous pressure is low, so veins do not need a thick muscular or elastic media. Their thin, distensible walls let them hold most of the circulating blood (about two-thirds), which is why they are called capacitance vessels. The thick collagenous adventitia supports and anchors them, and valves keep the slow flow moving toward the heart.

  • Resisting pulsatile pressure and recoiling is the job of elastic arteries, with their elastic media.
  • Regulating flow into capillary beds is the job of arterioles and precapillary sphincters.
L76Learning
What are venous valves made of?
  1. A. Extensions of the internal elastic lamina, covered by endothelium on both faces
  2. B. Folds of the media with smooth muscle, covered by endothelium on one face
  3. C. Folds of the intima and its subendothelial connective tissue, covered by endothelium on both faces
AnswerC. Folds of the intima and its subendothelial connective tissue, covered by endothelium on both faces
WhyA venous valve is a fold of the intima and subendothelial connective tissue projecting into the lumen, with endothelium on both surfaces.
Explanation

The lecture: "fold of intima and subendothelial connective tissue; projects into lumen". Each valve is a thin, cusp-like flap strengthened by collagen and elastic fibres. Valves usually come in pairs; blood flowing toward the heart pushes them open, and backflow fills the cusps and shuts them.

  • Folds of the media is wrong: the media does not enter the valve, and there is no smooth muscle in it.
  • The internal elastic lamina is an arterial structure.
Slides (2)
L77LearningBorderline
Where are venous valves most numerous, and where are they absent?
  1. A. Most numerous in the venules; absent from all medium and large veins
  2. B. Most numerous in the venae cavae; absent from the veins of the legs
  3. C. Most numerous in the veins of the legs; absent from the venae cavae
AnswerC. Most numerous in the veins of the legs; absent from the venae cavae
WhyValves are commonest where blood must climb against gravity, in the lower-limb veins; the venae cavae (and other great veins of the trunk) have none.
Explanation

Valves are characteristic of small and medium veins, both superficial and deep, and are most numerous in the legs, where they stop blood falling back toward the feet when we stand. The venae cavae, the hepatic portal system and the veins of the brain lack valves.

  • The reverse option swaps the two locations.
  • Venules are too small to have valves; valves are a feature of veins.
L78Learning
Venous pressure in the legs is low. What keeps venous blood moving up toward the heart?
  1. A. Valves that allow only one-way flow, together with the squeeze of contracting skeletal muscles
  2. B. A thick muscular media that contracts rhythmically to propel the blood
  3. C. Elastic lamellae in the vein wall that store energy in systole and recoil in diastole
AnswerA. Valves that allow only one-way flow, together with the squeeze of contracting skeletal muscles
WhyVenous valves plus the skeletal-muscle pump: contracting leg muscles squeeze the deep veins, and the valves make sure blood can only go toward the heart.
Explanation

When calf muscles contract they compress the deep veins and push blood upward; when they relax the vein refills from below, while the valves above close to stop backflow. Failure of the valves (venous insufficiency) lets blood pool and the veins dilate, producing varicose veins and swelling after prolonged standing.

  • Veins have a thin media; they do not pump.
  • Elastic recoil keeps blood moving in the elastic arteries, not in veins.
Slides (2)
L79Learning
Describe the wall of the vena cava.
  1. A. Thin intima; thin media of a few circular smooth-muscle layers; very thick adventitia with longitudinal smooth-muscle bundles and vasa vasorum
  2. B. Thick intima; media of many concentric elastic lamellae; thin adventitia with vasa vasorum
  3. C. Thin intima; very thick media of circular smooth muscle; thin adventitia without vasa vasorum
AnswerA. Thin intima; thin media of a few circular smooth-muscle layers; very thick adventitia with longitudinal smooth-muscle bundles and vasa vasorum
WhyThe vena cava (a large vein) has a thin intima and media; its adventitia is by far the thickest coat, holding longitudinal smooth-muscle bundles and vasa vasorum.
Explanation

The lab describes the vena cava: a thin intima of endothelium and subendothelial collagen and elastic fibres, up to an internal elastic membrane; a narrow media of a few layers of circular smooth muscle with collagen and fibroblasts; and the adventitia, the thickest coat, containing vasa vasorum. In H&E the adventitia is crowded with bundles of longitudinal smooth muscle, cut across in a transverse section.

  • Very thick muscular media describes a muscular artery.
  • Media of many elastic lamellae describes the aorta.
Slides (3)

Varicose veins and deep vein thrombosis

L80Learning
A 56-year-old man has painful, dilated, twisted knots under the skin of both legs, with ulcers over some of them. Which vessels are affected?
  1. A. Superficial lymphatic vessels
  2. B. Small arteries
  3. C. Superficial veins
AnswerC. Superficial veins
WhyDilated, tortuous, painful knots in the legs are varicose veins: enlarged superficial veins (great saphenous system).
Explanation

Varicose veins are superficial leg veins (the saphenous veins and their tributaries) that have become enlarged and tortuous. Upright posture puts a high column of blood on these veins, so they are common, especially in people who stand for long periods. The ulcers are venous (stasis) ulcers, typically around the ankle.

  • Lymphatic obstruction causes diffuse swelling (lymphoedema), not visible knots of dilated vessels.
  • Diseased small arteries cause pale, cold, painful limbs with weak pulses, not bulging superficial knots.
Slide (1)
L81Learning
What makes a leg vein varicose?
  1. A. Incompetent valves and/or a dilated vein wall → enlarged, tortuous veins
  2. B. Thickened valves and a narrowed vein wall → small, straight veins
  3. C. Atherosclerotic plaque in the leg arteries → enlarged, pulsating veins
AnswerA. Incompetent valves and/or a dilated vein wall → enlarged, tortuous veins
WhyVaricosities are enlarged and tortuous because of incompetent venous valves and/or dilation of the vessel; they are commoner in people who stand for long periods.
Explanation

When valves fail to close, blood falls back down the vein, raising the pressure in the segment below; the wall stretches, which pulls the valve cusps further apart, and a vicious circle sets in. Prolonged standing, pregnancy, obesity and age favour it.

  • Thickened valves and a narrowed wall is the opposite of what is seen.
  • Arterial plaque reduces arterial inflow; it does not make veins varicose or pulsatile.
Slide (1)
L82Learning
How do varicose veins damage the skin of the leg?
  1. A. Fast, laminar flow → the skin arterioles constrict → the skin starves of oxygen → dry gangrene
  2. B. Slow, turbulent flow → clots travel into the skin arteries → arterial ulcers and gangrene
  3. C. Slow, turbulent flow → the capillary beds become engorged → fluid leaks into the skin → stasis dermatitis and venous ulcers
AnswerC. Slow, turbulent flow → the capillary beds become engorged → fluid leaks into the skin → stasis dermatitis and venous ulcers
WhyIn varicose veins flow is slow and turbulent, the upstream capillary bed is engorged, and fluid leaks into the skin: stasis dermatitis and venous ulcers.
Explanation

The lab slide: blood flow in varicose veins is turbulent and slow, the capillary bed is engorged, and fluid leaks into the surrounding skin, causing stasis (venous) dermatitis: red-brown, itchy, thickened skin of the lower leg. Poorly nourished, oedematous skin breaks down into venous ulcers, usually above the medial ankle.

  • Clots in veins travel toward the heart and lungs, never into skin arteries.
  • Flow in varicose veins is slow, not fast, and the problem is venous congestion, not arteriolar constriction.
Slides (2)
L83Learning
A biopsy from a patient with varicose veins shows a dilated, thin-walled vein whose lumen contains thin, delicate leaflets projecting from the wall (arrows). What are they?
  1. A. Vasa vasorum cut in cross-section
  2. B. Venous valves, folds of the intima
  3. C. Fragments of elastic lamellae torn from the media
AnswerB. Venous valves, folds of the intima
WhyThin leaflets projecting into a dilated vein lumen are venous valves, folds of intima and subendothelial connective tissue covered by endothelium.
Explanation

The lab case biopsy shows a markedly dilated vein in the subcutaneous tissue with the arrows on its valve cusps. In varicose veins the valves are present but can no longer meet across the widened lumen, so they are incompetent.

  • Torn elastic lamellae would lie within an arterial media, not float as paired leaflets in a vein lumen.
  • Vasa vasorum are small vessels in the adventitia, outside the lumen.
Slide (1)
L84Learning
Are varicose veins a common cause of deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism?
  1. A. Yes: most pulmonary emboli start as clots in superficial varicose veins
  2. B. No: varicose veins are superficial, and their clots rarely embolise; pulmonary emboli come mainly from thrombi in the deep leg veins
  3. C. Yes: varicose veins are dilated deep veins, the usual site of deep vein thrombosis
AnswerB. No: varicose veins are superficial, and their clots rarely embolise; pulmonary emboli come mainly from thrombi in the deep leg veins
WhyNo. Varices are dilated superficial veins; thrombi in them seldom embolise. Deep vein thrombosis forms in the deep leg veins and is the usual source of pulmonary emboli.
Explanation

The lab asks this question next to a diagram of the deep veins of the leg. Superficial and deep veins are separate systems linked by perforating veins. Clots in superficial varicosities cause local, tender inflammation (superficial thrombophlebitis) but rarely travel. Deep vein thrombi (calf, popliteal, femoral, iliac veins) can break free and lodge in the pulmonary arteries.

  • Most emboli from superficial veins is false.
  • Varices are deep veins is false: varicose veins are the superficial (saphenous) system.
Slides (2)
L85Learning
What is deep vein thrombosis, and what is its main danger?
  1. A. A clot forming on the wall of a deep leg vein, which can break free and lodge in the lungs as a pulmonary embolus
  2. B. A clot forming on the wall of a superficial leg vein, which can break free and cause a stroke
  3. C. A plaque forming on the wall of a deep leg artery, which can rupture and cause limb ischaemia
AnswerA. A clot forming on the wall of a deep leg vein, which can break free and lodge in the lungs as a pulmonary embolus
WhyIn deep vein thrombosis a thrombus forms on the wall of a deep leg vein; a fragment can lodge in the lungs as a pulmonary embolus.
Explanation

The lab diagram: a thrombus begins to form on the wall of a deep vein, breaks free, and travels to the lungs. The embolus passes up the inferior vena cava, through the right atrium and ventricle, into the pulmonary arteries, where a large one blocks flow and can cause sudden chest pain, collapse and death.

  • Emboli from leg veins lodge in the lungs; reaching the brain (stroke) would need a hole between the right and left heart.
  • A plaque in an artery is atherosclerosis, not thrombosis of a vein.
Slide (1)

Lymphatic vessels

L86Learning
What do lymphatic vessels do?
  1. A. Carry lymph out of the blood and deliver it into the interstitial fluid
  2. B. Collect excess interstitial fluid left behind by the capillaries and return it to the blood as lymph
  3. C. Collect excess interstitial fluid and carry it to the kidney to be excreted as urine
AnswerB. Collect excess interstitial fluid left behind by the capillaries and return it to the blood as lymph
WhyLymphatics drain excess interstitial fluid (lymph) from the tissues, carry it through lymph nodes, and return it to the bloodstream via the thoracic or right lymphatic duct.
Explanation

Capillaries filter slightly more fluid into the tissues than they reabsorb. Lymphatic capillaries pick up this excess, along with proteins and cells that leaked out, and the lymphatic system carries it back to the great veins in the neck. On the way, lymph nodes filter it and immune responses begin.

  • The lymphatic system does not connect to the kidney; urine is made by filtering blood.
  • Flow is one way, from the tissues to the blood, not the reverse.
Slide (1)
L87Learning
Describe the structure of a lymphatic capillary.
  1. A. A blind-ended, very thin endothelial tube with many tight junctions and a continuous basal lamina
  2. B. An open-ended, thick-walled endothelial tube with many tight junctions and a continuous basal lamina
  3. C. A blind-ended, very thin endothelial tube with no tight junctions and an incomplete basal lamina
AnswerC. A blind-ended, very thin endothelial tube with no tight junctions and an incomplete basal lamina
WhyLymphatic capillaries are close-ended (blind), very thin endothelial tubes that lack tight junctions and have an incomplete basal lamina.
Explanation

The lecture: close-ended, very thin; incomplete basal lamina; interstitial fluid enters openings between endothelial cells. The lab adds that they lack tight junctions. This makes them far more permeable than blood capillaries, so they can take up large proteins, cells and fat droplets.

  • Open-ended and thick-walled is a common false statement.
  • Many tight junctions and a continuous basal lamina describes a continuous blood capillary.
Slide (1)
L88Learning
How does interstitial fluid get into a lymphatic capillary?
  1. A. By active transport across the endothelial cells
  2. B. Through openings between the endothelial cells
  3. C. Through fenestrae in the endothelial cells
AnswerB. Through openings between the endothelial cells
WhyInterstitial fluid enters through openings between endothelial cells, whose overlapping edges are not sealed by tight junctions.
Explanation

Lymphatic endothelial cells overlap loosely at their edges. When interstitial fluid pressure rises, the overlapping edges are pushed inward and fluid flows between the cells into the lumen; anchoring filaments hold the vessel open as the tissue swells.

  • Fenestrae are pores through the cytoplasm of fenestrated blood capillaries.
  • Entry is passive, driven by pressure, not active transport.
Slide (1)
L89Learning
What are the anchoring filaments of lymphatic capillaries?
  1. A. Smooth muscle cells tying neighbouring endothelial cells together, keeping the openings closed
  2. B. Fine fibres (collagen and elastin) tying the endothelial cells to the surrounding tissue, holding the openings open
  3. C. Fine fibres (collagen and elastin) tying the endothelial cells to their basal lamina, keeping the openings sealed
AnswerB. Fine fibres (collagen and elastin) tying the endothelial cells to the surrounding tissue, holding the openings open
WhyAnchoring filaments attach lymphatic endothelial cells to the surrounding connective tissue, so the vessel and its intercellular openings are pulled open, not squashed, when the tissue swells.
Explanation

The lab slide: openings between endothelial cells are held in place by fine anchoring filaments containing collagen and elastin. As tissue fluid accumulates, the tissue expands and the filaments pull on the endothelium, widening the openings so more fluid can enter. Textbooks describe them as microfibrils of the elastic-fibre system (fibrillin-rich).

  • Anchoring to the basal lamina to seal the openings is the opposite of their job.
  • Lymphatic capillaries have no smooth muscle.
Slide (1)
L90Learning
What stops lymph leaking back out of a lymphatic capillary into the tissue?
  1. A. Overlapping edges of the endothelial cells, which act as one-way flaps
  2. B. Tight junctions between the endothelial cells
  3. C. Contraction of pericytes around the capillary
AnswerA. Overlapping edges of the endothelial cells, which act as one-way flaps
WhyThe overlapping endothelial edges (folds) swing inward to let fluid in, then press shut when lymph pressure rises: they act as one-way flaps.
Explanation

The lab slide: endothelial folds prevent backflow of lymph into the interstitial space. When pressure inside the lymphatic exceeds tissue pressure, the overlapping flaps are pushed together and close the gaps, so lymph moves on into larger vessels with true valves.

  • Lymphatic capillaries lack tight junctions; that is why fluid can enter.
  • Pericytes belong to blood capillaries and venules, not lymphatics.
Slide (1)
L91Learning
How does the wall of a lymphatic vessel compare with that of a vein of the same size?
  1. A. About the same thickness, with a thick muscular media
  2. B. Thicker, with three clearly defined tunics
  3. C. Thinner, with layers that are hard to make out
AnswerC. Thinner, with layers that are hard to make out
WhyLymphatic vessels have thinner walls and less distinct layers than arteries and veins of similar size.
Explanation

The lab slide says so directly. Small lymphatic vessels are little more than endothelium with a wisp of connective tissue and smooth muscle; only the largest (such as the thoracic duct) show a recognisable three-layered wall resembling a vein.

  • Thicker, three clear tunics describes a muscular artery or a medium vein.
  • A thick muscular media belongs to arteries.
Slide (1)
L92Learning
What are the valves of lymphatic vessels made of, and what pushes lymph along?
  1. A. Paired infoldings of intima covered by endothelium; suction generated by the lymph nodes
  2. B. Single folds of media containing smooth muscle; the heartbeat transmitted along the vessel
  3. C. Paired infoldings of intima covered by endothelium; external pressure such as contracting skeletal muscle
AnswerC. Paired infoldings of intima covered by endothelium; external pressure such as contracting skeletal muscle
WhyLymphatic valves are paired intimal infoldings covered by endothelium; lymph is moved mainly by external compression, such as skeletal-muscle contraction.
Explanation

Like veins, larger lymphatic vessels have valves that support one-way flow and prevent backflow; the lab's longitudinal section shows the paired leaflets pointing in the direction of flow. Lymph has no pump of its own: compression by surrounding muscles, arterial pulsations and breathing movements, aided by weak contraction of the wall in larger vessels, squeezes it forward.

  • Valves contain no media or muscle, and the heartbeat does not drive lymph.
  • Lymph nodes filter lymph; they do not generate suction.
Slides (2)
L93Learning
On a slide, what is the quickest way to tell a lymphatic vessel from a venule or small vein?
  1. A. A prominent internal elastic lamina
  2. B. A thick muscular wall around a round lumen
  3. C. No red blood cells in its lumen
AnswerC. No red blood cells in its lumen
WhyLymphatics carry pale, protein-rich lymph with a few lymphocytes but no red blood cells; venules and veins are usually full of red cells.
Explanation

The lab slide: lymphatic vessels may contain lightly staining proteinaceous lymph, lymphocytes and other white cells, but lack red blood cells, which helps distinguish them from blood vessels. Other clues: a very thin wall with indistinct layers, an irregular, often collapsed outline, and valves.

  • A thick muscular wall around a round lumen identifies an artery or arteriole.
  • A prominent internal elastic lamina identifies a muscular artery.
Slides (2)
L94Learning
How does lymph get back into the blood?
  1. A. Through the thoracic duct or the right lymphatic duct, into the great veins at the root of the neck
  2. B. Through the thoracic duct, which empties directly into the right atrium
  3. C. Through lymphatic capillaries that open directly into the venules of each tissue
AnswerA. Through the thoracic duct or the right lymphatic duct, into the great veins at the root of the neck
WhyLymphatic vessels merge into larger vessels and finally the thoracic duct or the right lymphatic duct, which empty into the great veins at the root of the neck.
Explanation

The pathway: lymphatic capillaries → larger collecting lymphatic vessels (through one or more lymph nodes) → lymphatic trunks → the thoracic duct (left venous angle, where the left internal jugular joins the left subclavian vein) or the right lymphatic duct (right venous angle).

  • Lymphatic capillaries are blind-ended; they never open into venules.
  • The thoracic duct ends in the left subclavian/internal jugular junction, not in the heart.
Slide (1)
L95Learning
In a section of ileum, the core of each villus contains a clear, thin-walled channel lined only by flat endothelium, sometimes holding pale pink fluid and a few white blood cells but no red cells. What is it?
  1. A. A lacteal, a blind-ended lymphatic capillary
  2. B. A thoroughfare channel
  3. C. A fenestrated blood capillary
AnswerA. A lacteal, a blind-ended lymphatic capillary
WhyThe clear central channel of an intestinal villus is the lacteal, a blind-ended lymphatic capillary lined by simple squamous endothelium.
Explanation

The lab ileum slide: find a villus with a clear space at its core; that space is the lumen of a lacteal. It may hold lightly eosinophilic lymph and occasional white cells. Lacteals occur in villi throughout the small bowel. Only this lymphatic part of the gut slide is on the circulatory exam.

  • Fenestrated blood capillaries also run in the villus core, but they are narrow and carry red cells.
  • A thoroughfare channel is part of a capillary bed's bypass route, not a structure seen in the villus core.

L96LearningBorderline
How are absorbed dietary fats carried out of the small-intestinal villus?
  1. A. Into the fenestrated blood capillaries of the villus
  2. B. Into sinusoidal capillaries in the villus core
  3. C. Into the lacteals (lymphatic capillaries), as large lipid particles (chylomicrons)
AnswerC. Into the lacteals (lymphatic capillaries), as large lipid particles (chylomicrons)
WhyAbsorbed fat leaves the enterocytes as chylomicrons, which are too large for blood capillaries and enter the leaky lacteals, reaching the blood via the thoracic duct.
Explanation

Lymphatic capillaries lack tight junctions and have an incomplete basal lamina, so they take up particles that blood capillaries cannot, including the big lipoprotein droplets (chylomicrons) packaged by intestinal cells. Lymph from the gut after a fatty meal is milky (chyle), hence the name lacteal.

  • The villus fenestrated capillaries take up sugars and amino acids, not chylomicrons.
  • Villi do not contain sinusoids.
L97Learning
What is lymphoedema?
  1. A. Swelling from blood trapped in the tissue because the veins are blocked
  2. B. Swelling from fluid trapped in the tissue because lymphatic drainage is blocked
  3. C. Shrinkage of the tissue because leaky lymphatics remove too much fluid
AnswerB. Swelling from fluid trapped in the tissue because lymphatic drainage is blocked
WhyLymphoedema is tissue swelling caused by obstructed lymphatic drainage: the excess interstitial fluid cannot be returned to the blood.
Explanation

If lymphatic vessels or nodes are blocked or removed (parasites, surgery, radiation, tumour), the fluid and protein normally carried away by lymph collect in the tissue. The swelling is typically firm and non-pitting, and the overlying skin thickens.

  • Blocked veins cause congestion and pitting oedema by raising capillary pressure; blood does not collect in the tissue, and the lymphatics are not the problem.
  • Lymphatics cannot "over-drain" tissue.
Slide (1)
L98Learning
A 33-year-old man from a tropical region has massive swelling of the scrotum and left leg and is diagnosed with a filarial roundworm infestation. Which vessels have the parasites lodged in and obstructed?
  1. A. Lower-limb veins
  2. B. Lymphatic vessels
  3. C. Capillaries of the skin
AnswerB. Lymphatic vessels
WhyIn lymphatic filariasis adult roundworms live in and block lymphatic vessels, causing massive lymphoedema (elephantiasis) of a leg or the scrotum.
Explanation

Mosquitoes transmit the larvae of filarial nematodes (such as Wuchereria bancrofti). The worms mature in lymphatic vessels and nodes, causing inflammation and obstruction. Lymph cannot drain, protein-rich fluid builds up, and chronic swelling with thick, fibrotic skin develops: elephantiasis.

  • Venous obstruction (e.g. deep vein thrombosis) causes a swollen, red, warm leg but not this enormous, chronic swelling of leg and scrotum together.
  • Blocked skin capillaries would cause local ischaemia, not massive oedema.
Slide (1)
L99Learning
Several months after a left mastectomy with removal of the axillary lymph nodes, a woman develops firm, non-pitting swelling of her left arm. Which vessels have been disrupted?
  1. A. The axillary vein
  2. B. The axillary artery
  3. C. Lymphatic vessels draining the arm
AnswerC. Lymphatic vessels draining the arm
WhyRemoving the axillary lymph nodes cuts the lymphatic drainage of the arm, so protein-rich fluid collects: post-mastectomy lymphoedema.
Explanation

Lymph from the upper limb passes through the axillary nodes. Their surgical removal (or radiation damage) obstructs lymph flow, giving slowly progressive, non-pitting swelling of the arm, sometimes with thickened, orange-peel skin. An exam stem may describe the damaged structures as "vessels which arise from blind endings and have one-way valves": lymphatics.

  • Axillary vein obstruction would cause a congested, bluish arm with pitting oedema and distended superficial veins.
  • Axillary artery damage would make the arm pale, cold and pulseless, not swollen.

In his autobiography, the American swimmer Michael Phelps admitted to being affected by a form of Marfan Syndrome, a genetic disease in which the fibrillin protein component of elastic tissue may be abnormal. Individuals with Marfan syndrome commonly experience aortic dissection. What portion of the aortic wall might be expected to be most affected by abnormal elastic tissue?
Show figure

  3. C. Media (M)

  5. E. Vasa vasorum (V)

WhyFibrillin scaffolds elastin, and the many elastic lamellae of the aorta are in the tunica media, so Marfan syndrome weakens the media (cystic medial degeneration), predisposing to aneurysm and dissection.

Blood under pressure in aortic lumen may dissect into weakened wall of the aorta, a process known as “aortic dissection”.

Identify the cells whose nuclei are indicated by the arrows.
  1. (A) Adipocytes
  2. (B) Cardiac muscle cells
  3. (C) Fibroblasts
  4. (D) Macrophages
  5. (E) Smooth muscle cells

WhyThe nuclei in the aortic tunica media belong to smooth muscle cells arranged in circumferential layers between elastic lamellae; besides contracting, they synthesize the elastin, collagen and ground substance of the media.
Explanation from the source
Smooth muscle fibers form circumferential layers within the tunica media of large elastic arteries. Smooth muscle fibers typically appear as linear arrays of cells in cross-section (shown in the image). In addition to their contractile function, smooth muscle cells synthesize and secrete extracellular matrix components of the tunica media. These extracellular matrix molecules provide structural support to the vessel wall and help to convert the pulsatile blood flow leaving the heart to more continuous flow of blood in the microcirculation. Fibroblasts and macrophages (choices C and D) may migrate through the tunica media, but they would be difficult to identify without the use of special stains. None of the other cells are present in the tunica media of the vessel wall. Keywords: Arteries, tunica media, smooth muscle cell
ConceptNuclei in aortic tunica media belong to smooth muscle cells

Which of the following best describes the pathologic changes visible in this specimen? [Question 24] Microscopic examination of the autopsy specimen described in Question 23 at high magnification would most likely reveal which of the following pathologic changes? [Question 25] Lipid accumulation in the atheroma described in Questions 23 and 24 was primarily related to chronic injury and dysfunction of which of the following vascular components?
  1. (A) Adventitial connective tissue
  2. (B) Elastic lamellae
  3. (C) Endothelial cells
  4. (D) Smooth muscle cells
  5. (E) Subendothelial connective tissue
AnswerC. Endothelial cells
WhyEndothelial injury (from hyperlipidemia, hypertension, smoking) increases permeability to LDL, which oxidizes in the intima and is taken up by macrophages that become foam cells, starting the atheroma.
Explanation from the source
Loss of integrity of the vascular endothelial cell barrier initiates plaque formation in atherosclerosis. Hyperlipidemia, hyperglycemia, hypertension, smoking, and certain infections can lead to chronic injury and disruption of the endothelial cell barrier. Low-density lipoproteins (LDLs) in the blood carry lipids and cholesterol into the developing atheroma. Injured endothelial cells show increased permeability to LDL and increased production of reactive oxygen species such as O2 −, which oxidizes LDL. Oxidized LDL activates endothelial cells and recruits macrophages and other inflammatory cells into the tunica intima. Macrophages phagocytize oxidized LDL and become lipid-laden “foam” cells. Hyperplastic smooth muscle cells in the subendothelial layer of the tunica intima also participate in lipid accumulation. Keywords: Atherosclerosis, endothelial cells
ConceptEndothelial injury initiates lipid accumulation in atheromas

Explanation from the source
Lymphatic vessels convey protein-rich fluid to the bloodstream. Lymphatic channels play a crucial role in regulating interstitial fluid volume and in providing tissue debris to regional lymph nodes for immune surveillance. The smallest lymphatic vessels are lymphatic capillaries. These simple endothelial tubes have closed ends that are in close proximity to blood capillaries. They are most abundant in the skin and gastrointestinal tract. Lymphatic vessels converge and, ultimately, unite to form the thoracic duct (the largest lymphatic vessel) and the right lymphatic trunk. The thoracic duct and right lymphatic trunk empty lymph into the venous circulatory system at the junction of the internal jugular vein and the subclavian vein bilaterally. None of the other vessels exhibit histologic features of efferent lymphatic vessels. Keywords: Lymphatic system
ConceptLymphatic vessels: thin walls, pale proteinaceous lymph, no red cells

The answer is E: Smooth muscle cells. Smooth muscle fibers form circumferential layers within the tunica media of large elastic arteries. Smooth muscle fibers typically appear as linear arrays of cells in cross-section (shown in the image). In addition to their contractile function, smooth muscle cells synthesize and secrete extracellular matrix components of the tunica media. These extracellular matrix molecules provide structural support to the vessel wall and help to convert the pulsatile blood flow leaving the heart to more continuous flow of blood in the microcirculation. Fibroblasts and macrophages (choices C and D) may migrate through the tunica media, but they would be difficult to identify without the use of special stains. A 73-year-old man with a history of hypertension presents to the emergency room with “tearing” chest pain. His blood pressure is 85/45 mm Hg, and his pulse rate is 100 per minute. The patient expires shortly after admission. A dissecting aneurysm of the descending arch of the aorta is discovered at autopsy. Microscopic examination of the aortic wall reveals tearing/dissection along the outer third of the tunica media (shown in the image). This patient’s dissecting aneurysm was most likely caused by chronic injury (and subsequent failure) to which of the following vascular structures?
Show figure
  1. (A) Collagen fibers in the tunica adventitia
  2. (B) Elastic lamellae in the tunica media
  3. (C) Endothelial cells in the tunica intima
  4. (D) Subintimal connective tissue
  5. (E) Vasa vasorum in the tunica adventitia

WhyElastic lamellae are the main structural support of the aortic tunica media; chronic injury by hypertension fragments them, so blood can split the wall.
Explanation from the source
The answer is B: Elastic lamellae in the tunica media. Elastic lamellae are the principal structural support in the tunica media of elastic arteries. Chronic injury caused by hypertension and/or atherosclerosis can disrupt elastic lamellae, leading to vascular dilations (aneurysms) and aneurysmal tears (dissections). Patients with Marfan syndrome are also at risk for dissecting aortic aneurysms. These patients have missense mutations in the gene coding for fibrillin-1 (FBN1). Fibrillins are a family of connective tissue proteins analogous to collagens. They are widely distributed in many tissues in the form of fiber systems termed microfibrils. Deposition of elastin on microfibrils produces the distinctive concentric rings of elastic lamellae found in the aortic wall. Defects in the other structures would not be expected to disrupt elastic tissue in the tunic media of the aorta. Keywords: Dissecting aortic aneurysms, arteries, elastic lamellae
ConceptAortic dissection follows failure of elastic lamellae in the media

Arteries and veins that supply the adventitia and outer portions of the media are referred to as vasa vasorum. These blood vessels travel in the tunica adventitia and send branches into the outer layer of the tunica media (arrows, shown in the image). Nerves innervating the wall of large blood vessels are referred to as nervi vascularis (choice D). Nerves are present in the tunica adventitia, but they are not visible in this section. Adipocytes, collagen fibers, and elastic fibers (choices A, B, and C) are also present in the tunica adventitia, but these cells/structures do not exhibit the distinctive histologic features of the vasa vasorum. A section of the aorta is examined in the histology laboratory. The luminal surface of the vascular wall is shown at high magnification in the image. Which of the following describes the area indicated by the double arrow?

WhyThe band between the endothelium and the first elastic lamella is the subendothelial layer of the intima, loose connective tissue with occasional smooth muscle.
Explanation from the source
The answer is D: Subendothelium. The tunica intima is the innermost layer of arteries and veins. It is composed of endothelium with a basal lamina and an underlying (subendothelial) layer of connective tissue. Endothelial cells (choice B) form a physical barrier to the vascular compartment and help regulate coagulation, inflammation, and wound healing. Smooth muscle cells constitute the major cell type found in the subendothelial connective tissue and secrete a variety of extracellular matrix molecules, including collagen and elastin. The tunica intima of large elastic arteries is relatively thick compared to other arteries. Elastic lamellae (choice A) are components of the tunica media (choice E) visible in the lower part of the image. Internal elastic membrane (choice C) is an elastic lamella along the most external portion of the subendothelial layer. This membrane is more prominent in the tunica media of muscular arteries and arterioles. In large arteries, the internal elastic membrane is inconspicuous, since it is merely the inner layer of many elastic lamellae. Keywords: Arteries, tunica intima

Lipid accumulation in the atheroma described in Questions 23 and 24 was primarily related to chronic injury and dysfunction of which of the following vascular components?

  2. (B) Elastic lamellae
  3. (C) Endothelial cells
  4. (D) Smooth muscle cells

WhyChronic endothelial injury raises permeability to LDL, which oxidizes in the intima and is engulfed by macrophages that become foam cells of the atheroma.
Explanation from the source
The answer is C: Endothelial cells. Loss of integrity of the vascular endothelial cell barrier initiates plaque formation in atherosclerosis. Hyperlipidemia, hyperglycemia, hypertension, smoking, and certain infections can lead to chronic injury and disruption of the endothelial cell barrier. Low-density lipoproteins (LDLs) in the blood carry lipids and cholesterol into the developing atheroma. Injured endothelial cells show increased permeability to LDL and increased production of reactive oxygen species such as O2 −, which oxidizes LDL. Oxidized LDL activates endothelial cells and recruits macrophages and other inflammatory cells into the tunica intima. Macrophages phagocytize oxidized LDL and become lipid-laden “foam” cells. Hyperplastic smooth muscle cells in the subendothelial layer of the tunica intima also participate in lipid accumulation. Keywords: Atherosclerosis, endothelial cells
ConceptEndothelial injury initiates lipid accumulation in atheromas

WhyThe media of a muscular artery consists almost entirely of circumferential smooth muscle cells, which contract to control flow and pressure.
Explanation from the source
The answer is E: Smooth muscle cells. The tunica media in medium arteries is composed almost entirely of smooth muscle fibers. As large elastic arteries undergo branching morphogenesis and their diameter becomes smaller, the tunica media exhibits a gradual reduction in elastic tissue, and a corresponding increase in smooth muscle cells. Smooth muscle fibers are the predominant structural and functional component of the tunica media in mediumsized muscular arteries. Contraction of smooth muscle cells in medium arteries helps maintain systemic blood pressure. Collagen and reticular fibers (choices A and D) are interspersed between smooth muscle cells, but they are not the major structural component of the tunica media. Elastic lamellae (choice B) and fibroblasts (choice C) are not present in the tunica media of medium arteries. Smooth muscle cells synthesize the extracellular matrix components (including collagen and reticular fibers and ground substance) present in the tunica media of medium arteries. You watch a group of high school students playing football. Which of the following components of the circulatory system plays the most important role in directing increased blood flow to capillaries in the skeletal muscles of these young athletes?

WhyArterioles are resistance vessels whose smooth muscle dilates or constricts to redistribute blood into the capillary beds of active skeletal muscle.
Explanation from the source
The answer is B: Arterioles. Contraction and relaxation of smooth muscle fibers in arterioles regulate vasoconstriction and vasodilation, respectively. These structural changes enable arterioles to regulate (and redistribute) blood flow to capillary beds in regions of the body where arterial blood flow is most needed. Arterioles are commonly referred to as resistance vessels, because tonic contraction of their smooth muscle creates vascular resistance, which is considered to be the major determinant of systemic blood pressure. None of the other components of the circulatory system regulate regional blood flow. Keywords: Arterioles, vasoconstriction, vasodilation

A 55-year-old man complains of recurring dizziness and nausea for about 1 year. His blood pressure is 170/110 mm Hg. Which of the following contributes the most to the pathogenesis of systemic hypertension in this patient?
  1. (A) Arterial cystic medial necrosis
  2. (B) Increased heart rate
  3. (C) Increased peripheral vascular resistance
  4. (D) Increased vascular permeability
  5. (E) Vasodilation of arterioles
Answer(C) Increased peripheral vascular resistance
WhyNarrowed, hypertrophied small arteries and arterioles raise peripheral vascular resistance, the common end result in primary systemic hypertension.
Explanation from the source
The answer is C: Increased peripheral vascular resistance. Although different mechanisms may contribute to the pathogenesis of primary hypertension, the common end result for all of them is increased peripheral vascular resistance. In most cases of primary hypertension, small arteries and arterioles show structural narrowing and reduced luminal diameter, which may result from an increased number of smooth muscle cells in the vascular wall and/or increased active contraction of smooth muscle cells. Increased heart rate (choice B) does not necessarily lead to systemic hypertension. Vasodilation of arterioles (choice E) lowers blood pressure. Arterial cystic medial necrosis (choice A) and increased vascular permeability (choice D) may be consequences of hypertension, but they do not cause hypertension. Keywords: Systemic hypertension

WhyA tiny channel lined by one flattened endothelial cell and just wide enough for single erythrocytes, running between muscle fibers, is a capillary.
Explanation from the source
The answer is B: Capillary. Capillaries are the smallest blood vessels. They are composed of a single layer of endothelial cells (a simple squamous epithelium) surrounded by a delicate basal lamina. These narrow endothelial channels are just large enough to allow erythrocytes to pass through, one at a time, and thin enough to allow for efficient transendothelial diffusion. Capillaries form fine networks that facilitate the exchange of fluids, electrolytes, gases, nutrients, and metabolic waste products between blood and interstitial tissues of organs. None of the other blood vessels exhibit the distinctive histologic features of capillaries. Keywords: Capillaries

A 68-year-old man with a history of smoking presents with chest pain and mild fever. The patient is subsequently diagnosed with lung cancer. Examination of the surgical specimen reveals normal tissue along the tumor margin (shown in image). Which of the following best describes structural features of the capillary indicated by the arrow?
  1. (A) Continuous endothelial cells with continuous basal lamina
  2. (B) Discontinuous endothelial cells with discontinuous basal lamina
  3. (C) Endothelial cells with fenestrations covered by diaphragms
  4. (D) Fenestrated endothelial cells with continuous basal lamina
  5. (E) Sinusoidal capillary with discontinuous basal lamina
Answer(A) Continuous endothelial cells with continuous basal lamina
WhyAlveolar-septum capillaries are continuous capillaries, with an uninterrupted endothelium joined by tight junctions and a continuous basal lamina.
Explanation from the source
The answer is A: Continuous endothelial cells with continuous basal lamina. Three types of capillaries can be distinguished on the basis of their ultrastructural morphology: continuous, fenestrated, and discontinuous. Continuous capillaries have an uninterrupted endothelial lining, surrounded by a continuous layer of basal lamina. Endothelial cells are linked by tight junctions (zonula occludens). Continuous capillaries are found in the lungs, CNS, thymus, skeletal muscle, and bone. Fenestrated capillaries (choices C and D) have many small windows (fenestra) that facilitate the diffusion of biological molecules across the endothelium. The fenestrations may, or may not, be covered by a thin “diaphragm.” The basal lamina is continuous in fenestrated capillaries. Fenestrated capillaries with diaphragms are found in the intestines, endocrine organs, and kidney tubules (i.e., peritubular capillaries). Fenestrated capillaries without diaphragms facilitate the ultrafiltration of blood in the renal glomerulus. Discontinuous capillaries (also referred to as sinusoidal capillaries) display an incomplete endothelial lining and a fragmented basal lamina. These capillaries (choices B and E) facilitate communication between parenchymal cells and blood. Discontinuous capillaries are found in the liver, spleen, and bone marrow. Keywords: Capillaries, endothelial cells
ConceptLung alveolar-septum capillaries are continuous

You are asked to lead a small group discussion on topics related to the histology and physiology of the cardiovascular system. Which of the following best describes the biological function of arteriovenous shunts in the skin?
  1. (A) Activation of coagulation and hemostasis
  2. (B) Drainage of extravascular lymphedema
  3. (C) Regulation of capillary permeability
  4. (D) Regulation of granulocyte diapedesis during acute inflammation
  5. (E) Temperature-dependent regulation of blood flow
Answer(E) Temperature-dependent regulation of blood flow
WhyArteriovenous shunts let blood bypass skin capillary beds, so opening or closing them adjusts surface blood flow and heat loss with temperature.
Explanation from the source
The answer is E: Temperature-dependent regulation of blood flow. Precapillary arterioles generally convey blood into capillary networks that are drained by postcapillary venules. However, in many tissues, especially in the skin of the fingertips and in erectile tissues of the penis and clitoris, the capillary circulation can be bypassed via direct connections between terminal arterioles and postcapillary venules. These direct routes are termed arteriovenous anastomoses or arteriovenous shunts (AV shunts). AV shunts are enclosed in connective tissue capsules and are richly innervated. AV shunts in the skin are involved in thermoregulation at the body surface. When exposed to cold weather, AV shunts open and capillary beds are closed to prevent heat loss. In warm weather, AV shunts close, allowing blood to flow into capillary beds to augment heat dissipation. Keywords: Arteriovenous shunts
ConceptSkin arteriovenous shunts regulate blood flow for thermoregulation

The answer is C: Postcapillary venule. Postcapillary venules are the principal site where endothelial cells respond to vasoactive molecules, such as histamine and serotonin. In response to tissue injury, endothelial cells alter their membrane properties to (1) permit leakage of fluid and plasma components from the intravascular compartment and (2) facilitate the emigration of leukocytes from the vascular space into the surrounding extravascular tissue.
