  3. C. Tight junction (1) and basal lamina (2)
  4. D. Gap junction (1) and basal lamina (2)
  5. E. Intercellular cleft (1) and basal lamina (2)
AnswerA. Diaphragm of pore (1) and basal lamina (2)
WhyIn a fenestrated capillary each pore is spanned by a thin diaphragm (1), while the basal lamina (2) beneath the endothelium stays continuous.
ConceptFenestrated capillary TEM: pore diaphragm and continuous basal lamina
Slides (2)
164
In his autobiography, the American swimmer Michael Phelps admitted to being affected by a form of Marfan Syndrome, a genetic disease in which the fibrillin protein component of elastic tissue may be abnormal. Individuals with Marfan syndrome commonly experience aortic aneurysms. What portion of the aortic wall might be expected to be affected by abnormal elastic tissue?
  1. A. 1
  2. B. 2
  3. C. 3
  4. D. 4
  5. E. 5
AnswerC. 3
WhyLayer 3 is the thick elastic tunica media between intima and adventitia; its fibrillin-dependent elastic lamellae are what Marfan syndrome weakens.
Explanation from the source
In Marfan syndrome, mutation of the fibrillin-1 protein gene a)interferes with normal structural integrity of fibrillin-rich connective tissue, and b) also decreases the sequestration of TGF-β by fibrillin protein. The increased bioavailability of TGF-β leads to activation of matrix metalloproteinases that degrade elastic tissue. Compare elastic stain of aorta from individual with Marfan syndrome (left) with normal control (right). In Marfan’s syndrome, blood under pressure in the aortic lumen may dissect into the weakened wall of the aorta, a process known as “aortic dissection”.Observe the loss of elastic tissue in the aortic wall on this elastic stain
ConceptMarfan: pick the aortic tunica media (3) on the micrograph
Slide (1)
165
A wavy, dark line is visible at the junction between the tunica intima and tunica media of a muscular artery when stained with elastic tissue stain. What structure does this represent?
  1. A. External elastic lamina
  2. B. Reticular fiber network
  3. C. Basal lamina
  4. D. Internal elastic lamina
AnswerD. Internal elastic lamina
WhyThe internal elastic lamina is a fenestrated elastin sheet marking the intima-media border, seen as a wavy dark line and most prominent in muscular arteries.
Explanation from the source
An internal elastic lamina, a sheet of elastin with fenestrations, often separates the tunica intima from the tunica media, most prominent in muscular arteries.(Junqueira’s Basic Histology)
ConceptWavy elastic line between intima and media is the internal elastic lamina
Slides (2)
166
Which tunic is primarily responsible for controlling vasoconstriction and vasodilation?
  1. A. Tunica intima
  2. B. Tunica media
  3. C. Tunica adventitia
  4. D. Internal elastic lamina
AnswerB. Tunica media
WhyThe tunica media is mainly smooth muscle, so its contraction or relaxation narrows or widens the lumen to regulate blood flow and pressure.
Explanation from the source
The tunica media, composed largely of smooth-muscle cells, permits vasoconstriction and vasodilation to regulate blood flow and pressure. (Junqueira’s Basic Histology)
ConceptTunica media controls vasoconstriction and vasodilation
Slide (1)
167High-yield
During a liver biopsy, the pathologist notes large, irregular vascular spaces lined by discontinuous endothelium and gaps between cells that allow passage of plasma proteins and even blood cells. These findings are characteristic of which capillary type?
  1. A. Continuous capillary
  2. B. Fenestrated capillary
  3. C. Discontinuous capillary
  4. D. Arteriolar capillary
  5. E. Venule
AnswerC. Discontinuous capillary
WhyWide irregular channels with gaps between endothelial cells and a discontinuous basal lamina are discontinuous (sinusoidal) capillaries, found in liver, spleen and bone marrow.
Explanation from the source
Discontinuous (sinusoidal) capillaries have large lumens and gaps in both endothelium and basal lamina, allowing passage of macromolecules and cells. Found in the liver, spleen, and bone marrow organs where extensive exchange of large molecules or cells occurs.
ConceptLiver sinusoids are discontinuous capillaries
Slides (2)
168
A histologic section of brain tissue shows capillaries lined by endothelial cells joined by “tight junctions.” Which type of capillary is this?
  1. A. Fenestrated capillary
  2. B. Continuous capillary
  3. C. Discontinuous capillary
  4. D. Fenestrated capillary
  5. E. Discontinuous capillary
AnswerB. Continuous capillary – muscle, brain
WhyBrain capillaries are continuous capillaries: endothelial cells sealed by tight junctions on an unbroken basal lamina, forming the blood–brain barrier; fenestrated and discontinuous types have pores or gaps.
Explanation from the source
As you think about these questions try to understand the location and why you’d expect them there. Continuous- The Brain is tightly regulated which requires an Extremely picky capillary system. Otherwise we could get infections…etc. Discontinuous-Spleen and Bone they must be open to allow for large passage such as WBC, RBC, and filtration to occur.
ConceptBrain capillaries are continuous
Slide (1)
169
Within the spleen, blood passes through specialized capillaries before entering the splenic cords and sinusoids. Which of the following best describes the type and structural characteristics of these capillaries?
  1. A. Continuous capillaries lined by endothelial cells with tight junctions and a continuous basal lamina
  2. B. Fenestrated capillaries with diaphragms and an intact basal lamina for selective filtration
  3. C. Sinusoidal capillaries with discontinuous endothelium and discontinuous basal lamina allowing passage of blood cells
  4. D. Discontinuous capillaries with continuous endothelium but interrupted basal lamina
  5. E. Arteriovenous anastomoses allowing direct flow from arterioles to venules without capillary beds
AnswerC. Sinusoidal capillaries with discontinuous endothelium and discontinuous basal lamina allowing passage of blood cells
WhySplenic sinusoids are discontinuous capillaries with gapped endothelium and a fragmented basal lamina, so whole blood cells can move between cords and lumen.
ConceptSpleen sinusoids: discontinuous endothelium and basal lamina pass blood cells
Slides (2)
170
Both the exocrine and endocrine portions of the pancreas are highly vascularized. Which of the following best describes the type of capillaries supplying the islets of Langerhans?
  1. A. Continuous capillaries with tight junctions and continuous basal lamina, restricting molecular exchange
  2. B. Fenestrated capillaries with pores and diaphragms that facilitate rapid hormone diffusion into the bloodstream
  3. C. Sinusoidal capillaries with discontinuous endothelium and absent basal lamina, permitting blood cell passage
  4. D. Discontinuous capillaries with continuous endothelium but fragmented basal lamina
  5. E. Lymphatic capillaries draining secretory products from the exocrine acini
AnswerB. Fenestrated capillaries with pores and diaphragms that facilitate rapid hormone diffusion into the bloodstream
WhyEndocrine islets release hormones into fenestrated capillaries, whose diaphragm-covered pores over a continuous basal lamina permit rapid diffusion of hormones into blood.
ConceptPancreatic islets are supplied by fenestrated capillaries
Slides (2)
171
Which vessel wall structure best supports its primary function in maintaining continuous blood flow during both systole and diastole?
  1. A. Elastic artery: thick tunica media with many elastic lamellae
  2. B. Muscular artery: thin media and thick adventitia
  3. C. Arteriole: single layer of endothelial cells only
  4. D. Vein: thick tunica media with abundant smooth muscle
AnswerA. Elastic artery: thick tunica media with many elastic lamellae
WhyElastic arteries have a thick media of many elastic lamellae that stretch in systole and recoil in diastole, keeping blood flowing between heartbeats.
Explanation from the source
Elastic arteries, such as the aorta, have many elastic lamellae in the tunica media that expand during systole and recoil during diastole, helping to maintain blood pressure and a more uniform flow of blood. (Junqueira’s Basic Histology)
ConceptElastic arteries' lamellae maintain continuous flow in systole and diastole
Slides (2)
172High-yield
Why do large arteries and veins contain vasa vasorum within their tunica adventitia?
  1. A. To drain lymph from surrounding tissues
  2. B. To supply oxygen and nutrients to outer vessel wall layers
  3. C. To anchor the vessel to adjacent structures
  4. D. To monitor changes in blood pressure
AnswerB. To supply oxygen and nutrients to outer vessel wall layers
WhyLarge vessel walls are too thick for diffusion from the lumen, so vasa vasorum in the adventitia supply oxygen and nutrients to the outer layers.
Explanation from the source
In large vessels, the tunica adventitia contains small blood vessels (vasa vasorum) that supply the outer wall, since diffusion from the lumen is insufficient for these cells. (Junqueira’s Basic Histology)
ConceptVasa vasorum supply the outer wall of large vessels
Slide (1)
173High-yield
The ability of muscular arteries to direct blood to specific organs depends mainly on which structural feature?
  1. A. Abundant collagen in adventitia
  2. B. Multiple smooth-muscle layers in the tunica media
  3. C. Fenestrated endothelium
  4. D. Lack of elastic fibers
AnswerB. Multiple smooth-muscle layers in the tunica media
WhyMuscular (distributing) arteries have many smooth-muscle layers in the media, whose tone adjusts lumen size to direct blood to specific organs.
Explanation from the source
Muscular arteries have a prominent tunica media composed largely of smooth muscle that allows regulation of blood flow to organs. (Junqueira’s Basic Histology)
ConceptMuscular arteries distribute blood via many smooth-muscle layers in media
Slide (1)
174
A large vessel shows a thin tunica media and a thick tunica adventitia with collagen and smooth muscle bundles. What is the primary functional role of this wall design?
  1. A. Resist high pulsatile pressures
  2. B. Provide structural support and store large blood volumes under low pressure
  3. C. Regulate flow into capillary beds
  4. D. Permit diffusion and gas exchange
AnswerB. Provide structural support and store large blood volumes under low pressure
WhyLarge veins carry blood at low pressure, so a thin media and thick collagenous adventitia give support while the wide lumen stores large blood volumes.
Explanation from the source
Veins have thinner walls, a well-developed tunica adventitia, and valves that prevent backflow of blood under low pressure serving as capacitance vessels.(Junqueira’s Basic Histology)
ConceptLarge vein wall: thin media, thick adventitia for low-pressure capacitance
175
Loss of the vasa vasorum in large arteries (e.g. tertiary syphilis) results in:
  1. A. Aneurysm formation
  2. B. Hypertension
  3. C. Aortic valve stenosis
  4. D. Myocardial infarction
AnswerA. Aneurysm formation
WhyVasa vasorum nourish the outer media of large arteries; losing them, as in tertiary syphilis, causes ischemic necrosis that weakens the wall into an aneurysm.
Explanation from the source
Ischemic necrosis of tunica media → wall weakening → aneurysm
ConceptLoss of vasa vasorum causes ischemic media and aneurysm
176
Individuals with Marfan syndrome have mutations in the fibrillin gene and commonly experience aortic aneurysm. What portion of the arterial wall is most likely to be affected by the malformed fibrillin?
  1. A. Endothelium
  2. B. Tunica intima
  3. C. Tunica media
  4. D. Tunica adventitia
  5. E. Vasa vasorum
AnswerC. Tunica media
WhyFibrillin is the microfibril scaffold for elastin, and the aorta's elastic lamellae lie in the tunica media, so Marfan syndrome weakens the media and predisposes to aneurysm.
ConceptMarfan fibrillin defect weakens the tunica media of the aorta
Slide (1)
177High-yield
Which of the following describes the structure most likely damaged in this patient?
  1. A) Vessels which arise from blind endings and have one-way valves
  2. B) Forces blood at high pressure into large elastic vessels
  3. C) Vessels which carry blood away from the heart and have a thick layer of smooth muscle
  4. D) Vessels which carry blood towards the heart which have one way valves
AnswerA. Vessels which arise from blind endings and have one-way valves
WhyRemoving axillary nodes damages lymphatic vessels, which begin as blind-ended capillaries and carry lymph through valved vessels, so arm lymph drainage fails.
Explanation from the source
Lymphatic vessels for the arm are vulnerable to damage during mastectomies for breast cancer treatment. The destroyed lymphatic drainage causes lymphedema, which is local swelling caused by increased lymph in the tissues.
ConceptPost-mastectomy arm lymphedema: lymphatics are blind-ended with valves
Slides (2)
178
What is the function of precapillary sphincters in the microcirculation?
  1. A) Control the flow of blood from veins to capillaries
  2. B) Regulate the volume of blood flowing through the arterioles
  3. C) Act as "switches" to regulate blood flow into the capillary beds
  4. D) Prevent blood flow through metarterioles
AnswerC. Act as "switches" to regulate blood flow into the capillary beds
WhyPrecapillary sphincters are smooth-muscle rings at capillary origins that open or close like switches to regulate blood flow into capillary beds.
Explanation from the source
Explanation: Precapillary sphincters are bands of smooth muscle located at the entry of capillaries, which open or close to regulate blood flow into the capillary beds based on the needs of the tissues.
ConceptPrecapillary sphincters act as switches controlling capillary-bed flow

What is A? What type of artery is this? Take note of the appearance of the media! Do we see many or few elastic fibers?

What type of artery is this? How do you know?

Correct key: Aorta (elastic artery). Thick media of many wavy elastic lamellae with thin adventitia = large elastic artery/aorta; the long list of other keys are the answers to the deck's later, different picture slides (units 62–146).
WhyA thick media made largely of many wavy elastic lamellae with a relatively thin adventitia identifies a large elastic artery, the aorta.
Explanation from the source
The largest arteries contain considerable elastic material and expand with blood when the heart contracts. A transverse section through part of a large elastic artery shows a thick media (M) consisting largely of many well-developed elastic lamellae. Strong pressure of blood pulsating into such arteries during systole expands the arterial wall, reducing the pressure and allowing strong blood flow to continue during diastole. The intima (I) of the empty aorta is typically folded, and the dense irregular connective tissue of the adventitia (A) is thinner than the media.
ConceptLM elastic artery (aorta): thick media of wavy elastic lamellae

231Borderline
Which statement best explains how elastic fibers and lamellae contribute to the mechanical function of connective tissue?
  1. A) They form rigid scaffolds that prevent deformation under stress.
  2. B) They enable tissues such as arteries and lungs to stretch under pressure and recoil, maintaining continuous flow and ventilation.
  3. C) They store calcium ions for rapid release during contraction.
  4. D) They provide compressive resistance through hydrated proteoglycan aggregates.
AnswerB) They enable tissues such as arteries and lungs to stretch under pressure and recoil, maintaining continuous flow and ventilation.
WhyElastic fibers of elastin on fibrillin microfibrils stretch under pressure and recoil, keeping blood flow continuous in arteries and driving passive expiration in lungs.
Explanation from the source
Elastic fibers and lamellae, composed of elastin deposited on fibrillin microfibrils, create a resilient network that allows tissues to stretch and return to their original shape. Covalent desmosine cross‑links between elastin molecules give these fibers their rubberlike properties. In structures like arterial walls, lungs, and vertebral ligaments, this elasticity maintains functional recoil—essential for sustaining blood flow and ventilation without structural damage.
General connective-tissue question (elastic fibers, Foundations 2); the correct option uses elastic arteries/lungs as the example (HIST-7B elastic arteries).

Recognising capillaries (capillary loops) is HIST-7B vessel content, but the setting and the distractors (Meissner corpuscles, free nerve endings) are integument (skin), which is OUT.

A 59-year-old diabetic woman complains of declining visual acuity. Funduscopic examination of the patient’s retina reveals capillary microaneurysms and small hemorrhage. Loss of which of the following components from the capillary wall is the most likely cause of early-stage diabetic retinopathy in this patient?
  1. (A) Basal lamina
  2. (B) Elastic fibers
  3. (C) Endothelial cells
  4. (D) Pericytes
  5. (E) Smooth muscle cells
AnswerD. Pericytes
WhyPericytes stabilize capillary endothelium; in diabetes they are lost from retinal capillaries, which then form microaneurysms and small hemorrhages.
Explanation from the source
Pericytes are contractile cells associated with some continuous capillaries and postcapillary venules. Their branching cytoplasmic processes surround endothelial cells to provide support and stability. Loss of pericytes in patients with diabetes mellitus is believed to play a key role in the pathogenesis of early-stage diabetic retinopathy. Without the support of pericytes, the retinal capillaries form microaneurysms and small hemorrhages that are evident on funduscopic examination. These lesions do not usually impair vision. However, after many years, diabetic retinopathy becomes proliferative. Delicate new blood vessels grow toward the vitreous body, resulting in a reduction or loss of vision. Injury to the other vascular wall components does not lead to the development of diabetic retinopathy. Keywords: Diabetic retinopathy, pericyte
Needs diabetic retinopathy pathology; the CP1 part is pericytes of the capillary wall.
Slide (1)
234Borderline
A 39-year-old immigrant presents to the emergency room with a rapid pulse and cold clammy skin. A CT scan of the thorax reveals dilation of the ascending aorta. The fluorescent treponemal antibody (FTA) test is positive. The patient is subsequently diagnosed with a syphilitic aneurysm. Which of the following mechanisms of disease is the most likely cause of aortic aneurysm in this patient?
  1. (A) Atherosclerosis
  2. (B) Cystic medial necrosis
  3. (C) Endarteritis of the vasa vasorum
  4. (D) Fibrillin gene mutation
  5. (E) Systemic hypertension
Answer(C) Endarteritis of the vasa vasorum
WhyTertiary syphilis causes obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum, starving the outer aortic media, which necroses and weakens into an ascending aortic aneurysm.
Explanation from the source
The answer is C: Endarteritis of the vasa vasorum. Syphilis is a sexual transmitted disease caused by the bacterium Treponema pallidum. At one time, syphilis was the most common cause of aortic aneurysm. Syphilitic aneurysms typically affect the ascending aorta, where infection causes endarteritis of the vasa vasorum. Ischemia caused by obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum causes focal necrosis and loss of structural integrity in the tunica media. Blood flow during systole eventually stretches the aorta to form an aneurysmal dilation. As mentioned above, patients with Marfan syndrome are also at risk for dissecting aortic aneurysm. They have fibrillin gene mutations (choice D) that cause cystic medial necrosis in the tunica media (choice B). Atherosclerosis (choice A) and systemic hypertension (choice E) are important risk factors for aneurysms, but they would not be the most likely cause of an aneurysm affecting the ascending aorta in a woman with a history of untreated syphilis. Keywords: Syphilitic aneurysm, vasa vasorum
Needs the pathology of syphilitic aortitis (beyond the course); the in-scope part is the vasa vasorum of large vessels.
235Borderline
A 30-year-old man suffers a sudden and severe headache during a basketball game and loses consciousness. The patient is rushed to the hospital but expires 2 days later. Autopsy demonstrates a massive subarachnoid hemorrhage arising from a balloon-like outpouching near the origin of the posterior cerebral artery. Which of the following mechanisms of disease best explains the pathogenesis of this patient’s saccular (berry) aneurysm?
  1. (A) Cystic medial necrosis
  2. (B) Deficiency of smooth muscle
  3. (C) Endarteritis of the vasa vasorum
  4. (D) Formation of atheromatous plaque
  5. (E) Platelet aggregation and degranulation
Answer(B) Deficiency of smooth muscle
WhyCerebral berry aneurysms arise where the arterial media has a congenital gap in smooth muscle at circle of Willis branch points, letting the wall balloon.
Explanation from the source
The answer is B: Deficiency of smooth muscle. Saccular aneurysms, also referred to as berry aneurysms, are balloon-like outpouchings of the arterial wall. They are the most common type of aneurysm affecting cerebral arteries. Berry aneurysms typically occur at branch points in the circle of Willis. At these locations, the wall of the artery may be weak, owing to a congenital deficiency of smooth muscle. Rupture of a berry aneurysm leads to catastrophic subarachnoid hemorrhage. Cystic medial necrosis and formation of atheromatous plaque (choices A and D) are associated with aortic aneurysms. Endarteritis of the vasa vasorum (choice C) is associated with syphilitic aneurysms of the ascending aorta. Keywords: Saccular aneurysm
Needs the pathology of cerebral berry aneurysms (beyond the course); the in-scope part is the smooth-muscle tunica media of muscular arteries.

  1. (A) Basal lamina

Explanation from the source
The answer is D: Pericytes. Pericytes are contractile cells associated with some continuous capillaries and postcapillary venules. Their branching cytoplasmic processes surround endothelial cells to provide support and stability. Loss of pericytes in patients with diabetes mellitus is believed to play a key role in the pathogenesis of early-stage diabetic retinopathy. Without the support of pericytes, the retinal capillaries form microaneurysms and small hemorrhages that are evident on funduscopic examination. These lesions do not usually impair vision. However, after many years, diabetic retinopathy becomes proliferative. Delicate new blood vessels grow toward the vitreous body, resulting in a reduction or loss of vision. Injury to the other vascular wall components does not lead to the development of diabetic retinopathy. Keywords: Diabetic retinopathy, pericyte
Needs the pathology of diabetic retinopathy (pericyte loss, beyond the course); the in-scope part is pericytes of the capillary wall.

237Borderline
A 48-year-old woman presents with a painful, raised, red lesion on the dorsal surface of her right hand. Histologic examination of a skin biopsy reveals a benign tumor of the glomus body. Which of the following best describes the structure of a normal glomus body in the dermis of the skin?
  1. (A) Arteriovenous shunt
  2. (B) Capillary loop in the dermal papillae
  3. (C) Deep dermal venous plexus
  4. (D) Dilated lymphatic channel
  5. (E) Vascularized skin wart
Answer(A) Arteriovenous shunt
WhyA glomus body is a coiled, richly innervated arteriovenous shunt in the dermis of fingertips that bypasses capillaries for temperature regulation.
Explanation from the source
The answer is A: Arteriovenous shunt. Glomus bodies are neuromyoarterial receptors that are sensitive to temperature and are involved in body temperature regulation. The glomus body consists of an arteriovenous (AV) shunt surrounded by a richly innervated connective tissue capsule. Sympathetic stimulation of the glomus apparatus (body) causes vasoconstriction of the AV shunt, forcing blood to flow through the adjoining capillary bed. A glomus tumor is a benign tumor of the glomus body that is often extremely painful. The lesions are small, usually smaller than 1 cm in diameter. None of the other choices describe histologic features of the glomus body. Keywords: Glomus tumor, glomus body
Glomus body / glomus tumor of skin is beyond the course (integument); the in-scope part is the arteriovenous shunt of the microvasculature.

238Borderline
A kidney biopsy is stained with the trichrome reagent and examined in the pathology department (shown in the image). Blood that circulates through the glomerular capillary tuft within the renal corpuscle (indicated by the arrow) drains into which of the following renal blood vessels?
  1. (A) Afferent arteriole
  2. (B) Efferent arteriole
  3. (C) Peritubular capillary
  4. (D) Vasa recta
  5. (E) Venule
Answer(B) Efferent arteriole
WhyThe glomerulus is an arterial portal system: its capillary tuft drains into the efferent arteriole, which then feeds peritubular capillaries or vasa recta.
Explanation from the source
The answer is B: Efferent arteriole. Capillary networks typically receive blood from precapillary arterioles and are drained by postcapillary venules. However, this standard arrangement is altered in the kidney. Here, an arteriole is interposed between two capillary networks. Afferent arterioles (choice A) supply blood to the glomerulus (the capillary network within the renal corpuscle) and efferent arterioles drain blood away. The efferent arteriole leaves the renal corpuscle and branches into a secondary capillary network, either (1) peritubular capillaries (choice C) that envelope the tubules or (2) vasa recta (choice D) that surround the limbs of the loop of Henle. The peritubular capillaries and vasa recta are drained by venules (choice E). Another special capillary arrangement occurs in portal systems of the liver and pituitary. In the liver, the portal vein (containing blood from intestinal capillaries) branches into a sinusoid capillary network between cords of hepatocytes. Hepatic sinusoids drain via hepatic veins to the inferior vena cava. Keywords: Kidney, glomerulus
Kidney histology is OUT; the in-scope idea is the microvascular pattern of a capillary bed drained by an arteriole (arterial portal system, HIST-7B).

Which of the following describes the correct sequence leading to atherosclerosis?
  1. a. Injury to endothelial cells → foam cells form → LDL enters the bloodstream → collagen cap forms → vessel occlusion.
  2. b. LDL enters the intimal space → foam cells form → endothelial cells become permeable → collagen cap forms → macrophages engulf oxLDL.
  3. c. Injury to endothelial cells increases permeability → LDL enters intimal space and oxidizes → macrophages engulf oxLDL → foam cells form → plaque formation and partial vessel occlusion.
  4. d. Foam cells form → macrophages engulf LDL → LDL enters the bloodstream → plaque forms → thrombus breaks oﬀ, causing vessel occlusion.
AnswerC. Injury to endothelial cells increases permeability → LDL enters intimal space and oxidizes → macrophages engulf oxLDL → foam cells form → plaque formation and partial vessel occlusion.
WhyEndothelial injury raises permeability, LDL enters and oxidizes in the intima, macrophages engulf it as foam cells, and a plaque forms and narrows the lumen.
Explanation from the source
yes, eventually LDLR is downregulated, this leads to less LDL being cleared from the blood contributing to high LDL serum levels
Atherosclerosis is an official Topic 7 clinical correlate (endothelial injury/dysfunction, foam cells, intimal plaque → HIST-7B/7L); the source objective ("link between LDL levels, LDL oxidation and atherosclerosis") is CP2 lipoprotein biochemistry.

HIST-7L Circulatory lab

116 questions · 91 concepts · 27 high-yield
Learning questions 9

Identifying vessels on a slide

L1Learning
In a neurovascular bundle, how do you tell the artery from its companion vein?
  1. A. Artery: thick muscular wall around a smaller, round, regular lumen
    Vein: thin wall around a larger, irregular, often collapsed lumen
  2. B. Artery: thin wall around a larger, irregular, often collapsed lumen
    Vein: thick muscular wall around a smaller, round, regular lumen
  3. C. Artery: thick wall around an irregular, collapsed lumen
    Vein: thin wall around a small, round, open lumen
AnswerA. Artery: thick muscular wall around a smaller, round, regular lumen
Vein: thin wall around a larger, irregular, often collapsed lumen
WhyThe artery is the smaller vessel with the thicker wall and a round, regular lumen; the companion vein has a larger, irregular lumen and a much lower wall-to-lumen ratio.
Explanation

The lab neurovascular bundle shows a muscular (distributing) artery and a medium-sized vein side by side. The artery's thick smooth-muscle media holds its lumen open and round, and its internal elastic lamina is visible even in H&E. The vein's thin wall lets its lumen collapse into an irregular shape. In veins the ratio of wall thickness to lumen size is much smaller than in arteries.

  • The second option swaps artery and vein.
  • The third gives the artery a collapsed lumen and the vein a small round one, both reversed.
Slides (2)
L2Learning
In the same neurovascular bundle, how is the nerve told apart from the artery and the vein?
  1. A. It has valves and an irregular lumen
  2. B. It is solid, with no lumen
  3. C. It has a thin wall and a collapsed lumen
AnswerB. It is solid, with no lumen
WhyThe nerve is a solid round bundle of nerve fibres with no lumen; both vessels are hollow.
Explanation

The lab describes the nerve bundle as "the solid round structures next to the artery". In section it looks like a round, finely textured plug wrapped in a thin connective-tissue sheath (perineurium), with no central space and no blood.

  • Valves and an irregular lumen point to a vein.
  • A thin wall with a collapsed lumen is also the vein (or a lymphatic).
Slides (2)
L3Learning
An elastic-stained section shows a very thick vessel wall in which almost the whole media is packed with dozens of parallel, wavy, dark elastic lamellae, with only a thin layer of connective tissue outside. What vessel is it?
  1. A. Elastic artery
  2. B. Large vein
  3. C. Muscular artery
AnswerA. Elastic artery
WhyA media filled throughout with wavy elastic lamellae is the signature of an elastic artery such as the aorta.
Explanation

This is the lab's classic elastic artery (the aorta in an elastic stain). Steps: the wall is thick and its thickest layer is the media → an artery; the media is a stack of dark wavy lamellae rather than muscle → an elastic artery. It looks like a patch of curly ramen.

  • A muscular artery shows one dark wavy line (internal elastic lamina) at the inner edge, with smooth muscle behind it.
  • A large vein has a thin media and a thick adventitia with scattered elastic fibres, not stacked lamellae.
Slide (1)
L4Learning
An elastic-stained section shows a vessel wall with one sharp, dark, wavy line just under the endothelium, a thick band of closely packed smooth muscle cells, a second, less distinct dark line at its outer edge, and then collagenous connective tissue. What vessel is it?
  1. A. Medium-sized vein
  2. B. Elastic artery
  3. C. Muscular artery
AnswerC. Muscular artery
WhyA crisp internal elastic lamina, a thick smooth-muscle media and an outer external elastic lamina identify a muscular artery.
Explanation

The wavy line under the endothelium is the internal elastic lamina; the second line is the external elastic lamina; the media between them is smooth muscle, the thickest layer. A Weigert-stained artery from a neurovascular bundle looks the same.

  • An elastic artery would show lamellae throughout the media, not just two lines bordering it.
  • A medium-sized vein has only a few muscle layers and a thick adventitia, and usually no clear elastic laminae.
Slide (1)
L5Learning
A high-magnification H&E view of a vessel wall shows an endothelium with a thin subendothelial layer, a thin media of only a few scattered smooth muscle cells, and a much thicker, pale outer layer of loose collagen that forms most of the wall. What vessel is it?
  1. A. Medium-sized vein
  2. B. Arteriole
  3. C. Muscular artery
AnswerA. Medium-sized vein
WhyThickest layer adventitia with a media of a few muscle cells → vein; plain collagen without muscle bundles in the adventitia → medium-sized vein.
Explanation

The lab hint for this image: "There are 3 layers in this high-magnification view. Which layer is the thickest?" Thickest layer adventitia → vein. A medium vein's media is a few layers of circular smooth muscle; its adventitia is well-developed collagenous connective tissue. A large vein's adventitia would also be crowded with bundles of longitudinal smooth muscle.

  • A muscular artery has the media as its thickest layer and a prominent internal elastic lamina.
  • An arteriole is tiny, with a narrow lumen ringed by 1–3 muscle layers and almost no adventitia.
Slide (1)
L6Learning
An H&E section of a large vessel wall shows a thin intima and a thin media, while most of the wall is an outer coat crowded with large bundles of smooth muscle cut in cross-section, with small blood vessels among them. What vessel is it?
  1. A. Medium-sized vein
  2. B. Large vein
  3. C. Elastic artery
AnswerB. Large vein
WhyA thick adventitia packed with longitudinal smooth-muscle bundles (cut across in a transverse section) and vasa vasorum is the hallmark of a large vein.
Explanation

Thickest layer adventitia → vein; smooth-muscle bundles running lengthwise in that adventitia → a large vein, such as the inferior vena cava. The bundles crowding the adventitia are smooth muscle fibres, not collagen.

  • The aorta has a thick media of elastic lamellae and a relatively thin adventitia.
  • A medium-sized vein has a collagenous adventitia without these large longitudinal muscle bundles.
Slide (1)
L7Learning
Two elastic-stained sections of great vessels are compared. In (a) a thick middle coat is packed with dark wavy lamellae and the outer coat is thin. In (b) the middle coat is thin and the outer coat is far thicker, with scattered elastic fibres. Which is which?
  1. A. (a) vena cava; (b) aorta
  2. B. (a) muscular artery; (b) medium-sized vein
  3. C. (a) aorta; (b) vena cava
AnswerC. (a) aorta; (b) vena cava
WhyThick elastic media → aorta (elastic artery); thick adventitia with a thin media → vena cava (large vein).
Explanation

The lab objective "aorta versus vena cava" comes down to which tunic is thickest. Aorta: pale thin intima, very thick media of concentric fenestrated elastic membranes, relatively thin adventitia with vasa vasorum. Vena cava: thin intima, narrow media of a few smooth-muscle layers, and the adventitia as the thickest coat (with longitudinal muscle bundles and vasa vasorum).

  • The swapped option reverses the two.
  • A muscular artery would show smooth muscle, not stacked lamellae, in its media.
Slide (1)
L8Learning
In connective tissue, a small round vessel has a narrow lumen about as wide as its wall is thick; the endothelium sits directly on one to three layers of circular smooth muscle, with no visible elastic lamina and only a wisp of adventitia. What is it?
  1. A. Arteriole
  2. B. Muscular artery
  3. C. Venule
AnswerA. Arteriole
WhyA narrow lumen ringed by 1–3 layers of smooth muscle, with no elastic lamina and almost no adventitia, is an arteriole.
Explanation

The lecture's arteriole micrograph labels exactly this: endothelium (E), intima (I), a media (M) of a few smooth muscle cells, and a thin adventitia (Ad). Its giveaway is a thick, muscular wall around a narrow lumen.

  • A venule is wider, with a thin wall of endothelium and pericytes and no continuous muscle coat.
  • A muscular artery is much larger, with many muscle layers and a prominent internal elastic lamina.
Slide (1)
L9Learning
Beside a small artery, a small vein, a venule and an arteriole lie irregular, very thin-walled spaces lined only by flat endothelium. They hold a little pale pink fluid but no red blood cells. What are they?
  1. A. Sinusoidal capillaries
  2. B. Lymphatic vessels
  3. C. Postcapillary venules
AnswerB. Lymphatic vessels
WhyThin-walled, irregular channels with no red cells lying among blood vessels are lymphatic vessels (asterisks on the lab slide).
Explanation

The lab ID exercise marks these with asterisks next to the labelled small vein, small artery, venule and arteriole. Their wall is just endothelium with a little connective tissue, the outline is irregular, and the lumen holds lightly staining proteinaceous lymph, perhaps a few lymphocytes, but never red blood cells.

  • Postcapillary venules also have very thin walls, but they contain red blood cells (the labelled venule in the same field does).
  • Sinusoids occur only in particular organs (marrow, liver, spleen) and carry blood.

[Question 16] A 68-year-old man with a history of smoking and hypertension suffers sudden cardiac arrest and expires. The patient’s thoracic aorta is examined at autopsy. Identify layer “A” (shown in the image). [Question 18] A section of the aorta obtained from the patient described in Question 16 is treated with Verhoff van Gieson stain to visualize connective tissue elements in the tunica media (shown in the image). The dark wavy lines represent which of the following histologic structures?
  1. (A) Collagen fibers
  2. (B) Elastic lamellae
  3. (C) Nerve fibers
  4. (D) Reticular fibers
  5. (E) Smooth muscle fibers
AnswerB. Elastic lamellae
WhyVerhoeff stain colors elastin black, so the dark, wavy, concentric bands in the aortic media are fenestrated elastic lamellae, the hallmark of an elastic artery.
Explanation from the source
Elastic lamellae (sheets) are found in the tunica media of large elastic arteries. These lamellae are fenestrated to facilitate diffusion of oxygen and nutrients from the blood. Elastic lamellae are arranged in concentric layers. In cross section, these sheets appear as wavy bands, interspersed with layers of smooth muscle (not visible in this preparation). Collagen fibers and reticular fibers (choices A and D) may be present in the tunica media, but they are not visible in this preparation. Large elastic arteries buffer the pulsatile (intermittent) blood flow leaving the heart. None of the other structures exhibit histologic features of elastic lamellae in the tunica media. Keywords: Arteries, elastic lamellae
ConceptDark wavy lines in aortic media (Verhoeff stain) = elastic lamellae

[Question 23] A 69-year-old woman presents with crushing substernal chest pain and nausea. She is treated with plasminogen activator, oxygen, and morphine sulfate. The patient subsequently becomes hypotensive and suffers cardiac arrest. A cross-section of the patient’s anterior interventricular artery is examined at autopsy (shown in the image). Which of the following best describes the pathologic changes visible in this specimen? [Question 24] Microscopic examination of the autopsy specimen described in Question 23 at high magnification would most likely reveal which of the following pathologic changes?
  1. (A) Acute inflammation in the tunica adventitia
  2. (B) Bacterial colonies in the tunica media
  3. (C) Cystic medial necrosis in the tunica intima
  4. (D) Lipid deposition and smooth muscle cell hyperplasia in the tunica intima
  5. (E) Obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum
AnswerD. Lipid deposition and smooth muscle cell hyperplasia in the tunica intima
WhyAn atheroma is a plaque in the tunica intima of extracellular lipid, foam cells and proliferating smooth muscle cells with a fibrous cap; cystic medial necrosis and endarteritis are different lesions.
Explanation from the source
The classic lesion of atherosclerosis is best described as a fibroinflammatory lipid plaque (atheroma) in the tunica intima. Inflammatory and immune cells, hyperplastic smooth muscle fibers, cholesterol crystals, and other connective tissue components accumulate progressively in the tunica intima of large elastic and medium-sized muscular arteries. Microscopic examination of the atheroma reveals pools of extracellular lipid and numerous lipid-laden macrophages (foam cells). Atherosclerosis is not an infectious disease process or an acute inflammatory reaction (choices A and B). Cystic medial necrosis (choice C) is present in the tunica media in cases of dissecting aortic aneurysm. Obliterative endarteritis (choice E) describes the effects of tertiary syphilis. Keywords: Ischemic heart disease, atherosclerosis
ConceptAtheroma: intimal lipid deposition and smooth-muscle proliferation

[Question 27] A neurovascular bundle from the upper limb is collected at autopsy, and the tissue sections are processed using Weigert elastica staining reagent. The wall of a blood vessel is examined by light microscopy (shown in the image). Based on these histologic findings, this blood vessel is best identified as which of the following? [Question 28] Sections from the autopsy specimen described in Question 27 are processed using a different histochemical stain and examined by light microscopy (shown in the image). The layer of the artery indicated by the double arrow is primarily composed of which of the following vascular components?
  1. (A) Collagen fibers
  2. (B) Elastic lamellae
  3. (C) Fibroblasts
  4. (D) Reticular fibers
  5. (E) Smooth muscle cells
AnswerE. Smooth muscle cells
WhyThe media of a muscular artery consists almost entirely of circular smooth muscle cells, which also secrete its collagen and elastic fibres.
Explanation from the source
The tunica media in medium arteries is composed almost entirely of smooth muscle fibers. As large elastic arteries undergo branching morphogenesis and their diameter becomes smaller, the tunica media exhibits a gradual reduction in elastic tissue, and a corresponding increase in smooth muscle cells. Smooth muscle fibers are the predominant structural and functional component of the tunica media in medium-sized muscular arteries. Contraction of smooth muscle cells in medium arteries helps maintain systemic blood pressure. Collagen and reticular fibers (choices A and D) are interspersed between smooth muscle cells, but they are not the major structural component of the tunica media. Elastic lamellae (choice B) and fibroblasts (choice C) are not present in the tunica media of medium arteries. Smooth muscle cells synthesize the extracellular matrix components (including collagen and reticular fibers and ground substance) present in the tunica media of medium arteries. Keywords: Muscular arteries, tunica media, smooth muscle cells
ConceptMuscular artery media is mainly smooth muscle cells

[Question 41] A 56-year-old man presents with painful dilated knots in both legs. Ulcers are noted over some of the knots. A photograph of the patient is shown. Which of the following structures in the legs is most likely affected in this patient? [Question 42] A skin biopsy is taken from the patient described in Question 41. Microscopic examination reveals blood vessels in the subcutaneous tissue (shown in the image). Identify the structures indicated by the arrows.
  1. (A) Arteriovenous shunt
  2. (B) Lymphatic vessels
  3. (C) Smooth muscle fibers
  4. (D) Subendothelial connective tissue
  5. (E) Venous valves
AnswerE. Venous valves
WhyThe thin flaps projecting into the vein lumen are venous valves, endothelium-covered folds of the intima reinforced by collagen and elastic fibers; their incompetence underlies varicose veins.
Explanation from the source
Valves are characteristic features of medium-sized veins, in both superficial and deep veins. They are most numerous in the lower limb veins, because of the need to direct the flow of blood back to the heart against the force of gravity. Venous valves are cusp-like projections into the lumen of the vein. The valves are covered by endothelium, and they are strengthened by collagen and elastic fibers. They have cup-like valvular sinuses that fill from above. The valve cusps occlude the lumen of the vein when they are full, so as to prevent reflux of blood and ensure that the venous blood continues to flow in one direction back toward the heart. Keywords: Varicose veins, venous valves
ConceptVenous valves in a subcutaneous vein (H&E micrograph)

WhyElastic stain shows a wavy internal elastic lamina, a media of circular smooth muscle, and a distinct external elastic lamina, identifying a muscular artery rather than an elastic artery.
Explanation from the source
Diagram and photomicrograph of a muscular artery. a. In this schematic diagram of a muscular artery, the cellular and extracellular components are labeled. Note the distribution of cellular components in all three tunics and the locations of external and internal elastic membranes. b. In this photomicrograph of a cross-section through a muscular artery in Weigert’s resorcin-fuchsin elastic stain preparation, note two distinct layers of elastic tissue: a wavy-appearing inner layer of the internal elastic membrane and a well-deﬁned outer layer of the external elastic membrane. The relatively thick tunica media enclosed by the internal and external elastic membranes consists mainly of circularly arranged smooth muscle cells, collagen, and ﬁne elastic ﬁbers. The tunica intima in this preparation is indiscernible; the tunica adventitia is well deﬁned, consisting mostly of connective tissue with collagen and elastic ﬁbers. ×175.
ConceptMuscular artery in elastic stain: distinct internal and external elastic laminae

A 52-year-old man with a history of active pulmonary tuberculosis presents with difficulty breathing, chest pain, and abdominal discomfort. Physical examination reveals hepatomegaly, ascites, and pitting edema of the legs (signs of right-sided heart failure). Cardiac auscultation demonstrates a pericardial friction rub. The patient is subsequently diagnosed with constrictive pericarditis caused by spread of his mycobacterial infection to the pericardial cavity. Which of the following structures of the heart was most directly and severely affected by this patient’s infectious disease?
  1. (A) Conducting system of the heart
  2. (B) Coronary arteries
  3. (C) Endocardium
  4. (D) Myocardium
  5. (E) Pericardium
Answer(E) Pericardium
WhyIn constrictive pericarditis infection scars and fuses the visceral and parietal pericardium, obliterating the pericardial cavity and restricting cardiac filling.
Explanation from the source
The answer is E: Pericardium. The pericardium is a sac that surrounds and protects the heart. It is composed of an outer fibrous pericardium and an inner serous pericardium. The potential space between visceral and parietal layers of the serous pericardium defines the pericardial cavity. Infections within the pericardial cavity cause acute or chronic pericarditis. An exuberant healing response to pericarditis can obliterate the pericardial cavity. In these patients, visceral and parietal layers of the pericardium are fused together by dense deposits of collagenous scar tissue. As a result, the heart is compressed and cardiac filling is restricted. This condition is referred to as constrictive pericarditis. Keywords: Constrictive pericarditis, pericardium
ConceptConstrictive pericarditis primarily affects the pericardium

Heart tissue obtained at autopsy is embedded, sectioned at 6 μm, and stained with H&E (shown in the image). Identify the structure within the rectangular box.
  1. (A) Adipose tissue
  2. (B) Cardiac muscle fibers
  3. (C) Loose connective tissue
  4. (D) Purkinje fibers
  5. (E) Smooth muscle fibers
Answer(D) Purkinje fibers
WhyThe boxed cells are Purkinje fibres: much larger than neighbouring cardiomyocytes, with pale glycogen-rich cytoplasm and sparse peripheral myofibrils.
Explanation from the source
The answer is D: Purkinje fibers. Purkinje fibers are components of the conducting system of the heart. They are found within the subendocardial connective tissue of the ventricles and along both sides of the interventricular septum. Purkinje fibers are modified cardiac myocytes that are specialized for the conduction of action potentials (impulses). They are considerably larger than typical cardiac muscle fibers. Their cytoplasm shows a sparse distribution of myofibrils, located primarily near the periphery of the cells. Abundant intracellular deposits of glycogen provide an important energy reserve for these metabolically active cells. Because the glycogen deposits are extracted during tissue processing, the cytoplasm of Purkinje fibers typically appears pale (washed-out). None of the other structures demonstrate histologic features of Purkinje cells. Keywords: Heart, Purkinje fibers
ConceptIdentify Purkinje fibres in boxed subendocardial region

A section of the aorta obtained from the patient described in Question 16 is treated with Verhoff van Gieson stain to visualize connective tissue elements in the tunica media (shown in the image). The dark wavy lines represent which of the following histologic structures?
  1. (A) Collagen fibers
  2. (B) Elastic lamellae
  3. (C) Nerve fibers
  4. (D) Reticular fibers
  5. (E) Smooth muscle fibers
Answer(B) Elastic lamellae
WhyVerhoeff stain colours elastin black, so the dark wavy concentric bands in the aortic media are fenestrated elastic lamellae of an elastic artery.
Explanation from the source
The answer is B: Elastic lamellae. Elastic lamellae (sheets) are found in the tunica media of large elastic arteries. These lamellae are fenestrated to facilitate diffusion of oxygen and nutrients from the blood. Elastic lamellae are arranged in concentric layers. In cross section, these sheets appear as wavy bands, interspersed with layers of smooth muscle (not visible in this preparation). Collagen fibers and reticular fibers (choices A and D) may be present in the tunica media, but they are not visible in this preparation. Large elastic arteries buffer the pulsatile (intermittent) blood flow leaving the heart. None of the other structures exhibit histologic features of elastic lamellae in the tunica media. Keywords: Arteries, elastic lamellae
ConceptDark wavy lines in aortic media (Verhoeff stain) = elastic lamellae

A 69-year-old woman presents with crushing substernal chest pain and nausea. She is treated with plasminogen activator, oxygen, and morphine sulfate. The patient subsequently becomes hypotensive and suffers cardiac arrest. A cross-section of the patient’s anterior interventricular artery is examined at autopsy (shown in the image). Which of the following best describes the pathologic changes visible in this specimen?
  1. (A) Acute arteritis
  2. (B) Aneurysmal dilation
  3. (C) Atherosclerosis
  4. (D) Thrombosis
  5. (E) Vasodilation
Answer(C) Atherosclerosis
WhyThe coronary lumen is narrowed by a thick, eccentric intimal plaque, the hallmark of atherosclerosis, which predisposes to thrombosis and myocardial infarction.
Explanation from the source
The answer is C: Atherosclerosis. Atherosclerosis is the most common acquired abnormality of large- and medium-sized arteries. Major complications of atherosclerosis, including intermittent claudication, abdominal aortic aneurysm, coronary artery disease, cerebrovascular disease, and peripheral vascular disease, account for more than half of the annual deaths in the United States. Chest pain is the major complaint of patients with coronary artery disease (also referred to as ischemic heart disease). The pain typically occurs in the substernal portion of the chest and may radiate to the left arm, jaw, and/ or epigastrium. Diabetes mellitus and hyperlipidemia are risk factors for atherosclerosis. The image shows atherosclerosis in the narrowed lumen. Thrombosis of an atherosclerotic plaque can result in ischemic necrosis of the dependent cardiac muscle (myocardial infarction). None of the other choices describe histologic features of atherosclerosis. Keywords: Atherosclerosis, myocardial infarction
ConceptNarrowed coronary artery with intimal plaque = atherosclerosis

296High-yield
Microscopic examination of the autopsy specimen described in Question 23 at high magnification would most likely reveal which of the following pathologic changes?
  1. (A) Acute inflammation in the tunica adventitia
  2. (B) Bacterial colonies in the tunica media
  3. (C) Cystic medial necrosis in the tunica intima
  4. (D) Lipid deposition and smooth muscle cell hyperplasia in the tunica intima
  5. (E) Obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum
Answer(D) Lipid deposition and smooth muscle cell hyperplasia in the tunica intima
WhyAn atheroma is an intimal plaque of extracellular lipid, foam cells and proliferating smooth muscle, so the change lies in the tunica intima, not the media or adventitia.
Explanation from the source
The answer is D: Lipid deposition and smooth muscle cell hyperplasia in the tunica intima. The classic lesion of atherosclerosis is best described as a fibroinflammatory lipid plaque (atheroma) in the tunica intima. Inflammatory and immune cells, hyperplastic smooth muscle fibers, cholesterol crystals, and other connective tissue components accumulate progressively in the tunica intima of large elastic and medium-sized muscular arteries. Microscopic examination of the atheroma reveals pools of extracellular lipid and numerous lipid-laden macrophages (foam cells). Atherosclerosis is not an infectious disease process or an acute inflammatory reaction (choices A and B). Cystic medial necrosis (choice C) is present in the tunica media in cases of dissecting aortic aneurysm. Obliterative endarteritis (choice E) describes the effects of tertiary syphilis. Keywords: Ischemic heart disease, atherosclerosis
ConceptAtheroma: intimal lipid deposition and smooth-muscle proliferation

A neurovascular bundle from the upper limb is collected at autopsy, and the tissue sections are processed using Weigert elastica staining reagent. The wall of a blood vessel is examined by light microscopy (shown in the image). Based on these histologic findings, this blood vessel is best identified as which of the following?
  1. (A) Arteriole
  2. (B) Elastic artery
  3. (C) Large vein
  4. (D) Muscular artery
  5. (E) Small artery
Answer(D) Muscular artery
WhyA muscular artery shows a prominent folded internal elastic lamina, a thick smooth-muscle media and a thinner external elastic lamina, unlike the many lamellae of an elastic artery.
Explanation from the source
The answer is D: Muscular artery. The arteries that conduct oxygenated blood from the heart to the microcirculation are traditionally grouped into three types based on their size and wall morphology. These types include (1) large or elastic arteries, (2) medium or muscular arteries, and (3) small arteries. The aorta and its larger branches and the pulmonary arteries are classified as large elastic arteries, since elastic lamellae constitute the major structural component of their tunica media. As these arteries branch, they are referred to as medium or muscular arteries. Examples of medium arteries include ulnar, popliteal, splenic, renal, and mesenteric arteries. The tunica intima is thinner in muscular arteries compared to elastic arteries. The internal elastic membrane is a prominent and characteristic feature of medium artery. Owing to the contraction of smooth muscle cells after death, internal elastic membranes typically appear as a folded line in histologic sections (shown in the image). An external elastic membrane is observed as a wavy line separating the tunica media from the tunica adventitia. None of the other types of blood vessels exhibit histologic features of medium arteries. Keywords: Arteries, muscular arteries
ConceptWeigert elastic stain: folded internal elastic lamina = muscular artery

298
A colon biopsy is examined in the pathology department (shown in the image). Identify the blood vessel located within the submucosa of the appendix.
  1. (A) Arteriole
  2. (B) Elastic artery
  3. (C) Medium artery
  4. (D) Small artery
  5. (E) Small vein
Answer(A) Arteriole
WhyAn arteriole has only one to a few concentric smooth-muscle layers and a lumen roughly as wide as its wall is thick, plus a thin internal elastic lamina.
Explanation from the source
The answer is A: Arteriole. Medium arteries branch repeatedly into smaller arteries. The smallest and most terminal branches of the arterial system are termed arterioles. The diameter of an arteriole is generally smaller than 0.5 mm. The lumen is as wide as the wall is thick. There are only one to five layers of smooth muscle fibers in the media of an arteriole. These muscle fibers are oriented in concentric rings around the vascular lumen. Internal elastic membranes are present in larger arterioles (as shown in the image and indicated by the arrow), but they are lacking in smaller arterioles. The adventitia is rather inconspicuous and blends with surrounding connective tissue. Arterioles feed capillary beds and, therefore, represent the beginnings of the microvasculature. Keywords: Arterioles
ConceptArteriole: few smooth-muscle layers, lumen about equal to wall thickness

299
A 38-year-old man develops a painful femoral hernia, and the herniated intestinal segment is removed surgically. Microscopic examination of the submucosa reveals a series of small blood vessels (shown in the image). Identify the vessel indicated by the arrow.
  1. (A) Arteriole
  2. (B) Capillary
  3. (C) Muscular artery
  4. (D) Small vein
  5. (E) Venule
Answer(E) Venule
WhyA venule has a relatively wide, blood-filled lumen bounded by little more than endothelium and pericytes, unlike the thick muscular wall of the neighbouring arteriole.
Explanation from the source
The answer is E: Venule. Venules connect the distal ends of capillary beds with the venous system. Venules are composed of a layer of endothelial cells with a basal lamina. A thin layer of adventitia supports the venule and binds it to the surrounding connective tissue. Venules continuous with the capillaries are referred as postcapillary venules. The more distal and larger venules that connect to small veins are termed muscular venules. Although venules lack a smooth muscle coat, postcapillary venules are invested with pericytes. Muscular venules are distal to postcapillary venules; they are approximately 0.1 mm in diameter. Larger muscular venules have one or two layers of smooth muscle cells that form a tunica media. Pericytes are not associated with muscular venules. Keywords: Venules, pericytes
ConceptVenule: wide blood-filled lumen with very thin endothelial wall

A 56-year-old man presents with painful dilated knots in both legs. Ulcers are noted over some of the knots. A photograph of the patient is shown. Which of the following structures in the legs is most likely affected in this patient?
Show figure
  1. (A) Cutaneous nerves
  2. (B) Deep veins
  3. (C) Small arteries
  4. (D) Superficial lymphatic vessels
  5. (E) Superficial veins
Answer(E) Superficial veins
WhyVaricose veins are dilated, tortuous superficial veins (the saphenous veins and their tributaries) with incompetent valves, worsened by prolonged standing.
Explanation from the source
The answer is E: Superficial veins. Superficial varicosities of the saphenous veins and their tributaries in the lower limb are very common, owing to upright posture. Varicose veins are common in the posteromedial portions of the lower limbs. The incidence of varicose veins is greater in individuals whose occupations require them to stand for long periods of time. Varicosities are enlarged and tortuous, due to incompetence of venous valves and/ or dilation of the vessel. Blood flow in the varicose vein is turbulent and slow, and the capillary bed is engorged. Fluid leaks into the surrounding cutaneous tissue and causes stasis dermatitis. None of the other structures give rise to varicose leg veins. Keywords: Varicose veins
ConceptVaricose leg veins are the superficial veins

A skin biopsy is taken from the patient described in Question 41. Microscopic examination reveals blood vessels in the subcutaneous tissue (shown in the image). Identify the structures indicated by the arrows.
  1. (A) Arteriovenous shunt
  2. (B) Lymphatic vessels
  3. (C) Smooth muscle fibers
  4. (D) Subendothelial connective tissue
  5. (E) Venous valves
Answer(E) Venous valves
WhyThe thin flaps projecting into the vein lumen are venous valves, endothelium-covered folds of intima reinforced by collagen and elastic fibres that stop backflow.
Explanation from the source
The answer is E: Venous valves. Valves are characteristic features of medium-sized veins, in both superficial and deep veins. They are most numerous in the lower limb veins, because of the need to direct the flow of blood back to the heart against the force of gravity. Venous valves are cusp-like projections into the lumen of the vein. The valves are covered by endothelium, and they are strengthened by collagen and elastic fibers. They have cup-like valvular sinuses that fill from above. The valve cusps occlude the lumen of the vein when they are full, so as to prevent reflux of blood and ensure that the venous blood continues to flow in one direction back toward the heart. Keywords: Varicose veins, venous valves
ConceptVenous valves in a subcutaneous vein (H&E micrograph)

An ulnar neurovascular bundle is harvested at autopsy and examined using the trichrome stain to help distinguish between collagenous connective tissue, red blood cells, and smooth muscle (shown in the image). Identify this patient’s blood vessel.
  1. (A) Large vein
  2. (B) Muscular artery
  3. (C) Medium vein
  4. (D) Small artery
  5. (E) Venule
Answer(C) Medium vein
WhyA medium vein has a thin media of a few smooth-muscle layers between blue collagen, an adventitia thicker than the media, and a wide blood-filled lumen.
Explanation from the source
The answer is C: Medium vein. Medium-sized veins typically accompany muscular arteries in a common connective tissue sheath. Medium veins have a diameter range of 0.1 to 10 mm, and they exhibit all three vascular tunics. The tunica intima is composed of endothelium and a thin subendothelial layer. In larger medium-sized veins, a thin internal elastic membrane may be present. The tunica media is much thinner in medium veins compared to medium arteries. As shown in this image, there are only a few layers of circular smooth muscle fibers (red wavy lines) interspersed between blue-stained connective tissue fibers (collagen and elastin). The tunica adventitia is thicker than the tunica media, with an abundance of collagen and elastic fibers. None of the other vessels describe the characteristic structural features of the muscular vein. Keywords: Veins, muscular
ConceptMedium vein (trichrome): thin media, adventitia thicker than media

A segment of the inferior vena cava is obtained at autopsy and examined by routine H&E staining (shown in the image). Identify the structures indicated by the arrows.
  1. (A) Bundles of elastic fibers
  2. (B) Collagen fibers
  3. (C) Nervi vascularis
  4. (D) Smooth muscle fibers
  5. (E) Vasa vasorum
Answer(D) Smooth muscle fibers
WhyThe thickest layer of the vena cava, the adventitia, contains prominent bundles of longitudinal smooth muscle cut in cross-section, which are the structures marked.
Explanation from the source
The answer is D: Smooth muscle fibers. The venae cavae, pulmonary, subclavian, and portal veins are considered large veins in the human body. As seen in the image, the tunica adventitia (indicated by the double arrow) is the thickest layer of the wall of large veins. It contains aggregates of bundles of longitudinally arranged smooth muscle fibers. The tunica media of large veins is thin, with a few layers of smooth muscle fibers and abundant connective tissue. The other structures are found in the tunica adventitia of large veins, but they do not show histologic features of smooth muscle fibers. Keywords: Veins
ConceptVena cava adventitia contains longitudinal smooth-muscle bundles

A 28-year-old woman experiences sudden chest pain and is rushed to the emergency room. The patient is unable to maintain cardiac output and expires the following day. Autopsy reveals a thromboembolus at the bifurcation of the right pulmonary artery. Which of the following mechanisms of disease is the most likely cause of pulmonary thromboembolism in this patient?
  1. (A) Bacterial endocarditis
  2. (B) Complicated atherosclerotic plaque
  3. (C) Deep vein thrombosis
  4. (D) Paradoxical embolization
  5. (E) Right ventricular mural thrombus
Answer(C) Deep vein thrombosis
WhyThrombi from deep vein thrombosis in the legs travel through the vena cava and right heart to lodge in the pulmonary arteries as a pulmonary embolus.
Explanation from the source
The answer is C: Deep vein thrombosis. A thrombus is an aggregation of coagulated blood (platelets, fibrin, and cells) that forms within a vascular lumen. Deep vein thrombosis (DVT) represents the formation of coagulated blood in a deep vein. Most DVTs occur in the deep veins of the lower limb. If a DVT of the lower limb dislodges, it can be carried up to the inferior vena cava, through the heart, to the pulmonary arteries. A large pulmonary thromboembolus causes acute obstruction of the pulmonary arterial tree. As a result, the patient develops severe hypotension (cardiogenic shock) and may die within minutes. The other mechanisms of disease cause arterial thrombosis. Keywords: Pulmonary thromboembolism, deep vein thrombosis
ConceptPulmonary thromboembolism usually originates from deep vein thrombosis

A biopsy of the jejunum is examined in the histology laboratory. A section through an intestinal villus is shown in image. Identify the channel indicated by the arrow.
  1. (A) Arteriole
  2. (B) Capillary
  3. (C) Lymphatic capillary
  4. (D) Small vein
  5. (E) Venule
Answer(C) Lymphatic capillary
WhyThe clear central channel of an intestinal villus is a lacteal, a blind-ended lymphatic capillary lined by thin endothelium that absorbs chylomicrons.
Explanation from the source
The answer is C: Lymphatic capillary. Lymphatic capillaries are lined by a simple squamous endothelium, but they lack a continuous basal lamina. As a result, lymphatic capillaries are highly permeable. They convey large proteins, protein complexes, and large lipid micelles and chylomicrons. They are more efficient than blood capillaries in removing tissue fluid and necrotic debris. Lymphatic capillaries in the villi of the small intestine are referred as lacteals. Lacteals collect dietary fats absorbed by the intestinal villi. Emulsified triglycerides in the lumen of the small intestine pass through the simple columnar epithelial lining and enter the lamina propria of the intestinal villi. Here, triacylglycerol combines with phospholipids, cholesterol esters, and apolipoprotein B-48 to form chylomicrons. The chylomicrons are absorbed into the lacteals and form a milky substance known as chyle. Lacteals merge to form larger lymphatic vessels, which transport chyle to the bloodstream by way of the thoracic duct. None of the other channels exhibit histologic features of lymphatic capillaries. Keywords: Lacteal, lymphatic capillary
ConceptLacteal: lymphatic capillary in the villus core

The myocardium of a woman who died of a cardiac arrhythmia is examined in the pathology department. Which of the following statements describes an important feature of cardiac muscle that helps distinguish cardiac from skeletal muscle in routine H&E slide preparations?
Show figure
  1. (A) Connective tissue contains a rich capillary network.
  2. (B) Muscle fibers are composed of multiple cells.
  3. (C) Muscle fibers exhibit cross-striations.
  4. (D) Sarcomeres are located between adjacent Z lines.
  5. (E) Thin filaments contain actin.
Answer(B) Muscle fibers are composed of multiple cells.
WhyA cardiac fiber is composed of multiple cells joined end to end at intercalated discs, whereas a skeletal muscle fiber is a single multinucleated cell; striations, sarcomeres and actin occur in both.
Explanation from the source
The answer is B: Muscle fibers are composed of multiple cells. Unlike skeletal muscle, where muscle fibers are multinucleated cells, cardiac muscle fibers are composed of multiple cells that make tight end-to-end connections. Cardiac muscle cells may split and unite, giving cardiac muscle a typical “branching” morphology. Cardiac and skeletal muscles both exhibit cross-striations—their thick and thin contractile filaments exhibit the same organiza-tion (choices C, D, E). The nuclei of cardiac and skeletal muscle are, however, distinctly different. The nuclei of skeletal muscle cells are located at the periphery of the fiber, whereas the nucleus of a cardiac myocyte is located in the center of the cell (shown in the image). This dif-ference in nuclear location provides a useful means for distinguishing cardiac from skeletal muscle. Cardiac and skeletal muscle fibers are both invested with connective tissue that conveys nerves and capillaries (choice A).Keywords: Cardiac muscle
ConceptCardiac vs skeletal muscle on H&E: cells joined end-to-end

A 56-year-old man presents with painful dilated knots in both legs. Ulcers are noted over some of the knots. A photograph of the patient is shown below (left). Which structure in the legs is most likely affected in this patient?
Show figure
AnswerThe answer is E: Superficial veins.
WhyPainful dilated knots in the legs are varicose veins, which affect the superficial veins (great and small saphenous and tributaries) whose valves fail under the gravity load of standing.
Explanation from the source
The answer is E: Superficial veins. Superficial varicosities of the saphenous veins and their tributaries in the lower limb are very common, owing to upright posture. Varicose veins are common in the posteromedial portions of the lower limbs. The incidence of varicose veins is greater in individuals whose occupations require them to stand for long periods of time. Varicosities are enlarged and tortuous, due to incompetence of venous valves and/ or dilation of the vessel. Blood flow in the varicose vein is turbulent and slow, and the capillary bed is engorged. Fluid leaks into the surrounding cutaneous tissue and causes stasis dermatitis. None of the other structures give rise to varicose leg veins. Keywords: Varicose veins
ConceptVaricose leg veins are the superficial veins

A 56-year-old man presents with painful dilated knots in both legs. Ulcers are noted over some of the knots. A photograph of the patient is shown below (left). A skin biopsy is taken from the patient. Microscopic examination reveals blood vessels in the subcutaneous tissue (on the right). Identify the structures indicated by the arrows.
AnswerVenous Valves — The answer is E: Venous valves.
WhyThe arrows mark venous valves, endothelium-covered intimal folds that are most numerous in the lower limb veins, where they direct blood toward the heart against gravity.
Explanation from the source
The answer is E: Venous valves. Valves are characteristic features of medium-sized veins, in both superficial and deep veins. They are most numerous in the lower limb veins, because of the need to direct the flow of blood back to the heart against the force of gravity. Venous valves are cusp-like projections into the lumen of the vein. The valves are covered by endothelium, and they are strengthened by collagen and elastic fibers. They have cup-like valvular sinuses that fill from above. The valve cusps occlude the lumen of the vein when they are full, so as to prevent reflux of blood and ensure that the venous blood continues to flow in
ConceptVenous valves in a dilated vein (gross-section image)

  4. D. capillary
AnswerD. capillary
WhyEach marked vessel is a capillary: a single thin endothelial cell around a lumen just wide enough for one red blood cell, lying between cardiac muscle fibres.
Explanation from the source
D. capillary- ID the pericyte around it and thin Thin cell layer around the vessel
ConceptCapillaries between cardiac muscle fibres (cross-section)

355
Identify the tissue type
  1. A. Large vein
  2. B. Elastic Artery
  3. C. endothelial cell
  4. D. capillary
AnswerA. Large vein
WhyA large vein has a very thin media and a thick adventitia containing longitudinal smooth-muscle bundles, unlike an elastic artery's lamellar media.
Explanation from the source
Large vein- very thin tunica media and large Tunica adventitia
ConceptLarge vein: thin media, thick adventitia with muscle bundles

356
Mrs. Sanchez comes into your office complaining of twisted vessels that goes down her legs. She is concerned because they ache episodically and is worse when she sits or stand for long periods of time. Which of the following is true of this vessel?
  1. A. The tunica media layer is the thickest layer
  2. B. These vessels contain valves in the intimal layer to prevent backflow
  3. C. The adventitia layer of these vessels are thin
  4. D. These vessels contain cusps that projects into the lumen
  5. E. These vessels have small luminal diameter
AnswerB. These vessels contain valves in the intimal layer to prevent backflow
WhyVeins have valves formed by folds of the tunica intima projecting into the lumen to prevent backflow, and their adventitia, not media, is the thickest layer.

The tunica ADVENTITIA layer is the thickest layer The adventitia layer of these vessels are THICK These vessels contain VALVES ALONG WITH ENDOTHELIAL CONNECTIVE TISSUE that projects into the lumen Size of veins: Venules < small veins < medium size veins < large veins
ConceptVaricose veins: valves are intimal folds that prevent backflow

357
Which of these has one way valves?
Show figure
  1. a. Inferior vena cava
  2. b. Capillaries
  3. c. Femoral artery
  4. d. Arterioles
  5. e. Lymph vessels
AnswerE. Lymph vessels
WhyLymph vessels contain paired intimal valves that keep lymph moving one way, whereas arteries, arterioles, capillaries and the inferior vena cava lack them.

E. Lymph vessels have a little bit of contractile By the time you reach the inferior vena cava there are no valves.

The following is a PAS stained slide of the heart wall, identify the cells indicated by the black arrows.
Answer supplied — the source gives no keyPurkinje fibers

359
Which histological feature uniquely identifies cardiac muscle fibers?
  1. A. Intercalated discs
  2. B. Dyads
  3. C. Sarcolemma
  4. D. Peripheral nuclei

WhyIntercalated discs, the step-like junctions joining cardiomyocytes end-to-end, are found only in cardiac muscle; sarcolemma is universal and peripheral nuclei mark skeletal muscle.

Cardiac muscle-linked by adherent and gap junctions at prominent intercalated discs (Junqueira).

360
Q1. A 62-year-old male patients dies after suffering a myocardial infarction. A sample section of normal myocardium is obtained in autopsy, stained with H&E, and is presented below. Which of the following features confirm that this is a section of cardiac muscle and not skeletal muscle?
  1. A. The presence of sarcomeres between Z lines

  3. C. The presence of actin microfilaments

  5. E. Alternating pattern of A and I bands

  2. B. Foam cells → collagen formation → plaque → endothelial damage → LDL enters → macrophages → vessel occlusion

HIST-8 Respiratory system lecture

212 questions · 163 concepts · 48 high-yield
Learning questions 150

Two ways to divide the tract

L1Learning
Anatomically, which structures make up the upper and the lower respiratory tract?
  1. A. Upper: nasal cavity, sinuses, pharynx, larynx
    Lower: trachea, bronchi, lungs
  2. B. Upper: nasal cavity, sinuses, pharynx
    Lower: larynx, trachea, bronchi, lungs
  3. C. Upper: nasal cavity, sinuses
    Lower: pharynx, larynx, trachea, bronchi, lungs
AnswerB. Upper: nasal cavity, sinuses, pharynx
Lower: larynx, trachea, bronchi, lungs
WhyThe anatomical line falls between the pharynx and the larynx: nasal cavity, sinuses and pharynx are upper; larynx and everything below are lower.
Explanation

The anatomical division is a gross-anatomy split at the laryngeal inlet. The upper tract is the nasal cavities, the paranasal sinuses and the pharynx; the lower tract starts with the larynx and continues through the trachea, bronchi and lungs (bronchioles and alveoli).

  • Putting the larynx in the upper tract moves the line one level too low.
  • Putting the pharynx in the lower tract moves it one level too high.

Keep this apart from the histological (functional) division into conducting and respiratory portions, which cuts much further down, after the terminal bronchiole.

Slide (1)
L2Learning
What is the conducting portion of the respiratory system, and what does it do?
  1. A. Nasal cavity → terminal bronchioles; conditions and carries air, no gas exchange
  2. B. Nasal cavity → respiratory bronchioles; conditions air and exchanges some gas
  3. C. Trachea → alveolar ducts; conditions and carries air, no gas exchange
AnswerA. Nasal cavity → terminal bronchioles; conditions and carries air, no gas exchange
WhyThe conducting portion runs from the nasal cavity to the terminal bronchioles: it warms, moistens, cleans and carries air but exchanges no gas.
Explanation

The histological (functional) division asks one question of each segment: does gas exchange happen here? Everything from the nasal cavity, nasopharynx, larynx, trachea and bronchi down to the terminal bronchioles is conducting: its wall has no alveoli, so it only conditions (warms, humidifies, filters) and delivers air.

  • To the respiratory bronchioles goes one step too far: respiratory bronchioles have alveoli in their wall and already exchange gas, so they start the respiratory portion.
  • Trachea → alveolar ducts is wrong at both ends: the nasal cavity, pharynx and larynx are conducting, and alveolar ducts are respiratory.
Slide (1)
L3Learning
What makes up the respiratory portion, and what does it do?
  1. A. Respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts, alveoli — gas exchange
  2. B. Terminal bronchioles, respiratory bronchioles, alveoli — gas exchange
  3. C. Alveolar ducts and alveoli only — gas exchange
AnswerA. Respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts, alveoli — gas exchange
WhyThe respiratory portion is every segment with alveoli in its wall: respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts and alveoli, where O2 and CO2 are exchanged.
Explanation

Gas exchange needs alveoli, the thin-walled sacs wrapped in capillaries. The first segment that has alveoli opening from its wall is the respiratory bronchiole, so the respiratory portion = respiratory bronchioles → alveolar ducts → alveolar sacs and alveoli.

  • Terminal bronchioles have a complete wall with no alveoli: they are the last conducting segment, not the first respiratory one.
  • Alveolar ducts and alveoli only leaves out the respiratory bronchioles, which already exchange some gas through their scattered alveoli.
Slide (1)
L4Learning
What is the most distal (last) segment of the conducting portion?
  1. A. Respiratory bronchiole
  2. B. Larger bronchiole
  3. C. Terminal bronchiole
AnswerC. Terminal bronchiole
WhyThe terminal bronchiole is the last purely conducting airway; the next branch, the respiratory bronchiole, has alveoli in its wall.
Explanation

A terminal bronchiole is the final, smallest bronchiole whose wall is complete: cuboidal epithelium with club cells, one or two layers of smooth muscle, and no alveoli opening from it. Each one branches into respiratory bronchioles.
