  • The respiratory bronchiole is one step further: alveoli bud from its wall, so it belongs to the respiratory portion.
  • A larger bronchiole is conducting, but it is not the last one: it still branches down to terminal bronchioles.

Exam tip: "most distal conducting" = terminal bronchiole; "first respiratory" = respiratory bronchiole.

Slide (1)

Nasal cavity, sinuses and pharynx

L5Learning
What lines the nasal vestibule (just inside the nostril)?
  1. A. Non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium with seromucous glands and no hairs
  2. B. Pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium with goblet cells and seromucous glands
  3. C. Keratinized stratified squamous epithelium (skin) with sweat and sebaceous glands and vibrissae
AnswerC. Keratinized stratified squamous epithelium (skin) with sweat and sebaceous glands and vibrissae
WhyThe outer vestibule is ordinary skin: keratinized stratified squamous epithelium with sweat and sebaceous glands and coarse hairs (vibrissae).
Explanation

The vestibule is the dilated entrance of each nasal cavity. Its outer part is continuous with the facial skin, so it has a keratinized stratified squamous epithelium, sebaceous and sweat glands and thick hairs called vibrissae that filter out large particles. Hyaline cartilage of the nose supports it.

  • Non-keratinized stratified squamous with seromucous glands describes a wet mucosa (like the vocal fold), not skin; and it omits the hairs that define the vestibule.
  • Pseudostratified ciliated columnar with goblet cells is respiratory epithelium, which begins only further back, after the transition zone.
Slide (1)
L6Learning
What are vibrissae?
  1. A. Coarse filtering hairs of the nasal vestibule
  2. B. Motile cilia of the nasal respiratory epithelium
  3. C. Non-motile cilia of the olfactory neurons
AnswerA. Coarse filtering hairs of the nasal vestibule
WhyVibrissae are the thick hairs of the nasal vestibule's skin; they catch large inhaled particles before air reaches the mucosa.
Explanation

Vibrissae are true hairs growing from hair follicles in the skin of the vestibule. They are the first, coarse filter of the airway; finer particles are trapped later by mucus and moved by cilia.

  • Motile cilia are microtubule-based projections (9 + 2) on ciliated columnar cells, hundreds per cell; they move mucus, they are not hairs.
  • The non-motile cilia of olfactory neurons are the "olfactory hairs" that carry odorant receptors, high in the nasal roof, far from the vestibule.
Slide (1)
L7Learning
What happens to the vestibular lining as it passes deeper into the nasal cavity?
  1. A. It gains keratin in a transition zone and becomes thicker skin
  2. B. It loses its keratin in a transition zone and becomes respiratory epithelium
  3. C. It turns straight into olfactory epithelium, with no transition zone
AnswerB. It loses its keratin in a transition zone and becomes respiratory epithelium
WhyThe inner vestibule is a transition zone: the skin loses its keratin and gives way to the ciliated respiratory epithelium of the nasal cavity proper.
Explanation

The vestibule has two parts: an outer part that is skin (keratinized stratified squamous with hairs and glands) and an inner part that is a transition zone. There the epithelium becomes non-keratinized and then changes into the pseudostratified ciliated columnar (respiratory) epithelium that lines most of the nasal cavity.

  • Gains keratin reverses the direction: the keratin is on the outside, at the nostril.
  • Straight into olfactory epithelium is wrong: olfactory epithelium is found only on the superior concha and roof, far from the vestibule.
Slide (1)
L8Learning
Which nasal surfaces carry olfactory epithelium, and which carry respiratory epithelium?
  1. A. Olfactory: middle concha and septum
    Respiratory: superior and inferior conchae and the rest
  2. B. Olfactory: superior concha and roof
    Respiratory: middle and inferior conchae and the rest
  3. C. Olfactory: inferior concha and floor
    Respiratory: superior and middle conchae and the rest
AnswerB. Olfactory: superior concha and roof
Respiratory: middle and inferior conchae and the rest
WhyOlfactory epithelium covers the superior concha and roof of the nasal cavity; the middle and inferior conchae and the rest are respiratory epithelium.
Explanation

The conchae (turbinates) are three shelves of bone on the lateral nasal wall. Smell receptors sit only at the top: the superior concha and the roof, under the cribriform plate through which the olfactory nerves pass. The middle and inferior conchae, septum and floor carry ordinary respiratory epithelium, which warms and cleans the air.

  • Middle concha and inferior concha are respiratory; putting olfactory epithelium there swaps the levels.

Hook: smell goes up, to the top shelf next to the brain.

Slide (1)
L9Learning
How does the nasal cavity condition inhaled air?
  1. A. Secretions humidify
    Vascular loops and venous plexus warm
    Mucus traps particles
    Plasma cells add immunoglobulin A (IgA)
  2. B. Secretions humidify
    Vascular loops and venous plexus warm
    Mucus traps particles
    Plasma cells add immunoglobulin G (IgG)
  3. C. Secretions humidify
    Vascular loops and venous plexus warm
    Mucus traps particles
    Goblet cells add immunoglobulin A (IgA)
AnswerA. Secretions humidify
Vascular loops and venous plexus warm
Mucus traps particles
Plasma cells add immunoglobulin A (IgA)
WhyThe nasal mucosa humidifies (secretions), warms (vascular loops, venous plexus), traps particles (mucus) and adds IgA from plasma cells.
Explanation

Air must reach the alveoli warm, moist and clean. In the nasal cavity:

  • seromucous gland and goblet-cell secretions moisten it;
  • the rich capillary loops and large venous plexus of the lamina propria warm it;
  • sticky mucus traps dust and microbes, which cilia then sweep to the pharynx;
  • plasma cells in the lamina propria secrete IgA, which is carried into the mucus.

Wrong choices: mucosal plasma cells make IgA, the secretory antibody, not IgG; and goblet cells make mucus, not antibody.

Slide (1)
L10Learning
How does the lining of the paranasal sinuses and nasopharynx differ from the rest of the nasal respiratory mucosa?
  1. A. Thicker epithelium, more goblet cells, many large glands
  2. B. Thinner epithelium, fewer goblet cells, few and small glands
  3. C. Thinner epithelium, more goblet cells, many large glands
AnswerB. Thinner epithelium, fewer goblet cells, few and small glands
WhyThe sinuses and nasopharynx have a thin respiratory epithelium with few goblet cells and only few, small glands in the lamina propria.
Explanation

The paranasal sinuses are air spaces in the frontal, maxillary, ethmoid and sphenoid bones that open into the nasal cavity. They keep the same type of lining (pseudostratified ciliated columnar respiratory epithelium) but in a reduced form: a thinner epithelium, fewer goblet cells, and few, small glands. Their mucus is moved out through narrow openings by cilia, which is why poor ciliary clearance leads to sinusitis.

  • Both wrong choices give the sinuses more goblet cells and large glands; they have less secretory equipment than the main nasal cavity, not more.
Slide (1)
L11Learning
What muscle and structures are found in the pharynx and nasopharynx?
  1. A. Pharynx: smooth muscle
    Nasopharynx: pharyngeal tonsil, maxillary sinus opening
  2. B. Pharynx: skeletal muscle
    Nasopharynx: lingual tonsil, nasolacrimal duct opening
  3. C. Pharynx: skeletal muscle
    Nasopharynx: pharyngeal tonsil, auditory (Eustachian) tube opening
AnswerC. Pharynx: skeletal muscle
Nasopharynx: pharyngeal tonsil, auditory (Eustachian) tube opening
WhyThe pharyngeal wall is skeletal muscle; the nasopharynx holds the pharyngeal tonsil and the opening of the auditory (Eustachian) tube.
Explanation

Unlike the nasal cavity and sinuses (supported by bone and cartilage), the pharynx is a muscular tube of skeletal (striated) muscle, the constrictors, used in swallowing. Its upper part, the nasopharynx, is lined by respiratory epithelium and carries the pharyngeal tonsil (adenoid) on its posterior wall and the openings of the auditory tubes on its lateral walls.

  • Smooth muscle is wrong: the pharynx is voluntary skeletal muscle.
  • The maxillary sinus and nasolacrimal duct open into the nasal cavity (middle and inferior meatus), not the nasopharynx; the lingual tonsil is on the back of the tongue.
Slides (2)
L12Learning
A teenager with a cold has a "stuffy nose". Which feature of the nasal lamina propria normally warms inhaled air and, when engorged, causes the congestion?
  1. A. A dense layer of seromucous glands
  2. B. A large, thin-walled venous plexus
  3. C. Abundant lymphoid nodules (MALT)
AnswerB. A large, thin-walled venous plexus
WhyThe nasal lamina propria holds a large venous plexus that warms air; in a cold it engorges and leaks fluid, so the mucosa swells and blocks the airway.
Explanation

The lamina propria of the nasal cavity and sinuses contains capillary loops and a large plexus of thin-walled veins (sometimes called swell bodies). Warm blood flowing close to the surface heats the passing air. In a cold or allergic rhinitis, inflammation engorges these venous spaces and makes them leaky; the lamina propria swells with blood and oedema fluid and narrows the airway, the "stuffy nose".

  • Seromucous glands humidify the air; their extra secretion causes a runny nose, not the swelling that blocks it.
  • Lymphoid nodules are immune tissue; they do not warm air or swell enough to block the nose.
Slide (1)

Respiratory epithelium

L13Learning
What type of epithelium is respiratory epithelium, and what does it rest on?
  1. A. Pseudostratified ciliated columnar, on a thick basement membrane
  2. B. Pseudostratified ciliated columnar, on a thin basement membrane
  3. C. Stratified ciliated columnar, on a thick basement membrane
AnswerA. Pseudostratified ciliated columnar, on a thick basement membrane
WhyRespiratory epithelium is pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium with goblet cells, resting on a conspicuously thick basement membrane.
Explanation

Respiratory epithelium lines most of the conducting portion: nasal cavity (except vestibule and olfactory area), sinuses, nasopharynx, most of the larynx, trachea and bronchi. It is pseudostratified (one layer that looks like several), its tall cells are ciliated columnar, and goblet cells are scattered among them. Beneath it lies a thick basement membrane, seen as a pink band in H&E, which thickens further in smokers and asthmatics.

  • A thin basement membrane is a feature of olfactory epithelium, a useful way to tell the two apart.
  • Stratified ciliated columnar would need true layers of cells; in respiratory epithelium every cell touches the basement membrane.
Slide (1)
L14LearningBorderline
Why is respiratory epithelium called pseudostratified?
  1. A. Only the basal cells touch the basement membrane, but all cells reach the lumen
  2. B. The cells form true layers, but the cilia make the surface look single
  3. C. All cells touch the basement membrane, but their nuclei sit at different heights
AnswerC. All cells touch the basement membrane, but their nuclei sit at different heights
WhyIn pseudostratified epithelium every cell rests on the basement membrane, but not all reach the lumen, so the nuclei line up at several levels and mimic layers.
Explanation

"Pseudo" means false: the epithelium looks stratified but is really a single layer. Tall ciliated and goblet cells reach the lumen; short basal cells do not. Because the cells are of different heights, their nuclei sit at different levels, which gives the false impression of several layers.

  • Only basal cells touching the membrane would make it truly stratified, the opposite of the definition.
  • True layers is simply stratified epithelium; cilia have nothing to do with the name.
L15Learning
Which five cell types make up respiratory epithelium?
  1. A. Ciliated columnar, goblet, basal, brush, club (Clara)
  2. B. Ciliated columnar, goblet, basal, sustentacular, olfactory neuron
  3. C. Ciliated columnar, goblet, basal, brush, small granule (Kulchitsky)
AnswerC. Ciliated columnar, goblet, basal, brush, small granule (Kulchitsky)
WhyRespiratory epithelium has ciliated columnar, goblet, basal, brush and small granule (Kulchitsky) cells.
Explanation
  • Ciliated columnar cells: move mucus.
  • Goblet cells: secrete mucin.
  • Basal cells: stem cells on the basement membrane.
  • Brush cells: chemosensory cells with blunt microvilli.
  • Small granule (Kulchitsky) cells: neuroendocrine cells of the diffuse neuroendocrine system (DNES).

Wrong choices: club (Clara) cells belong to the bronchiolar epithelium, not to the pseudostratified respiratory epithelium of the nose, trachea and bronchi. Sustentacular cells and olfactory neurons belong to olfactory epithelium.

Slide (1)
L16Learning
Roughly what share of respiratory epithelium does each main cell type make up?
  1. A. Ciliated: about 60%
    Goblet, basal: about 15% each
    Small granule: about 10%
  2. B. Ciliated, goblet, basal: about 30% each
    Small granule: about 10%
  3. C. Ciliated, goblet, basal: about 30% each
    Small granule: about 3%
AnswerC. Ciliated, goblet, basal: about 30% each
Small granule: about 3%
WhyThe lecture gives ciliated, goblet and basal cells about 30% each; small granule (Kulchitsky) cells are only about 3%, and brush cells are few.
Explanation

The three common cell types share the epithelium roughly equally (about 30% each). The remaining few percent are the rarer cells: small granule cells are about 3% of all cells and hard to see in routine H&E, and brush cells are much less numerous than the main three.

  • Ciliated about 60% is not the course figure; textbooks call ciliated cells the most abundant, but the lecture splits the main three evenly.
  • Small granule about 10% overstates them threefold: they are a sparse neuroendocrine population.
Slides (2)
L17Learning
Which cell is the most numerous in respiratory epithelium?
  1. A. Goblet cell
  2. B. Basal cell
  3. C. Ciliated columnar cell
AnswerC. Ciliated columnar cell
WhyCiliated columnar cells are the most abundant cells of respiratory epithelium, each carrying 250–300 cilia.
Explanation

Ciliated columnar cells are tall cells reaching from the basement membrane to the lumen, with a dense tuft of motile cilia on top. Textbooks and the lab review call them the most abundant cell type. The lecture's own figures (about 30% each for ciliated, goblet and basal cells) put the three close together, so on an exam that asks for the single most numerous cell, choose the ciliated cell.

  • Goblet cells are numerous and can predominate in some areas (and increase in smokers and asthmatics), but overall they are fewer than ciliated cells.
  • Basal cells are small stem cells hugging the basement membrane; common, but not the most numerous.
Slide (1)
L18Learning
How many cilia does each ciliated cell carry, and which way do they move mucus?
  1. A. 250–300 motile cilia — toward the alveoli
  2. B. 250–300 motile cilia — toward the pharynx
  3. C. 20–30 motile cilia — toward the pharynx
AnswerB. 250–300 motile cilia — toward the pharynx
WhyEach ciliated cell has about 250–300 motile cilia; coordinated beating moves the mucus sheet up toward the pharynx, where it is swallowed or coughed out.
Explanation

This is the mucociliary escalator. Goblet cells and glands lay down a sheet of mucus that traps particles and microbes; the cilia beat in coordinated waves so the sheet slides upward from the bronchi and trachea (and backward from the nose) to the pharynx.

  • Toward the alveoli would carry trapped dirt and bacteria into the gas-exchange surface, the opposite of the purpose.
  • 20–30 cilia is ten times too few; the dense tuft of hundreds of cilia per cell is what makes the brush-like border visible in the light microscope.
Slides (2)
L19Learning
What is the dominant apical specialization seen on respiratory epithelium in the light microscope?
  1. A. Motile cilia
  2. B. Stereocilia
  3. C. A brush border of microvilli
AnswerA. Motile cilia
WhyRespiratory epithelium carries motile cilia: long, 9 + 2 microtubule-based projections that beat to move mucus.
Explanation

Motile cilia are long (about 5–10 µm) projections with a 9 + 2 axoneme of microtubules and dynein arms, anchored in basal bodies. In the trachea and bronchi they form a dense, even fringe on the ciliated columnar cells.

  • Stereocilia are very long, non-motile microvilli (actin core) found in the epididymis and inner ear, not the airway.
  • A brush border of short microvilli is the absorptive surface of intestinal and kidney tubule cells. In the airway only the scattered brush cells carry (blunt) microvilli, and they are too few to form a border.

Olfactory epithelium also has cilia, but they are non-motile and belong to the receptor neurons.

Slides (2)
L20Learning
In the trachea, what forms the thin dark line just under the cilia?
  1. A. Tight junctions
  2. B. Basal bodies
  3. C. Glycocalyx coat
AnswerB. Basal bodies
WhyThe dark line under the cilia is the row of basal bodies, the centriole-like anchors from which each cilium grows.
Explanation

Every cilium sprouts from a basal body, a short cylinder of nine microtubule triplets in the apical cytoplasm. Because hundreds of basal bodies line up side by side at the same level in each ciliated cell, they stain as a continuous dark line just below the cilia in H&E sections of the trachea.

  • Tight junctions sit at the apical edges between neighbouring cells; they are far too small to form a visible band in the light microscope.
  • The glycocalyx is a carbohydrate coat on the outer surface of the membrane, above (not below) the base of the cilia, and it is not seen as a dark line in H&E.
Slide (1)
L21Learning
How do goblet cells look in respiratory epithelium?
  1. A. Basal nucleus; apex covered by sparse, blunt microvilli
  2. B. Basal nucleus; apex swollen with pale mucin granules
  3. C. Apical nucleus; base full of small dense-core granules
AnswerB. Basal nucleus; apex swollen with pale mucin granules
WhyGoblet cells have a narrow base with the nucleus and a swollen apex packed with mucin granules, which look pale (empty) in H&E.
Explanation

Goblet cells are mucus-secreting cells shaped like a wine glass: the nucleus is squeezed into the narrow base and the apical cytoplasm is filled with mucin granules (glycoproteins, mostly carbohydrate). In H&E the mucin washes out and looks pale; it stains strongly with periodic acid–Schiff (PAS) or Alcian blue.

  • Sparse, blunt microvilli on the apex describe the brush cell.
  • Dense-core granules at the base describe the small granule (Kulchitsky) neuroendocrine cell, which releases its contents toward the blood, not the lumen.
Slide (1)
L22Learning
What is the role of the basal cells of respiratory epithelium?
  1. A. Stem (progenitor) cells that replace the other cell types
  2. B. Secrete mucus onto the epithelial surface
  3. C. Sense chemicals and signal to afferent nerves
AnswerA. Stem (progenitor) cells that replace the other cell types
WhyBasal cells are the mitotically active stem and progenitor cells that regenerate ciliated, goblet and other cells of the epithelium.
Explanation

Basal cells are small, rounded cells that sit on the basement membrane and do not reach the lumen; their nuclei form the lowest row of the pseudostratified epithelium. They divide and differentiate to replace worn-out or injured cells, which is how the airway lining repairs itself (and, under chronic irritation, how it can change type, as in squamous metaplasia).

  • Mucus secretion is the job of goblet cells (and submucosal glands).
  • Chemosensation with afferent nerve contacts is the job of brush cells.
Slide (1)
L23Learning
Which description fits the brush cell of respiratory epithelium?
  1. A. Basal dense-core granules; endocrine, releasing a calcitonin-like peptide
  2. B. Long motile cilia; mechanosensory, in synaptic contact with efferent nerve endings
  3. C. Sparse, blunt microvilli; chemosensory, in synaptic contact with afferent nerve endings
AnswerC. Sparse, blunt microvilli; chemosensory, in synaptic contact with afferent nerve endings
WhyBrush cells are columnar cells with blunt microvilli; they are chemosensory receptors that synapse on afferent nerve endings at their base.
Explanation

Brush cells are a small population of columnar cells named for their apical tuft of short, blunt microvilli. The course calls them neurosensory cells: they carry the same signal-transduction machinery as taste cells and make synaptic contact with afferent (sensory) nerve endings on their basal surface, so they report the chemical content of the airway.

  • Dense-core granules with a calcitonin-like peptide describe the small granule (Kulchitsky) cell.
  • Brush cells have microvilli, not cilia, and their nerves are afferent, not efferent.
Slide (1)
L24Learning
Small granule (Kulchitsky) cells belong to which system, and what do they contain?
  1. A. Diffuse neuroendocrine system (DNES) — pale granules of mucin glycoprotein
  2. B. Diffuse neuroendocrine system (DNES) — dense-core granules of peptide hormone
  3. C. Mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT) — lysosomal granules of hydrolase
AnswerB. Diffuse neuroendocrine system (DNES) — dense-core granules of peptide hormone
WhySmall granule (Kulchitsky) cells are neuroendocrine cells of the DNES, filled with 100–300 nm dense-core granules of peptide hormones.
Explanation

The diffuse neuroendocrine system is a set of scattered hormone-secreting cells in epithelia (airway and gut) rather than in an endocrine gland. In the airway, small granule cells sit near the basement membrane, are hard to tell from basal cells in H&E, and contain many dense-core granules (100–300 nm) that release peptides locally. In human bronchi these cells contain a calcitonin-like peptide, similar to the hormone of thyroid C cells.

  • Mucin granules belong to goblet cells.
  • MALT is lymphoid tissue (lymphocytes, plasma cells), not epithelial endocrine cells.
Slide (1)
L25Learning
Respiratory epithelium is immunostained with an antibody to a peptide hormone. Which cells turn brown?
  1. A. Small granule (Kulchitsky) cells
  2. B. Goblet (mucin-secreting) cells
  3. C. Brush (chemosensory) cells
AnswerA. Small granule (Kulchitsky) cells
WhyA peptide-hormone immunostain marks the small granule (Kulchitsky) neuroendocrine cells, which are almost invisible in routine H&E.
Explanation

Immunohistochemistry uses an antibody against a specific protein; a brown reaction product shows where it is. Because small granule cells store peptide hormones in dense-core granules, an antibody to such a peptide lights them up as scattered brown cells near the basement membrane, which is the standard way to demonstrate them.

  • Goblet cells contain mucin (carbohydrate-rich glycoprotein); they are shown with periodic acid–Schiff (PAS) or Alcian blue, not a hormone antibody.
  • Brush cells are chemosensory receptor cells with microvilli; they do not store peptide hormones.
Slide (1)
L26Learning
Which lung cancer arises from the airway's small granule (Kulchitsky) cells?
  1. A. Small cell lung cancer
  2. B. Squamous cell carcinoma
  3. C. Adenocarcinoma
AnswerA. Small cell lung cancer
WhySmall cell lung cancer is a neuroendocrine tumour of the Kulchitsky (K) cell lineage; it can secrete peptide hormones such as calcitonin.
Explanation

Small granule cells are the airway's neuroendocrine cells, and small cell carcinoma is the lung's main neuroendocrine cancer. Like their cell of origin, the tumour cells carry dense-core granules and can make peptide hormones: the lecture notes that bronchial K cells contain a calcitonin-like peptide and that small cell cancer is often associated with high blood calcitonin.

  • Squamous cell carcinoma arises from squamous metaplasia of the bronchial lining in smokers.
  • Adenocarcinoma is a gland-forming cancer, usually of the peripheral lung.
L27Learning
In a section of trachea, in which layers are mucus-secreting glandular cells found?
  1. A. Only the epithelium, as goblet cells among the ciliated cells
  2. B. Only the connective tissue, as seromucous glands beneath the epithelium
  3. C. Both: goblet cells in the epithelium and seromucous glands beneath it
AnswerC. Both: goblet cells in the epithelium and seromucous glands beneath it
WhyMucus comes from two levels: goblet cells within the epithelium and seromucous glands in the lamina propria and submucosa.
Explanation

Goblet cells are unicellular glands sitting among the ciliated cells. Below the epithelium, seromucous glands (mucous tubules capped by serous cells) lie in the submucosa, with a few in the lamina propria, and their ducts open onto the surface. Together they produce the watery mucus blanket that the cilia move.

  • Epithelium only ignores the large seromucous glands, a defining feature of the trachea and bronchi.
  • Connective tissue only ignores the goblet cells, which are glandular cells too.

Glands stop at the bronchi; goblet cells continue a little further, into the larger bronchioles.

Slide (1)
L28Learning
A lab micrograph shows a tall epithelium with nuclei at several levels, apical cilia and pale goblet cells, resting on a thick pink basement membrane over a band of hyaline cartilage. How is the epithelium classified?
  1. A. Stratified columnar
  2. B. Stratified cuboidal
  3. C. Pseudostratified columnar
AnswerC. Pseudostratified columnar
WhyNuclei at several levels, cilia and goblet cells on a thick basement membrane = pseudostratified (ciliated) columnar respiratory epithelium, here in the trachea or a bronchus.
Explanation

Use the clues in order: the cells are tall (columnar); the nuclei are at several heights but the cells all reach a single basement membrane (pseudostratified); cilia and goblet cells make it respiratory epithelium; the hyaline cartilage below places it in the trachea or a bronchus.

  • Stratified columnar epithelium (rare: large ducts, conjunctiva) has true layers with only the surface layer columnar, and no ciliated-goblet mix.
  • Stratified cuboidal epithelium (sweat gland ducts) is two layers of cube-shaped cells, far shorter than this.
Slides (2)

Olfactory mucosa

L29Learning
How does olfactory epithelium differ from respiratory epithelium?
  1. A. Taller pseudostratified; thin basement membrane; no goblet cells
  2. B. Shorter pseudostratified; thick basement membrane; many goblet cells
  3. C. Taller pseudostratified; thick basement membrane; many goblet cells
AnswerA. Taller pseudostratified; thin basement membrane; no goblet cells
WhyOlfactory epithelium is a tall pseudostratified epithelium on a thin basement membrane, with no goblet cells (and no motile ciliated cells).
Explanation

Both are pseudostratified, but the olfactory version is built for sensing, not clearing:

OlfactoryRespiratory
HeightVery tall, many rows of nucleiTall
Basement membraneThinThick
Goblet cellsNoneMany
CiliaNon-motile, on neuronsMotile
Lamina propriaSerous Bowman's glandsSeromucous glands

The wrong choices give it a thick basement membrane and goblet cells, which belong to respiratory epithelium.

Slides (3)
L30Learning
Which cell perceives smell, and where are its nuclei in the olfactory epithelium?
  1. A. Sustentacular (supporting) cell — nuclei form the middle rows
  2. B. Multipolar olfactory neuron — nuclei form the basal row
  3. C. Bipolar olfactory neuron — nuclei form the middle rows
AnswerC. Bipolar olfactory neuron — nuclei form the middle rows
WhyThe receptor is the bipolar olfactory neuron; its nuclei fill the middle rows of the epithelium, between the supporting-cell nuclei above and the basal-cell nuclei below.
Explanation

Olfactory receptor cells are true bipolar neurons: one dendrite runs up to the surface and ends in a knob with olfactory cilia; one axon runs down through the basement membrane to join the olfactory nerve. Their nuclei make up most of the epithelium's thickness, in an irregular middle zone.

  • Sustentacular cells support the neurons; their nuclei form the top row.
  • The neurons are bipolar, not multipolar, and the basal row belongs to the basal stem cells.

Nuclear layers, top to bottom: supporting → olfactory neurons → basal.

Slide (1)
L31Learning
Which description fits the supporting (sustentacular) cells of olfactory epithelium?
  1. A. Motile cilia and mucin granules; nuclei nearest the basement membrane
  2. B. Microvilli and ion channels; nuclei in the middle rows
  3. C. Microvilli and ion channels; nuclei nearest the surface
AnswerC. Microvilli and ion channels; nuclei nearest the surface
WhySupporting cells are tall columnar cells with apical microvilli and ion channels; their nuclei form the uppermost row of the olfactory epithelium.
Explanation

Sustentacular cells span the full height of the epithelium and hold the olfactory neurons between them, much as glial cells support neurons in the brain. Their apical microvilli reach into the surface mucus, and their ion channels help keep the ionic environment the neurons need. Their nuclei sit closest to the lumen.

  • Motile cilia and mucin belong to the ciliated and goblet cells of respiratory epithelium; olfactory epithelium has neither.
  • The middle rows of nuclei are the olfactory neurons'.
Slide (1)
L32Learning
What does the dendrite of an olfactory neuron end in?
  1. A. A knob bearing short motile cilia that sweep mucus toward the pharynx
  2. B. A knob bearing long non-motile cilia ("olfactory hairs") that carry the odorant receptors
  3. C. A single primary cilium buried in the basement membrane
AnswerB. A knob bearing long non-motile cilia ("olfactory hairs") that carry the odorant receptors
WhyEach olfactory neuron's dendrite ends at the surface in a knob with long non-motile cilia, the olfactory hairs, whose membranes hold the odorant receptors.
Explanation

The dendrite rises between the supporting cells and swells at the surface into an olfactory knob (vesicle). From it, several long, non-motile cilia spread out flat in the surface fluid. Odorant molecules dissolved in that fluid bind receptor proteins on these cilia and trigger the neuron.

  • Motile cilia that sweep mucus belong to the ciliated cells of respiratory epithelium.
  • The basement membrane is at the other end of the cell, where the axon leaves; nothing sensory is buried there.
Slide (1)
L33Learning
Where do the axons of olfactory neurons go?
  1. A. Through the cribriform plate of the ethmoid as the olfactory nerve
  2. B. Through the optic canal as the olfactory nerve
  3. C. Through the cribriform plate of the ethmoid as the trigeminal nerve
AnswerA. Through the cribriform plate of the ethmoid as the olfactory nerve
WhyOlfactory axons gather into bundles (fila olfactoria) in the lamina propria and pass through the cribriform plate as the olfactory nerve (cranial nerve I) to the olfactory bulb.
Explanation

The axon leaves the base of each bipolar neuron, crosses the thin basement membrane and joins others in unmyelinated nerve bundles in the lamina propria (seen as pale nerve profiles beside Bowman's glands). These fila olfactoria pass upward through the perforations of the cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone and synapse in the olfactory bulb.

  • The optic canal carries the optic nerve and ophthalmic artery.
  • The trigeminal nerve gives general sensation (touch, pain) to the nasal mucosa; it does not carry smell.
Slide (1)
L34Learning
What is the giveaway of olfactory mucosa in the lamina propria?
  1. A. Mixed seromucous glands
  2. B. Serous von Ebner's glands
  3. C. Serous Bowman's (olfactory) glands
AnswerC. Serous Bowman's (olfactory) glands
WhyBowman's glands, purely serous tubuloalveolar glands in the lamina propria (with olfactory nerve bundles), identify olfactory mucosa.
Explanation

The olfactory lamina propria is packed with Bowman's (olfactory) glands whose ducts cross the epithelium to the surface, along with olfactory nerve bundles and many blood vessels. Seeing serous glands plus nerve bundles under a thick, goblet-free epithelium tells you this is the olfactory region.

  • Mixed seromucous glands are the glands of respiratory mucosa (nasal cavity, larynx, trachea, bronchi).
  • Von Ebner's glands are serous glands of the tongue, opening into the trenches of the circumvallate papillae.
Slide (1)
L35Learning
What do Bowman's glands secrete onto the olfactory surface, and why?
  1. A. Watery serous fluid that dissolves odorants and rinses them away
  2. B. Thick mucus that traps inhaled dust for the cilia to clear
  3. C. A surfactant-like lipid that stops the surface from sticking
AnswerA. Watery serous fluid that dissolves odorants and rinses them away
WhyBowman's glands make a watery serous fluid: it dissolves odorant molecules so they reach the receptors, and its steady flow washes them away so new smells can be detected.
Explanation

Odorants must dissolve in the surface fluid before they can bind receptors on the olfactory cilia. Bowman's glands keep that fluid layer watery and constantly renewed, so the epithelium is "reset" for the next odour.

  • Thick mucus that traps dust is the job of goblet cells and seromucous glands of respiratory epithelium, and clearance by cilia needs motile cilia, which olfactory epithelium lacks.
  • A surfactant-like lipid is secreted by club cells in the bronchioles (and true surfactant by type II alveolar cells), not in the nose.
Slide (1)
L36Learning
Is olfactory epithelium ciliated?
  1. A. Yes — mostly by motile ciliated columnar cells, as in the trachea
  2. B. Only by the non-motile cilia of its neurons; it has no motile ciliated cells
  3. C. Yes — by motile cilia on the sustentacular cells
AnswerB. Only by the non-motile cilia of its neurons; it has no motile ciliated cells
WhyOlfactory epithelium has no motile ciliated cells; its only cilia are the non-motile olfactory hairs on the neurons' dendritic knobs.
Explanation

The lecture lists "absence of goblet cells and ciliated cells" for olfactory epithelium, meaning there are no ciliated columnar cells and no motile cilia. The receptor neurons do carry long non-motile cilia, and some tables (one shown in the course) therefore mark olfactory epithelium "ciliated: yes". Both statements fit once you separate motile ciliated cells (absent) from neuronal sensory cilia (present).

  • Mostly ciliated columnar cells describes respiratory epithelium.
  • Sustentacular cells carry microvilli, not cilia.
Slides (2)
L37Learning
A 48-year-old woman loses her sense of smell during a viral upper respiratory infection; it returns a week later. Which cells restored it?
  1. A. Sustentacular (supporting) cells
  2. B. Basal stem cells of the olfactory epithelium
  3. C. Surviving olfactory neurons dividing
AnswerB. Basal stem cells of the olfactory epithelium
WhyOlfactory neurons are among the few neurons replaced throughout life: basal stem cells on the basement membrane divide and differentiate into new receptor neurons.
Explanation

The virus damages the olfactory epithelium and its receptor neurons. Because the basal cells are stem cells, they regenerate new bipolar neurons (and supporting cells), whose dendrites reach the surface and whose axons grow back through the intact cribriform plate to the olfactory bulb, so smell returns in days to weeks.

  • Sustentacular cells support and insulate the neurons; they do not turn into neurons.
  • Mature olfactory neurons, like other neurons, do not divide.
Slide (1)
L38LearningBorderline
After a baseball fractures his ethmoid bone, a man cannot smell coffee, and the loss proves permanent. What was most likely damaged?
  1. A. Basal stem cells of the olfactory epithelium
  2. B. Olfactory axons torn at the cribriform plate
  3. C. Bowman's glands of the olfactory lamina propria
AnswerB. Olfactory axons torn at the cribriform plate
WhyAn ethmoid (cribriform plate) fracture shears the olfactory axons on their way to the bulb; scarring blocks regrowth, so the anosmia is usually permanent.
Explanation

The olfactory nerve is a set of fine axon bundles that pass through the holes of the cribriform plate. A fracture there tears them where they cross the bone. Even though basal cells keep making new receptor neurons, their axons cannot reconnect through the scarred plate, so the loss lasts.

  • Loss of basal stem cells is not the usual result of a fracture, and the epithelium itself sits below the plate; contrast toxic fumes or viruses, which damage the epithelium and give temporary loss because basal cells regenerate it.
  • Damage to Bowman's glands would at worst dry the surface; it would not abolish smell permanently.
Slide (1)
L39Learning
A biopsy from the roof of the nasal cavity shows a very thick pseudostratified epithelium with many rows of nuclei and no goblet cells, over a lamina propria full of serous tubuloalveolar glands and nerve bundles. What tissue is it?
  1. A. Olfactory mucosa
  2. B. Respiratory mucosa
  3. C. Nasopharyngeal mucosa
AnswerA. Olfactory mucosa
WhyThick goblet-free epithelium + Bowman's glands + nerve bundles in the lamina propria = olfactory mucosa of the superior concha and nasal roof.
Explanation

Read the clues: roof of the nasal cavity (olfactory region), an unusually thick pseudostratified epithelium with many rows of nuclei (supporting cells on top, neurons in the middle, basal cells below), no goblet cells, and serous glands with nerve bundles beneath it.

  • Respiratory mucosa would show goblet cells, motile cilia, a thick basement membrane and mixed seromucous glands.
  • Nasopharyngeal mucosa is a thin respiratory epithelium with few goblet cells and small glands, often with lymphoid tissue (pharyngeal tonsil), not nerve bundles and Bowman's glands.
Slides (2)

Cilia and primary ciliary dyskinesia

L40Learning
What goes wrong in the airway in primary ciliary dyskinesia?
  1. A. A defective chloride channel dehydrates the mucus, so it is too thick to move
  2. B. Faulty cilia fail to beat together, so mucus with dirt and bacteria builds up
  3. C. Cilia beat normally, but goblet cells make no mucus to trap particles
AnswerB. Faulty cilia fail to beat together, so mucus with dirt and bacteria builds up
WhyIn primary ciliary dyskinesia the cilia are structurally faulty and do not beat in coordinated waves, so the mucociliary escalator stops and mucus, dirt and bacteria pile up.
Explanation

Normally the cilia lining the trachea and bronchi beat in wave-like motions that carry the mucus sheet toward the mouth. In primary ciliary dyskinesia (Kartagener syndrome when situs inversus is present) an inherited defect makes the cilia immotile or uncoordinated. Mucus stagnates, bacteria grow in it, and the patient has chronic sinusitis, otitis, bronchitis and bronchiectasis.

  • A defective chloride channel with thick, dehydrated mucus is cystic fibrosis: the cilia are normal there, but the mucus is too viscous.
  • Mucus production is normal in PCD; the problem is moving it.
Slide (1)
L41LearningBorderline
What structural defect most often underlies primary ciliary dyskinesia (Kartagener syndrome)?
  1. A. Defective tubulin, so no axonemal microtubules form
  2. B. Absent basal bodies, so no cilia form at all
  3. C. Missing or defective dynein arms on the 9 + 2 axoneme
AnswerC. Missing or defective dynein arms on the 9 + 2 axoneme
WhyMost PCD is caused by mutations in dynein arm proteins: the cilia are present with a normal 9 + 2 microtubule pattern, but without dynein they cannot bend and beat.
Explanation

A motile cilium's core, the axoneme, is nine outer microtubule doublets around a central pair (9 + 2). Dynein arms on each doublet are ATP-driven motors that slide neighbouring doublets against each other; that sliding is what bends the cilium. In PCD the commonest defect is in the outer (and/or inner) dynein arms, so the cilia are immotile. The same machinery drives the sperm tail, so affected men are infertile.

  • With no microtubules or no basal bodies there would be no cilia; in PCD the cilia are there and look nearly normal in the light microscope, they just do not move.
L42Learning
In primary ciliary dyskinesia, where does mucus build up, and what else is affected?
  1. A. Trachea, bronchi and lungs only; fertility in men only
  2. B. Nasal cavity, sinuses, middle ear, trachea, bronchi and lungs; fertility in both sexes
  3. C. Nasal cavity, sinuses and middle ear only; fertility in women only
AnswerB. Nasal cavity, sinuses, middle ear, trachea, bronchi and lungs; fertility in both sexes
WhyEvery surface cleared by motile cilia is affected: nose, sinuses, middle ear, trachea, bronchi and lungs; fertility is impaired in both sexes.
Explanation

Motile cilia line the whole conducting airway and also the middle ear and auditory tube, so patients have chronic rhinosinusitis, ear infections, bronchitis and bronchiectasis. The same axonemal defect immobilizes the sperm flagellum (male infertility) and the cilia of the uterine tube that move the egg (reduced female fertility, ectopic pregnancy). In about half of patients the embryonic nodal cilia also fail, giving situs inversus (Kartagener syndrome).

  • Both wrong choices restrict the disease to part of the airway and to one sex; the defect is in every motile cilium.
Slide (1)

Larynx and epiglottis

L43Learning
Which laryngeal surfaces are covered by non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium, and why?
  1. A. Laryngeal surface of the epiglottis and the vestibular folds — they take friction and abrasion
  2. B. Lingual surface of the epiglottis and the vocal folds — they take friction and abrasion
  3. C. Lingual surface of the epiglottis and the ventricles — they trap inhaled particles
AnswerB. Lingual surface of the epiglottis and the vocal folds — they take friction and abrasion
WhyThe two stratified squamous sites are the lingual surface of the epiglottis (rubbed by food) and the vocal folds (struck by vibration and fast air); squamous layers resist abrasion.
Explanation

Most of the larynx is lined by respiratory epithelium, but two surfaces need a tougher, wet, non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium: the lingual (anterior) surface of the epiglottis, which swallowed food slides over, and the true vocal folds, which slap together thousands of times a minute during speech. On the laryngeal (posterior) surface of the epiglottis the squamous lining changes to respiratory epithelium.

  • The vestibular (false) folds are covered by respiratory epithelium.
  • The ventricles are also respiratory epithelium, and trapping particles is the job of mucus and cilia, not of a squamous lining.
Slide (1)
L44Learning
Which epithelium lines the vestibular (false) vocal folds?
  1. A. Non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium
  2. B. Pseudostratified ciliated columnar (respiratory) epithelium
  3. C. Keratinized stratified squamous epithelium
AnswerB. Pseudostratified ciliated columnar (respiratory) epithelium
WhyThe vestibular (false) folds, like the rest of the larynx except the vocal folds and lingual epiglottis, are covered by respiratory epithelium.
Explanation

The vestibular folds are the upper pair of laryngeal folds. They do not vibrate in speech, so they keep the ordinary pseudostratified ciliated columnar lining, with many seromucous glands and lymphoid tissue beneath. The squamous change is confined to the vocal folds below them and to the lingual surface of the epiglottis.

  • Non-keratinized stratified squamous lines the true vocal folds, one level lower; mixing up the two pairs of folds is the classic error.
  • Keratinized epithelium is skin; it is not found in the normal larynx.
Slides (2)
L45Learning
What type of cartilage supports the epiglottis, and what else does the epiglottis contain?
  1. A. Hyaline cartilage — with perichondrium, seromucous glands and taste buds
  2. B. Elastic cartilage — with perichondrium, seromucous glands and taste buds
  3. C. Fibrocartilage — without perichondrium, with mucous glands only
AnswerB. Elastic cartilage — with perichondrium, seromucous glands and taste buds
WhyThe epiglottis has a core of elastic cartilage with perichondrium, seromucous glands in its lamina propria and taste buds in its epithelium.
Explanation

Elastic cartilage contains a dense network of elastic fibres, so the epiglottis can bend down over the laryngeal inlet during swallowing and spring back afterward. Around the cartilage is a perichondrium; the mucosa has seromucous glands and, on the lingual side, stratified squamous epithelium with scattered taste buds.

  • Hyaline cartilage forms the thyroid and cricoid cartilages and the tracheal rings; it is stiffer and can calcify with age.
  • Fibrocartilage (intervertebral discs, pubic symphysis) has no perichondrium and does not occur in the larynx.
Slide (1)
L46Learning
What cartilage forms the thyroid and cricoid cartilages?
  1. A. Elastic cartilage, which stays flexible
  2. B. Fibrocartilage, without a perichondrium
  3. C. Hyaline cartilage, which may ossify with age
AnswerC. Hyaline cartilage, which may ossify with age
WhyThe thyroid and cricoid are hyaline cartilage; like other hyaline cartilage they can calcify and form bone with age.
Explanation

The larynx is built on a framework of large hyaline cartilages (thyroid, cricoid, most of the arytenoids) and smaller elastic cartilages (epiglottis, corniculate, cuneiform, tips of the arytenoids). Hyaline cartilage tends to calcify and even ossify in older adults, which is why the lab asks you to look for bone formation in the cricoid ring.

  • Elastic cartilage is the epiglottis's; it stays flexible and does not ossify.
  • Fibrocartilage is not part of the larynx.
Slide (1)
L47Learning
What does the laryngeal lamina propria contain?
  1. A. Serous Bowman's glands, dense regular tissue and olfactory nerve bundles
  2. B. Mixed seromucous glands, areolar tissue and mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT)
  3. C. Sweat and sebaceous glands, dense irregular tissue and hair follicles
AnswerB. Mixed seromucous glands, areolar tissue and mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT)
WhyThe laryngeal lamina propria is loose areolar tissue with mixed seromucous glands and MALT (lymphoid nodules).
Explanation

Beneath the laryngeal epithelium lies a loose (areolar) connective tissue with many mixed seromucous glands, especially in the vestibular folds, and lymphoid tissue (MALT, often as lymphatic nodules). In the vocal folds it also holds the elastic vocal ligament.

  • Bowman's glands and olfactory nerve bundles are the signature of the olfactory mucosa high in the nose.
  • Sweat and sebaceous glands with hair follicles belong to skin, such as the nasal vestibule.
Slide (1)
L48Learning
What lies in each true vocal fold beneath its epithelium?
  1. A. The elastic vocal ligament over smooth muscle and seromucous glands
  2. B. The elastic vestibular ligament over the smooth trachealis muscle
  3. C. The elastic vocal ligament over the striated vocalis muscle
AnswerC. The elastic vocal ligament over the striated vocalis muscle
WhyEach vocal fold holds the vocal ligament (elastic, the free upper edge of the conus elasticus) and, lateral to it, the vocalis muscle, which is striated (skeletal).
Explanation

Sound is made when air passes between the vocal folds and sets them vibrating. The vocal ligament is a band of dense elastic tissue along the free edge of the fold; it is the upper border of the conus elasticus (cricovocal membrane). The vocalis is part of the thyroarytenoid muscle, a voluntary skeletal muscle that adjusts the tension and so the pitch.

  • Smooth muscle is wrong: the intrinsic laryngeal muscles are all skeletal.
  • The vestibular ligament lies in the false fold above, and the trachealis is the smooth muscle of the trachea.
Slide (1)
L49Learning
What separates each true vocal fold from the vestibular fold above it?
  1. A. The piriform recess (extending up into a small saccule)
  2. B. The laryngeal ventricle (extending up into a small saccule)
  3. C. The vallecula (extending up into a small saccule)
AnswerB. The laryngeal ventricle (extending up into a small saccule)
WhyBetween the vestibular fold and the vocal fold on each side is a lateral recess, the laryngeal ventricle, whose upward pouch is the saccule.
Explanation

In a coronal section the larynx shows, from top to bottom: laryngeal vestibule → vestibular (false) folds → a slit-like ventricle on each side → vocal (true) folds → infraglottic cavity → trachea. The ventricle extends upward as the saccule, whose glands lubricate the vocal folds.

  • The piriform recess is a groove of the laryngopharynx beside the larynx, outside the airway.
  • The vallecula is the pouch between the tongue and the epiglottis.
Slide (1)
L50Learning
What is a singer's nodule?
  1. A. A mucus-filled cyst of the laryngeal saccule from voice overuse, covered by respiratory epithelium
  2. B. A callus-like growth on the vestibular fold from voice overuse, covered by respiratory epithelium
  3. C. A callus-like growth at the midpoint of the vocal fold from voice overuse, covered by stratified squamous epithelium
AnswerC. A callus-like growth at the midpoint of the vocal fold from voice overuse, covered by stratified squamous epithelium
WhyA singer's (vocal cord) nodule is a benign, callus-like thickening at the midpoint of the vocal fold caused by repeated overuse or misuse of the voice.
Explanation

Repeated hard contact between the vocal folds, most forcefully at the middle of their vibrating length, injures the stratified squamous covering. Like a callus on the hand, the epithelium and the tissue beneath thicken (sometimes with keratinization or abnormal vessels), and the voice becomes hoarse. It is commonest in women aged 20–50 and in singers, teachers and others who use their voice heavily; it is reversible with voice rest.

  • A saccular cyst is a different lesion.
  • The vestibular folds do not vibrate in normal speech and are covered by respiratory epithelium.
Slide (1)
L51Learning
A 23-year-old singer becomes hoarse; laryngoscopy shows a small nodule on a true vocal cord. Which epithelium normally covers the vocal fold?
  1. A. Non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium
  2. B. Pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium
  3. C. Keratinized stratified squamous epithelium
AnswerA. Non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium
WhyThe true vocal fold is covered by a wet, non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium, which protects it from the abrasion of vibration and fast airflow.
Explanation

The nodule grows from the vocal fold surface, so it is covered by the same epithelium: several layers of cells flattening toward the surface, kept moist by glandular secretions and without a keratin layer. This tough lining lets the folds strike each other during phonation without being damaged by everyday use.

  • Pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium covers the vestibular folds and most of the larynx, but not the true folds.
  • Keratinized epithelium is skin (nasal vestibule). The normal vocal fold is non-keratinized; keratin may appear only on a chronically injured nodule.
Slide (1)
L52Learning
A low-power coronal section shows a midline airway with two pairs of lateral folds separated by a slit-like recess: the upper pair is glandular under respiratory epithelium, the lower pair is covered by stratified squamous epithelium over a large mass of striated muscle. What organ is it?
  1. A. Larynx
  2. B. Trachea
  3. C. Nasopharynx
AnswerA. Larynx
WhyTwo pairs of folds (vestibular above, vocal below) separated by a ventricle, with the striated vocalis in the lower fold, identify the larynx.
Explanation

The upper folds are the vestibular (false) folds: respiratory epithelium over seromucous glands and lymphoid nodules. The recess below is the ventricle. The lower folds are the vocal (true) folds: stratified squamous epithelium over the vocal ligament and the large vocalis skeletal muscle.

  • The trachea is a simple tube with a C-shaped hyaline cartilage ring, seromucous glands and smooth trachealis muscle; it has no folds or striated muscle.
  • The nasopharynx has thin respiratory epithelium, skeletal muscle in its wall and the pharyngeal tonsil, but no paired vocal and vestibular folds.
Slides (2)

Trachea

L53Learning
List the layers of the tracheal wall from the lumen outward.
  1. A. Mucosa → hyaline cartilage → submucosa → adventitia
  2. B. Mucosa → submucosa → elastic cartilage → adventitia
  3. C. Mucosa → submucosa → hyaline cartilage → adventitia
AnswerC. Mucosa → submucosa → hyaline cartilage → adventitia
WhyTrachea, inside out: mucosa (respiratory epithelium + lamina propria) → submucosa (seromucous glands) → hyaline cartilage (C-rings) → adventitia.
Explanation

The trachea has no muscularis mucosae, so lamina propria and submucosa blend; an elastic membrane marks the boundary. The glands sit in the submucosa, and the C-shaped hyaline cartilage rings lie between the submucosa and the adventitia, the outer loose connective tissue that binds the trachea to its neighbours.

  • Cartilage before submucosa puts the rings directly under the mucosa; in fact the glandular submucosa lies between them.
  • Elastic cartilage is the epiglottis's; the trachea uses hyaline cartilage.
Slide (1)
L54Learning
What makes up the tracheal mucosa?
  1. A. Olfactory epithelium and a lamina propria with Bowman's glands, bounded by a collagen membrane
  2. B. Respiratory epithelium and a lamina propria with lymphoid tissue, bounded by an elastic membrane
  3. C. Stratified squamous epithelium and a lamina propria with sebaceous glands, bounded by smooth muscle
AnswerB. Respiratory epithelium and a lamina propria with lymphoid tissue, bounded by an elastic membrane
WhyThe tracheal mucosa is respiratory epithelium plus a lamina propria with a few glands and lymphoid tissue; an elastic membrane separates it from the submucosa.
Explanation

The lamina propria is loose connective tissue rich in elastic fibres, with scattered lymphocytes and lymphoid tissue (part of MALT) and only a few glands. Its deep edge is a condensed layer of elastic fibres, the elastic membrane, which takes the place of a muscularis mucosae and marks where the gland-rich submucosa begins.

  • Olfactory epithelium with Bowman's glands is found only high in the nasal cavity.
  • Stratified squamous epithelium with sebaceous glands is skin (nasal vestibule); there is no smooth muscle layer bounding the tracheal mucosa.
Slides (2)
L55Learning
Which glands lie in the tracheal submucosa, and what do they secrete?
  1. A. Sebaceous glands (a few also in the lamina propria) — oily sebum
  2. B. Seromucous glands (a few also in the lamina propria) — watery mucus
  3. C. Serous Bowman's glands (only in the lamina propria) — watery fluid
AnswerB. Seromucous glands (a few also in the lamina propria) — watery mucus
WhyThe tracheal submucosa is full of seromucous glands, mucous tubules capped by serous demilunes, whose ducts deliver watery mucus to the surface.
Explanation

Seromucous (mixed) glands contain both mucous cells (pale, foamy) and serous cells (darker, often arranged as serous demilunes). Their excretory ducts cross the lamina propria and open on the epithelial surface. The mixture keeps the mucus watery enough for the cilia to move and adds antimicrobial proteins. The lecture places them in the submucosa, with only a few in the lamina propria; the lab review describes them in the lamina propria, because the two layers blend in the trachea.

  • Sebaceous glands are skin glands of the nasal vestibule.
  • Bowman's glands are purely serous olfactory glands of the nasal roof.
Slides (2)
L56Learning
What is the tracheal cartilage like, and what does it do?
  1. A. Complete rings of elastic cartilage without perichondrium — let the lumen collapse in expiration
  2. B. C-shaped plates of fibrocartilage that never calcify — anchor the trachea to the oesophagus
  3. C. C-shaped rings of hyaline cartilage with perichondrium (may ossify with age) — hold the lumen open
AnswerC. C-shaped rings of hyaline cartilage with perichondrium (may ossify with age) — hold the lumen open
WhyAbout 16–20 C-shaped hyaline cartilage rings, each wrapped in perichondrium, keep the trachea permanently open against pressure changes and outside force.
Explanation

The rings lie between submucosa and adventitia, stacked one above the other and joined by fibroelastic tissue. Their stiffness holds the lumen open during forced breathing and protects it from being crushed by a blow to the neck. Like other hyaline cartilage they can calcify and even contain bone in older people. The open (posterior) side of each C faces the oesophagus.

  • Elastic cartilage is the epiglottis's, and a collapsing trachea would block airflow.
  • Fibrocartilage is not used in the airway.
Slides (3)
L57Learning
What bridges the open posterior ends of the tracheal cartilage rings?
  1. A. The trachealis muscle (smooth)
  2. B. The trachealis muscle (skeletal)
  3. C. Plates of elastic cartilage
AnswerA. The trachealis muscle (smooth)
WhyThe gap at the back of each C-ring is spanned by the trachealis, a bundle of smooth muscle (with fibroelastic tissue) facing the oesophagus.
Explanation

The posterior wall of the trachea has no cartilage. Instead the free ends of each C-ring are joined by the trachealis muscle, a band of smooth muscle. This soft wall lets a swallowed bolus bulge the oesophagus forward, and contraction of the trachealis narrows the trachea, raising airflow speed during coughing.

  • Skeletal muscle is wrong: the trachealis is involuntary smooth muscle (the skeletal muscles of the airway are in the pharynx and larynx).
  • Elastic cartilage plates are not found in the trachea.
Slide (1)
L58Learning
What does the tracheal adventitia contain?
  1. A. Smooth muscle, elastic membrane and perichondrium
  2. B. Seromucous glands, MALT and hyaline cartilage
  3. C. Vessels, nerves, lymphatics and fat
AnswerC. Vessels, nerves, lymphatics and fat
WhyThe adventitia is the outer loose connective tissue of the trachea, carrying blood vessels, nerves, lymphatics and fat (sometimes lymph nodules).
Explanation

The trachea has no serosa: its outermost layer is adventitia, loose connective tissue that blends with the neck and mediastinal tissues and carries the larger vessels, nerves and lymphatics that supply the wall, together with adipose tissue.

  • The elastic membrane lies under the mucosa, and the perichondrium wraps the cartilage; smooth muscle (trachealis) is in the posterior wall, not the adventitia.
  • Seromucous glands and MALT are in the submucosa and lamina propria, and the hyaline cartilage lies inside the adventitia, not within it.
Slide (1)
L59Learning
A cross-section shows a wide airway encircled by a thick C-shaped band of hyaline cartilage, open posteriorly where a smooth muscle bundle bridges the gap beside the oesophagus; seromucous glands fill the submucosa and no lung tissue surrounds it. What is it?
  1. A. Intrapulmonary bronchus
  2. B. Trachea
  3. C. Large bronchiole
AnswerB. Trachea
WhyA single C-shaped hyaline ring, trachealis muscle beside the oesophagus and no surrounding alveoli identify the trachea.
Explanation

Read the wall from the outside in. A complete-looking C of cartilage with a posterior smooth-muscle bridge is the trachea's signature; the oesophagus lies right behind it in the neck and superior mediastinum; and the airway is wrapped in loose adventitia rather than lung.

  • An intrapulmonary bronchus has several separate cartilage plates around the wall and is surrounded by alveoli.
  • A large bronchiole has no cartilage and no glands, only folded epithelium and prominent smooth muscle.
Slides (2)

Bronchi

L60Learning
Name the bronchi in order, starting at the carina.
  1. A. Primary (lobar) → secondary (main) → tertiary (segmental)
  2. B. Primary (main) → secondary (segmental) → tertiary (lobar)
  3. C. Primary (main) → secondary (lobar) → tertiary (segmental)
AnswerC. Primary (main) → secondary (lobar) → tertiary (segmental)
WhyThe trachea splits at the carina into two primary (main) bronchi, which give secondary (lobar) bronchi, one per lobe, which give tertiary (segmental) bronchi, one per bronchopulmonary segment.
Explanation

The bronchial tree: trachea → primary (main) bronchi (right and left) → secondary (lobar) bronchi (3 right, 2 left) → tertiary (segmental) bronchi → smaller bronchi → bronchioles → terminal bronchioles. The names follow what each branch supplies: the whole lung, a lobe, a segment.

  • Both wrong choices swap two names. Hook: M-L-S, main-lobar-segmental, from big to small.
Slide (1)
L61Learning
What cartilage supports the primary (main) bronchi before they enter the lung?
  1. A. Rings of hyaline cartilage, like the trachea's
  2. B. Separate plates of hyaline cartilage, like the intrapulmonary bronchi's
  3. C. No cartilage — only smooth muscle
AnswerA. Rings of hyaline cartilage, like the trachea's
WhyThe extrapulmonary primary bronchi are built like the trachea, with rings of hyaline cartilage; plates appear only once the bronchi enter the lung.
Explanation

Outside the lung the primary bronchi copy the tracheal wall: respiratory epithelium, seromucous glands and hyaline cartilage rings. Sources differ on the ring shape: the summary table calls them C-shaped like the trachea's, while the lab review describes a complete ring in primary bronchi; either way they are rings, not plates.

  • Separate plates are the hallmark of intrapulmonary bronchi, the change that happens as the bronchus enters the lung.
  • No cartilage describes bronchioles.
Slide (1)
L62Learning
What form does the cartilage take in intrapulmonary bronchi?
  1. A. Separate irregular plates of hyaline cartilage
  2. B. C-shaped rings of hyaline cartilage
  3. C. Separate irregular plates of elastic cartilage
AnswerA. Separate irregular plates of hyaline cartilage
WhyInside the lung the rings break up into separate, irregular plates of hyaline cartilage in the submucosa, spread around the circumference.
Explanation

As a bronchus enters the lung, the C-shaped rings are replaced by isolated plates of hyaline cartilage scattered all around the wall. They still keep the lumen open but allow branching and flexibility. The plates get smaller and fewer in smaller bronchi and disappear completely in the bronchioles.

  • C-shaped rings belong to the trachea and extrapulmonary bronchi.
  • The plates are hyaline, not elastic; elastic cartilage in the airway is the epiglottis's.
Slide (1)
L63Learning
Why does the bronchial mucosa look folded in histological sections?
  1. A. The cartilage plates pull on the submucosa and pleat the mucosa
  2. B. Its smooth muscle layer contracts (after death or fixation) and pleats the mucosa
  3. C. The submucosal glands swell and push the mucosa into folds
AnswerB. Its smooth muscle layer contracts (after death or fixation) and pleats the mucosa
WhyBronchi have a layer of smooth muscle between mucosa and cartilage; its contraction throws the epithelium and lamina propria into longitudinal folds.
Explanation

In intrapulmonary bronchi a distinct layer of spiral smooth-muscle bundles encircles the lumen in the lamina propria, between epithelium and cartilage plates. When it contracts, as it does after death and during fixation, the overlying mucosa cannot shorten and so buckles into folds. The same happens, even more strongly, in bronchioles, which are almost all muscle.

  • Cartilage plates are rigid supports outside the muscle; they hold the wall open rather than pleating it.
  • Glands lie in the submucosa and do not cause folding.
Slide (1)
L64Learning
Which large vessel runs alongside the bronchi and bronchioles inside the lung, branching with them?
  1. A. A branch of the pulmonary vein
  2. B. A branch of the internal thoracic artery
  3. C. A branch of the pulmonary artery
AnswerC. A branch of the pulmonary artery
WhyPulmonary artery branches travel with the airways, branching with them, down to the respiratory bronchioles; the pulmonary veins run separately in the connective tissue between segments.
Explanation

Each bronchus and bronchiole is accompanied by a branch of the pulmonary artery carrying oxygen-poor blood toward the capillaries around the alveoli; in sections the thick-walled artery is often seen right beside the airway (for example next to a terminal bronchiole). The airway wall itself is fed by small bronchial arteries from the aorta.

  • Pulmonary veins collect blood at the periphery of the units and run in the interlobular and intersegmental septa, away from the airways.
  • The internal thoracic artery runs inside the anterior chest wall and does not enter the lung.
Slide (1)
L65Learning
How does the bronchial wall change as the bronchi get smaller?
  1. A. Epithelium gets taller; glands and goblet cells become more numerous
  2. B. Epithelium gets shorter; cartilage rings become complete
  3. C. Epithelium gets shorter; glands and goblet cells become fewer
AnswerC. Epithelium gets shorter; glands and goblet cells become fewer
WhyGoing distally, the respiratory epithelium shortens and glands and goblet cells thin out, while cartilage plates shrink and smooth muscle becomes relatively more prominent.
Explanation

The bronchial tree simplifies as it narrows. The pseudostratified epithelium becomes lower, approaching simple columnar; the number of submucosal glands and goblet cells falls; the cartilage plates become smaller and sparser. Smooth muscle, by contrast, makes up a growing share of the wall, which is why the smallest airways are the ones that constrict most.

  • Taller epithelium with more glands reverses the trend.
  • Complete cartilage rings belong to the large extrapulmonary airways; distally the cartilage breaks into plates and then vanishes.
Slide (1)
L66Learning
How do you tell an intrapulmonary bronchus from an extrapulmonary one on a slide?
  1. A. Separate cartilage plates around the wall, and lung tissue (alveoli) right against its adventitia
  2. B. C-shaped cartilage rings, and loose adventitia instead of lung tissue around it
  3. C. No cartilage at all, and a thick layer of smooth muscle instead
AnswerA. Separate cartilage plates around the wall, and lung tissue (alveoli) right against its adventitia
WhyAn intrapulmonary bronchus has irregular cartilage plates instead of rings and is surrounded by alveoli; extrapulmonary bronchi have rings and loose connective tissue around them.
Explanation

Two quick checks: the cartilage (rings outside the lung, plates inside) and what surrounds the airway (loose adventitia in the mediastinum, alveolar lung tissue inside the lung). The lining is respiratory epithelium in both.

  • C-shaped rings with loose adventitia describe the extrapulmonary bronchus (and trachea), the opposite of what was asked.
  • No cartilage, thick smooth muscle describes a bronchiole, which is smaller still.
Slide (1)
L67Learning
A lung section shows an airway with folded respiratory epithelium, a layer of spiral smooth muscle, seromucous glands, lymphoid tissue and several separate plates of hyaline cartilage, with alveoli right outside its wall. What is it?
  1. A. Intrapulmonary bronchus
  2. B. Extrapulmonary bronchus
  3. C. Large bronchiole
AnswerA. Intrapulmonary bronchus
WhyCartilage plates + glands + smooth muscle + surrounding alveoli = intrapulmonary bronchus (for example a tertiary, segmental bronchus).
Explanation

The intrapulmonary bronchus wall, inside out: folded respiratory epithelium (few goblet cells); lamina propria with spiral smooth-muscle bundles, MALT and serous and mucous glands; submucosa with isolated hyaline cartilage plates; adventitia with vessels and nerves; then lung tissue.

  • An extrapulmonary bronchus has cartilage rings and lies outside the lung, so no alveoli surround it.
  • A large bronchiole has no cartilage and no glands.
Slides (2)

Bronchioles and club cells

L68Learning
About how wide are bronchioles, and what do their walls lack?
  1. A. Less than 1 mm — no cartilage and no glands
  2. B. Less than 5 mm — no cartilage, but many glands
  3. C. Less than 1 mm — cartilage plates, but no glands
AnswerA. Less than 1 mm — no cartilage and no glands
WhyBronchioles are airways under about 1 mm across whose walls have no cartilage and no glands.
Explanation

The change from bronchus to bronchiole is defined by the wall, not just size: the last cartilage plates and submucosal glands disappear. What remains is folded mucosa, a well-developed smooth-muscle layer and an adventitia of dense connective tissue tethered to the surrounding alveoli.

  • Many glands is wrong: glands end with the bronchi.
  • Cartilage plates are the mark of a bronchus; any airway with cartilage is not a bronchiole.
Slide (1)
L69Learning
What supports a bronchiole wall in place of cartilage?
  1. A. Abundant seromucous glands in a folded mucosa
  2. B. Complete rings of elastic cartilage in a folded mucosa
  3. C. Well-developed smooth muscle in a folded mucosa
AnswerC. Well-developed smooth muscle in a folded mucosa
WhyWith no cartilage, the bronchiole wall is mostly smooth muscle under a folded mucosa, held open by the pull of the elastic alveolar tissue around it.
Explanation

Bronchioles have the thickest smooth muscle relative to their size of any airway. The surrounding alveolar walls, attached to the bronchiolar adventitia, pull outward and keep the lumen open during inspiration. Elastic fibres run with the muscle.

  • Seromucous glands are absent from bronchioles.
  • There is no cartilage of any kind in a bronchiole; elastic cartilage is found in the epiglottis.

This muscle-rich, cartilage-free wall is why bronchioles narrow so much in asthma.

Slide (1)
L70Learning
How does the epithelium change along the bronchioles, from large to terminal?
  1. A. Ciliated low columnar → stratified squamous; brush cells go from few to predominant
  2. B. Pseudostratified columnar → simple squamous; type I alveolar cells take over
  3. C. Ciliated low columnar → mostly non-ciliated cuboidal; club cells go from few to predominant
AnswerC. Ciliated low columnar → mostly non-ciliated cuboidal; club cells go from few to predominant
WhyDown the bronchioles the lining goes from ciliated low columnar to cuboidal, from ciliated to largely non-ciliated, and from few to predominantly club cells.
Explanation

Large bronchioles still carry a respiratory-type lining (ciliated, a few goblet cells), shortening to simple ciliated columnar. By the terminal bronchiole the epithelium is simple cuboidal, only some cells are ciliated, goblet cells are gone and club (Clara) cells dominate.

  • Stratified squamous appears in bronchi only as pathological squamous metaplasia, and brush cells stay rare.
  • Simple squamous epithelium with type I cells lines the alveoli, in the respiratory portion.
Slide (1)
L71Learning
What epithelium lines the terminal bronchiole?
  1. A. Stratified cuboidal (some sources say stratified columnar)
  2. B. Simple squamous (some sources say flattened cuboidal)
  3. C. Simple cuboidal (some sources say low columnar)
AnswerC. Simple cuboidal (some sources say low columnar)
WhyThe terminal bronchiole is lined by simple cuboidal epithelium (club cells and some ciliated cells); some atlases label it low columnar.
Explanation

The lecture and summary table give simple cuboidal; the lab review says "non-ciliated cuboidal or low columnar", and one atlas figure labels it "simple columnar". All agree it is a single layer of short cells, no longer pseudostratified, and without goblet cells.

  • Stratified cuboidal or columnar epithelium lines large gland ducts, not airways.
  • Simple squamous epithelium appears only in the alveolar ducts and alveoli, beyond the terminal bronchiole.
Slides (2)
L72Learning
Which cells make up the terminal bronchiole epithelium?
  1. A. Mostly club cells; some ciliated cells; a few brush and small granule cells
  2. B. Mostly goblet cells; some ciliated cells; a few basal and brush cells
  3. C. Mostly type I alveolar cells; some type II cells; a few club cells
AnswerA. Mostly club cells; some ciliated cells; a few brush and small granule cells
WhyThe terminal bronchiole lining is dominated by club (Clara) cells, with some ciliated cells and a few brush and small granule cells; goblet cells are gone.
Explanation

By this level the mucus-making machinery of the bigger airways has disappeared: there are no goblet cells (and no glands), because mucus this far down could not be cleared. The club cells take over secretion and protection, while a few remaining ciliated cells still move fluid upward and scattered brush and neuroendocrine cells persist.

  • Mostly goblet cells is the opposite of the truth: goblet cells end in the larger bronchioles.
  • Type I and type II alveolar cells line the alveoli, which do not open from a terminal bronchiole wall.
Slides (2)
L73Learning
What surrounds the terminal bronchiole epithelium, and what is missing from its wall?
  1. A. A thick spiral layer of skeletal muscle; no elastic fibres in the wall
  2. B. One or two layers of smooth muscle with elastic fibres; no alveoli open from the wall
  3. C. Separate hyaline cartilage plates with seromucous glands; no smooth muscle in the wall
AnswerB. One or two layers of smooth muscle with elastic fibres; no alveoli open from the wall
WhyA terminal bronchiole has only 1–2 layers of smooth muscle with elastic fibres, and a complete wall: no glands, no cartilage and no alveoli opening from it.
Explanation

The terminal bronchiole is the last conducting airway, so its wall must still be continuous: epithelium → lamina propria with thin smooth muscle and elastic fibres → adventitia. Alveoli lie all around it in the lung tissue but none open into it; the first alveolar outpockets appear in the respiratory bronchiole.

  • Skeletal muscle is found only in the pharynx and larynx, and elastic fibres run all the way to the alveoli.
  • Cartilage plates and glands ended with the bronchi.
Slides (2)
L74Learning
Where in the airway are club (Clara) cells found?
  1. A. In the trachea and primary bronchi, among the ciliated cells
  2. B. In the bronchioles, predominant in terminal and respiratory bronchioles
  3. C. In the alveolar walls, among the type I alveolar cells
AnswerB. In the bronchioles, predominant in terminal and respiratory bronchioles
WhyClub cells are the non-ciliated cuboidal cells of the bronchiolar epithelium: few in large bronchioles, predominant in terminal and respiratory bronchioles.
Explanation

Club cells (bronchiolar exocrine cells, formerly Clara cells) increase in number as the bronchioles narrow and become the main cell of the terminal and respiratory bronchioles. They are absent from the pseudostratified respiratory epithelium of the trachea and bronchi.

  • Trachea and primary bronchi: their epithelium is ciliated, goblet, basal, brush and small granule cells, with no club cells.
  • Alveolar walls are lined by type I and type II alveolar cells; type II cells share some club-cell functions (surfactant) but are a different cell.
Slides (2)
L75Learning
What do club cells secrete?
  1. A. Calcitonin-like peptide hormones
  2. B. Surfactant-like lipoproteins and mucins
  3. C. Thick mucin from apical goblet granules
AnswerB. Surfactant-like lipoproteins and mucins
WhyClub cells secrete surfactant-like phospholipid/lipoprotein and mucins, which line the bronchioles and help stop them collapsing and sticking shut.
Explanation

Their apical granules contain a surface-active, phospholipid-rich material resembling alveolar surfactant, plus mucins. Spread over the bronchiolar lining, it lowers surface tension so the small airways do not collapse at the end of expiration. They also secrete protective proteins (see the immune question).

  • Calcitonin-like peptides come from small granule (Kulchitsky) cells, the neuroendocrine cells.
  • Goblet cells are absent from terminal bronchioles; club cells take over secretion there.
Slide (1)
L76Learning
How do club cells detoxify inhaled chemicals?
  1. A. Abundant rough ER with secretory enzymes
  2. B. Abundant smooth ER with cytochrome P450 enzymes
  3. C. Abundant lysosomes with hydrolytic enzymes
AnswerB. Abundant smooth ER with cytochrome P450 enzymes
WhyClub cells have abundant smooth endoplasmic reticulum (SER) whose cytochrome P450 enzymes inactivate inhaled xenobiotics, as liver cells do.
Explanation

The SER is the cell's site of lipid synthesis and of oxidative detoxification. Its cytochrome P450 enzymes modify foreign compounds (xenobiotics) such as those in smoke and pollutants so they can be removed. Club cells sit exactly where inhaled chemicals settle in the small airways, and their large SER makes them the airway's detoxifying cells.

  • Rough ER makes secretory and membrane proteins; it does not detoxify.
  • Lysosomes digest material taken in by endocytosis or phagocytosis, the job of macrophages, not club cells.
Slide (1)
L77Learning
What do club cells contribute to local immune defence?
  1. A. IgG antibodies, interferon-γ and complement proteins
  2. B. IgE antibodies, histamine and leukotriene mediators
  3. C. Secretory component of IgA, antimicrobial peptides, cytokines
AnswerC. Secretory component of IgA, antimicrobial peptides, cytokines
WhyClub cells secrete the secretory component of IgA, antimicrobial peptides (such as lysozyme) and cytokines that regulate local inflammation.
Explanation

Plasma cells in the lamina propria make dimeric IgA, but it needs an epithelial receptor to reach the lumen; club cells provide this, releasing the secretory component with the IgA into the bronchiolar fluid. They also secrete antimicrobial peptides active against bacteria and viruses and cytokines that tune the local immune response.

  • IgG and interferon-γ are made by plasma cells and lymphocytes, not epithelial cells.
  • IgE, histamine and leukotrienes are the products of plasma cells and mast cells in allergy and asthma.
Slide (1)
L78Learning
Besides secretion and defence, what other role do some club cells have?
  1. A. Stem cells for the bronchiolar epithelium
  2. B. Phagocytes that ingest inhaled dust
  3. C. Chemoreceptors that signal to afferent nerves
AnswerA. Stem cells for the bronchiolar epithelium
WhySome club cells are stem (progenitor) cells that divide to renew the bronchiolar epithelium after injury.
Explanation

Bronchioles have few or no basal cells, so the cuboidal cells themselves include the progenitors: dividing club cells replace both club and ciliated cells after injury, for example after smoke inhalation.

  • Phagocytes that ingest dust are alveolar macrophages (dust cells).
  • Chemoreceptors with afferent nerve contacts are brush cells.

Parallel to remember: basal cells renew the respiratory and olfactory epithelia, club cells renew the bronchioles, and type II alveolar cells renew the alveolar lining.

Slide (1)
L79Learning
A lung section shows an airway with a wide lumen, tall ciliated epithelium thrown into deep folds and a prominent ring of smooth muscle, supported only by fibrous connective tissue, with no glands and no cartilage. What is it?
  1. A. Large bronchiole
  2. B. Intrapulmonary bronchus
  3. C. Terminal bronchiole
AnswerA. Large bronchiole
WhyFolded respiratory-type epithelium and thick smooth muscle with no cartilage and no glands = large bronchiole.
Explanation
