The decisive clue is what is missing: no cartilage plates and no glands rules out every bronchus. Among bronchioles, a large one still has tall, ciliated (respiratory-type) epithelium and a lumen much wider than the neighbouring alveoli.

  • An intrapulmonary bronchus would show hyaline cartilage plates and seromucous glands.
  • A terminal bronchiole is small (about alveolar size), lined by low cuboidal mostly non-ciliated club cells, with only one or two layers of smooth muscle.
Slide (1)
L80Learning
A small airway, about the size of the alveoli around it, has a slightly folded lining of cuboidal cells, many with dome-shaped apices, ringed by one or two layers of smooth muscle; it has no cartilage, no glands and no alveoli opening from its wall. What is it?
  1. A. Respiratory bronchiole
  2. B. Large bronchiole
  3. C. Terminal bronchiole
AnswerC. Terminal bronchiole
WhyCuboidal club-cell lining, thin smooth muscle and a complete wall with no alveoli = terminal bronchiole, the last conducting airway.
Explanation

Small size, cuboidal epithelium dominated by dome-shaped club cells, only 1–2 layers of smooth muscle and no cartilage or glands all point to a terminal bronchiole. The unbroken wall is the key to telling it from the next segment.

  • A respiratory bronchiole has the same kind of cuboidal lining but its wall is interrupted by alveoli opening directly from it.
  • A large bronchiole is much wider than an alveolus, with tall ciliated epithelium and a thick, prominent muscle layer.
Slide (1)
L81Learning
In the epithelium of a terminal bronchiole, the most abundant cells are non-ciliated, with dome-shaped apices bulging into the lumen and full of granules. What are they?
  1. A. Small granule (Kulchitsky) cells
  2. B. Club (Clara) cells
  3. C. Goblet cells
AnswerB. Club (Clara) cells
WhyNon-ciliated cuboidal cells with dome-shaped, granule-filled apices bulging into a bronchiole are club (Clara) cells.
Explanation

Club cells are bronchiolar exocrine cells: cuboidal, without cilia, with an apical cytoplasm that bulges above the ciliated cells and contains secretory granules (surfactant-like material), and a large SER. They dominate the terminal bronchiole lining.

  • Small granule cells are scattered, basally placed neuroendocrine cells whose dense-core granules lie at the base and need special stains to see.
  • Goblet cells have pale mucin-filled apices and are absent from terminal bronchioles.
Slide (1)

Wall features down the tree

L82Learning
Hyaline cartilage: where is it last seen, and where is it gone?
  1. A. Last in the bronchi (rings, then plates) → gone from the bronchioles
  2. B. Last in the terminal bronchioles (plates) → gone from the alveolar ducts
  3. C. Last in the bronchioles (plates) → gone from the respiratory bronchioles
AnswerA. Last in the bronchi (rings, then plates) → gone from the bronchioles
WhyCartilage runs from the trachea through all the bronchi (rings, then plates) and stops at the bronchioles.
Explanation

The loss of cartilage defines the bronchiole. Its sequence is: C-shaped rings (trachea, extrapulmonary bronchi) → irregular plates (intrapulmonary bronchi, getting smaller) → none (bronchioles onward).

FeatureLast seenGone from
Cartilage, glandsBronchiBronchioles
Goblet cellsLarger bronchiolesTerminal bronchioles
CiliaRespiratory bronchiolesAlveolar ducts
Smooth muscleAlveolar ductsAlveoli
Elastic fibresAll the way to the alveoli
Slide (1)
L83Learning
Glands: where are they last seen, and where are they gone?
  1. A. Last in the bronchi → gone from the bronchioles
  2. B. Last in the trachea → gone from the bronchi
  3. C. Last in the respiratory bronchioles → gone from the alveolar ducts
AnswerA. Last in the bronchi → gone from the bronchioles
WhySubmucosal glands stop together with the cartilage: present through the bronchi, absent from the bronchioles.
Explanation

Seromucous glands are found from the nasal cavity through the larynx, trachea and bronchi (fewer in smaller bronchi). Bronchioles have no glands, which is one of the two absences (with cartilage) that define them.

  • Gone from the bronchi stops a level too early: intrapulmonary bronchi still have serous and mucous glands.
  • Respiratory bronchioles have no glands at all.

Hook: cartilage and glands leave together at the bronchiole.

Slide (1)
L84Learning
Goblet cells: where are they last seen, and where are they gone?
  1. A. Last in the bronchi → gone from all bronchioles
  2. B. Last in the terminal bronchioles → gone from the respiratory bronchioles
  3. C. Last in the larger bronchioles → gone from the terminal bronchioles
AnswerC. Last in the larger bronchioles → gone from the terminal bronchioles
WhyGoblet cells outlast the glands by one step: a few remain in the larger bronchioles, and terminal bronchioles have none.
Explanation

Goblet cells thin out steadily along the bronchial tree. The summary table lists them "only in larger" bronchioles and "none" in terminal bronchioles, where club cells take over. Mucus produced too far down could not be cleared, so it would plug the smallest airways.

  • Gone from all bronchioles stops one step too early: large bronchioles still have a few.
  • Present in terminal bronchioles goes one step too far.
Slide (1)
L85Learning
Cilia: where are they last seen, and where are they gone?
  1. A. Last in the respiratory bronchioles (a few) → gone from the alveolar ducts
  2. B. Last in the terminal bronchioles → gone from the respiratory bronchioles
  3. C. Last in the alveolar ducts (a few) → gone from the alveoli
AnswerA. Last in the respiratory bronchioles (a few) → gone from the alveolar ducts
WhyCiliated cells reach furthest of all the epithelial specializations: some remain in terminal and respiratory bronchioles, and none are found from the alveolar ducts on.
Explanation

Ciliated cells become fewer down the tree, but a few persist in terminal and respiratory bronchioles so that fluid and debris can still be moved upward from the gas-exchange region. The alveolar ducts and alveoli are lined by simple squamous cells with no cilia.

  • Gone from the respiratory bronchioles stops one step too early.
  • Present in the alveolar ducts goes one step too far: their lining is simple squamous.
Slide (1)
L86Learning
Smooth muscle: where is it last seen, and where is it gone?
  1. A. Last in the alveolar ducts (at alveolar openings) → gone from the alveoli
  2. B. Last in the terminal bronchioles → gone from the respiratory bronchioles
  3. C. Last in the respiratory bronchioles → gone from the alveolar ducts
AnswerA. Last in the alveolar ducts (at alveolar openings) → gone from the alveoli
WhySmooth muscle outlasts the conducting portion: it persists in respiratory bronchioles and in alveolar ducts as knobs ringing the alveolar openings; alveolar walls have none.
Explanation

The smooth-muscle layer thins but does not stop at the end of the conducting portion. Respiratory bronchioles keep some, and in the alveolar ducts small bundles sit at the rims of the alveolar openings (seen as knobs between the alveoli). The alveolar walls themselves are muscle-free.

  • Stopping at the terminal or respiratory bronchioles ends too early: respiratory bronchioles still have muscle, and the last bundles ring the alveolar openings of the ducts.
Slide (1)
L87Learning
Which wall component runs all the way down the airway to the alveoli?
  1. A. Smooth muscle
  2. B. Elastic fibres
  3. C. Ciliated cells
AnswerB. Elastic fibres
WhyElastic fibres are the only wall component present from the trachea to the alveoli; they even become a larger share of the wall distally.
Explanation

Elastic fibres in the lamina propria of the airways and in the alveolar walls give the lung its elastic recoil: they stretch during inspiration and spring back to push air out passively during expiration. As cartilage, glands, goblet cells, cilia and muscle drop out one by one, elastic fibres remain, so they make up a growing proportion of the wall. Their destruction in emphysema is why those lungs cannot recoil.

  • Smooth muscle ends at the alveolar ducts.
  • Ciliated cells end at the respiratory bronchioles.
Slide (1)

Asthma and smoking

L88Learning
What is asthma, and which cells drive it?
  1. A. Chronic inflammation of the alveolar walls — neutrophils, macrophages, B lymphocytes
  2. B. Chronic inflammation of the bronchial tree — mast cells, eosinophils, T lymphocytes
  3. C. Chronic fibrosis of the lung interstitium — fibroblasts and type II alveolar cells
AnswerB. Chronic inflammation of the bronchial tree — mast cells, eosinophils, T lymphocytes
WhyAsthma is chronic inflammation of the bronchial tree with episodes of bronchospasm, driven by mast cells, eosinophils and T lymphocytes.
Explanation

In allergic asthma, inhaled antigens activate T helper cells and IgE-coated mast cells in the airway wall. Mast cells release histamine and other mediators that constrict smooth muscle and make vessels leak; eosinophils (cells of allergic disease) and T lymphocytes keep the inflammation going and remodel the wall.

  • Alveolar-wall inflammation with neutrophils describes pneumonia; asthma is an airway disease.
  • Interstitial fibrosis is a restrictive lung disease, not asthma.
Slide (1)
L89Learning
What is the sequence of events in an acute asthmatic bronchospasm?
  1. A. Antigen → mast cells degranulate → bronchiolar smooth muscle contracts suddenly
  2. B. Antigen → mast cells degranulate → bronchiolar smooth muscle relaxes suddenly
  3. C. Antigen → eosinophils degranulate → tracheal cartilage collapses suddenly
AnswerA. Antigen → mast cells degranulate → bronchiolar smooth muscle contracts suddenly
WhyIn an attack, a specific antigen triggers mast-cell degranulation, and the released mediators make bronchiolar smooth muscle contract suddenly (bronchospasm).
Explanation

The antigen cross-links IgE on mast cells in the airway wall; the mast cells degranulate, releasing histamine, leukotrienes and other mediators. These cause sudden constriction of the smooth muscle of the bronchioles, plus oedema and mucus secretion, so the lumen narrows and the patient wheezes. Severity ranges from mild to life-threatening.

  • Smooth muscle relaxing would widen the airway: that is what the treatment does.
  • The trachea's cartilage keeps it open; asthma narrows the cartilage-free bronchioles.
Slide (1)
L90Learning
Why are the bronchioles the airways most susceptible to bronchospasm?
  1. A. The most goblet cells and glands, so mucus plugs form there first
  2. B. Relatively the thinnest smooth muscle, and complete cartilage rings that cannot flex
  3. C. Relatively the thickest smooth muscle, and no cartilage to hold them open
AnswerC. Relatively the thickest smooth muscle, and no cartilage to hold them open
WhyBronchioles have no cartilage to resist narrowing and a proportionally thick smooth-muscle layer, so when that muscle contracts the lumen can nearly close.
Explanation

In the trachea and bronchi, rings and plates of hyaline cartilage keep the airway open whatever the muscle does. Bronchioles have lost all cartilage (and glands), and smooth muscle forms a large share of their wall. Contraction of that muscle therefore folds the mucosa inward and shrinks a lumen that was already less than 1 mm wide; airflow resistance rises steeply, and expiration suffers most.

  • Bronchioles have no glands and few goblet cells; mucus contributes to asthma but is not why bronchioles are most affected.
  • Bronchioles have no cartilage at all, and their muscle is relatively thick, not thin.
Slide (1)
L91Learning
What chronic changes does asthma produce in the airway wall?
  1. A. Smooth-muscle atrophy
    Thinned basement membrane
    Fewer goblet and basal cells
    Loss of mucus
    Ciliated hyperplasia
  2. B. Smooth-muscle atrophy
    Thickened basement membrane
    More club cells
    Alveolar wall destruction
    Columnar metaplasia
  3. C. Smooth-muscle hypertrophy
    Thickened basement membrane
    More goblet and basal cells
    Excess mucus (plugs)
    Squamous metaplasia
AnswerC. Smooth-muscle hypertrophy
Thickened basement membrane
More goblet and basal cells
Excess mucus (plugs)
Squamous metaplasia
WhyChronic asthma remodels the airway: hypertrophied smooth muscle, a thickened basement membrane, more goblet and basal cells with mucus plugs, and patches of squamous metaplasia.
Explanation

Repeated inflammation changes the wall permanently. The smooth-muscle layer thickens, so spasms narrow the airway more; the basement membrane beneath the epithelium becomes visibly thick; goblet cells multiply (goblet cell hyperplasia/metaplasia), producing excess mucus that can plug the lumen with trapped inflammatory cells; basal cells increase; and parts of the injured epithelium may turn squamous.

  • The first wrong choice reverses every change.
  • Alveolar wall destruction is emphysema, and muscle atrophies in neither disease.
Slide (1)
L92Learning
How do epinephrine and other sympathomimetic drugs relieve an asthma attack?
  1. A. They contract bronchiolar smooth muscle, stiffening the bronchioles
  2. B. They relax bronchiolar smooth muscle, widening the bronchioles
  3. C. They stimulate goblet cells, flushing mucus out of the bronchioles
AnswerB. They relax bronchiolar smooth muscle, widening the bronchioles
WhyEpinephrine and other sympathomimetics (for example inhaled β2-agonists) act on the smooth muscle to relax it and increase bronchiolar diameter.
Explanation

Sympathetic stimulation of β2-adrenergic receptors on airway smooth muscle relaxes it, so the narrowed bronchioles open up and airflow returns. That is why these drugs are given during attacks.

  • Contracting the muscle is what the disease already does; it would worsen the attack.
  • More goblet-cell mucus would add to the obstruction; the target of the drug is the muscle.
Slide (1)
L93Learning
A 45-year-old man with a 30 pack-year smoking history has a chronic cough. What would a bronchial biopsy most likely show?
  1. A. Ciliated pseudostratified columnar epithelium replaced by stratified squamous epithelium
  2. B. Stratified squamous epithelium replaced by ciliated pseudostratified columnar epithelium
  3. C. Ciliated pseudostratified columnar epithelium replaced by simple cuboidal epithelium
AnswerA. Ciliated pseudostratified columnar epithelium replaced by stratified squamous epithelium
WhyChronic smoke injures the bronchial lining, and basal stem cells replace it with tougher stratified squamous epithelium: squamous metaplasia (columnar → squamous).
Explanation

Smoke paralyses and kills ciliated cells. Under constant irritation the basal stem cells change their differentiation and produce a stratified squamous epithelium, which resists chemical injury better but has no cilia and no goblet cells. The change is reversible if smoking stops, but if irritation continues the metaplastic epithelium can become dysplastic and give rise to squamous cell carcinoma.

  • Squamous → columnar is the reverse direction (columnar metaplasia, as in Barrett oesophagus).
  • Simple cuboidal epithelium is the normal lining of terminal bronchioles, not a smoker's change in bronchi.
Slide (1)
L94Learning
Replacement of one mature epithelium by another type in response to chronic irritation, as in a smoker's bronchi, is called:
  1. A. Metaplasia
  2. B. Dysplasia
  3. C. Hyperplasia
AnswerA. Metaplasia
WhyMetaplasia is a reversible switch from one fully differentiated cell type to another (here columnar → squamous) that copes better with the irritant.
Explanation

In metaplasia the stem cells of the tissue are reprogrammed to make a different mature epithelium: in the smoker's bronchus, pseudostratified ciliated columnar → stratified squamous. The cells are normal-looking cells of the new type, and the change can revert if the irritation stops.

  • Dysplasia is disordered growth with abnormal, atypical cells (loss of uniformity and orientation); it can follow persistent metaplasia and is precancerous.
  • Hyperplasia is an increase in the number of cells of the same type, such as goblet cell hyperplasia in asthma.
Slide (1)
L95Learning
Why does squamous metaplasia in a smoker's bronchi impair mucus clearance?
  1. A. Squamous cells resist smoke but have no cilia, so mucus is not moved upward
  2. B. Squamous cells have motile cilia that beat toward the alveoli
  3. C. Squamous cells secrete thick mucin that the cilia cannot move
AnswerA. Squamous cells resist smoke but have no cilia, so mucus is not moved upward
WhyThe metaplastic stratified squamous epithelium is tougher but has no cilia (and no goblet cells), so the mucociliary escalator stops and mucus must be coughed up.
Explanation

Trading ciliated columnar cells for squamous cells protects the bronchus from chemical injury but costs the clearing mechanism. Mucus from the remaining glands accumulates, bacteria and particles are no longer swept to the pharynx, and the smoker develops a chronic productive cough and frequent infections.

  • Squamous cells have no cilia at all, in any direction.
  • Squamous cells do not secrete mucin; mucus comes from goblet cells and submucosal glands.
Slide (1)

Respiratory bronchiole: where gas exchange begins

L96Learning
Which list contains only structures of the respiratory portion of the airway?
  1. A. Terminal bronchioles, respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts
  2. B. Respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts, alveoli
  3. C. Bronchioles, alveolar ducts, alveolar sacs
AnswerB. Respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts, alveoli
WhyThe respiratory portion is every segment where alveoli appear: respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts and alveoli (with their sacs). Terminal bronchioles still conduct.
Explanation

The airway is divided by function. The conducting portion (nasal cavity → terminal bronchioles) only moves, warms, moistens and cleans air. The respiratory portion starts where alveoli open into the airway wall, because only an alveolar wall is thin enough, and close enough to capillaries, for gas to diffuse.

  • The list starting with terminal bronchioles fails on its first item: the terminal bronchiole is the last conducting segment, with a complete wall and no alveoli.
  • The list starting with bronchioles fails for the same reason: ordinary bronchioles are conducting airways with smooth muscle and no alveoli.

Hook: no alveoli, no exchange, no respiratory portion.

Slide (1)
L97Learning
Where does the respiratory portion of the airway, and with it gas exchange, begin?
  1. A. In the alveolar duct, which branches from the respiratory bronchiole
  2. B. In the terminal bronchiole, which branches from the last ordinary bronchiole
  3. C. In the respiratory bronchiole, which branches from the terminal bronchiole
AnswerC. In the respiratory bronchiole, which branches from the terminal bronchiole
WhyGas exchange starts in the respiratory bronchiole, the branch after the terminal bronchiole, because it is the first airway with alveoli in its wall.
Explanation

Each terminal bronchiole divides into two or more respiratory bronchioles. These are still tubes with a cuboidal lining, but alveoli bud from their walls at intervals, so some gas exchange already happens here. Further out, the alveolar ducts and sacs are almost all alveoli, and most exchange happens there.

  • The terminal bronchiole has a complete wall with no alveoli; it is the most distal conducting segment.
  • The alveolar duct does exchange gas, but it is the second respiratory segment, not the first.
Slide (1)
L98Learning
What is the key feature that separates a respiratory bronchiole from a terminal bronchiole?
  1. A. Alveoli open directly from the respiratory bronchiole's wall
  2. B. Hyaline cartilage plates support the respiratory bronchiole's wall
  3. C. Goblet cells line the respiratory bronchiole's wall
AnswerA. Alveoli open directly from the respiratory bronchiole's wall
WhyA respiratory bronchiole is a bronchiole whose wall is interrupted by alveoli; a terminal bronchiole has a complete wall with no alveoli.
Explanation

Both segments have a simple cuboidal lining with club cells and some smooth muscle, so the lining alone does not separate them. The wall does: in the respiratory bronchiole, alveolar outpockets open straight into the lumen and break the epithelium into short stretches. That is why gas exchange begins here.

  • Goblet cells are gone before the terminal bronchiole and never reappear distally.
  • Hyaline cartilage ends with the bronchi; no bronchiole has cartilage.

Hook: look for holes in the wall. None = terminal; some = respiratory.

Slides (2)
L99Learning
What lines the wall of a respiratory bronchiole between its alveoli?
  1. A. Pseudostratified ciliated columnar cells with goblet cells, over plates of hyaline cartilage
  2. B. Small cuboidal cells (some ciliated) and club cells, with some smooth muscle beneath
  3. C. Only type I and type II pneumocytes, with no smooth muscle beneath
AnswerB. Small cuboidal cells (some ciliated) and club cells, with some smooth muscle beneath
WhyBetween its alveoli, a respiratory bronchiole keeps the terminal bronchiole's lining: small cuboidal cells and club cells, with some smooth muscle.
Explanation

The respiratory bronchiole is a transition segment. Where its wall is intact it looks like the terminal bronchiole: low cuboidal epithelium (a few cells still ciliated), many club (Clara) cells and a little smooth muscle in the lamina propria. Where an alveolus opens, the lining changes abruptly to the flat type I and rounded type II cells of the alveolar wall.

  • Pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium with goblet cells over cartilage is the bronchial wall; goblet cells and cartilage have both disappeared well before this level.
  • Only pneumocytes and no smooth muscle describes the alveolus itself, not the tube between the alveoli.
Slides (2)
L100Learning
Which vessel runs alongside a respiratory bronchiole?
  1. A. A branch of the pulmonary artery
  2. B. A branch of the bronchial vein
  3. C. A tributary of the pulmonary vein
AnswerA. A branch of the pulmonary artery
WhyPulmonary artery branches travel with the airways down to the respiratory bronchioles, then break up into the capillaries of the alveolar septa.
Explanation

The pulmonary arteries carry oxygen-poor blood from the right ventricle and branch in step with the bronchial tree, so a branch sits beside each bronchiole; the lecture micrographs label it next to the terminal and respiratory bronchioles. At the alveoli it opens into the capillary plexus of the septa.

  • Pulmonary vein tributaries do not travel with the airways; they run apart, in the connective-tissue septa between lobules and segments.
  • Bronchial veins drain only the larger airways near the hilum.

Hook: the artery hugs the airway; the vein keeps its distance.

Slide (1)

Alveolar ducts, sacs and alveoli

L101Learning
Going outward from a terminal bronchiole, in what order do the parts of the respiratory portion follow?
  1. A. Respiratory bronchiole → alveolar sac → alveolar duct → alveolus
  2. B. Alveolar duct → respiratory bronchiole → alveolar sac → alveolus
  3. C. Respiratory bronchiole → alveolar duct → alveolar sac → alveolus
AnswerC. Respiratory bronchiole → alveolar duct → alveolar sac → alveolus
WhyRespiratory bronchiole → alveolar duct → alveolar sac → alveolus: alveoli take over the wall step by step until only alveoli are left.
Explanation

The order follows how much of the wall is made of alveoli:

  • Respiratory bronchiole: a tube with scattered alveoli.
  • Alveolar duct: a passage whose wall is almost entirely alveolar openings.
  • Alveolar sac: the blind end of a duct, a shared space ringed by alveoli.
  • Alveolus: the single air pocket where exchange occurs.

Putting the duct first places a passage made of alveolar openings before the bronchiole that feeds it. Putting the sac before the duct places the dead end ahead of the passage that leads to it.

Slide (1)
L102Learning
What makes up the wall of an alveolar duct?
  1. A. A continuous cuboidal lining with club cells, over a complete layer of smooth muscle
  2. B. Little but alveolar openings, with small knobs of smooth muscle between them
  3. C. Little but alveolar openings, with small plates of hyaline cartilage between them
AnswerB. Little but alveolar openings, with small knobs of smooth muscle between them
WhyAn alveolar duct has almost no wall of its own: it is a row of alveolar openings, with smooth-muscle knobs at the rims between them.
Explanation

On a section the duct looks like a long corridor whose walls are the mouths of alveoli. Between neighbouring mouths sits a small knob: a bundle of smooth muscle with elastic and reticular fibres, capped by epithelium. On H&E the knobs show as pink dots lining the corridor.

  • A continuous cuboidal lining with club cells over complete smooth muscle describes the terminal bronchiole, which has no alveoli at all.
  • Cartilage never reaches this level; it ends with the bronchi.

Analogy from the TA review: a duct is a hallway lined with doors; a sac is the room at the end.

Slide (1)
L103Learning
What is an alveolar sac?
  1. A. A single alveolus budding from the wall of a respiratory bronchiole
  2. B. A wide airway that divides to give rise to several respiratory bronchioles
  3. C. The dead-end space of an alveolar duct, ringed by alveoli opening into it
AnswerC. The dead-end space of an alveolar duct, ringed by alveoli opening into it
WhyAn alveolar sac is the blind end of an alveolar duct: a shared space that several alveoli open into.
Explanation

Each alveolar duct ends in one or more sacs. The sac is the shared chamber; the alveoli are the pockets around it. The hierarchy is duct (corridor) → sac (dead-end room) → alveoli (alcoves off that room).

  • A single alveolus on a respiratory bronchiole is an alveolar outpocket, not a sac.
  • The airway that gives rise to respiratory bronchioles is the terminal bronchiole.
Slide (1)
L104Learning
From the alveolar ducts onward, what lines the airspaces and what supports them?
  1. A. Simple squamous epithelium, supported by elastic and collagen (reticular) fibres
  2. B. Simple cuboidal epithelium, supported by hyaline cartilage and smooth muscle
  3. C. Pseudostratified columnar epithelium, supported by dense collagen and cartilage plates
AnswerA. Simple squamous epithelium, supported by elastic and collagen (reticular) fibres
WhyAlveolar ducts and alveoli are lined by simple squamous cells (pneumocytes) on a matrix of elastic and collagen (reticular) fibres.
Explanation

Gas exchange needs the thinnest possible wall, so the lining flattens to simple squamous epithelium, mostly type I pneumocytes. No cartilage or glands remain. The framework is a fine mesh of elastic fibres, which stretch on inspiration and recoil on expiration, and reticular (type III collagen) fibres, which limit overstretching and support the capillaries.

  • Simple cuboidal epithelium with cartilage mixes a bronchiolar lining with a bronchial support; neither belongs here.
  • Pseudostratified columnar epithelium with cartilage plates is the intrapulmonary bronchus.
Slide (1)
L105Learning
In the alveolar ducts and alveoli, where is smooth muscle found?
  1. A. Only around the openings of the alveoli
  2. B. Only in the walls of the alveolar sacs
  3. C. Throughout every interalveolar septum
AnswerA. Only around the openings of the alveoli
WhyPast the respiratory bronchiole, smooth muscle survives only as small bundles ringing the alveolar openings; the alveolar walls have none.
Explanation

Smooth muscle thins steadily down the tree. In the alveolar ducts it is reduced to knobs at the rims of the alveolar openings. Beyond them, in the sacs and the interalveolar septa, there is no muscle: the septa hold capillaries, elastic and reticular fibres, fibroblasts and macrophages.

  • Every interalveolar septum: no; muscle there would thicken the diffusion barrier.
  • Only in the sac walls: the sacs are walls of alveoli and have no muscle.

One older review key stops smooth muscle at the respiratory bronchioles; the lecture and its histology table place the last of it at the alveolar openings of the ducts.

Slide (1)
L106Learning
What do the elastic fibres around the alveoli do during breathing?
  1. A. Hold alveoli rigid on inspiration and prop them open on expiration
  2. B. Let alveoli stretch on inspiration and recoil passively on expiration
  3. C. Lower surface tension so alveoli do not collapse at end-expiration
AnswerB. Let alveoli stretch on inspiration and recoil passively on expiration
WhyElastic fibres stretch as alveoli fill and recoil when the inspiratory muscles relax, pushing air out passively.
Explanation

Quiet expiration is passive: the energy stored in the stretched elastic network of the alveolar walls drives the air back out. Elastic fibres are the one wall component that continues, and increases in proportion, all the way to the alveoli.

  • Holding alveoli rigid is the opposite of elastic behaviour; a rigid lung could not inflate.
  • Lowering surface tension is the job of surfactant from type II pneumocytes, not of fibres.

Clinical link: emphysema destroys the elastin, recoil is lost and air is trapped.

L107Learning
Where does most gas exchange take place, and what makes it possible there?
  1. A. In the respiratory bronchioles: their cuboidal walls carry the densest capillary network
  2. B. In the alveolar ducts: their smooth-muscle knobs pump air across the wall
  3. C. In the alveoli: alveolar air lies against a dense capillary network across a very thin wall
AnswerC. In the alveoli: alveolar air lies against a dense capillary network across a very thin wall
WhyThe alveoli are the main exchange site: their septa carry a dense capillary plexus separated from the air by a very thin barrier.
Explanation

Hundreds of millions of alveoli give an enormous surface. Each interalveolar septum is packed with capillaries, and over much of it the air is separated from blood only by a type I cell, a fused basal lamina and an endothelial cell. Diffusion depends on area and thinness, so the alveoli do almost all of the exchange.

  • Respiratory bronchioles exchange gas only through their scattered alveoli; their cuboidal stretches are too thick.
  • The smooth-muscle knobs of the ducts do not pump air; gas crosses by diffusion, and ventilation is driven by the respiratory muscles.
Slides (3)

Type I and type II pneumocytes

L108Learning
What does a type I pneumocyte look like?
  1. A. Cuboidal and rounded, joined to its neighbours by occluding (tight) junctions
  2. B. Squamous and extremely thin, with no junctions between neighbouring cells
  3. C. Squamous and extremely thin, joined to its neighbours by occluding (tight) junctions
AnswerC. Squamous and extremely thin, joined to its neighbours by occluding (tight) junctions
WhyType I pneumocytes are very thin squamous cells sealed to each other by occluding (tight) junctions; on H&E only their flat, dark nucleus shows.
Explanation

The type I cell spreads its cytoplasm into a sheet so thin (well under a micrometre) that the light microscope cannot resolve it; you see only a flattened, dark nucleus along the septum. Its few organelles cluster around the nucleus, leaving the rest of the cell free for diffusion. Neighbouring type I and type II cells are linked by occluding junctions.

  • Cuboidal and rounded describes the type II pneumocyte.
  • No junctions would leave gaps through which tissue fluid could flood the alveoli.
Slide (1)
L109LearningBorderline
Type I pneumocytes are sealed together by occluding junctions. What do these junctions prevent?
  1. A. Tissue fluid leaking from the septum into the alveolar air space
  2. B. Electrical signals spreading directly from cell to cell
  3. C. Type I cells pulling apart under the stretch of inspiration
AnswerA. Tissue fluid leaking from the septum into the alveolar air space
WhyOccluding (tight) junctions seal the gaps between alveolar cells, so interstitial fluid cannot leak into the alveoli.
Explanation

The zonula occludens fuses the outer membranes of neighbouring cells into a seal that closes the route between cells. In the alveolus this keeps the air space dry: fluid in the septal connective tissue cannot seep between the cells into the lumen, where it would lengthen the diffusion path.

  • Resisting pulling apart under mechanical stress is the job of anchoring junctions (desmosomes and adherens junctions).
  • Passing electrical signals from cell to cell is the job of gap junctions, as in cardiac muscle.
L110Learning
What is the role of type I pneumocytes?
  1. A. They divide to replace damaged alveolar cells and secrete surfactant onto the surface
  2. B. They cover almost the whole alveolar surface and are the wall gas diffuses across
  3. C. They cover almost the whole alveolar surface and phagocytose inhaled dust and microbes
AnswerB. They cover almost the whole alveolar surface and are the wall gas diffuses across
WhyType I cells line about 95% of the alveolar surface and form the epithelial layer of the blood–air barrier, across which gas exchange occurs.
Explanation

Type I cells are outnumbered by type II cells, but each spreads over a huge area, so together they cover about 95% of the alveolar surface. Their thin cytoplasm is the epithelial layer of the blood–air barrier. Type I cells cannot divide; when they die, type II cells replace them.

  • Phagocytosing dust is the job of alveolar macrophages (dust cells).
  • Dividing and secreting surfactant are the jobs of type II pneumocytes.
Slide (1)
L111Learning
What are the other names for the type II pneumocyte?
  1. A. Club cell; Clara cell
  2. B. Septal cell; great alveolar cell
  3. C. Dust cell; heart failure cell
AnswerB. Septal cell; great alveolar cell
WhyThe type II pneumocyte is also called the septal cell or the great alveolar cell.
Explanation

'Great alveolar cell' reflects its size and rounded shape next to the flat type I cell; 'septal cell' reflects where it sits, often at the corners where septa meet. It is also called the type II alveolar cell.

  • Dust cell and heart failure cell are names for alveolar macrophages (carbon-laden and iron-laden).
  • Club cell and Clara cell are two names for the bronchiolar secretory cell; it shares some functions with type II cells but lines bronchioles, not alveoli.
Slide (1)
L112Learning
How do you recognise a type II pneumocyte on an H&E slide?
  1. A. A large cell free in the alveolar lumen, its cytoplasm packed with brown or black granules
  2. B. A flat cell hugging the septum, with a dark elongated nucleus and no visible cytoplasm
  3. C. A rounded cuboidal cell bulging into the alveolus, often where septa meet, with pale foamy cytoplasm
AnswerC. A rounded cuboidal cell bulging into the alveolus, often where septa meet, with pale foamy cytoplasm
WhyType II cells are rounded and cuboidal and bulge into the alveolus, often at septal corners; their cytoplasm looks foamy because the lamellar bodies wash out.
Explanation

On light microscopy the type II cell has a round nucleus and pale, bubbly ('foamy') cytoplasm: the lipid in its lamellar bodies dissolves during processing and leaves vacuoles. It belongs to the epithelial lining, so it is part of the wall, not loose in the lumen.

  • A free cell with brown or black granules in the lumen is an alveolar macrophage.
  • A flat cell with a dark elongated nucleus is a type I pneumocyte (or an endothelial cell).
Slide (1)
L113Learning
On TEM, which organelle identifies a type II pneumocyte, and what does it store?
  1. A. Lamellar bodies, which store surfactant
  2. B. Weibel–Palade bodies, which store von Willebrand factor
  3. C. Lamellar bodies, which store elastase
AnswerA. Lamellar bodies, which store surfactant
WhyLamellar bodies mark the type II cell; they store surfactant until it is secreted onto the alveolar surface.
Explanation

Surfactant lipids and proteins are made in the rough endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi, packed into lamellar bodies and released by exocytosis at the apical surface, where they spread over the alveolar lining. On TEM the type II cell also shows short apical microvilli.

  • Elastase is released by neutrophils and macrophages, not stored in lamellar bodies; its unopposed action causes emphysema.
  • Weibel–Palade bodies are rod-shaped granules of endothelial cells that store von Willebrand factor.
Slide (1)
L114Learning
On TEM, what does a lamellar body look like?
  1. A. A membrane-bound granule (100–300 nm) with a single dense, dark core
  2. B. A rod-shaped granule with fine parallel tubules running along its length
  3. C. A membrane-bound granule (100–400 nm) of closely stacked, parallel membrane layers
AnswerC. A membrane-bound granule (100–400 nm) of closely stacked, parallel membrane layers
WhyA lamellar body is a 100–400 nm membrane-bound granule packed with closely stacked parallel lamellae of surfactant lipid.
Explanation

The stacked membranes look like the layers of an onion or a fingerprint. They are the surfactant lipids (mainly dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine) and proteins, continuously made and released at the apical surface.

  • A granule with a dense core (100–300 nm) is the neuroendocrine granule of the small granule (Kulchitsky) cell.
  • A rod-shaped granule with parallel tubules is the Weibel–Palade body of endothelial cells.
Slide (1)
L115Learning
After severe alveolar damage, such as a viral pneumonia, which cells restore the alveolar lining?
  1. A. Type II pneumocytes, which divide and give rise to both type I and type II cells
  2. B. Alveolar macrophages, which transform into new type I and type II cells
  3. C. Type I pneumocytes, which divide and give rise to both type I and type II cells
AnswerA. Type II pneumocytes, which divide and give rise to both type I and type II cells
WhyType II pneumocytes are the stem cells of the alveolar lining: they divide and differentiate into both type I and type II cells.
Explanation

Type I cells are terminally differentiated and cannot divide. When diffuse alveolar damage (viral pneumonia, toxic inhalation) kills them, surviving type II cells proliferate, cover the bare basement membrane and then flatten into new type I cells.

  • Type I pneumocytes cannot divide.
  • Alveolar macrophages come from blood monocytes and never become epithelial cells.
Slide (1)

Surfactant

L116Learning
Which cell secretes pulmonary surfactant into the alveoli?
  1. A. Alveolar macrophage
  2. B. Type II pneumocyte
  3. C. Type I pneumocyte
AnswerB. Type II pneumocyte
WhyType II pneumocytes make surfactant and release it from their lamellar bodies onto the alveolar surface.
Explanation

The type II cell synthesises surfactant lipids and proteins, stores them in lamellar bodies and exocytoses them at its apical surface. The secretion spreads over the whole alveolar lining as a thin film.

  • Type I pneumocytes form the thin exchange surface; they have no secretory granules.
  • Alveolar macrophages take up and clear old surfactant, but they do not make it.

Club cells secrete a surfactant-like material in the bronchioles, but alveolar surfactant comes from type II cells.

Slide (1)
L117Learning
How is surfactant arranged on the alveolar surface?
  1. A. A layer of mucus and mucins over a thin layer of triglycerides
  2. B. A film of phospholipids and lipoproteins over a thin layer of water
  3. C. A film of water over a thin layer of phospholipids and lipoproteins
AnswerB. A film of phospholipids and lipoproteins over a thin layer of water
WhySurfactant is a film of phospholipids and lipoproteins spread over a thin aqueous layer that coats the alveolar cells.
Explanation

A thin film of water covers the alveolar epithelium. Surfactant phospholipids are amphipathic: their polar heads sit in this water and their fatty-acid tails point into the air. Spread at the air–water interface, they weaken the pull between water molecules that creates surface tension.

  • Water over phospholipids reverses the layers; water exposed to air is exactly what produces high surface tension.
  • Mucus over triglycerides describes nothing in the alveolus; mucus belongs to the conducting airways.
Slide (1)
L118Learning
Which components make up surfactant?
  1. A. Dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine (DPPC)
    Triglycerides
    Club cell secretory protein
  2. B. Dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine (DPPC)
    Mucins
    Surfactant proteins A, B, C, D
  3. C. Dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine (DPPC)
    Cholesterol
    Surfactant proteins A, B, C, D
AnswerC. Dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine (DPPC)
Cholesterol
Surfactant proteins A, B, C, D
WhyType II cells secrete DPPC, cholesterol and surfactant proteins A, B, C and D.
Explanation

DPPC is the main surface-active phospholipid. Cholesterol and other lipids keep the film fluid and stable. SP-B and SP-C (water-repelling) help the lipid film spread; SP-A and SP-D (water-soluble) also help local immune defence by coating microbes.

  • Mucins come from goblet cells and, in the bronchioles, club cells. One TA key lists 'lipoproteins and mucins' as surfactant; that pair is the club cell's secretion.
  • Triglycerides and club cell secretory protein are not surfactant components.
Slide (1)
L119Learning
Which molecule is the main surface-active lipid of surfactant?
  1. A. Dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine (DPPC)
  2. B. Sphingomyelin
  3. C. Cholesterol
AnswerA. Dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine (DPPC)
WhyDPPC (dipalmitoyl lecithin) is the main phospholipid of surfactant and the one that lowers surface tension.
Explanation

DPPC is a phosphatidylcholine (lecithin) with two saturated palmitate chains. Its straight tails pack tightly at the air–water interface as the alveolus shrinks, which brings surface tension very low at the end of expiration.

  • Sphingomyelin is the reference lipid in the amniotic-fluid lecithin/sphingomyelin ratio used to judge fetal lung maturity; it is not the active surfactant lipid.
  • Cholesterol is present in surfactant, but it keeps the film fluid; it does not do the surface-tension work.
L120Learning
How does surfactant work, and what does it achieve?
  1. A. Raises surface tension → alveoli recoil harder at end-expiration and empty with less force → less work of breathing
  2. B. Lowers surface tension → alveoli stay open at end-expiration and inflate with less force → less work of breathing
  3. C. Adds elastin to the alveolar wall → alveoli stretch further on inspiration → more work of breathing
AnswerB. Lowers surface tension → alveoli stay open at end-expiration and inflate with less force → less work of breathing
WhySurfactant lowers surface tension, so alveoli stay open at end-expiration and inflate more easily, cutting the work of breathing.
Explanation

The water lining a tiny curved alveolus pulls inward (surface tension) and tends to collapse it, most of all at small volume at the end of expiration. Surfactant weakens this pull. With it, alveoli stay open when emptied and re-inflate with less inspiratory force.

  • Raised surface tension is what happens without surfactant: alveoli collapse (atelectasis) and breathing becomes hard work.
  • Surfactant adds no elastin; elastic fibres belong to the septal connective tissue and are made by fibroblasts.
Slide (1)
L121Learning
Type II pneumocytes share surfactant secretion and other functions with which airway cell?
  1. A. Basal cells
  2. B. Brush cells
  3. C. Club (Clara) cells
AnswerC. Club (Clara) cells
WhyClub cells of the bronchioles share many type II functions, including secretion of surfactant-like lipoproteins.
Explanation

Club (Clara) cells are non-ciliated, dome-shaped cells of the terminal and respiratory bronchioles. They secrete surfactant lipoproteins (and mucins), which help keep the small bronchioles from collapsing, and some act as stem cells for the bronchiolar lining, as type II cells do for the alveolar lining.

  • Basal cells are the stem cells of the pseudostratified respiratory epithelium; they secrete nothing.
  • Brush cells carry blunt microvilli and are chemosensory.
Slide (1)
L122Learning
A viral pneumonia destroys most of a patient's type II pneumocytes. Which functional problem follows directly?
  1. A. Alveoli tend to collapse because surface tension rises
  2. B. Ciliary beating in the bronchi slows and mucus builds up
  3. C. Bronchiolar smooth muscle contracts and narrows the airways
AnswerA. Alveoli tend to collapse because surface tension rises
WhyLosing type II cells means losing surfactant: surface tension rises and alveoli collapse (atelectasis).
Explanation

Type II cells are the only source of alveolar surfactant, and the stem cells for repair. Without fresh surfactant, the fluid lining pulls the alveoli shut, especially at end-expiration, so the ventilated surface shrinks and the patient becomes hypoxic. The same mechanism explains the collapsed alveoli of premature infants.

  • Bronchiolar smooth-muscle contraction (bronchospasm) is driven by mast-cell mediators in asthma, not by the loss of pneumocytes.
  • Ciliary beating belongs to the conducting-airway epithelium, which has no type II cells.
Slides (2)

Alveolar macrophages (dust cells)

L123Learning
What are alveolar macrophages also called, where do they come from, and where do they sit?
  1. A. Septal cells; from type II pneumocytes; within the alveolar epithelial lining
  2. B. Dust cells; from type II pneumocytes; only free in the alveolar air spaces
  3. C. Dust cells; from blood monocytes; in the alveolar lumen or in the interalveolar septa
AnswerC. Dust cells; from blood monocytes; in the alveolar lumen or in the interalveolar septa
WhyAlveolar macrophages, or dust cells, derive from blood monocytes and sit in the alveoli or in the interalveolar septa.
Explanation

Monocytes leave the septal capillaries, enter the connective tissue of the septum, mature into macrophages and crawl onto the alveolar surface. On H&E they are larger than pneumocytes, often free in the lumen, and frequently full of dark inhaled particles, hence 'dust cells'.

  • Septal cell is another name for the type II pneumocyte, an epithelial cell, not a phagocyte.
  • Macrophages do not come from type II pneumocytes, which give rise only to alveolar epithelial cells; and macrophages sit in the septa as well as the lumen.
Slide (1)
L124Learning
What do alveolar macrophages phagocytose?
  1. A. Inhaled particles and red cells that escape from the capillaries
  2. B. Inhaled particles and the healthy type I cells of the septa
  3. C. Surfactant and dead type I cells, but no inhaled particles
AnswerA. Inhaled particles and red cells that escape from the capillaries
WhyDust cells engulf inhaled particles (dust, carbon, microbes) and erythrocytes that leak into the alveoli.
Explanation

Alveolar macrophages are the defence of the alveoli, where cilia and mucus no longer reach. They take up particles that slip past the mucociliary blanket of the conducting airways and clear red cells that leak out of congested capillaries, digesting the haemoglobin and storing the iron as haemosiderin. They also take up worn-out surfactant.

  • Saying they take up no inhaled particles contradicts their main job and their name.
  • They do not destroy healthy type I cells; they remove only dead cells and debris.
Slide (1)
L125Learning
How do debris-laden alveolar macrophages leave the lung?
  1. A. Through the pores of Kohn and on into the pulmonary veins
  2. B. On the mucociliary escalator up the airways, or via the lymphatics
  3. C. Across the visceral pleura and out into the pleural cavity
AnswerB. On the mucociliary escalator up the airways, or via the lymphatics
WhyLoaded dust cells are cleared by mucociliary clearance (carried up the airways, then swallowed or coughed out) or via the lymphatics.
Explanation

Some macrophages migrate from the alveoli into the bronchioles, reach the ciliated epithelium and ride the mucus blanket up to the pharynx, where they are swallowed or coughed out. Others enter the septal connective tissue and then lymphatics, and settle in peribronchial lymphoid tissue and hilar lymph nodes; this is why carbon pigment collects there.

  • Pores of Kohn connect neighbouring alveoli; they do not open into veins.
  • The pleural cavity is not an exit route for alveolar contents.
Slide (1)
L126Learning
What are heart failure cells?
  1. A. Alveolar macrophages full of brown lipofuscin from cardiac muscle cells that die in heart failure
  2. B. Alveolar macrophages full of brown haemosiderin from red cells that leak into congested alveoli
  3. C. Type II pneumocytes full of brown haemosiderin from red cells that leak into congested alveoli
AnswerB. Alveolar macrophages full of brown haemosiderin from red cells that leak into congested alveoli
WhyHeart failure cells are alveolar macrophages that have eaten leaked red cells and store the iron as golden-brown haemosiderin.
Explanation

In congestive heart failure, blood backs up into the pulmonary capillaries, red cells leak into the alveoli and macrophages engulf them. Their lysosomes break down the haemoglobin, and the iron is stored as haemosiderin granules: golden-brown on H&E, blue with an iron stain.

  • Type II pneumocytes are epithelial secretory cells; they do not phagocytose red cells.
  • Lipofuscin is the wear-and-tear pigment of long-lived cells such as cardiac muscle cells; it has nothing to do with lung macrophages.
Slide (1)
L127LearningBorderline
A patient with chronic left-sided heart failure has heart failure cells in the lungs. How did they form?
  1. A. Pressure backs up into the systemic veins → red cells leak into the alveoli → macrophages eat them and store the iron as haemosiderin
  2. B. Pressure backs up into the pulmonary veins and capillaries → red cells leak into the alveoli → macrophages eat them and store the iron as lipofuscin
  3. C. Pressure backs up into the pulmonary veins and capillaries → red cells leak into the alveoli → macrophages eat them and store the iron as haemosiderin
AnswerC. Pressure backs up into the pulmonary veins and capillaries → red cells leak into the alveoli → macrophages eat them and store the iron as haemosiderin
WhyLeft heart failure congests the pulmonary capillaries; macrophages eat the red cells that leak out and store their iron as haemosiderin.
Explanation

A failing left ventricle cannot empty the left atrium, so pressure rises back through the pulmonary veins into the alveolar capillaries. Red cells cross the congested capillary walls into the alveoli. Macrophages phagocytose them, and the iron from the haemoglobin is stored in their lysosomes as haemosiderin. These iron-laden macrophages are the heart failure cells.

  • Systemic venous congestion is the result of right heart failure (leg oedema, liver congestion); systemic veins do not drain the alveolar capillaries.
  • Lipofuscin is an age pigment made of lipid debris; iron from red cells is stored as haemosiderin.
Slide (1)
L128Learning
A lung biopsy shows alveoli and interalveolar tissue with large cells laden with black carbon particles. What are these cells?
  1. A. Alveolar macrophages
  2. B. Type II pneumocytes
  3. C. Fibroblasts
AnswerA. Alveolar macrophages
WhyLarge cells packed with carbon in the alveoli and septa are alveolar macrophages (dust cells) that have phagocytosed inhaled particles.
Explanation

Inhaled carbon from smoke, coal dust or city air slips past the mucociliary blanket, reaches the alveoli and is engulfed by alveolar and interstitial macrophages. The pigment cannot be digested, so it stays in the cells for years (anthracosis).

  • Type II pneumocytes are large and rounded, but their cytoplasm is pale and foamy (lamellar bodies), not black, and they are not phagocytes.
  • Fibroblasts are spindle-shaped cells of the septal connective tissue that make fibres; they do not collect particles.
Slides (2)
L129Learning
In anthracosis, where do the carbon-laden macrophages accumulate?
  1. A. Beside lymphatics, in lymphoid tissue along the bronchi, and at the hilum
  2. B. Free in the pleural cavity and spread along the parietal pleura
  3. C. Inside the type I pneumocytes lining the alveoli and covering the capillaries
AnswerA. Beside lymphatics, in lymphoid tissue along the bronchi, and at the hilum
WhyCarbon-laden macrophages follow the lymphatics: they collect in connective tissue next to lymphatics, in peribronchial lymphoid tissue and at the hilum, which turn black.
Explanation

Anthracosis is the most harmless coal-related lung lesion, seen in coal miners and to some degree in city dwellers and smokers. Macrophages that swallow carbon move into the interstitium and toward the lymphatics, so the pigment gathers in perilymphatic connective tissue, peribronchial lymphoid tissue and the hilar lymph nodes. This is why the hilar nodes of an adult cadaver often look jet black.

  • Type I pneumocytes are not phagocytic and do not store carbon.
  • The pigment stays inside macrophages in the lung tissue and its lymphatics; it does not float free in the pleural cavity.
Slide (1)

Interalveolar septum and blood–air barrier

L130Learning
What does an interalveolar septum contain?
  1. A. Type I and II cells on both faces
    No capillaries (gas reaches the bronchial arteries instead)
    Connective tissue: fibroblasts, elastic and reticular fibres, macrophages
  2. B. Ciliated and goblet cells on both faces
    A dense capillary plexus (red cells and leukocytes)
    Connective tissue: fibroblasts, elastic and reticular fibres, macrophages
  3. C. Type I and II cells on both faces
    A dense capillary plexus (red cells and leukocytes)
    Connective tissue: fibroblasts, elastic and reticular fibres, macrophages
AnswerC. Type I and II cells on both faces
A dense capillary plexus (red cells and leukocytes)
Connective tissue: fibroblasts, elastic and reticular fibres, macrophages
WhyAn interalveolar septum is the wall between two alveoli: pneumocytes on both faces, a capillary plexus inside and connective tissue with fibroblasts, elastic and reticular fibres and macrophages.
Explanation

Each septum serves two alveoli at once, so it is lined on both sides by alveolar epithelium (mostly type I, some type II cells). Inside runs one of the densest capillary networks in the body, holding erythrocytes and leukocytes. The rest is a thin interstitium: fibroblasts, elastic and reticular fibres, and macrophages. There is no cartilage, gland or (beyond the alveolar openings) smooth muscle.

  • No capillaries is wrong: the septal capillaries are where gas exchange happens. Bronchial arteries feed the airway walls, not the septa.
  • Ciliated and goblet cells belong to the conducting airway; none line an alveolus.
Slides (3)
L131Learning
What is the difference between the interalveolar septum and the blood–air barrier?
  1. A. Septum: the wall of an alveolar duct
    Barrier: the wall of an alveolar sac
  2. B. Septum: the whole wall between two alveoli
    Barrier: only the thinnest layers within it that gas crosses
  3. C. Septum: only the thinnest layers that gas crosses
    Barrier: the whole wall between two alveoli
AnswerB. Septum: the whole wall between two alveoli
Barrier: only the thinnest layers within it that gas crosses
WhyThe septum is the whole partition between alveoli (cells, capillaries, connective tissue); the blood–air barrier is just the thin path gas crosses within it.
Explanation

The septum contains everything between two alveolar air spaces: epithelium, fibroblasts, fibres, macrophages and capillaries. The blood–air barrier is a small part of it: where a capillary presses against the epithelium, gas crosses only surfactant, a type I cell, a fused basal lamina and the endothelium. That is the septum's thin portion; where connective tissue lies between the layers, the septum is thicker and is not the main exchange site.

  • The reversed pairing swaps the whole for its part.
  • Duct walls and sac walls are both made of alveoli, and both contain septa and barrier; the two terms do not separate them.
Slides (2)
L132Learning
List the layers of the blood–air barrier from air to blood.
  1. A. Surfactant (counted by some sources) → type II cell → fused basal laminae → capillary endothelium
  2. B. Surfactant (counted by some sources) → type I cell → fused basal laminae → capillary endothelium
  3. C. Surfactant (counted by some sources) → type I cell → septal connective tissue → capillary endothelium
AnswerB. Surfactant (counted by some sources) → type I cell → fused basal laminae → capillary endothelium
WhyAir → surfactant → type I cell → fused basal laminae → capillary endothelium → blood.
Explanation

O2 diffuses from alveolar air into capillary blood, and CO2 the other way, through:

  • the surfactant film and its watery layer (the lecture lists it; some books leave it out);
  • the thin cytoplasm of a type I pneumocyte;
  • the fused basal laminae of the epithelium and the endothelium;
  • the thin cytoplasm of a continuous capillary endothelial cell.

The type II cell is not part of the barrier: it is thick and sits at septal corners. A layer of septal connective tissue between the cells marks the thick portion of the septum, not the barrier.

Slides (2)
L133Learning
Which of these is NOT part of the blood–air barrier?
  1. A. Type II pneumocyte
  2. B. Fused basal laminae
  3. C. Capillary endothelial cell
AnswerA. Type II pneumocyte
WhyThe barrier is type I cell + fused basal laminae + endothelium (plus surfactant); the type II pneumocyte is not part of it.
Explanation

Gas crosses where the alveolar lining is thinnest: over type I cells. Type II pneumocytes are cuboidal, bulge into the alveolus at septal corners and cover only a small part of the surface; their jobs are surfactant secretion and repair, not exchange.

  • The fused basal laminae are the middle layer of the barrier.
  • The capillary endothelial cell is its blood-side layer.
Slide (1)
L134Learning
What kind of capillary endothelium forms the blood side of the blood–air barrier?
  1. A. Fenestrated endothelium with diaphragms
  2. B. Discontinuous (sinusoidal) endothelium
  3. C. Thin, continuous endothelium
AnswerC. Thin, continuous endothelium
WhyAlveolar capillaries have thin, continuous endothelium: no pores, but so thin that gas diffuses through easily.
Explanation

O2 and CO2 are small, lipid-soluble molecules that cross cell membranes directly, so no pores are needed. A continuous endothelium (cells sealed by tight junctions, an intact basal lamina) keeps plasma and blood cells out of the alveoli, and its very thin cytoplasm keeps the diffusion path short.

  • Fenestrated capillaries (with pores) suit fluid filtration and absorption, as in the gut and endocrine glands; pores here would flood the alveoli.
  • Sinusoidal capillaries, with gaps, are found in the liver, spleen and bone marrow, where cells must pass through.
Slide (1)
L135Learning
On TEM, what is the thin portion of the alveolar septum?
  1. A. Where fibroblasts and fibres lie between a type I cell and the endothelium: the main site of gas exchange
  2. B. Where a type I cell and the endothelium share one fused basal lamina with nothing between them: a site with no gas exchange
  3. C. Where a type I cell and the endothelium share one fused basal lamina with nothing between them: the main site of gas exchange
AnswerC. Where a type I cell and the endothelium share one fused basal lamina with nothing between them: the main site of gas exchange
WhyIn the thin portion, the epithelial and endothelial basal laminae fuse with no connective tissue between: the shortest diffusion path and the main gas-exchange site.
Explanation

On one side of each septal capillary, the type I cell and the endothelial cell lie back to back on a single fused basal lamina, a fraction of a micrometre thick in total. This thin portion is the blood–air barrier proper, where most O2 and CO2 cross. Fusion of the two basal laminae is the key structural adaptation for gas exchange.

  • Saying the thin portion has no gas exchange reverses its function.
  • Fibroblasts and fibres between the layers define the thick portion, where diffusion is slower.
Slides (2)
L136Learning
On TEM, what is the thick portion of the alveolar septum?
  1. A. Where smooth muscle and cartilage lie between the epithelium and the endothelium
  2. B. Where connective-tissue cells and fibres lie between the epithelium and the endothelium
  3. C. Where type II cells pile up in several layers over the capillary
AnswerB. Where connective-tissue cells and fibres lie between the epithelium and the endothelium
WhyIn the thick portion, the two basal laminae are separated by interstitial connective tissue: fibroblasts, elastic and reticular fibres and tissue fluid.
Explanation

On the other side of the capillary, the epithelial and endothelial layers part, and the space between them holds fibroblasts, fibres, ground substance, interstitial fluid and sometimes macrophages. This portion gives the septum its support and is where tissue fluid collects; it is a much poorer route for gas.

  • Type II cells sit singly in the epithelium; they do not pile up in layers.
  • Smooth muscle and cartilage are absent from the alveolar septa.
Slides (2)

Pores of Kohn and pleura

L137Learning
What are the pores of Kohn?
  1. A. Small holes through the interalveolar septa that connect neighbouring alveoli
  2. B. Small holes through the capillary endothelium that connect alveoli to the blood
  3. C. Small openings that connect terminal bronchioles directly to alveolar ducts
AnswerA. Small holes through the interalveolar septa that connect neighbouring alveoli
WhyPores of Kohn (alveolar pores) are small openings in the interalveolar septa that link adjacent alveoli.
Explanation

They are gaps in the septal wall through which air passes between neighbouring alveoli, including alveoli on different ducts or sacs. They show on scanning electron micrographs and on diagrams of the alveolar wall.

  • Terminal bronchioles open into respiratory bronchioles, not straight into alveolar ducts, and airway branches are ordinary lumens, not pores.
  • Holes from alveoli into the blood would let blood flood the air spaces; the blood–air barrier has no pores.
Slide (1)
L138Learning
What do the pores of Kohn do?
  1. A. Let loaded macrophages leave the lung and drain fluid into the lymphatics when an alveolus floods
  2. B. Equalise air pressure between alveoli and let air reach an alveolus from the side if its airway is blocked
  3. C. Let gas bypass the blood–air barrier and enter the blood directly when the barrier is thickened
AnswerB. Equalise air pressure between alveoli and let air reach an alveolus from the side if its airway is blocked
WhyPores of Kohn equalise pressure between alveoli and provide collateral ventilation when the local airway is blocked.
Explanation

If a small bronchiole is plugged by mucus, the alveoli it serves would collapse; air reaching them sideways through the pores keeps them inflated. The same openings let pressure even out between neighbouring alveoli.

  • No route lets gas bypass the barrier; gas must always diffuse across it.
  • Macrophages leave by mucociliary clearance or the lymphatics; the pores are not a drainage route.
Slides (2)
L139Learning
In lobar pneumonia, fluid and bacteria pass from alveolus to alveolus until a whole lobe is consolidated. Which structure allows this spread?
  1. A. Pores of Kohn
  2. B. Blood–air barrier
  3. C. Alveolar capillaries
AnswerA. Pores of Kohn
WhyInfected fluid passes between adjacent alveoli through the pores of Kohn, so the infection spreads through the whole lobe.
Explanation

The openings that provide collateral ventilation also give exudate a direct path to neighbouring alveoli, without going through the airways. Streptococcus pneumoniae spreads this way until the whole lobe is filled (consolidation), which shows on X-ray as a dense white lobe.

  • The blood–air barrier separates air from blood; it does not connect alveoli to each other.
  • Spread through the alveolar capillaries would be bloodstream spread (bacteraemia), not alveolus-to-alveolus spread.
Slide (1)
L140Learning
What is the pleura made of?
  1. A. Ciliated columnar epithelium on thin connective tissue; visceral layer on the lung, parietal layer on the chest wall
  2. B. Mesothelium (simple squamous) on thin connective tissue; parietal layer on the lung, visceral layer on the chest wall
  3. C. Mesothelium (simple squamous) on thin connective tissue; visceral layer on the lung, parietal layer on the chest wall
AnswerC. Mesothelium (simple squamous) on thin connective tissue; visceral layer on the lung, parietal layer on the chest wall
WhyThe pleura is mesothelium, a simple squamous epithelium on thin connective tissue: visceral on the lung, parietal on the chest wall.
Explanation

Both layers are a single sheet of flat mesothelial cells on thin connective tissue with elastic and collagen fibres, blood vessels and lymphatics. The mesothelium produces a thin film of serous fluid in the pleural cavity between the layers, so the lung glides against the chest wall.

  • Ciliated columnar epithelium lines airways, not serous cavities.
  • The names are swapped in the third choice: visceral means on the organ (the lung); parietal means on the wall.
Slide (1)

Hyaline membrane disease (neonatal respiratory distress syndrome)

L141Learning
What causes hyaline membrane disease, and in whom?
  1. A. Surfactant deficiency from immature type II cells, in premature infants
  2. B. Surfactant excess from overactive type II cells, in premature infants
  3. C. Surfactant deficiency from destroyed type I cells, in elderly smokers
AnswerA. Surfactant deficiency from immature type II cells, in premature infants
WhyHyaline membrane disease (neonatal respiratory distress syndrome) is surfactant deficiency because type II cells are still immature in premature infants.
Explanation

Type II cells make enough surfactant only in the last weeks of gestation, so a baby born early has too little. Its alveoli collapse with each breath, it works hard to breathe and becomes hypoxic, and the injured alveoli leak protein that forms the hyaline membranes.

  • Excess surfactant would make alveoli easier to keep open; it would not cause distress.
  • Type I cells do not make surfactant, and this is a disease of newborns, not smokers.
Slides (2)
L142Learning
What happens to the lungs of an infant with hyaline membrane disease?
  1. A. Airways constrict (bronchospasm) → wheezing
  2. B. Alveoli collapse (atelectasis) → hypoxia
  3. C. Alveoli over-inflate (emphysema) → air trapping
AnswerB. Alveoli collapse (atelectasis) → hypoxia
WhyWithout surfactant, high surface tension makes alveoli collapse (atelectasis); collapsed alveoli are not ventilated, so the infant becomes hypoxic.
Explanation

Each expiration empties the alveoli to small volumes, where surface tension is strongest; without surfactant they close and need great force to reopen. Blood still flows past alveoli that are no longer ventilated, so it cannot pick up O2. Fluid and protein leak from the damaged capillaries and line the remaining open airspaces as hyaline membranes.

  • Bronchospasm is smooth-muscle constriction of bronchioles in asthma.
  • Over-inflation with loss of elastic recoil is emphysema, the opposite of collapse.
Slides (2)
L143Learning
What are hyaline membranes made of?
  1. A. Fragments of elastin mixed with haemosiderin
  2. B. Debris of dead type I cells mixed with collagen
  3. C. Debris of dead type II cells mixed with fibrin
AnswerC. Debris of dead type II cells mixed with fibrin
WhyHyaline membranes are necrotic debris of type II pneumocytes mixed with fibrin from plasma that leaks out of injured capillaries.
Explanation

Damaged capillaries leak fibrinogen-rich plasma into the alveoli; it clots into fibrin and mixes with the debris of dead alveolar cells to form glassy, eosinophilic (pink) membranes along the alveolar ducts and alveoli. The lecture names type II cell debris; pathology texts say 'necrotic alveolar epithelial cells'. Similar membranes appear in adults with diffuse alveolar damage.

  • Collagen is laid down later, in healing (fibrosis), not in the membranes.
  • Elastin and haemosiderin are not components; haemosiderin is the iron pigment of heart failure cells.
L144Learning
What does hyaline membrane disease look like in a lung section?
  1. A. Many enlarged airspaces; thin, broken septa with black pigmented macrophages
  2. B. Many collapsed alveoli; the few open airspaces lined by bright pink hyaline membranes
  3. C. Many open alveoli; septa thickened by granulomas around food particles
AnswerB. Many collapsed alveoli; the few open airspaces lined by bright pink hyaline membranes
WhyLook for collapsed alveoli (solid-looking areas) with the remaining airspaces lined by pink hyaline membranes.
Explanation

At low power the lung looks dense because most alveoli have collapsed. The few airspaces that stay open (often alveolar ducts) are coated by a smooth, glassy, eosinophilic band, the hyaline membrane, sometimes with trapped cells.

  • Granulomas around food particles describe pulse (lentil) aspiration pneumonia.
  • Enlarged airspaces with thin, broken septa describe emphysema; black macrophages suggest anthracosis.
Slide (1)
L145Learning
An infant born at 28 weeks grunts, flares the nostrils and becomes cyanotic soon after birth. Which cells are too immature to do their job?
  1. A. Type I pneumocytes
  2. B. Alveolar macrophages
  3. C. Type II pneumocytes
AnswerC. Type II pneumocytes
WhyNeonatal respiratory distress syndrome comes from immature type II pneumocytes that cannot make enough surfactant.
Explanation

The signs (rapid breathing, grunting, nasal flaring, rib retractions, cyanosis) come from alveoli collapsing at every expiration. The defect is functional immaturity of the surfactant-secreting cell. Corticosteroids given to the mother before delivery speed up its maturation, and surfactant can be instilled into the baby's airways.

  • Type I pneumocytes form the gas-exchange surface but do not make surfactant.
  • Alveolar macrophages defend the alveoli and clear debris; immature macrophages would not make alveoli collapse.
Slides (2)

Emphysema and pulse aspiration pneumonia

L146Learning
What is emphysema?
  1. A. Destruction of alveolar walls with loss of elasticity; a form of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD)
  2. B. Thickening of alveolar walls with excess elasticity; a form of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD)
  3. C. Destruction of alveolar walls with loss of elasticity; a form of restrictive lung disease
AnswerA. Destruction of alveolar walls with loss of elasticity; a form of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD)
WhyEmphysema is destruction of alveolar walls with loss of elastic recoil; it is one of the chronic obstructive pulmonary diseases (COPD).
Explanation

The airspaces beyond the terminal bronchiole enlarge permanently because the septa between them are destroyed. Losing elastic tissue removes the recoil that pushes air out and holds the small airways open, so they collapse on expiration and trap air: an obstructive pattern with a hyperinflated, barrel-shaped chest.

  • Thickened walls with excess elasticity is the opposite of what happens.
  • Restrictive disease (such as fibrosis) stiffens the lung and shrinks its volumes; emphysema obstructs outflow and enlarges them.
Slides (2)
L147Learning
How does smoking cause emphysema?
  1. A. Excess antitrypsin activity → elastase from macrophages builds up elastin
  2. B. Loss of elastase activity → antitrypsin from macrophages destroys elastin
  3. C. Loss of antitrypsin activity → elastase from macrophages destroys elastin
AnswerC. Loss of antitrypsin activity → elastase from macrophages destroys elastin
WhySmoking inactivates α1-antitrypsin, so elastase from macrophages (and neutrophils) destroys the elastin of the alveolar walls.
Explanation

Smoke recruits and activates alveolar macrophages and neutrophils, which release elastase. Normally α1-antitrypsin, a protease inhibitor made by the liver, neutralises it. Oxidants in smoke inactivate antitrypsin, so elastase digests the elastic fibres of the septa unopposed and the walls break down.

  • Elastase never builds elastin; it digests it, and more antitrypsin would protect the lung.
  • The third choice swaps the roles: elastase is the destructive enzyme and antitrypsin its inhibitor.
Slide (1)
L148Learning
A 34-year-old who has never smoked has emphysema and an inherited α1-antitrypsin deficiency. What destroys his alveolar walls?
  1. A. Excess collagen from septal fibroblasts, thickening and stiffening the septa
  2. B. Elastase from neutrophils and macrophages, working without its inhibitor
  3. C. Antitrypsin from neutrophils and macrophages, working without its inhibitor
AnswerB. Elastase from neutrophils and macrophages, working without its inhibitor
WhyWithout α1-antitrypsin, elastase released by neutrophils and macrophages digests alveolar elastin unchecked, even without smoking.
Explanation

α1-antitrypsin is the main inhibitor of neutrophil elastase in the lung. When a mutation leaves too little of it in the blood, the normal background elastase from inflammatory cells slowly destroys the septal elastin and causes emphysema at a young age; smoking makes it worse and earlier. The lecture names macrophage elastase; textbooks stress neutrophil elastase. Both contribute.

  • Antitrypsin is the protective inhibitor, made by the liver; it is not a destructive enzyme.
  • Excess collagen thickening the septa is pulmonary fibrosis, a restrictive disease, not emphysema.
Slide (1)
L149Learning
What does emphysema do to the alveoli, and with what result?
  1. A. Many small alveoli → fewer, larger, floppy spaces → less surface for exchange and less recoil to push air out
  2. B. Few large alveoli → many smaller, stiff spaces → more surface for exchange and more recoil to push air out
  3. C. Many small alveoli → fewer, larger, floppy spaces → more surface for exchange and more recoil to push air out
AnswerA. Many small alveoli → fewer, larger, floppy spaces → less surface for exchange and less recoil to push air out
WhyEmphysema merges many small alveoli into fewer, larger, floppy spaces: less exchange surface and less elastic recoil.
Explanation

When septa are destroyed, neighbouring alveoli fuse into large airspaces. Total surface falls (many small bubbles have more surface than a few big ones holding the same air), so O2 uptake and CO2 removal suffer. With the elastin gone, the lung no longer recoils, air is trapped and the chest becomes barrel-shaped.

  • Larger spaces with more surface is geometrically wrong: merging bubbles reduces surface.
  • Smaller, stiffer spaces is the opposite of emphysema.
Slide (1)
L150Learning
What is pulse (lentil) aspiration pneumonia?
  1. A. A non-infectious granulomatous pneumonitis from inhaled legumes (e.g. lentils), imaged as small, poorly defined nodules
  2. B. An infectious bacterial pneumonia from inhaled legumes (e.g. lentils), imaged as one consolidated lobe
  3. C. A non-infectious granulomatous pneumonitis from inhaled coal dust, imaged as large, well-defined masses
AnswerA. A non-infectious granulomatous pneumonitis from inhaled legumes (e.g. lentils), imaged as small, poorly defined nodules
WhyAspirated legumes (lentils, peas, beans) cause a non-infectious granulomatous pneumonitis with small, poorly defined nodular opacities.
Explanation

'Pulse' means the dry edible seeds of legumes. When such food is aspirated, the plant material lodges in the small airways and alveoli and provokes a foreign-body granulomatous reaction, with macrophages and giant cells around the particles. Imaging shows multiple small, ill-defined nodules.

  • The reaction is not infectious and does not look like lobar consolidation.
  • Coal dust causes anthracosis or coal workers' pneumoconiosis, not pulse pneumonia.
Slide (1)
364
In the tissue depicted in this micrograph, the surface facing the lumen contains [blank 1] . The cells where these projections originate are [blank 2] . The middle of this slide shows the [blank 3] , which produce mucus to coat epithelial surface.
  1. Blank 1: nerve dendrites | cilia | stereocilia | nerve axons
  2. Blank 2: pseudounipolar neurons | bipolar neurons | goblet cells | columnar epithelial cells
  3. Blank 3: club cells | goblet cells | striated ducts | bowman’s glands
AnswerBlank 1 → nerve dendrites
Blank 2 → bipolar neurons
Blank 3 → bowman’s glands
WhyThe luminal processes are dendrites (knobs with non-motile cilia) of bipolar olfactory neurons, and the lamina propria glands are serous Bowman's glands.
Explanation from the source
This is a medium power view of the olfactory epithelium that contains a meshwork of sustentacular microvilli and olfactory non-motile cilia on the surface. The epithelium is pseudostratified columnar and it is hard to differentiate between the olfactory receptor cells, sustentacular cells and basal epithelial cells. However, the nuclei of the sustentacular cells tend to be in the top portion of the layer, the nuclei of the olfactory receptor cells tend to be in the middle portion, and the nuclei of the basal epithelial cells tend to be in the bottom portion. One can also see the an afferent nerve bundle. The dendrites of the olfactory neurons are sometimes called "non-motile cilia", due to the fact that at light microscopy they resemble cilia. However, they are in fact dendrites.

Below the epithelial layer there is a lamina propria. This lamina propria is composed of connective tissue, and is where we find the bowman’s glands, which produce mucus to trap odorants and eventually wash them away. Below the bowman’s glands is a bundle of nerves, formed by the axons of the bipolar neurons, which will run through the cribriform plate to the olfactory cortex via the olfactory nerve.
ConceptOlfactory epithelium image: dendritic surface processes of bipolar neurons over Bowman's glands

[Question 6] A segment of trachea is obtained at autopsy. Paraffin sections are stained with H&E and examined by light microscopy (shown in the image). Identify the structure within the oval. [Question 7] Which of the following best describes the function of the structure identified in Question 6?

Small particles and pathogens become trapped within the mucus and are removed by the coordinated ciliary action of the respiratory epithelium.
