[Question 8] A 14-year-old girl with the common cold presents with a “stuffy nose” due to nasal congestion. Which of the following represents a hallmark of the lamina propria in the nasal cavity? [Question 9] Which of the following mechanisms of disease best describes the pathogenesis of nasal congestion in the patient described in Question 8?
  1. (A) Increased secretion from mucous glands in the lamina propria
  2. (B) Increased secretion from serous glands in the lamina propria
  3. (C) Infiltration of the lamina propria with chronic inflammatory cells
  4. (D) Overproduction of mucus by goblet cells in the respiratory epithelium
  5. (E) Swelling of the lamina propria of the nasal mucosa
AnswerE. Swelling of the lamina propria of the nasal mucosa
WhyThe nasal lamina propria has venous swell bodies; in a cold they engorge and plasma leaks out (edema), so swelling of the lamina propria narrows the passage and causes congestion.
Explanation from the source
The nasal mucosa contains a rich vascular plexus. These venous sinusoids are known as “swell bodies.” Allergic reactions and inflammation related to “colds” and “flu” can cause abnormal engorgement of the sinusoidal swell bodies. Increased hydrostatic pressure and increased vascular permeability lead to an accumulation of extravascular edema fluid in the lamina propria of the nasal mucosa, resulting in the sensation of “stuffy nose.” Although the other choices describe changes associated with inflammation, they are not related to nasal congestion in patients with the common cold. Keywords: Nasal cavity, swell body
ConceptNasal congestion results from swelling of the lamina propria

  1. (A) Pseudostratified columnar

To protect the mucosa from abrasion by the rapidly moving stream of air, the vocal folds are lined by a protective, stratified squamous epithelium. None of the other choices describe this histologic feature of the vocal folds. Keywords: Larynx, vocal folds

[Question 20] A 50-year-old woman with lung cancer develops respiratory insufficiency and expires. A transverse section of the trachea is examined at autopsy. The posterior aspect of the patient’s trachea appears normal (shown in the image). Which of the following structures is essential for maintaining an open tracheal air passage? [Question 21] The posterior aspect of the trachea described in Question 20 is examined at higher magnification (shown in the image). Identify the structure indicated by the arrow.
  1. (A) Adventitia
  2. (B) Dense regular connective tissue
  3. (C) Hyaline cartilage
  4. (D) Smooth muscle

WhyPosteriorly, where the C-shaped cartilage rings are open next to the esophagus, the gap is bridged by the trachealis, a band of smooth muscle linking the free ends of the cartilage.
Explanation from the source
Cartilaginous support is absent along the posterior aspect of the trachea adjacent to the esophagus. This histologic feature of the trachea facilitates the passage of food through the esophagus to the stomach. The gap between free ends of the two C-shaped cartilaginous rings is filled by smooth muscle and a connective tissue that is rich in both elastic and collagen fibers. The smooth muscle identified by the arrow in the image is termed the trachealis muscle. None of the other choices identify smooth muscle. Keywords: Trachea, trachealis muscle

[Question 27] A 54-year-old woman with a history of smoking presents with hemoptysis and chest pain. A CT scan of the thorax reveals a 5-cm mass in the middle lobe of the right lung. The mass is removed using a pulmonary segmentectomy. Which of the following pulmonary units best characterizes the structural basis for your surgical resection? [Question 28] The specimen obtained at surgery from the patient described in Question 27 reveals an adenocarcinoma, with a margin of normal lung parenchyma. Examination of the tumor margin shows an intrapulmonary bronchus (shown in the image). Which of the following histologic features distinguishes this intrapulmonary bronchus from an extrapulmonary primary bronchus?
  1. (A) Absence of submucosal glands
  2. (B) Adventitia composed of connective tissue
  3. (C) Lack of cartilage in the bronchial wall
  4. (D) Loss of respiratory epithelium
  5. (E) Presence of cartilage plates
AnswerE. Presence of cartilage plates
WhyExtrapulmonary bronchi have C-shaped rings like the trachea; once inside the lung, intrapulmonary bronchi have irregular cartilage plates. Glands, respiratory epithelium and smooth muscle are present in both.
Explanation from the source
The histologic features of extrapulmonary segments of the primary bronchi are similar to those of the trachea. However, once primary bronchi enter the lung and become intrapulmonary, their structure changes. The first major histologic change is that C-shaped cartilage rings are replaced by small cartilaginous plates. These irregular-shaped cartilage plates are distributed around the circumference of the bronchial wall to prevent collapse of the bronchial air passage. As the bronchi continue to branch and become smaller in diameter, these cartilage plates decrease significantly in size. They eventually disappear at the point where the most distal bronchi become bronchioles. None of the other choices distinguish extra- from intrapulmonary bronchi. Keywords: Intrapulmonary bronchi
ConceptIrregular cartilage plates distinguish intrapulmonary bronchi

[Question 27] A 54-year-old woman with a history of smoking presents with hemoptysis and chest pain. A CT scan of the thorax reveals a 5-cm mass in the middle lobe of the right lung. The mass is removed using a pulmonary segmentectomy. Which of the following pulmonary units best characterizes the structural basis for your surgical resection? [Question 28] The specimen obtained at surgery from the patient described in Question 27 reveals an adenocarcinoma, with a margin of normal lung parenchyma. Examination of the tumor margin shows an intrapulmonary bronchus (shown in the image). Which of the following histologic features distinguishes this intrapulmonary bronchus from an extrapulmonary primary bronchus? [Question 29] The wall of the intrapulmonary bronchus described in Question 28 is examined at higher magnification (shown in the image). Identify the structure indicated by the arrow.
  1. (A) Basement membrane
  2. (B) Dense connective tissue
  3. (C) Lamina propria
  4. (D) Muscularis mucosa
  5. (E) Submucosa
AnswerD. Muscularis mucosa
WhyIntrapulmonary bronchi gain a distinct layer of spirally arranged smooth muscle (the muscularis mucosae) between the lamina propria and submucosa, which controls airway diameter.
Explanation from the source
Another distinction between extra- and intrapulmonary bronchi is the appearance of a distinct layer of smooth muscle between the lamina propria and the submucosa in the intrapulmonary air passages. In larger bronchi, this muscularis mucosa forms a continuous layer. However, as the bronchi become smaller, the muscularis mucosa becomes discontinuous. This muscle layer characterizes the bronchopulmonary tree as far distally as the alveolar ducts, where smooth muscle fibers are observed as knoblike structures within interalveolar septa. Contractions of the muscularis mucosae regulate the diameter of the conducting airways of the respiratory system. Keywords: Intrapulmonary bronchi
ConceptSmooth-muscle layer (muscularis mucosae) in intrapulmonary bronchus

[Question 33] A lung specimen (shown in the image) is examined in the pathology department. Identify the structure within the oval. [Question 34] Another area from the specimen described in Question 33 is examined by light microscopy (shown in the image). Identify the structure within the oval line.
  1. (A) Alveolar duct
  2. (B) Bronchiole
  3. (C) Intrapulmonary bronchus
  4. (D) Respiratory bronchiole
  5. (E) Terminal bronchiole
AnswerD. Respiratory bronchiole
WhyThe circled airway has a cuboidal-lined wall interrupted by alveolar outpocketings (arrows), the defining feature of a respiratory bronchiole.
Explanation from the source
Large bronchioles undergo continuous branching, before reaching the respiratory portion of the lungs. Respiratory bronchioles arise from terminal bronchioles. They serve as a transition between the conducting and the respiratory portions of the respiratory system. They are involved in both air conducting and gas exchange. The feature that distinguishes respiratory bronchioles from terminal bronchioles (choice E) is the presence of an incomplete wall that is interrupted by alveoli (arrows, shown in the image). A respiratory bronchiole, along with the alveolar ducts, alveolar sacs, and alveoli that it supplies, forms the smallest functional component of the respiratory system, termed respiratory bronchiolar unit. Keywords: Respiratory bronchioles
ConceptBronchiole wall interrupted by alveoli: respiratory bronchiole

WhyThe arrowheads mark plump, rounded cells with round nuclei bulging at septal junctions, type II alveolar cells, unlike the flat nuclei of type I cells.
Explanation from the source
Type II alveolar cells, also termed type II pneumocytes, are rounded cells with rounded nuclei. They are interspersed among the type I alveolar cells and account for about 60% of cells in the alveolar wall. Type II alveolar cells tend to cluster at junctions between the alveolar septa and bulge into the alveolar lumen. [Question 52] A 32-year-old woman delivers a baby prematurely at 25 weeks of gestation. Shortly after birth, the neonate becomes short of breath, with intercostal retraction and nasal flaring during respiration. Respiratory distress in your patient is most likely caused by injury to which of the following components of the respiratory system? [Question 53] Respiratory distress syndrome described in Question 52 was most likely caused by lack of fetal development (immaturity) of which of the following cells?
  1. (A) Brush cells
  2. (B) Clara cells
  3. (C) Goblet cells
  4. (D) Type I alveolar cells
  5. (E) Type II alveolar cells

WhySurfactant is made by type II alveolar cells, which mature late in gestation; at 25 weeks too little surfactant is secreted, so alveoli collapse, causing respiratory distress syndrome.

Pulmonary surfactant is secreted by type II alveolar cells. However, these cells do not appear in fetal alveoli until late in pregnancy (typically after week 35). Pulmonary surfactant is released into amniotic fluid, where it can be sampled by amniocentesis to assess fetal lung maturity. Administration of exogenous surfactant to neonates that are born prematurely has greatly improved their survival. None of the other cells listed secrete pulmonary surfactant. Keywords: Respiratory distress syndrome of the neonate, surfactant
ConceptRDS in premature infant: type II pneumocytes are too immature

  4. D. Hyperplasia of goblet cells causing airway obstruction
AnswerA. Reduced surfactant synthesis by immature Type II pneumocytes leading to increased alveolar surface tension
WhyPremature type II pneumocytes make too little surfactant, so alveolar surface tension rises, alveoli collapse, and fibrin-rich hyaline membranes line the airspaces.
ConceptNeonatal RDS: immature type II cells make too little surfactant

  2. B. Type I pneumocyte → fused basal laminae → capillary endothelial cell

A 5-year-old girl with cystic fibrosis is admitted to the hospital with pneumonia. As you examine the patient, you recall the anatomy and histology of the respiratory system. Which of the following air passages is the most distal part of the conducting portion of the patient’s lungs?
  1. (A) Alveolar ducts
  2. (B) Respiratory bronchioles
  3. (C) Secondary bronchi
  4. (D) Segmental bronchi
  5. (E) Terminal bronchioles
Answer(E) Terminal bronchioles
WhyTerminal bronchioles are the smallest branches of the bronchial tree and the last purely conducting segment; respiratory bronchioles and alveolar ducts already exchange gas.
Explanation from the source
The answer is E: Terminal bronchioles. The respiratory system is composed of a conducting and a respiratory portion. The conducting portion includes air passages outside and inside the lungs. The nasal cavities, nasopharynx, larynx, trachea, and paired primary bronchi are air passages external to the lungs (extrapulmonary). Upon entering the lungs, the paired primary bronchi undergo branching to form the intrapulmonary bronchial tree. The branches become smaller and lead to the respiratory portion of the lungs, where gas exchange takes place. Components of the bronchial tree include the primary bronchi, lobar (secondary) bronchi, segmental (tertiary) bronchi, and bronchioles. Terminal bronchioles are the smallest components of the bronchial tree and the terminal part of the conducting portion of the respiratory system. Cystic fibrosis is an autosomal recessive disorder that affects children. It is characterized by (1) chronic pulmonary disease, (2) deficient exocrine pancreatic function, and (3) other complications of retained (inspissated) mucus in a number of organs, including the small intestine, the liver, and the reproductive tract. All of the pathologic consequences of cystic fibrosis can be attributed to the presence of abnormally thick mucus. Keywords: Terminal bronchioles, cystic fibrosis
ConceptTerminal bronchioles are the most distal conducting airway

During a problem-based learning session, your facilitator asks about proper usage of the term “bronchial tree.” Which of the following structures is a component of the bronchial tree in the respiratory system?
  1. (A) Alveolar ducts
  2. (B) Alveolar sacs
  3. (C) Bronchioles
  4. (D) Larynx
  5. (E) Trachea
Answer(C) Bronchioles
WhyThe bronchial tree is the intrapulmonary conducting system of bronchi and bronchioles; larynx and trachea are extrapulmonary and alveolar ducts and sacs are respiratory.
Explanation from the source
The answer is C: Bronchioles. The term “bronchial tree” refers to intrapulmonary air conducting passages of the respiratory system. This tree is composed of internal bronchi that bifurcate from the primary bronchi and also the bronchioles. Larynx and trachea (choices D and E) are extrapulmonary air conducting passages. Alveolar ducts and sacs (choices A and B) are components of the respiratory portion of the lungs and are sites for gas exchange. Keywords: Bronchioles
ConceptBronchioles are part of the intrapulmonary bronchial tree
426
The respiratory portion of the respiratory system begins at which of the following locations in the lungs?
  1. (A) Alveolar ducts
  2. (B) Alveolar sacs
  3. (C) Alveoli
  4. (D) Respiratory bronchioles
  5. (E) Terminal bronchioles
Answer(D) Respiratory bronchioles
WhyRespiratory bronchioles have alveoli opening from their walls, so they are the first segment where gas exchange occurs and the start of the respiratory portion.
Explanation from the source
The answer is D: Respiratory bronchioles. Respiratory bronchioles are branches from air conducting, terminal bronchioles. In turn, respiratory bronchioles give rise to alveolar ducts, alveolar sacs, and finally to alveoli where gas exchange occurs. Alveoli are small air cavities, approximately 200 μm in diameter, enveloped by a rich capillary bed. Respiratory bronchioles have discontinuous walls that open directly to numerous alveoli. Therefore, respiratory bronchioles are included in the respiratory portion of the respiratory system, along with the alveolar ducts, alveolar sacs, and terminal alveoli. Keywords: Respiratory bronchioles
ConceptRespiratory portion begins at respiratory bronchioles

The parents of an 8-year-old boy with bronchial asthma ask about the anatomy and physiology of the lungs, to better understand their child’s medical condition. Which of the following components of the respiratory system is the major site of gas exchange?
  1. (A) Alveoli
  2. (B) Respiratory bronchioles
  3. (C) Secondary bronchi
  4. (D) Segmental bronchi
  5. (E) Terminal bronchioles
Answer(A) Alveoli
WhyGas exchange begins in respiratory bronchioles, but the vast surface of thin-walled alveoli wrapped in capillaries makes them the major exchange site.
Explanation from the source
The answer is A: Alveoli. Fresh air reaches the respiratory portion of the respiratory system through the extra- and intrapulmonary conducting ducts. Gas exchange begins within the respiratory bronchioles (choice B), because these air passages have alveoli connected to them. However, the major site of gas exchange in the lungs takes place within the smallest air spaces—the alveoli. Alveoli are organized as clusters. These clusters open to a common space that is referred to as the alveolar sac. Moving proximally in the respiratory tract, the alveoli and alveolar sacs are observed to open into larger, elongated spaces termed alveolar ducts. The other structures listed do not participate in gas exchange. Asthma in this patient is a chronic lung disease caused by increased responsiveness of the airways to a variety of stimuli. Patients typically exhibit paroxysms of wheezing, dyspnea, and cough. Keywords: Asthma, alveolus
ConceptAlveoli are the major site of gas exchange

Which of the following anatomic relationships best describes the structural basis for gas exchange in the lungs?
  1. (A) Association of pulmonary veins with the bronchial tree
  2. (B) Close association of alveolar spaces and pulmonary capillaries
  3. (C) Continuous branching of the bronchopulmonary tree
  4. (D) Dual blood supply to the lungs
  5. (E) Intimate relationship of pulmonary arteries and veins
Answer(B) Close association of alveolar spaces and pulmonary capillaries
WhyAir in alveoli lies only a fraction of a micrometre from blood in septal pulmonary capillaries, the structural basis of diffusion.
Explanation from the source
The answer is B: Close association of alveolar spaces and pulmonary capillaries. The alveolar air spaces are separated from one another by alveolar septa. Capillaries arising from the pulmonary arteries travel within these very thin interstitial spaces. Fresh air in the alveolus is only several hundred nanometers removed from deoxygenated blood in the pulmonary capillaries. This intimate relationship of air and pulmonary capillaries provides the structural basis for gas exchange in the lungs. Dual blood supply to the lungs (choice D) explains the pathologic finding that geographic areas of pulmonary necrosis are typically red (hemorrhagic infarcts). None of the other choices describe or explain the structural basis for gas exchange. Keywords: Alveoli
ConceptGas exchange rests on close apposition of alveoli and capillaries

  1. (A) Artery
  2. (B) Lymphoid follicle
  3. (C) Mucous gland

The answer is C: Mucous gland. Mucous and serous glands are found along most of the conducting portion of the respiratory tract, within the mucosa and the submucosa. Goblet cells located within the respiratory epithelium also produce abundant mucus. Serous glands (choice E) would stain with eosin. None of the other choices exhibit the distinctive morphology of tracheal mucous glands. Keywords: Mucous and serous glands

Which of the following best describes the function of the structure identified in Question 6?
  1. (A) Conditioning of inhaled air
  2. (B) Polypeptide hormone secretion
  3. (C) Production of secretory IgA antibody
  4. (D) Source of pulmonary surfactant
  5. (E) Substrate for inflammatory cell adhesion
Answer(A) Conditioning of inhaled air
WhySecretions of airway seromucous glands moisten inhaled air and trap particles for ciliary clearance, part of conditioning of inhaled air.
Explanation from the source
The answer is A: Conditioning of inhaled air. The mucus, produced by glands and goblet cells, coats the luminal surface over most of the conducting portion of the respiratory tract. Mucous and serous secretions help moisten, warm, and clean the inhaled air, before it reaches the delicate and fragile alveolar air spaces. Small particles and pathogens become trapped within the mucus and are removed by the coordinated ciliary action of the respiratory epithelium. A 14-year-old girl with the common cold presents with a “stuffy nose” due to nasal congestion. Which of the following represents a hallmark of the lamina propria in the nasal cavity?
  1. (A) Elastic fibers
  2. (B) Loose connective tissue
  3. (C) Lymphocytes
  4. (D) Reticular fibers
  5. (E) Rich vascular plexus
Answer(E) Rich vascular plexus
WhyThe nasal lamina propria holds a rich vascular plexus of capillary loops and venous swell bodies that warms inhaled air.
Explanation from the source
The answer is E: Rich vascular plexus. The two nasal cavities, separated by a nasal septum, comprise the uppermost part of the respiratory system. The nasal cavities communicate with nasopharynx posteriorly, as well as the paranasal sinuses and lacrimal sacs laterally and superiorly. The most anterior portion of the nasal cavity is the nasal vestibule, which is lined by skin. The nasal cavity posterior to the vestibule can be divided into two parts: (1) the inferior two-thirds represent the respiratory region and (2) the superior one-third represents the olfactory region. The respiratory region is covered by a ciliated, pseudostratified columnar epithelium (respiratory epithelium). The lamina propria is connected to periosteum or perichondrium of the underlying bone and cartilage. It exhibits an extensive vascular plexus with complex sets of capillary loops. This vascular latticework serves to warm the inhaled air to protect the lungs. The other choices are components of loose connective tissue that are found in many organs. Rhinovirus is the most frequent cause of the “common cold.” Keywords: Nasal cavity, nasal mucosa
ConceptNasal lamina propria hallmark: rich vascular plexus

432
Which of the following mechanisms of disease best describes the pathogenesis of nasal congestion in the patient described in Question 8?
  1. (A) Increased secretion from mucous glands in the lamina propria
  2. (B) Increased secretion from serous glands in the lamina propria
  3. (C) Infiltration of the lamina propria with chronic inflammatory cells
  4. (D) Overproduction of mucus by goblet cells in the respiratory epithelium
  5. (E) Swelling of the lamina propria of the nasal mucosa
Answer(E) Swelling of the lamina propria of the nasal mucosa
WhyEngorged venous swell bodies plus edema expand the nasal lamina propria during colds and allergy, narrowing the passage and causing a stuffy nose.
Explanation from the source
The answer is E: Swelling of the lamina propria of the nasal mucosa. The nasal mucosa contains a rich vascular plexus. These venous sinusoids are known as “swell bodies.” Allergic reactions and inflammation related to “colds” and “flu” can cause abnormal engorgement of the sinusoidal swell bodies. Increased hydrostatic pressure and increased vascular permeability lead to an accumulation of extravascular edema fluid in the lamina propria of the nasal mucosa, resulting in the sensation of “stuffy nose.” Although the other choices describe changes associated with inflammation, they are not related to nasal congestion in patients with the common cold. Keywords: Nasal cavity, swell body
ConceptNasal congestion results from swelling of the lamina propria

A 48-year-old woman with a 3-day history of an upper respiratory infection complains that she has lost her sense of smell. Her perception of smell recovers about 1 week later. The epithelial lining of which portion of the respiratory system was temporally affected in this patient?
  1. (A) Larynx
  2. (B) Nasal vestibule
  3. (C) Nasopharynx
  4. (D) Olfactory region of nasal cavity
  5. (E) Respiratory region of nasal cavity
Answer(D) Olfactory region of nasal cavity
WhySmell depends on the olfactory mucosa of the nasal roof and superior conchae; inflammation there causes temporary anosmia until basal cells regenerate neurons.
Explanation from the source
The answer is D: Olfactory region of nasal cavity. Three bony plates in the nasal cavity (superior, middle, and inferior conchae) project inferomedially from the lateral wall. The middle and inferior conchae are covered by respiratory epithelium and form the lateral wall of the respiratory region of the nasal cavity. By contrast, the superior conchae in the olfactory region at the roof of the nasal cavity are covered by a specialized olfactory mucosa (epithelium and lamina propria). The olfactory epithelium contains olfactory chemoreceptors. Damage to the olfactory mucosa caused by inflammation can result in the loss of smell. Epithelia in the other anatomic regions listed are not specialized for olfactory perception. Keywords: Nasal cavity, olfactory region

A biopsy of the olfactory mucosa is examined by light microscopy (shown in the image). Which of the following cells in the olfactory epithelium is responsible for the sense of smell?
  1. (A) Basal cells
  2. (B) Brush cells
  3. (C) Goblet cells
  4. (D) Neurons
  5. (E) Supporting cells
Answer(D) Neurons
WhyOlfactory neurons span the olfactory epithelium, with dendritic knobs bearing non-motile cilia that hold odorant receptors and axons that form the olfactory nerve.
Explanation from the source
The answer is D: Neurons. The olfactory epithelium of the nasal cavity is a ciliated, pseudostratified columnar epithelium but includes many other cells that are not found in typical respiratory epithelium. Olfactory neurons, also referred to as olfactory cells or olfactory receptor cells, span the entire thickness of the olfactory epithelium. The dendrite extends above the surface of the epithelium and forms a knoblike swelling termed the olfactory vesicle. Long, nonmotile cilia that arise from the olfactory vesicle function as receptors for chemical odorants. Axonal processes of these neurons leave the epithelium, unite as small nerve bundles within the basal lamina, and pass through the cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone to form the olfactory nerve, which enters the brain. Toxic fumes and physical injury can damage olfactory neurons resulting in a temporary loss of the sense of smell. Fortunately, olfactory neurons can be replaced by regeneration from proliferative stem cells in the epithelium. Other cells found in the olfactory epithelium include basal cells, brush cells, and supporting cells (choices A, B, and E). Keywords: Olfactory epithelium, olfactory neurons
ConceptOlfactory neurons are the cells that detect odorants

The cell described in Question 11 is best characterized as which of the following types of neurons?
  1. (A) Bipolar
  2. (B) Interneuron
  3. (C) Motor
  4. (D) Multipolar
  5. (E) Pseudounipolar
Answer(A) Bipolar
WhyEach olfactory receptor cell has one dendrite to the surface and one axon to the olfactory bulb, making it a bipolar neuron.
Explanation from the source
The answer is A: Bipolar. Olfactory neurons have one dendritic process and an axon. Cilia arising from the dendritic process serve as chemoreceptors for odorants. The neuronal axon extends from the olfactory epithelium to the central nervous system. None of the other types of neurons listed show the distinctive features of olfactory neurons. Keywords: Olfactory epithelium, olfactory neuron
ConceptOlfactory receptor cells are bipolar neurons

Which of the following cells of the olfactory epithelium is equivalent functionally to neuroglial cells of the central nervous system?

  3. (C) Goblet cells
  4. (D) Olfactory neurons
  5. (E) Supporting cells
Answer(E) Supporting cells
WhyTall supporting (sustentacular) cells with apical nuclei give mechanical and metabolic support to olfactory neurons, much like neuroglia in the CNS.
Explanation from the source
The answer is E: Supporting cells. Supporting cells, also termed sustentacular cells, are similar to neuroglial cells of the central nervous system. They are the most numerous type of cell in the olfactory epithelium. These tall, columnar cells have nuclei that are located close to the apical surface of the epithelium. They provide mechanical and metabolic support to the olfactory neurons. Supporting cells secrete odorant-binding proteins (OBPs) that transport odorant chemicals to olfactory receptors (specialized proteins) that are present in the plasma membranes of cilia in the olfactory vesicles. None of the other choices provide structural and metabolic support to olfactory neurons. Keywords: Olfactory epithelium, supporting cells

A 49-year-old woman with a history of recurrent paranasal sinusitis presents with facial pain and fever. Which of the following types of epithelium normally lines the paranasal sinus cavities?

The answer is A: Ciliated, pseudostratified columnar epithelium with goblet cells. The paranasal sinuses are bilateral open spaces within frontal, maxillary, ethmoid, and sphenoid bones. These spaces are lined by respiratory epithelium, and they communicate with nasal cavities through narrow openings. Other regions of the respiratory system that are covered by a respiratory epithelium include respiratory region of the nasal cavities, nasopharynx, larynx (excluding vocal folds and epiglottis), trachea, bronchi, and large bronchioles. Keratinized, stratified squamous epithelium (choice B) is found in the skin. Nonkeratinized, stratified squamous epithelium (choice C) is found in the esophagus and uterine cervix. Loss of function of which of the following cells or subcellular structures is a likely cause of chronic sinusitis?
  1. (A) Basal cells
  2. (B) Cilia
  3. (C) Goblet cells
  4. (D) Microvilli
  5. (E) Mucous glands
Answer(B) Cilia
WhyCoordinated cilia sweep sinus mucus through the narrow ostia; without them mucus stagnates, ostia block and infections recur as chronic sinusitis.
Explanation from the source
The answer is B: Cilia. Cilia are delicate projections of the plasma membrane that produce a coordinated, sweeping motion along the apical surface of an epithelium. Mucus that is produced by goblet cells and mucous glands in the respiratory system is swept into the nasal cavities by the coordinated motion of innumerable cilia. Defective ciliary action leads to an accumulation of mucus within the paranasal sinuses. Mucus accumulation in the sinuses leads to chronic obstruction of the drainage orifices and recurrent bouts of paranasal infections (chronic sinusitis). The other choices are unlikely causes of chronic sinusitis. Keywords: Sinusitis, cilia

A 29-year-old opera singer complains about recent changes in the frequency of her vibrato and the quality of her vocal sound. Phonation in your patient is initiated and shaped by which of the following structures of the head and neck?

  2. (B) Oropharynx

Its wall is composed of a series of cartilage plates connected by skeletal muscles and ligaments. Two anteroposterior mucosal folds, vocal folds, project toward the lumen of the larynx (voice box). Ligaments and skeletal muscles generate tension in these vocal folds and, thereby, control phonation. The vocal folds control the flow of air passing through the larynx, and they vibrate to produce sound. Injury or inflammation to the vocal folds may cause changes in phonation. None of the other choices are related to vocal sound. Keywords: Larynx, vocal folds, phonation

Lamina propria (choice B) is the underlying loose connective tissue layer that contains lymphatic vessels (choice C). The submucosa (choice E) of the trachea is composed of loose connective tissue and is difficult to distinguish from the lamina propria in routine histological preparations. A thin layer of elastic tissue forms a boundary between the mucosa (choice D) and the submucosa. Keywords: Trachea, basement membrane
ConceptThick basement membrane beneath tracheal epithelium

The specimen obtained at surgery from the patient described in Question 27 reveals an adenocarcinoma, with a margin of normal lung parenchyma. Examination of the tumor margin shows an intrapulmonary bronchus (shown in the image). Which of the following histologic features distinguishes this intrapulmonary bronchus from an extrapulmonary primary bronchus?
  1. (A) Absence of submucosal glands
  2. (B) Adventitia composed of connective tissue
  3. (C) Lack of cartilage in the bronchial wall
  4. (D) Loss of respiratory epithelium
  5. (E) Presence of cartilage plates
Answer(E) Presence of cartilage plates
WhyExtrapulmonary primary bronchi have C-shaped rings like the trachea; intrapulmonary bronchi have irregular cartilage plates, while glands, respiratory epithelium and adventitia are not distinguishing.
Explanation from the source
The answer is E: Presence of cartilage plates. The histologic features of extrapulmonary segments of the primary bronchi are similar to those of the trachea. However, once primary bronchi enter the lung and become intrapulmonary, their structure changes. The first major histologic change is that C-shaped cartilage rings are replaced by small cartilaginous plates. These irregular-shaped cartilage plates are distributed around the circumference of the bronchial wall to prevent collapse of the bronchial air passage. As the bronchi continue to branch and become smaller in diameter, these cartilage plates decrease significantly in size. They eventually disappear at the point where the most distal bronchi become bronchioles. None of the other choices distinguish extra- from intrapulmonary bronchi. Keywords: Intrapulmonary bronchi
ConceptIrregular cartilage plates distinguish intrapulmonary bronchi

The wall of the intrapulmonary bronchus described in Question 28 is examined at higher magnification (shown in the image). Identify the structure indicated by the arrow.
  1. (A) Basement membrane
  2. (B) Dense connective tissue
  3. (C) Lamina propria
  4. (D) Muscularis mucosa
  5. (E) Submucosa
Answer(D) Muscularis mucosa
WhyThe arrowed eosinophilic band between lamina propria and cartilage plates is the bronchial smooth muscle layer (muscularis mucosae), spiral bundles that control airway diameter.
Explanation from the source
The answer is D: Muscularis mucosa. Another distinction between extra- and intrapulmonary bronchi is the appearance of a distinct layer of smooth muscle between the lamina propria and the submucosa in the intrapulmonary air passages. In larger bronchi, this muscularis mucosa forms a continuous layer. However, as the bronchi become smaller, the muscularis mucosa becomes discontinuous. This muscle layer characterizes the bronchopulmonary tree as far distally as the alveolar ducts, where smooth muscle fibers are observed as knoblike structures within interalveolar septa. Contractions of the muscularis mucosae regulate the diameter of the conducting airways of the respiratory system. Keywords: Intrapulmonary bronchi
ConceptSmooth-muscle layer (muscularis mucosae) in intrapulmonary bronchus

You are involved in a research project to study the biology of Clara cells. As part of your research, you develop a monoclonal antibody that identifies these cells in paraffin-embedded sections.   4. (D) Segmental bronchi
  5. (E) Terminal bronchioles

Explanation from the source
The answer is E: Terminal bronchioles. Larger bronchioles are lined by typical respiratory epithelium. However, with terminal bronchioles, the lining epithelium begins to assume a simple cuboidal morphology with Clara cells interspersed among ciliated cells. Clara cells increase in number as the bronchioles narrow to become respiratory bronchioles. Clara cells become the major cell population present in the epithelium of distal respiratory bronchioles. Clara cells are not typically found in other pulmonary locations listed. Keywords: Clara cells

  2. (B) Fluid uptake via pinocytosis
  3. (C) Production of inflammatory cytokines
  4. (D) Receptors for binding pathogens
  5. (E) Secretion of surfactant

The answer is E: Secretion of surfactant. Clara cells are also referred to as exocrine bronchiolar cells. These cells secrete a surface-active lipoprotein that helps prevent luminal adhesion and collapse of the bronchioles, particularly during expiration. Clara cells are also reserve stem cells that can repopulate respiratory bronchioles following injury (e.g., following smoke inhalation). You are asked to discuss the physiology of pulmonary gas exchange during a laboratory meeting. Gas exchange begins at what point in the respiratory tree?

  3. (C) Respiratory bronchioles
  4. (D) Segmental bronchi
  5. (E) Terminal bronchioles
Answer(C) Respiratory bronchioles
WhyRespiratory bronchioles have alveoli opening from their walls, so they are the first site of gas exchange; terminal bronchioles are the last purely conducting segment.
Explanation from the source
The answer is C: Respiratory bronchioles. In this transitional zone, respiratory bronchioles function as both conducting passages (delivering air to and from alveoli) and sites of gas exchange. The anatomic basis for gas exchange at this location is that respiratory bronchioles open directly to alveoli, as well as alveolar ducts and sacs. It is not the major site for gas exchange, but it is the initial site for gas exchange in the lungs. Alveoli (choice A) are the primary site of gas exchange. Choices B, D, and E are not related to gas exchange. Keywords: Respiratory bronchioles

The squamous epithelial cells that cover most (95%) of the surface area of the pulmonary alveoli are connected to one another through junctions that prevent the leakage of interstitial fluid into the alveolar air spaces. Which of the following types of intercellular junctions serve this important biological function?
  1. (A) Cadherins
  2. (B) Hemidesmosomes
  3. (C) Macula adherens
  4. (D) Zonula adherens
  5. (E) Zonula occludens
Answer(E) Zonula occludens
WhyType I alveolar cells are sealed by zonula occludens (tight junctions), which block interstitial fluid from leaking into airspaces.
Explanation from the source
The answer is E: Zonula occludens. Tight junctions between type I alveolar cells form an effective barrier that prevents leakage of interstitial fluid into the air spaces of the lungs. Without this barrier, patients would develop pulmonary edema. Type I alveolar cells also form a blood–air barrier that is thin enough for efficient gas exchange. Cadherins (choice A) are Ca2+-dependent cell adhesion molecules that localize to zonula adherens (choice D); these junctions are found in type I alveolar cells, but they do not prevent fluid leakage. None of the other choices provide a barrier to the movement of interstitial fluid into the alveolar air spaces. Keywords: Type I alveolar cells, zonula occludens
ConceptType I alveolar cells are joined by tight junctions

Which of the following best describes the function of type II alveolar cells?
  1. (A) Cytokine production
  2. (B) Fluid transport
  3. (C) IgA antibody production
  4. (D) Phagocytosis of pathogens
  5. (E) Secretion of surfactant
Answer(E) Secretion of surfactant
WhyType II alveolar cells synthesize surfactant, store it in lamellar bodies and secrete it to lower surface tension and keep alveoli open.
Explanation from the source
The answer is E: Secretion of surfactant. Although type II alveolar cells are the most numerous cells in the alveolar epithelium, they cover only less than 5% of the alveolar surface area. These cells secrete surfactant, a surface-active lipoprotein mixture that coats the alveolar lining epithelium. Surfactant lipids and proteins form a protective layer that reduces surface tension within the alveoli, to stabilize alveolar spaces and prevent their collapse. Keywords: Alveolus, type II alveolar cells, surfactant
ConceptType II alveolar cells secrete surfactant

455High-yield
A 50-year-old woman with leukemia undergoes chemotherapy. During treatment, she develops increasing cough and shortness of breath. Sputum cultures are negative, and the patient does not respond to antibiotic therapy. If this patient has acquired a viral pneumonia, with alveolar damage, which of the following cells can regenerate the alveolar epithelium during healing?
  1. (A) Clara cells
  2. (B) Enterochromaffin cells
  3. (C) Small granular cells
  4. (D) Type I alveolar cells
  5. (E) Type II alveolar cells
Answer(E) Type II alveolar cells
WhyType I cells cannot divide, so after diffuse alveolar damage type II alveolar cells proliferate and differentiate to replace both type I and type II cells.
Explanation from the source
The answer is E: Type II alveolar cells. The alveolar surface is continuously exposed to inhaled pathogens and is vulnerable to many destabilizing forces. As described in this clinical vignette, viral infections of the pulmonary parenchyma produce interstitial pneumonia with diffuse alveolar damage. Necrosis of type I alveolar cells results in pathologic changes that are indistinguishable from diffuse alveolar damage in other settings (e.g., toxic smoke inhalation). Type I alveolar cells are mature cells that are not capable of proliferation and differentiation. By contrast, type II alveolar cells are pluripotent reserve cells that divide to repopulate the alveolar epithelium following injury. These stem cells are able to replace both type I and type II alveolar cells. Diffuse alveolar damage is characteristically associated with hyperplasia of type II alveolar cells (a key pathologic finding). None of the other cells listed are stem cells for regeneration of the alveolar epithelium. Keywords: Alveolus, type II alveolar cells
ConceptType II alveolar cells regenerate alveolar epithelium after injury

456High-yield
An electron micrograph of the alveolus is examined for evidence of structural changes. The barrier that separates atmospheric gasses from blood features which of the following important biological adaptations?
  1. (A) Fusion of epithelial and endothelial basal laminae
  2. (B) Gap junctions between epithelial and endothelial cells
  3. (C) Interdigitation of microvilli on adjacent epithelial and endothelial cells
  4. (D) Sinusoidal alveolar capillaries
  5. (E) Tight junctions between epithelial and endothelial cells
Answer(A) Fusion of epithelial and endothelial basal laminae
WhyIn the thin part of the blood-air barrier, the basal laminae of type I cell and capillary endothelium fuse into one, minimizing diffusion distance.
Explanation from the source
The answer is A: Fusion of epithelial and endothelial basal laminae. Gas exchange occurs when (1) O2 in the alveolus moves into capillary blood and (2) CO2 moves in the opposite direction. The structural components that separate the alveolar air space from blood are collectively referred to as the “blood–air barrier.” This physical barrier is remarkably thin and attenuated to permit efficient gas exchange. The thinnest portion of the blood–air barrier is composed of a layer of surfactant within the lumen of the alveolus, the type I alveolar cell and its basal lamina, and the capillary endothelial cell and its basal lamina. EM studies demonstrate that the basal laminae of type I alveolar cells and endothelial cells are fused together in the thinnest portions of the air–blood barrier. Most gas exchange is believed to occur at this location. None of the other choices describe the blood–air barrier in the lungs. Keywords: Alveoli, blood–air barrier
ConceptBlood-air barrier features fused epithelial and endothelial basal laminae

A 67-year-old smoker presents with increasing shortness of breath and dry cough. He is constantly “gasping for air” and walks with difficulty because he becomes breathless after only a few steps. A chest x-ray discloses hyperinflation of the lungs, and the patient is diagnosed with pulmonary emphysema. This disease is caused by smoking-related injury to which of the following components of the respiratory system?
  1. (A) Alveolar septa
  2. (B) Capillary endothelial cells
  3. (C) Respiratory epithelial cells
  4. (D) Submucosal cartilage plates
  5. (E) Submucosal mucous glands
Answer(A) Alveolar septa
WhySmoking-related protease damage breaks down the elastic alveolar septa, merging alveoli into enlarged airspaces with lost recoil, the lesion of emphysema.
Explanation from the source
The answer is A: Alveolar septa. Emphysema is a chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). It is characterized by enlargement of air spaces distal to the terminal bronchioles, with destruction of their walls, but without fibrosis or inflammation. The major cause of emphysema is cigarette smoking. Moderate to severe emphysema is rare in nonsmokers. Smokers develop squamous metaplasia of the respiratory epithelium (choice C) and hyperplasia of submucosal mucous glands (choice E); however, these pathologic changes do not explain the pathogenesis of respiratory distress in patients with emphysema. None of the other choices are related to the pathogenesis of pulmonary emphysema. Keywords: Emphysema
ConceptEmphysema destroys alveolar septa

A 32-year-old woman delivers a baby prematurely at 25 weeks of gestation. Shortly after birth, the neonate becomes short of breath, with intercostal retraction and nasal flaring during respiration. The neonate is placed on a ventilator but dies of respiratory insufficiency. Respiratory distress in your patient is most likely caused by injury to which of the following components of the respiratory system?
  1. (A) Alveoli
  2. (B) Bronchioles
  3. (C) Main stem bronchi
  4. (D) Segmental bronchi
  5. (E) Trachea
Answer(A) Alveoli
WhyWithout surfactant the alveoli collapse (atelectasis), leaving perfused but unventilated units and fibrin-rich hyaline membranes, so the alveolus is the injured site.
Explanation from the source
The answer is A: Alveoli. The pathogenesis of respiratory distress syndrome (RDS) of the newborn is intimately linked to a deficiency of surfactant. Collapse of the alveoli (atelectasis) secondary to surfactant deficiency results in perfused but not ventilated alveoli, a situation that leads to hypoxia and acidosis. The leak of fibrin-rich fluid into the alveoli from the injured vascular bed contributes to the typical clinical and pathologic features of RDS. On gross examination, the lungs are dark red and airless. None of the other choices describe the pathogenesis of respiratory distress syndrome of the neonate. Keywords: Respiratory distress syndrome of the neonate
ConceptNeonatal RDS targets the alveoli (surfactant deficiency)

Respiratory distress syndrome described in Question 52 was most likely caused by lack of fetal development (immaturity) of which of the following cells?

  2. (B) Clara cells
  3. (C) Goblet cells
  4. (D) Type I alveolar cells
  5. (E) Type II alveolar cells
Answer(E) Type II alveolar cells
WhyType II alveolar cells secrete surfactant but mature late in gestation; their immaturity in a premature infant means too little surfactant, alveolar collapse and respiratory distress syndrome.
Explanation from the source
The answer is E: Type II alveolar cells. Pulmonary surfactant is secreted by type II alveolar cells. However, these cells do not appear in fetal alveoli until late in pregnancy (typically after week 35). Pulmonary surfactant is released into amniotic fluid, where it can be sampled by amniocentesis to assess fetal lung maturity. Administration of exogenous surfactant to neonates that are born prematurely has greatly improved their survival. None of the other cells listed secrete pulmonary surfactant. Keywords: Respiratory distress syndrome of the neonate, surfactant
ConceptRDS in premature infant: type II pneumocytes are too immature

2. An infant born prematurely in gestational week 25 has neonatal respiratory distress syndrome. Which of the following would be expected in this infant?
  1. (A) Arterial PO2 of 100 mm Hg
  2. (B) Collapse of the small alveoli
  3. (C) Increased lung compliance
  4. (D) Normal breathing rate
  5. (E) Lecithin:sphingomyelin ratio of greater than 2:1 in amniotic fluid
Answer(B) Collapse of the small alveoli
WhyWithout type II cell surfactant, surface tension stays high and small alveoli collapse (atelectasis), lowering compliance and blood oxygen in neonatal respiratory distress syndrome.
Explanation from the source
2. The answer is B [II D 2]. Neonatal respiratory distress syndrome is caused by lack of adequate surfactant in the immature lung. Surfactant appears between the 24th and the 35th gestational week. In the absence of surfactant, the surface tension of the small alveoli is too high. When the pressure on the small alveoli is too high (P = 2T/r), the small alveoli collapse into larger alveoli. There is decreased gas exchange with the larger, collapsed alveoli, and ventilation/perfusion (V/Q) mismatch, hypoxemia, and cyanosis occur. The lack of surfactant also decreases lung compliance, making it harder to inflate the lungs, increasing the work of breathing, and producing dyspnea (shortness of breath). Generally, lecithin:sphingomyelin ratios greater than 2:1 signify mature levels of surfactant.
ConceptNeonatal RDS: surfactant lack causes collapse of small alveoli

  5. E. Secretion of anti-microbial peptides
AnswerB. Found within the lower trachea and primary bronchus – Clara cells are found in Bronchioles

Clara (Club) Cells Bulging of cytoplasm into lumen Granules at the apical surface Found within the lower trachea and primary bronchus – Clara cells are found in Bronchioles Prevention of airway collapse Via secretion of surfactant Secretion of antimicrobial peptides and IgA
ConceptClub cells are bronchiolar, not tracheal or bronchial (NOT true)

337. Q1: A 28-year-old man presents with progressive shortness of breath and a family history of early-onset emphysema. Genetic testing reveals a mutation that prevents proper secretion of α1-antitrypsin (AAT). Which of the following best explains the pathophysiology of this patient's condition?
  1. A. Increased fibroblast activity causing excessive elastin production in alveolar walls
  2. B. Impaired degradation of surfactant leading to alveolar collapse
  3. C. Excessive collagen deposition due to unchecked TGF-β signaling
  4. D. Unopposed neutrophil elastase activity leading to destruction of alveolar elastin
AnswerD. Unopposed neutrophil elastase activity leading to destruction of alveolar elastin
WhyHepatic α1-antitrypsin is the main inhibitor of neutrophil elastase; when it is not secreted, elastase destroys alveolar wall elastin, producing early-onset panacinar emphysema.
Explanation from the source
Answer: D. Unopposed neutrophil elastase activity leading to destruction of alveolar elastin Neutrophils constantly release low levels of elastase, a serine protease that degrades elastin; alpha-1 antitrypsin (AAT), made in the liver, is the main elastase inhibitor in the lung. When AAT is absent or inactive, elastase works unopposed and destroys alveolar elastin, and the damage cannot be repaired. Emphysema is not caused by excess elastin, collagen or surfactant problems, or by trypsin activity.
ConceptAlpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency leaves neutrophil elastase unchecked

Which of the following statements about the olfactory system is true?
  1. (A) The receptor cells are neurons

Answer(A) The receptor cells are neurons
WhyOlfactory receptor cells are true bipolar neurons that are regularly replaced from basal stem cells, which is why the other statements fail.

Olfactory receptor cells are unique in that they are true neurons that are continuously replaced from undifferentiated stem cells.

What is the differential basis of the liver and lung pathology seen in α1-antitrypsin deficiency?
AnswerWith α1-antitrypsin (AAT) deficiency, the cirrhosis that can result is due to polymerization and retention of AAT in the liver, its site of synthesis. Learning questions 8

Naming it on a slide

L1Learning
On a low-power lung section, how do you tell the parts of the distal airway apart?
  1. A. Terminal bronchiole: cuboidal-and-muscle wall interrupted by alveolar openings
    Respiratory bronchiole: complete cuboidal-and-muscle wall, no alveoli
    Alveolar duct: only a row of alveolar mouths with muscle knobs
    Alveolar sac: the dead-end cluster of alveoli
  2. B. Terminal bronchiole: complete cuboidal-and-muscle wall, no alveoli
    Respiratory bronchiole: that wall interrupted by alveolar openings
    Alveolar duct: only a row of alveolar mouths with muscle knobs
    Alveolar sac: the dead-end cluster of alveoli
  3. C. Terminal bronchiole: complete cuboidal-and-muscle wall, no alveoli
    Respiratory bronchiole: only a row of alveolar mouths with muscle knobs
    Alveolar duct: that wall interrupted by alveolar openings
    Alveolar sac: the dead-end cluster of alveoli
AnswerB. Terminal bronchiole: complete cuboidal-and-muscle wall, no alveoli
Respiratory bronchiole: that wall interrupted by alveolar openings
Alveolar duct: only a row of alveolar mouths with muscle knobs
Alveolar sac: the dead-end cluster of alveoli
WhyFollow the wall: complete (terminal) → interrupted by alveoli (respiratory) → only alveolar mouths and knobs (duct) → dead-end cluster (sac).
Explanation

At each step the deciding feature is how much wall is left:

  • Terminal bronchiole: a round tube with an unbroken cuboidal lining and one or two layers of smooth muscle; no alveoli open into it.
  • Respiratory bronchiole: the same lining in short stretches, broken by alveoli that open straight into the lumen.
  • Alveolar duct: no continuous wall, only alveolar openings with small pink knobs of smooth muscle between them.
  • Alveolar sac: the blind end, a space ringed by alveoli.

The wrong choices swap the respiratory bronchiole with one of its neighbours.

Slides (3)
L2Learning
Low-power lung: the pointer touches a tube whose wall is short stretches of cuboidal epithelium over a little smooth muscle, interrupted at intervals by alveoli opening into its lumen. What is it?
  1. A. Alveolar duct
  2. B. Terminal bronchiole
  3. C. Respiratory bronchiole
AnswerC. Respiratory bronchiole
WhyA tube that still has a cuboidal-and-muscle wall, but one interrupted by alveoli, is a respiratory bronchiole.
Explanation

Two clues together settle it: there is still a recognisable airway wall (cuboidal cells, club cells, smooth muscle), and alveoli bud from it. At low power the wall looks like a dashed line: thick segments alternating with alveolar mouths.

  • A terminal bronchiole has the same lining but a complete, unbroken wall with no alveoli.
  • An alveolar duct has no stretches of continuous wall: it is all alveolar openings, with only small knobs between them.
Slide (1)
L3Learning
Low-power lung: the pointer lies in a long airspace with no wall of its own; its sides are a row of alveolar openings with tiny pink knobs between them. What is it?
  1. A. Alveolar sac
  2. B. Respiratory bronchiole
  3. C. Alveolar duct
AnswerC. Alveolar duct
WhyA corridor whose sides are only alveolar mouths separated by smooth-muscle knobs is an alveolar duct.
Explanation

The pink knobs are small bundles of smooth muscle, with elastic and reticular fibres, at the rims of the alveolar openings. They line up along both sides of the duct and outline its course.

  • A respiratory bronchiole still has stretches of continuous cuboidal wall between its alveoli.
  • An alveolar sac is a rounded dead-end chamber at the end of a duct, not a long passage lined by knobs.
Slides (2)
L4Learning
At high power on H&E, how do you tell a type I pneumocyte, a type II pneumocyte and an alveolar macrophage apart?
  1. A. Flat, dark nucleus hugging the wall → type I
    Plump rounded cell with foamy cytoplasm, bulging from the wall → macrophage
    Large cell free in the lumen with brown or black granules → type II
  2. B. Flat, dark nucleus hugging the wall → type I
    Plump rounded cell with foamy cytoplasm, bulging from the wall → type II
    Large cell free in the lumen with brown or black granules → macrophage
  3. C. Flat, dark nucleus hugging the wall → type II
    Plump rounded cell with foamy cytoplasm, bulging from the wall → type I
    Large cell free in the lumen with brown or black granules → macrophage
AnswerB. Flat, dark nucleus hugging the wall → type I
Plump rounded cell with foamy cytoplasm, bulging from the wall → type II
Large cell free in the lumen with brown or black granules → macrophage
WhyFlat dark nucleus = type I; plump foamy cell in the wall = type II; big granular cell free in the lumen = macrophage.
Explanation

Three questions settle it: Is the cell flat or round? Is it part of the wall or loose in the lumen? Does it hold pigment?

  • Type I: only a thin, dark, flattened nucleus is visible; its cytoplasm is too thin to see.
  • Type II: cuboidal, often at the corners where septa meet, with a round nucleus and pale vacuolated cytoplasm (lamellar bodies); it is part of the lining.
  • Macrophage: larger, often free in the alveolus or in the septum, full of phagocytosed dust, carbon or haemosiderin.

On TEM, lamellar bodies mean type II.

Slides (2)
L5Learning
TEM of an alveolar wall: cell X lines the air space with a flattened nucleus and a very thin sheet of cytoplasm; cell Y is rounded, has apical microvilli and many granules of stacked membranes. What are X and Y?
  1. A. X type I pneumocyte; Y type II pneumocyte
  2. B. X type II pneumocyte; Y type I pneumocyte
  3. C. X capillary endothelial cell; Y alveolar macrophage
AnswerA. X type I pneumocyte; Y type II pneumocyte
WhyThe thin cell lining the air space is type I; the rounded cell with microvilli and lamellar bodies is type II.
Explanation

On TEM the type I cell is a nucleus with a long, thin sheet of cytoplasm on the alveolar side of the septum, part of the blood–air barrier. The type II cell is cuboidal, bulges into the alveolus, has short microvilli and is packed with lamellar bodies, round granules full of concentric or parallel membrane layers of surfactant.

  • Reversing them ignores the lamellar bodies, the one definitive marker.
  • An endothelial cell lines the capillary lumen, not the air space; a macrophage holds phagosomes and lysosomes full of debris, not lamellar bodies.
Slides (2)
L6Learning
H&E of lung: many large rounded cells in the alveoli and septa, their cytoplasm packed with coarse dark brown-black granules. What are they?
  1. A. Type II pneumocytes
  2. B. Alveolar macrophages
  3. C. Mast cells
AnswerB. Alveolar macrophages
WhyBig cells stuffed with dark phagocytosed particles, in the lumen and the septa, are dust cells: alveolar macrophages.
Explanation

The granules are phagocytosed material: black carbon in smokers and city dwellers, golden-brown haemosiderin in heart failure. The cells sit both free in the alveoli and within the interalveolar septa.

  • Type II pneumocytes belong to the epithelial lining and have pale, foamy cytoplasm, not dark pigment.
  • Mast cells are connective-tissue cells with fine granules of histamine and heparin; they are not pigment-laden phagocytes.
Slides (2)
L7Learning
TEM of the thin portion of a septum, from alveolus to capillary: A is a thin sheet of cytoplasm facing the air, B a thin dense line, C a thin sheet of cytoplasm facing the capillary lumen. What are A, B and C?
  1. A. A type I pneumocyte; B fused basal laminae; C capillary endothelium
  2. B. A type II pneumocyte; B elastic fibre; C capillary endothelium
  3. C. A capillary endothelium; B fused basal laminae; C type I pneumocyte
AnswerA. A type I pneumocyte; B fused basal laminae; C capillary endothelium
WhyFrom air to blood: type I cell → fused basal laminae → capillary endothelium.
Explanation

On TEM the barrier is three thin layers. The layer facing the alveolus is the thin cytoplasm of a type I pneumocyte; the dense band in the middle is the fused basal lamina shared by the two cells; the layer facing the red cells is the capillary endothelium.

  • Swapping A and C puts the endothelium on the air side; endothelium always faces blood.
  • A type II cell is thick and full of lamellar bodies, and the dense line between the cells in the thin portion is basal lamina, not an elastic fibre.
Slide (1)
L8Learning
A chronic smoker with a barrel chest has a lung biopsy: a few very large airspaces separated by thin, broken septa. What has been destroyed?
  1. A. The bronchiolar smooth muscle
  2. B. The bronchial cartilage plates
  3. C. The alveolar septa
AnswerC. The alveolar septa
WhyFew, huge airspaces with broken septa mean emphysema: smoking-related destruction of the alveolar septa.
Explanation

Normal lung has many small alveoli separated by intact septa. In emphysema, elastase digests the septal elastin, the walls break and neighbouring alveoli merge into large, thin-walled spaces that do not recoil. The barrel chest reflects the trapped air.

  • Bronchial cartilage is not lost in emphysema; smokers' bronchi show squamous metaplasia and gland hyperplasia instead.
  • Bronchiolar smooth muscle thickens in asthma; its loss is not the lesion here.

WhyMoving distally: 1 terminal bronchiole (complete wall), 2 respiratory bronchiole (wall interrupted by alveoli), 3 alveolar duct (wall made of alveolar openings), 4 alveolar sac (common space), 5 an individual alveolus.

Alfredo is a 45 year-old man with a 30 pack-year history of smoking cigarettes. He now presents to his doctor with a chronic cough. What changes would you expect to find in the patient’s respiratory mucosa?
AnswerSquamous Metaplasia
WhySmoke immobilizes cilia and injures the bronchial lining, which changes from pseudostratified ciliated columnar to stratified squamous epithelium (squamous metaplasia).
Explanation from the source
The chronic presence or accumulation of toxins that occur with heavy cigarette smoking or industrial air pollution affects the respiratory epithelium beginning in the nasal cavities. Immobilization of the cilia causes failure to clear mucus containing filtered material and exacerbates the problem, leading eventually to squamous metaplasia, a change from pseudostratified ciliated columnar to stratified squamous epithelium. This can produce precancerous cell dysplasia in this tissue.
ConceptSmoker bronchial biopsy shows squamous metaplasia

Q1. A 48 year-old woman with a 3-day history of an upper respiratory infection complains that she has lost her sense of smell. Her perception of smell returns one week later. Which of the following cells are responsible for the recovery of this patient’s olfactory sensation?
  1. A. Olfactory neurons
  2. B. Sustentacular cells
  3. C. Goblet cells
  4. D. Basal stem cells
  5. E. Ciliated cells
AnswerD. Basal stem cells
WhyOlfactory basal cells are stem cells that divide to replace olfactory neurons (normally every one to two months), so smell returns after a viral infection damages the receptor neurons.
Explanation from the source
Basal cells (B): stem cells which replace both olfactory neurons every one or two months and supporting cells less often
ConceptBasal stem cells regenerate olfactory neurons after anosmia

Q2. Regarding the region of the nasal cavity that contains olfactory epithelium, which of the following is a distinct and characteristic feature of the lamina propria of this region?
  1. A. Hyaline cartilage
  2. B. Bowman’s glands
  3. C. Abundant, thick collagen bundles
  4. D. Scant capillaries
  5. E. Absence of nerves
AnswerB. Bowman’s glands
WhyThe olfactory lamina propria contains serous Bowman's (olfactory) glands, whose watery secretion dissolves odorants and rinses the receptor surface; this feature is absent from respiratory mucosa.
Explanation from the source
Olfactory (Bowman) glands (BG): serous glands in lamina propria secrete watery fluid containing innate immune factors (lysozyme, IgA) and odorant-binding proteins

Q3. A 23 year-old singer is seeing her ENT after noticing marked changes in her voice. A laryngoscopy reveals the presence of a small nodule on the vocal cord. Which of the following epithelial types lines the surface of the vocal fold (“true vocal cord”) and the vocal cord nodule?

  3. C. Simple columnar with goblet cells

AnswerE. Stratified squamous non-keratinized

Q7. A 22 year-old woman has just given birth to a premature infant who begins showing clinical signs of hypoxia and respiratory difficulty. He is taken to the NICU where he is diagnosed with respiratory distress syndrome (RDS). In this condition, which of the following cells lacks the maturity to perform their usual function adequately?
  1. A. Type I pneumocytes
  2. B. Type II pneumocytes
  3. C. Macrophages
  4. D. Erythrocytes
  5. E. Fibroblasts
AnswerB. Type II pneumocytes
WhyImmature type II pneumocytes in a premature infant secrete too little surfactant, so alveolar surface tension stays high and alveoli collapse, causing respiratory distress syndrome.
Explanation from the source
The secreted material acts as pulmonary surfactant by spreading over the entire inner alveolar surface as a complex film of phospholipids and lipoproteins. The surfactant film lowers surface tension at the air-epithelium interface, which helps prevent alveolar collapse at exhalation and allows alveoli to be inflated with less force at inspiraton, easing the work of breathing.
ConceptNeonatal RDS: immature type II pneumocytes

Streptococcus can replicate and spread throughout a lobe of the lung via [blank 1]
Show figure
  1. A. e-cadherin
  2. B. pores of Cohn
  3. C. catenin complex dissociation
  4. D. inflammatory destruction of tight junctions via toll like receptors
  5. E. facilitated diffusion
AnswerB. pores of Cohn
WhyAlveolar pores (of Kohn) connect neighboring alveoli to equalize pressure and allow collateral ventilation, but they also let bacteria and exudate spread through a lobe, producing lobar pneumonia.
Explanation from the source
Pores of Cohn connect the alveoli of a particular lobe, allowing the lobe to inflate uniformly and avoid obstruction or hyperinflation of individual alveoli. Unfortunately, they also allow Strep Pneumoniae to spread throughout the lobe, causing lobar pneumonia as shown in the picture.
ConceptPores of Kohn spread lobar pneumonia

Asthma is a common condition produced by chronic inflammation within the bronchial tree of the lungs. The disorder is characterized by sudden constrictions of the smooth muscle in bronchioles called bronchospasms, or bronchial spasms. Constriction is caused by mast cell degranulation triggered by the presence of specific antigens. The resulting difficulty in breathing can be very mild to severe. Epinephrine and other sympathomimetic drugs relax the muscle and increase the bronchiole diameter by stimulating the sympathetic nervous system, and they are administered during asthma attacks. Why are the bronchioles most susceptible to bronchospasm?
Show figure
Answer supplied — the source gives no keyBronchioles have no cartilage (and no glands) to hold the lumen open, and their wall has a relatively thick, well-developed layer of smooth muscle, so contraction of that muscle (bronchospasm) can markedly narrow or close the lumen.
WhyBronchioles have no cartilage or glands to hold them open and a relatively thick smooth muscle layer, so its contraction can nearly close the lumen.
ConceptBronchioles most susceptible to bronchospasm: no cartilage, thick smooth muscle
Slide (1)

Correct key: Tertiary (segmental) bronchus, i.e., an intrapulmonary bronchus. This is Junqueira Fig 17-7: folded respiratory epithelium (E), smooth muscle (SM), hyaline cartilage plates (C), seromucous glands (G), and lung tissue around it = tertiary (segmental) intrapulmonary bronchus. The Exam 5 Pulm key (unit 33) is right and the Vidal 'Intra-pulmonary Bronchi' says the same thing; the other entries are keys of other slides.
WhyFolded respiratory epithelium, smooth muscle, separate hyaline cartilage plates and seromucous glands, surrounded by lung tissue, identify an intrapulmonary tertiary (segmental) bronchus.
Explanation from the source
In a cross section of a large bronchus, the lining of respiratory epithelium (E) and the mucosa are folded due to contraction of its smooth muscle (SM). At this stage in the bronchial tree, the wall is also surrounded by many pieces of hyaline cartilage (C) and contains many seromucous glands (G) in the submucosa which drain into the lumen. In the connective tissue surrounding the bronchi can be seen arteries and veins (V), which are also branching as smaller and smaller vessels in the approach to the respiratory bronchioles. All bronchi are surrounded by distinctive lung tissue (LT) showing the many empty spaces of pulmonary alveoli. (X56; H&E)
ConceptIdentify intrapulmonary (tertiary) bronchus, Junqueira Fig 17-7

What is the main epithelium type lining the nasal cavity?
Answer supplied — the source gives no keyRespiratory epithelium: pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium with goblet cells (most of the nasal cavity, middle and inferior conchae); the roof and superior conchae carry olfactory epithelium (also pseudostratified) and the vestibule is lined by keratinized stratified squamous epithelium.
WhyMost of the nasal cavity is lined by respiratory epithelium, pseudostratified ciliated columnar with goblet cells; the roof has olfactory epithelium and the vestibule is skin.
ConceptNasal cavity mainly lined by respiratory epithelium

What other cell types are present? Describe in detail.
Answer supplied — the source gives no keyOlfactory epithelium: olfactory receptor cells (bipolar neurons with non-motile cilia on a dendritic knob), supporting (sustentacular) cells with microvilli, basal (stem) cells; serous Bowman’s glands lie in the lamina propria. Respiratory epithelium: ciliated columnar cells, goblet cells, brush cells, small granule (Kulchitsky/neuroendocrine) cells and basal stem cells.
WhyOlfactory epithelium has bipolar receptor neurons, supporting cells and basal stem cells, while respiratory epithelium has ciliated, goblet, brush, small granule and basal cells.
ConceptCell types of olfactory and respiratory epithelium

The submucosa is dense connective tissue with various glands embedded in it. What is the composition of these glands?

WhyTracheal submucosal glands are seromucous (mixed): mucous tubules capped by serous demilunes whose ducts open onto the epithelium and add watery mucus.

Which epithelium lines the bronchioles (also, which distinct cell types are present?)

WhyBronchioles are lined by simple ciliated columnar epithelium becoming simple cuboidal distally, with ciliated cells, increasing club cells, few goblet, brush and neuroendocrine cells.

What are Clara cells? (Describe their appearance, role and location)
Answer supplied — the source gives no keyClub (Clara) cells: non-ciliated cuboidal cells with dome-shaped apices containing secretory granules and abundant SER, found in the epithelium of bronchioles (predominant in terminal and respiratory bronchioles); they secrete surfactant-like lipoproteins/mucins and protective proteins, detoxify inhaled xenobiotics with SER (cytochrome P450) enzymes, contribute to local immunity, and act as progenitor cells for bronchiolar epithelium.
WhyClub cells are non-ciliated dome-shaped cuboidal cells of terminal and respiratory bronchioles with secretory granules and SER, secreting protective proteins, detoxifying, and acting as stem cells.

How would you distinguish between the two types of pneumocytes?
Answer supplied — the source gives no keyType I pneumocytes are very thin squamous cells with flattened nuclei that line ~95% of the alveolar surface; type II pneumocytes are rounded/cuboidal cells, often at septal junctions, with round nuclei and foamy, vacuolated cytoplasm (lamellar bodies on EM).
WhyType I pneumocytes are thin squamous cells with flat nuclei covering most of the alveolus; type II are rounded cells with foamy cytoplasm, often at septal corners.
ConceptDistinguishing type I from type II pneumocytes

634
What is the function of each pneumocyte and of the alveolar macrophages?
Answer supplied — the source gives no keyType I: thin gas-exchange surface of the blood–air barrier (joined by occluding junctions). Type II: secrete surfactant from lamellar bodies and divide to replace type I and type II cells after injury. Alveolar macrophages (dust cells): phagocytose inhaled particles, microbes and extravasated erythrocytes (hemosiderin-laden “heart failure cells”), then leave via the mucociliary escalator or lymphatics.
WhyType I cells form the thin gas-exchange surface, type II cells secrete surfactant and regenerate alveolar epithelium, and macrophages phagocytose particles, microbes and erythrocytes.
ConceptFunctions of type I, type II pneumocytes and alveolar macrophages

635
What are the components of the blood-air barrier? (describe in detail and identify some of these components on your section).
Answer supplied — the source gives no keySurfactant layer, the thin cytoplasm of the type I alveolar cell, the fused basal laminae of the type I cell and the capillary endothelium, and the thin cytoplasm of the continuous capillary endothelial cell.
WhyThe blood-air barrier is surfactant, thin type I cell cytoplasm, the fused basal laminae of epithelium and endothelium, and thin continuous capillary endothelium.
ConceptComponents of the blood-air barrier

636
What is the function of surfactant?
Answer supplied — the source gives no keyLowers surface tension at the alveolar air–liquid interface, preventing alveolar collapse at end-expiration (atelectasis) and reducing the force needed to inflate the alveoli; surfactant proteins A and D also aid local defense.
WhySurfactant lowers surface tension at the alveolar air-liquid interface, preventing alveolar collapse at end-expiration and reducing the force needed to inflate alveoli.
ConceptFunction of surfactant

[Question 38] A section of normal lung tissue is examined by light microscopy at low magnification (shown in the image). Identify the space indicated by the asterisk. There is an increase in the number of alveolar openings along the walls of respiratory bronchioles as these air passages move distally. The continuity of the wall of the respiratory bronchiole is all but lost at the point where alveolar ducts originate. Alveolar ducts are lined almost entirely by openings of the alveoli. [Question 38] A section of normal lung tissue is examined by light microscopy at low magnification (shown in the image). Identify the space indicated by the asterisk. [Question 40] Another area of the specimen described in Question 38 is examined at low magnification (shown in the image). Which of the numbered spaces represents an alveolar duct? [Question 41] In the image shown for Question 40, the space indicated by number 1 is best identified as which of the following components of the respiratory system?
  1. (A) Alveolar duct
  2. (B) Alveolar sac
  3. (C) Alveolus
  4. (D) Respiratory bronchiole
  5. (E) Terminal bronchiole
AnswerB. Alveolar sac
WhyAn alveolar sac is the common space at the end of an alveolar duct into which a cluster of alveoli opens; it has no wall of its own beyond the alveoli.
Explanation from the source
Clusters of alveoli surround and open into common air spaces termed alveolar sacs. Moving proximally in the respiratory system, alveolar sacs open into alveolar ducts that further connect to respiratory bronchioles. None of the other choices exhibit histologic features of alveolar sacs. Keywords: Alveolar sacs

641
[Question 38] A section of normal lung tissue is examined by light microscopy at low magnification (shown in the image). Identify the space indicated by the asterisk. [Question 40] Another area of the specimen described in Question 38 is examined at low magnification (shown in the image). Which of the numbered spaces represents an alveolar duct? [Question 42] In the image shown for Question 40, which of the numbered spaces represents a respiratory alveolus?
  1. (A) Space 1
  2. (B) Space 2
  3. (C) Space 3
  4. (D) Space 4
  5. (E) Space 5
AnswerE. Space 5
WhySpace 5 is an alveolus, a small thin-walled terminal air pocket bounded by interalveolar septa that opens into a respiratory bronchiole, alveolar duct or alveolar sac.
Explanation from the source
Alveoli are sites of respiration in the lungs. They are terminal air spaces that form as pocket-like evaginations of the respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts, and alveolar sacs. These thin-walled cavities give the lungs a characteristic spongy texture and they dramatically increase the total surface area for gas exchange in the lungs. The alveoli are defined by alveolar septa (the scaffold for pulmonary architecture) that are composed of a very thin delicate connective tissue. Capillaries arising from the pulmonary arteries course through the alveolar septa, providing a rich blood supply to each alveolus. Alveolar septa contain elastin, collagen, and reticular fibers that provide support and mechanical strength to the lung. Loss of elasticity of alveolar septa underlies the pathogenesis of pulmonary emphysema. Emphysema is a chronic lung disease characterized by enlargement of air spaces distal to the terminal bronchioles, with destruction of their walls, but without fibrosis or inflammation. It is largely a disease of smokers. Keywords: Alveoli
ConceptIdentify alveolus (space 5)

[Question 56] A lung carcinoma is resected, and the tumor margin is carefully examined in the pathology department (shown in the image). The arteriole indicated by the arrow on the image is a branch from which of the following arteries? [Question 57] The artery indicated by the dagger on the image shown in Question 56 supplies blood to which of the following structures of the respiratory system?
  1. (A) Alveoli and alveolar septa
  2. (B) Connective tissue at hilum of lungs
  3. (C) Large-diameter bronchioles
  4. (D) Segmental bronchi
  5. (E) Terminal bronchioles
AnswerA. Alveoli and alveolar septa
WhyPulmonary arteries follow the airways but carry deoxygenated blood to the alveolar septal capillaries for gas exchange; airway walls get bronchial arteries.
Explanation from the source
Pulmonary arteries and their branches travel with corresponding segments of the conducting airways and bring deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle to capillaries in the alveolar septa for gas exchange. Oxygenated blood leaves alveoli via pulmonary venous capillaries and returns to the left atrium of the heart via the four pulmonary veins. Tributaries of the pulmonary veins travel in the connective septa, between bronchopulmonary segments, at a distance from the pulmonary arteries and conducting airways. The other structures listed receive blood from the bronchial arteries. Keywords: Pulmonary artery, alveoli
ConceptPulmonary artery supplies alveoli and alveolar septa

643
Identify the type of epithelium
AnswerRespiratory epithelium.
WhyCiliated columnar cells with goblet cells and basal cells on a thick basement membrane form respiratory epithelium, pseudostratified ciliated columnar.
Explanation from the source
Details of its structure vary in different regions of the respiratory tract, but it usually rests on a very thick basement membrane (BM) and has several cell types, some columnar, some basal, and all contacting the basement membrane. Ciliated columnar cells are most abundant, with hundreds of long robust cilia (C) on each of their bulging apical ends that provide a lush cover of cilia on the luminal surface. Most of the small rounded cells at the basement membrane are stem cells and their differentiating progeny, which together make up about 30% of the epithelium. Mucus-secreting goblet cells (G) and intraepithelial lymphocytes and dendritic cells are also present in respiratory epithelium. The lamina propria is well-vascularized (V). (X400; Mallory trichrome)
ConceptIdentify respiratory epithelium (trichrome, thick basement membrane)

Identify what organ this is from
AnswerOlfactory mucosa.
